bg: In spring 2011 a bookmaker's in Waterford was robbed three times. On 10 May 2011 two gardaí went to the suspect's home with a search warrant issued by a Garda superintendent under s.29(1) of the Offences Against the State Act 1939. They went in, arrested him in his bed and brought him to Waterford Garda Station, where he was cautioned, got legal advice and made statements admitting his involvement.

In February 2012 the Supreme Court struck down s.29(1) in Damache v DPP. At his Circuit Court trial later in 2012 the judge applied the strict rule in Kenny: entering the home on the invalid warrant breached the inviolability of his dwelling, the arrest and detention flowed from that entry, so the statements had to be excluded. Without them there was no case, and he was acquitted.

The DPP used the new 'with prejudice' appeal in s.23 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2010, which lets the prosecution appeal an acquittal where compelling evidence was wrongly excluded. That turned the case into a direct challenge to Kenny.
People (DPP) v JC.q: Must evidence obtained in breach of constitutional rights be excluded whenever the act that caused the breach was deliberate (the Kenny test), even where the gardaí had no idea they were breaching anyone's rights? Or should the court look at what the gardaí knew, and admit the evidence where the breach was a genuine mistake?
dec: On 15 April 2015 the Supreme Court overruled Kenny by 4–3 (Denham CJ, O'Donnell, Clarke and MacMenamin JJ; Murray, Hardiman and McKechnie JJ dissenting). The majority accepted that excluding evidence protects rights. But a rule that automatically shuts out reliable evidence where gardaí acted in good faith on a law that looked valid goes further than protecting rights requires, and left Ireland out of line with every other common law country.

Clarke J's test, adopted by the majority, has four steps. First, the prosecution must prove the evidence is admissible. Where it is said to have been obtained unconstitutionally, the prosecution must show either that it wasn't, or that it should be admitted anyway, and any facts it relies on must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Second, evidence obtained by a deliberate and conscious breach is excluded save in exceptional circumstances. 'Deliberate and conscious' now means knowing that the conduct was unconstitutional (Kenny had looked only at whether the act itself was deliberate). The knowledge that counts is not only the garda at the door's: senior officers, and Garda policies and practices, count too.

Third, any other breach carries a presumption of exclusion. The prosecution can overcome it by proving the breach was inadvertent, or that it arose from a later legal development, such as a court striking down a law the gardaí had relied on. Recklessness or gross negligence about rights is not inadvertence. Fourth, evidence that could never have been obtained constitutionally is excluded whatever anyone knew.

Applying the test, the gardaí in JC had acted on a statutory warrant, valid on its face, that the law presumed to be constitutional. It was invalidated only later, by Damache. That was a textbook later legal development, so the trial judge was wrong to exclude the statements.

The dissents were strong. Hardiman J said the new test put a premium on ignorance of the law and handed the gardaí immunity from oversight. McKechnie J thought the knowledge test unworkable and said there was no evidence that Kenny was causing injustice. Murray J would have dismissed the appeal and was troubled by applying a new rule to a past acquittal.
In a later ruling (reported July 2015), the whole Court refused to order a retrial. He had been acquitted three years earlier, and the interests of justice favoured leaving it there.

later: Criminal Assets Bureau v Murphy (Supreme Court, February 2018, O'Malley J for a unanimous court): the principle isn't confined to criminal trials. Cash had been seized under a pre-Damache s.29 warrant. Before making proceeds-of-crime orders, the High Court had to ask whether it would be lending its process to a deliberate and conscious breach of rights. Where the breach was reckless or grossly negligent, it has a discretion, with a presumption against making the order. The case was sent back for rehearing.

DPP v Smyth [2024] IESC 22: JC also governs evidence obtained in breach of EU Charter rights. Phone traffic and location data accessed under the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011, later found contrary to EU law, was admissible: the gardaí had relied on an Act in force, and its downfall was a later legal development. The Court read the 'never obtainable constitutionally' backstop narrowly, as aimed at things like torture or duress.

DPP v Dwyer [2024] IESC 39 (Collins J): admissibility of the same kind of retained phone data was decided under JC and the data was properly admitted at a murder trial. The Court rejected any absolute exclusion rule as exacting too high a price.

Academic commentators (Daly; Hamilton; Clooney) criticise the test as hard to apply and too easy for the prosecution to satisfy. In practice the defence goes after exactly what the garda knew, was trained in and was told.
job: JC protects honest mistakes, not carelessness. The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that any breach was inadvertent, so expect to be asked in the box what you knew, what training you'd had and why you acted as you did.
Knowing the rule and ignoring it means exclusion. So does cutting corners on the basis that 'JC will cover it'. That's the deliberate and conscious breach JC still excludes.
Write down your reasons at the time (notebook, custody record, PULSE). A note made then, showing why you believed a power applied, is what proves inadvertence months later.

If you're unsure whether a power covers what you're about to do, stop and check with your sergeant or inspector, or get advice. A reasonable check that turns out wrong looks like inadvertence. A guess doesn't.
Knowledge is institutional. If a practice or instruction is known higher up to be unlawful, the evidence can be lost even though you personally didn't know.

Acting on a law or warrant that's later struck down is the textbook 'later legal development', and the evidence is usually saved. Once a court has ruled, though, carrying on with the old practice is not inadvertent, so keep up to date.
People (DPP) v JC.law: Yes. JC is the leading authority on unconstitutionally obtained evidence. The Supreme Court applied it again in 2024 (Smyth; Dwyer) and extended it to breaches of EU Charter rights. Evidence obtained illegally but without breaching a constitutional right is still a matter for the trial judge's discretion under People (AG) v O'Brien [1965].

bg: A garda swore an information before a peace commissioner under s.26 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977. It said only that he suspected, on information in his possession, that controlled drugs were in the accused's flat, without saying what that information was. The peace commissioner didn't ask. The warrant recited that he was satisfied on the sworn information.

Gardaí forced entry to the flat on the warrant and found heroin. Nothing on the face of the warrant showed the defect, and the gardaí believed it was valid. At trial the warrant was held valid and he was convicted of possession and possession for sale or supply (ss.3 and 15).

The Court of Criminal Appeal held the warrant invalid, because the peace commissioner had not exercised his own judgment on the grounds (the point established in Byrne v Grey [1988]). But it did not treat that as a deliberate and conscious violation, because the garda had done what he believed was needed to get a valid warrant. The point went to the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Kenny.q: The test from People (AG) v O'Brien [1965] excluded evidence obtained by a 'deliberate and conscious' violation of constitutional rights. Did that mean the garda had to know he was breaching rights? Or was it enough that the act itself, forcing entry to a home, was deliberate, even though everyone thought the warrant was good?
dec: By 3–2 (Finlay CJ, Walsh and Hederman JJ; Griffin and Lynch JJ dissenting), on 20 March 1990, the Supreme Court excluded the heroin and allowed the appeal.

Finlay CJ saw two possible reasons for excluding such evidence: deterring future breaches, or protecting the citizen's rights. Article 40.3 obliges the courts to defend and vindicate personal rights as far as practicable, so he chose protection. A court should not take the benefit of a breach of constitutional rights, however good the garda's faith.

So the test looked at the act, not the garda's knowledge. If the act that breached the right (here, forcing entry to a dwelling) was deliberate, the evidence was out. There were only two exceptions: the breach was unintentional or accidental, or there were extraordinary excusing circumstances (O'Brien gave the examples of imminent destruction of vital evidence and the need to rescue someone in peril).
The public interest in convicting the guilty was not enough to outweigh that duty, even if it meant a guilty person went free.
The dissenters (Griffin and Lynch JJ) preferred to look at knowledge: the gardaí had acted in good faith on a warrant that looked valid, so there was no deliberate and conscious violation.

keys.q: a stronger and more effective defence and vindication of the right concerned
keys.w: Finlay CJ, on why he chose the protection principle

keys.q: committed unintentionally or accidentally
keys.w: Finlay CJ — the first exception

keys.q: extraordinary excusing circumstances
keys.w: Finlay CJ — the second exception

later: Followed for 25 years, it was the strictest exclusionary rule in the common law world. It drew heavy criticism: Charleton J in DPP v Cash (High Court, 2007), the Balance in Criminal Law Review Group (2007), and O'Donnell J in DPP v Mallon [2011] IECCA 29.

Overruled by People (DPP) v JC [2015] IESC 31 (4–3). 'Deliberate and conscious' now means knowing the conduct was unconstitutional, and the prosecution can save evidence by proving the breach was inadvertent.
Hardiman J, dissenting in JC, called Kenny one of the great monuments of Irish constitutional law, and academics still argue it was right.
Its warrant point still stands: whoever issues a warrant must be personally satisfied that there are reasonable grounds, and cannot just rubber-stamp a garda's say-so (Byrne v Grey).
job: Don't cite Kenny as the exclusion test. Use JC. But Kenny's facts are still the classic example of how a warrant fails.

When you swear an information, set out the grounds for your suspicion (what kind of information, how recent, anything that backs it up), not just 'I suspect on information received'. The judge has to be able to assess it independently.
Be ready for the judge to question you, and note what you told them.
Even under JC, a warrant obtained on a bare assertion invites the argument that the breach was careless rather than inadvertent.
People (DPP) v Kenny.law: Not on exclusion: the Kenny test was overruled by JC in 2015, so don't rely on it as the current test. Its point that a warrant issuer must be independently satisfied on sworn grounds is still good law.

bg: In 2010 gardaí were investigating an alleged conspiracy to murder a Swedish cartoonist over drawings of the Prophet Muhammad, and a threatening phone call made in January 2010 to a person in the United States.

In March 2010 a detective superintendent who was himself involved in the investigation issued a warrant to search the suspect's home in Waterford. He used s.29(1) of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 (as amended in 1976), which let a superintendent or higher issue a search warrant to a sergeant or higher. The house was searched.

The suspect was arrested for conspiracy to murder but was charged with sending a menacing message by phone (s.13 Post Office (Amendment) Act 1951). He brought judicial review proceedings claiming s.29(1) was unconstitutional. The High Court refused and he appealed.
Damache v DPP.q: Can the law let a Garda officer who is involved in an investigation issue the warrant to search a suspect's home? Or does the Constitution's protection of the dwelling require someone independent to decide?
dec: On 23 February 2012 a five-judge Supreme Court (judgment of Denham CJ) declared s.29(1) unconstitutional.

Article 40.5 makes the dwelling inviolable: it may not be forcibly entered except in accordance with law. A search warrant is the State's authority to override that. So deciding whether to issue one, although an administrative act, must be done judicially. The issuer has to weigh the State's interest in investigating crime against the person's rights, impartially, and be satisfied there are reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed and that evidence may be found there. Any interference has to be proportionate.

Someone running or involved in the investigation can't do that balancing impartially, because they would effectively be judging their own case. Section 29(1) allowed exactly that, and the Court couldn't read it any other way to save it, so it fell. The Court accepted that genuine urgency can justify a different arrangement, but s.29(1) wasn't limited to urgent cases.

keys.q: should be an independent person
keys.w: Denham CJ, on who may issue a search warrant

keys.q: must be exercised judicially
keys.w: Denham CJ, on the power to issue a warrant

later: The Criminal Justice (Search Warrants) Act 2012 was rushed through within months and substituted a new s.29. A District Court judge issues on a sworn information from a sergeant or above. A superintendent may issue only where urgency makes going to a judge impracticable, and only if not in charge of or involved in the investigation. A superintendent's warrant lasts 48 hours and the grounds must be recorded. The same safeguards were added to drug-trafficking warrants (s.8 Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act 1996).

People (DPP) v JC [2015] IESC 31: statements made after entry on a pre-Damache s.29 warrant were not excluded. The gardaí had relied on a law presumed valid, and its invalidity was a later legal development.
Criminal Assets Bureau v Murphy (Supreme Court, 2018): cash seized under a pre-Damache s.29 warrant. The JC approach applies in proceeds-of-crime proceedings too.

DPP v Behan [2022] IESC 23: the Supreme Court examined whether a divisional detective superintendent was independent when he issued an urgent warrant under the new s.29 and later became involved in the investigation. The conviction stood because the other evidence (CCTV, clothing, DNA) made an acquittal remote.

The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would overhaul search warrant law again, including warrants tailored to electronic devices. It was still before the Oireachtas in mid-2026, so check whether it has been enacted.
job: Go to a District Court judge for a warrant unless genuine urgency makes that impracticable.
An urgent superintendent's warrant must come from a superintendent with no part in your investigation, not the DS or superintendent running the case. Record why it was urgent.
A superintendent's warrant lasts 48 hours, and the grounds must be recorded at the time or as soon as practicable. Make sure that's done.
Keep the issuing superintendent out of the investigation afterwards. Later involvement invites the argument that they were never independent (Behan).
The independence principle applies to every warrant power, not just s.29. Before you execute, ask: who signed this, and were they independent?
If the warrant is challenged, you'll need to prove who issued it, on what information, and that they weren't involved.
Damache v DPP.law: Yes. Damache is still the foundation of the rule that whoever issues a search warrant must be independent. It is now built into s.29 (as substituted in 2012) and other warrant powers.

bg: Gormley was arrested in a sexual offence investigation and was later convicted of attempted rape. In custody he asked for a solicitor. The gardaí didn't hold off until the solicitor could reasonably arrive. They started interviewing him, and before he'd had any legal advice he made admissions that became a material part of the case against him.
The Court of Criminal Appeal (July 2009) upheld the conviction, accepting that the gardaí had made genuine efforts to contact the solicitor.
White, in a separate case, had forensic samples taken in custody after he asked for a solicitor but before he got advice. They were samples the law required him to give.
The Supreme Court heard the two appeals together.
People (DPP) v Gormley; People (DPP) v W.q: Once a detainee asks for a lawyer, must the gardaí hold off questioning until the legal advice has been received? And does the same apply to taking forensic samples?
dec: On 6 March 2014 a unanimous five-judge Supreme Court (Denham CJ, Murray, Hardiman, McKechnie and Clarke JJ) allowed Gormley's appeal and dismissed White's. Clarke J gave the main judgment and Hardiman J a concurring one.

Irish law already recognised a constitutional right of reasonable access to a solicitor in custody (DPP v Healy, 1990). The open question was whether the gardaí had to pause the investigation until that access was given.

Clarke J held that the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial (Article 38.1) is engaged from arrest, because what happens in custody shapes the evidence at trial. Drawing on Strasbourg case law (Salduz v Turkey, 2008) and practice in comparable countries, he held that a suspect who has asked for a lawyer is entitled not to be interrogated until that advice has been obtained.

Only wholly exceptional circumstances can justify questioning before then: a pressing and compelling need, such as protecting life. Gormley's admissions were a material part of the evidence, so his conviction could not stand.

White was different. The samples were objective evidence that he was legally obliged to give, and advice couldn't have changed that. Taking them before his solicitor arrived didn't make his trial unfair.
The Court left open whether the right extends to having a solicitor in the interview room.

keys.q: wholly exceptional circumstances involving a pressing and compelling need
keys.w: Gormley — the only exception to waiting for legal advice (quoted in the Garda Code of Practice)

later: After Gormley and White, the DPP advised in 2014 that a suspect's request to have a solicitor present at interview should be allowed. The Garda Code of Practice on Access to a Solicitor (April 2015) sets out the practice.

People (DPP) v Doyle [2017] IESC 1: there is no constitutional right to have the solicitor in the interview room, and the remarks in Gormley on presence weren't binding. Allowing presence continues as practice under the Code.

DPP v McDonald [2022] IESC 29: samples given by consent (outside the statutory scheme) were valid where the detainee had already had a short phone consultation with his solicitor; the solicitor didn't need to be there. A physical sample is different from evidence drawn from the suspect's mind, but the process must not be coercive or unfair.

The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would put the right to consult a solicitor before and during interview on a statutory footing. It was still before the Oireachtas in mid-2026, so check whether it has been enacted and commenced.
job: If they ask for a solicitor, don't interview them about the offence until they've had legal advice (a phone consultation counts) or have clearly waived it.
A waiver must be explicit, clear and documented. Remind them of their rights at the start of every interview, and record any change of mind in the custody record.
No 'informal chat' while you wait. Questioning aimed at getting evidence is interrogation, whatever you call it.

Solicitor not responding? Under the Code a phone consultation is expected within about 30 minutes. Call again, and after repeated failures offer them the choice of another solicitor. Never deliberately pick one you know will be slow to arrive.
Samples the law compels can be taken while you wait, but never misstate the legal basis to the suspect. For consent samples, make sure they've had the chance of advice first (McDonald).
Question before advice only in a genuine emergency, a pressing and compelling need such as a risk to life, and record exactly why.
Where possible, tell the solicitor in advance when samples will be taken, and mention the samples in the next recorded interview (Code).
People (DPP) v Gormley; People (DPP) v W.law: Yes. Gormley is the leading authority on access to legal advice before questioning. Read it with Doyle (2017) on solicitor presence, and watch for the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026, which would put the right into statute.

bg: In February 2009 the accused was arrested and detained over a fatal shooting. Over about 60 hours he was interviewed many times by two teams of gardaí, all on video. For most of the interviews he wouldn't engage, and he had short consultations with his solicitor.

Before the fifteenth interview he asked for his solicitor, who came to the station and consulted him. A few minutes into the interview the solicitor rang and spoke to him again, and the questioning then resumed. In that interview he admitted the shooting, described it and drew a map of the scene. He had not asked for the solicitor to sit in on the interview.
He was convicted of murder, and the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. On further appeal he argued that he had a constitutional right to have his solicitor present in the interview room.
People (DPP) v Doyle (2017).q: Does the constitutional right of access to a lawyer (recognised in Gormley) include a right to have the solicitor present during Garda interviews, or is it a right to consult before and between them?
dec: On 18 January 2017 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by 6–1. Denham CJ, O'Donnell, Charleton, Laffoy, MacMenamin and O'Malley JJ were in the majority, with McKechnie J dissenting.

The constitutional right (grounded in the fair-trial guarantee in Article 38.1) is one of reasonable access to legal advice, not a right to the lawyer's presence during interview. Doyle had consulted his solicitor before interview 15 and spoken to him again during it, so the right was met.
What the Court had said about solicitor presence in Gormley wasn't part of the decision there (the question never arose), so it wasn't binding.

Charleton J noted that the US recognises a presence right (Miranda) but held that Ireland's safeguards, namely consultation before questioning and video-recorded interviews, meant a constitutional presence right wasn't needed. O'Donnell J accepted that Strasbourg had recognised a lawyer's role during questioning (Salduz) but said that grew out of different, civil-law systems.
MacMenamin and O'Malley JJ, though in the majority, said they would be open to recognising a presence right in a future case. McKechnie J would have recognised it now.
His other grounds, based on Damache (decided after his trial) and on alleged threats or inducements in interview, also failed.

keys.q: The right is one of access to a lawyer
keys.w: Denham CJ

keys.q: not of the presence of a lawyer during an interview
keys.w: Denham CJ

keys.q: any statements on such issue are obiter dicta
keys.w: Denham CJ, on what Gormley said about presence

later: Doyle v Ireland (European Court of Human Rights, 23 May 2019): the 2009 Garda practice of refusing solicitors in the interview room was a blanket one, with no assessment of the individual, so it wasn't justified by compelling reasons. There was still no violation of Article 6: he wasn't vulnerable, could challenge his confession at every stage, the interviews were on video and shown to the jury, and the trial as a whole was fair.

In practice, solicitors have been allowed in interviews on request since the DPP's 2014 direction, and the Garda Code of Practice on Access to a Solicitor (April 2015) sets out their role and the limits on it.

The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would put the right to consult a solicitor before and during interview on a statutory footing. It was still before the Oireachtas in mid-2026, so check whether it has been enacted and commenced.
job: Before questioning, tell the suspect they may have a solicitor present, and if they ask, facilitate it. That's the Code and DPP practice, whatever Doyle says about the Constitution.
Never refuse a solicitor's presence as a blanket policy. Strasbourg requires compelling reasons specific to the person, and a refusal now would be very hard to defend.

Under the Code a solicitor can be asked to leave only if they prevent or unreasonably obstruct questioning, with a superintendent's prior authority (or an inspector's if no superintendent is available). It's a last resort, and the suspect must then be allowed another solicitor.
Video-record every interview and keep the recording. That was central to both courts finding the trial fair.
Record every consultation, phone call and request in the custody record, with times. In Doyle that record is what showed the right of access had been met.
People (DPP) v Doyle (2017).law: Partly. Doyle is still the Supreme Court's answer on the Constitution: there is no constitutional right to a solicitor's presence. But Strasbourg said in 2019 that Article 6 does extend to presence, so Irish practice allows it on request. The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would make consultation during interview statutory.

bg: On 31 August 1942 Liverpool police arrested a man without a warrant at his warehouse. They genuinely and reasonably suspected he had stolen, or received knowing it was stolen, a bale of cloth, but they didn't tell him that.

Instead they told him he was being arrested for 'unlawful possession' under a local Liverpool Act. Because they knew his name and address, that charge gave them no power to arrest without a warrant. The officer admitted he chose it as the most convenient course. A magistrate remanded him and he spent a week in prison.

When the Liverpool charge was withdrawn on 15 September, he was held at the court until officers from Leicester arrived to charge him with larceny. He sued the Liverpool officers for false imprisonment.
Christie v Leachinsky.q: Is an arrest without a warrant lawful if the police have good grounds but don't tell the person the real reason, or give a reason that wouldn't justify arresting them?
dec: In 1947 the House of Lords (Viscount Simon, Lords Thankerton, Simonds and du Parcq, with Lord Macmillan agreeing) held that the first arrest and detention was unlawful, so damages were due up to the magistrate's remand. The second detention, when he was told the real ground, was lawful.

Viscount Simon set out five propositions. (1) A person arrested without a warrant must ordinarily be told the true ground of arrest. (2) If not, the officer is liable for false imprisonment. (3) There's no need where the person must already know the general nature of the offence. (4) No technical or precise language is needed: it's a matter of substance. (5) A person who makes telling them impracticable, by violent resistance or running away, can't complain.

Lord du Parcq explained why: a citizen is only obliged to submit to a lawful arrest, so they must know why they are being arrested in order to know whether to submit. Where telling them at the moment of arrest is excused, the duty arises at the first reasonable opportunity, and the police must justify the whole period of detention, not just its start.
The police couldn't arrest on a ground that gave no power of arrest and then fall back on a suspicion they had kept to themselves. Giving the formal caution and charge later didn't cure it.

keys.q: the true ground of arrest
keys.w: Viscount Simon, on what the person must be told

keys.q: technical or precise language need not be used
keys.w: Viscount Simon

keys.q: The liberty of a man is a thing specially favoured by the common law
keys.w: Viscount Simon, quoting Dalton's Country Justice

later: Followed in Ireland. In People v Towson (Court of Criminal Appeal, 1978) it was distinguished: an arrest for a firearms offence was valid where the gardaí's suspicion of murder necessarily included suspicion of that offence. Christie applies where the stated ground gives no legal authority at all.

DPP v Mooney [1992] 1 IR 548 (High Court, Blayney J): telling a driver he was arrested 'for drunken driving' was enough for the Road Traffic Act arrest. No technical language is needed, provided the person understands why.

Reinforced by the Custody Regulations 1987 (reg. 8: the member in charge must tell an arrested person, in ordinary language, the offence or matter they were arrested for) and by Article 5(2) ECHR (reasons given promptly, in a language the person understands).
job: Tell them they're under arrest and why, in plain words, at the time: 'I'm arresting you for the theft of a phone from a shop on Talbot Street earlier today.'
Give the real reason, the offence you actually suspect. Don't use a convenient holding charge you can't justify, and don't keep the real reason to yourself to rely on later.
If they fight, run, or are too drunk to take it in, tell them at the first reasonable opportunity, and note when and how.
Write down your exact words, the time and their reply. The defence will ask.
Where there's a language barrier, get the reason across in a language they understand (interpreter or translation tool) and record how you did it.
If the investigation moves to a different offence, tell them the new reason, and check that the power you're holding them under covers it.
Christie v Leachinsky.law: Yes. Christie is still the foundation of the duty to give the reason for an arrest, and Irish courts apply it, with the Custody Regulations and Article 5(2) ECHR built on top. Substance matters, not formula.

bg: The accused had been returned for trial on charges of larceny, breaking and entering, malicious damage, receiving, resisting arrest and assault. All of them were alleged to have been committed while he was already on bail on earlier charges.
The superintendent objected to bail, describing him as an aggressive type who would interfere with witnesses if released. Beyond that opinion, there was no specific evidence of interference.

In the High Court, Murnaghan J refused bail. He listed twelve considerations he thought relevant, including the likelihood of further offences on bail. He gave three reasons: the superintendent's view about witnesses, the risk of further offending (as the new charges arose while on bail), and the likely substantial sentence given his record.
People (AG) v O'Callaghan.q: Can a court refuse bail to stop an accused committing more offences while awaiting trial? And what kind of evidence justifies refusing bail at all?
dec: In 1966 the Supreme Court granted bail.

Ó Dálaigh CJ held that the single question on a bail application is whether the applicant is likely to stand trial. Taking someone's liberty before conviction is punishment unless it's needed to secure their attendance. Refusing bail because the person might offend again is preventive detention, and neither the law nor the Constitution provided for it.

Walsh J said the object of bail is to secure the accused's attendance at trial, not to punish or prevent. The presumption of innocence applies before trial too, not only at it. Predicting future offending is speculative in most cases, even with a bad record.

Interference with witnesses or evidence is a valid ground, but only where it is reasonably probable, as an aspect of evading justice. A bare opinion is not enough. The prosecution's objection is relevant but not a ground in itself. Bail can't be used to put someone in protective custody against their will. The prospect of an early trial counts only in favour of bail.
He accepted that liberty might be restricted before conviction only in extraordinary and highly limited circumstances, and only if the Oireachtas spelled them out.

keys.q: neither punitive nor preventative
keys.w: Walsh J, on the object of bail

keys.q: a form of preventative justice which has no place in our legal system
keys.w: Walsh J

keys.q: a denial of the whole basis of our system of law
keys.w: Ó Dálaigh CJ, on refusing bail to prevent future crime

keys.q: a very real thing
keys.w: Walsh J, on the presumption of innocence

later: Ryan v DPP [1989] IR 399 (Supreme Court, Finlay CJ): the DPP asked the Court to depart from O'Callaghan and allow refusal because the accused would keep offending. Refused: the proper answers are police surveillance, speedy trials and deterrent sentences.

The Sixteenth Amendment (1996) changed the Constitution (Article 40.4) to allow refusal of bail to prevent serious offending, and s.2 Bail Act 1997 put it into effect. Bail may be refused where reasonably considered necessary to prevent a serious offence (a scheduled offence carrying 5 years or more). The court weighs the seriousness of the charge, the strength of the evidence, the likely sentence, offences committed on bail, previous convictions, other pending charges, drug addiction and persistent serious offending, and must consider whether conditions would do instead.
DPP v Vickers [2009] IESC 58: refusal under s.2 must be proportionate, and refusal is harder to justify where the feared offence is less serious.

The Criminal Justice Act 2017 added more bail conditions and a limited power to arrest without warrant for certain breaches where immediate arrest is needed to protect a victim or witness. A 2025–26 review (Staines) concluded bail law has gone as far as the Constitution allows; the Bar of Ireland's July 2026 submission urged better PULSE flagging of bail status.
job: Objecting on O'Callaghan grounds (flight, or interfering with witnesses or evidence)? Bring specific, sworn facts: threats made, contact with witnesses, no ties here, a passport and travel, previous failures to appear. 'He's an aggressive type' lost this case.
Fear of further offending is not an O'Callaghan ground. Use s.2 Bail Act 1997, and only for a serious offence (scheduled, 5 years or more), with evidence of the risk of another serious offence.
Give the court what it must weigh: the strength of the evidence, the likely sentence, offences committed while on bail, previous convictions, pending charges, and addiction where relevant.
Offer conditions as the alternative, because the court must consider them: residence, signing on, curfew, no contact with named people, staying away from an area, surrendering a passport.
Check PULSE for existing bail and conditions before any hearing, and tell the court if the person is already on bail.
If conditions are breached, apply under s.9 Bail Act 1997, or use the 2017 arrest power where immediate arrest is needed to protect a victim or witness.
People (AG) v O'Callaghan.law: Yes. O'Callaghan still sets the common-law grounds (flight; interfering with witnesses or evidence) and the presumption of innocence behind them. Section 2 of the Bail Act 1997, made possible by the Sixteenth Amendment, is the only route to refusing bail to prevent offending.

bg: On 2 July 1997 a shop in Limerick was robbed. Its surveillance camera recorded the robbery, and a garda who viewed the tape was satisfied that it clearly showed the accused doing it.

He was arrested under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 on the strength of the video alone. In custody he made and signed a statement admitting the robbery. After that the tape was given back to the shop, and it was gone by the time it was wanted.

He wasn't charged until about nine months after his arrest, and the defence then looked for the tape. The first trial (March 1999) ended with the jury unable to agree. At the retrial (April 1999) the judge excluded stills taken from the video because the tape itself couldn't be produced, and the jury was discharged.
He applied to stop any further trial. The High Court refused, because the prosecution was now relying on the confession, not the tape.
Braddish v DPP.q: What duty do gardaí have to keep evidence that bears on guilt or innocence? And where they have lost it, can the accused still get a fair trial?
dec: On 18 May 2001 the Supreme Court (Hardiman J, with Denham and Geoghegan JJ agreeing) allowed the appeal and prohibited any further trial.

Because of their unique investigative role, gardaí must seek out and preserve all evidence that has a bearing, or a potential bearing, on guilt or innocence. The duty isn't absolute: it's limited by what is practicable and by resources, and where the relevance of an item isn't direct and obvious it is applied fairly and reasonably on the facts.

The tape was real evidence of the crime itself, not background. The garda who gave it back believed it showed the accused, which made disposing of it very hard to justify. Gardaí have no right to dispose of evidence at will.

Relying on the confession instead didn't solve the problem. The accused disputed the confession, and confessions are best supported by independent evidence. The video could just as easily have shown it wasn't him, and the defence was entitled to examine it.
It was no answer that the defence asked for the tape late: he hadn't even been charged until nine months after his arrest.

keys.q: unique investigative role
keys.w: Hardiman J, on where the gardaí's duty comes from

keys.q: seek out and preserve all evidence having a bearing or potential bearing
keys.w: Hardiman J

later: Dunne v DPP [2002] IESC 27: CCTV at a filling station was never collected. The duty covers seeking out evidence, not just keeping what you have, and the trial was prohibited. McGuinness J's test: the evidence must be clearly relevant, there must be at least a strong probability it was available, and it must in reality bear on guilt or innocence.

Savage v DPP [2008] IESC 39 (Denham J): a car was destroyed after it had been examined and reports made. The accused must show a real and serious risk of an unfair trial, and here the reports were enough. The Court said gardaí should, as best practice, notify an accused before destroying such evidence.

Wall v DPP [2013] IESC 56 (O'Donnell J; Hardiman J dissenting): a steering wheel was never fingerprinted. That wasn't material enough to stop the trial, and the trial judge has the primary role in ensuring fairness. Stopping a trial for missing evidence is now rare; the gap is usually dealt with at trial.
job: Treat CCTV as an exhibit from the first visit. Get a full copy fast, before it's overwritten, and record the system time against real time, who downloaded it and continuity.
Look for everything that might be relevant, including what might clear the suspect: neighbouring premises, buses, doorbells, dashcams, phones. The duty is to seek out, not just keep.
Never return, release or destroy evidence while a prosecution is possible. Get direction first, and consider telling the defence before anything is disposed of (Savage).
If you rely on stills, keep the footage they came from, and note what the full footage shows, including anything that doesn't fit your case.
If footage can't be got (overwritten, system broken, owner refuses), record every attempt: when, who you spoke to, what you were told. That's your answer in court.
Before releasing a vehicle or other property, ask whether the defence could reasonably want to examine it, and record the decision.
Braddish v DPP.law: Yes. Braddish is still the foundation of the Garda duty to seek out and preserve evidence. But since Savage and Wall the courts rarely stop a trial over missing evidence: the accused must show a real risk of an unfair trial, and the trial judge usually deals with the gap.

bg: On 18 January 1998 a filling station in Palmerstown, Dublin, was robbed. The station had video cameras, they were working that night, and gardaí had collected tapes from the same station in earlier, unrelated cases.

This time no garda asked for or took the tapes. The investigating officer, who hadn't been at the scene, said no tape was ever obtained, and none of the gardaí who attended swore an affidavit explaining why.

The case against the accused rested on a short written statement he allegedly made admitting the robbery. The Circuit Court refused to order disclosure of the tapes because it couldn't be shown a video existed. The High Court (Kearns J) refused to stop the trial, saying he had delayed in looking for the footage and pointing to his early statement.
Dunne v DPP.q: Braddish dealt with evidence the gardaí had and lost. Does the duty also cover evidence they never collected, and can a trial be stopped because obvious footage was never sought?
dec: On 25 April 2002 the Supreme Court stopped the trial by 2–1 (McGuinness and Hardiman JJ; Fennelly J dissenting).

McGuinness J said that because the tapes were never in garda hands, this wasn't a failure to preserve evidence. The real question was a failure to seek out evidence bearing on guilt or innocence, and the Braddish duty covers that too. But the duty mustn't be read too widely: it doesn't demand an exhaustive search at any cost. To stop a trial, the evidence must be clearly relevant, there must be at least a strong probability that it was available, and it must in reality bear on guilt or innocence.

Hardiman J said CCTV is now so common in public places that its value to an investigation is obvious, and a garda attending a robbery should have asked about it. Where video was likely available, the gardaí must explain why it wasn't obtained, and they gave no explanation. With a case resting on a few lines of statement, the missing independent evidence mattered, and it would be harsh to refuse relief for delay.

Fennelly J dissented. A duty to seek out evidence was a big new step. Until then, stopping a trial had needed proof of prosecution misconduct, and chance events shouldn't let an accused avoid trial. He also warned that trials could become about the quality of the investigation rather than the accused's guilt.

keys.q: disproportionate commitment of manpower or resources
keys.w: McGuinness J, on the limit of the duty to seek out evidence

keys.q: very significant new step in the law
keys.w: Fennelly J (dissenting)

later: Savage v DPP [2008] IESC 39: the accused must show a real and serious risk of an unfair trial. The trial wasn't stopped where examination reports on a destroyed car still existed.
Wall v DPP [2013] IESC 56: the trial judge, not judicial review, is the main safeguard, so missing evidence now rarely stops a trial. The judge deals with it during the trial instead.
The duty to seek out evidence still stands. With CCTV, doorbell cameras and dashcams everywhere, expect the defence to ask exactly what you did to find footage.
job: At every scene, ask about CCTV straight away: the premises, neighbours, buses, taxis, doorbells, dashcams. Note who you asked, when, and what they said.
If footage exists, secure it the same day if you can. Systems overwrite fast.
If you decide not to collect something, record why: the camera faced away, or the system wasn't recording, and how you checked.
Look just as hard for footage that might help the suspect. The duty runs both ways.
Give the investigating member a written note of your CCTV enquiries, so the evidence about them can be given properly in court.
Dunne v DPP.law: Yes, on the duty: gardaí must seek out, not just keep, evidence that may bear on guilt or innocence. But stopping a trial over missing evidence is now exceptional (Savage; Wall).

bg: In 1995 a supermarket manager in Greater Manchester was shot dead. The applicant was arrested and, on legal advice, stayed silent in police interviews.

The police then secretly recorded his cell, the prison visiting area and his conversations with a fellow prisoner. They also put a long-standing police informant into his cell, with instructions to push him for information.
The informant's evidence of what the applicant had told him, along with the recordings, was used at trial. He was convicted of murder in 1998, and his appeal failed.
Allan v United Kingdom.q: Was it fair to use what a police informant drew out of a detained suspect who had chosen to stay silent? And was secret recording in custody lawful?
dec: On 5 November 2002 the European Court of Human Rights found breaches of Articles 8, 6 and 13.
Article 8 (privacy): at the time there was no statutory system regulating police use of covert recording devices, so the bugging was not 'in accordance with the law'.

Article 6 (fair trial): the right to silence and the privilege against self-incrimination protect a suspect's choice whether to speak to the police. The informant hadn't just listened. Primed by the police, he persistently questioned the applicant and steered the talk towards the killing. What he got wasn't spontaneous; it was drawn out in a way that amounted to an interrogation, with none of the safeguards of a formal interview, and against the applicant's choice to stay silent. Using it made the trial unfair.
Using the covert recordings of his conversations with others did not breach Article 6. He could challenge them at every stage, and they weren't obtained by pressure.
Article 13: there was no effective domestic remedy for the privacy breach.

keys.q: push him for what you can
keys.w: Police instructions to the informant

keys.q: the functional equivalent of interrogation
keys.w: European Court of Human Rights

keys.q: in defiance of the will of the applicant
keys.w: European Court of Human Rights

later: Bykov v Russia (Grand Chamber, 2009): an informant wearing a hidden transmitter recorded a suspect at his own premises, before arrest. There was no Article 6 breach: he was at liberty, under no pressure and free to end the conversation. The Court distinguished Allan, where the suspect was detained, had chosen silence and was worked on by a police-primed informant. Article 8 was breached, as there was no legal framework for the device.

In Ireland, covert surveillance devices now need authority under the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009: a District Court authorisation, or in urgent cases a superior officer's approval lasting up to 72 hours, with a written record within 8 hours.

Allan is still the leading Strasbourg case on informants and cell-mates. Read it with Gormley: a detainee who has asked for a lawyer must not be questioned by anyone acting for the gardaí before getting advice.
job: Never use a cell-mate, informant or undercover garda to question a detainee who has chosen silence. The court will treat it as an interview without the safeguards.
If a prisoner offers to 'get' admissions from another detainee, don't prime them or give them questions. Report it up the line.
Remarks a detainee makes without prompting are different. Note them word for word, with the time and context, and put them to the detainee in a recorded interview.

Any covert recording needs lawful authority. In Ireland that's the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009: a District Court authorisation, or in urgency a superior officer's approval for no more than 72 hours.
Allan v United Kingdom.law: Yes. Allan is the leading Strasbourg authority on informants in custody and is consistently applied. Irish courts give effect to Article 6 through the ECHR Act 2003, alongside the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial.

bg: In September 1976 two women went missing in the west of Ireland. On 26 September two men were detained in Galway, and one of them was the accused.

He was held at Galway Garda Station. On Monday 27 September a District Court sat in Galway and a judge was available from about 10.30 a.m., but he wasn't brought before it. He was held until the Wednesday. The superintendent regarded finding the second woman, who might still be alive, as more important than charging him with the relatively minor offences he could then be charged with.

During that extra detention he made statements and went with gardaí on a journey through Connemara. In February 1978 he was convicted of murder, rape and false imprisonment. The Court of Criminal Appeal refused leave to appeal but certified a point of law for the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Shaw.q: Was it lawful to keep him in custody after he could have been brought before a court, because the gardaí were trying to save a woman who might still be alive? And were the statements he made during that time admissible?
dec: The Supreme Court (Walsh, Henchy, Griffin, Kenny and Parke JJ) gave judgment on 17 December 1980, and the conviction stood.

Walsh J restated the basic rules. Arrest is only for bringing someone before a court at the earliest reasonable opportunity, and nobody can be arrested or held just to be questioned. Calling it 'helping the police with their inquiries' doesn't change that: it is false imprisonment. Detention for questioning now exists only where a statute provides for it.

Where his right to liberty clashed with the missing woman's right to life, the higher right prevailed. Kenny J said there is a hierarchy of constitutional rights, and that ranking her right to life above his right to liberty for those three days was the correct decision.

The judges split on what a 'deliberate and conscious' violation means. Griffin J, for the majority, said it looks at the violation of rights: evidence is excluded only where the gardaí knew they were breaching the suspect's rights. Walsh J said the act was what counted, not the garda's knowledge of constitutional law. Both reached the same result on the facts.

On confessions, a statement is admissible only if it is voluntary, meaning not obtained by threats or inducements from a person in authority, or by oppression. Even a voluntary statement can be excluded where it was obtained in breach of basic or fundamental fairness. Irish courts still go back to Griffin J's statement of these principles in Shaw.

keys.q: There is a hierarchy of constitutional rights
keys.w: Kenny J

keys.q: that which ranks higher must prevail
keys.w: Kenny J, on conflicts between constitutional rights

keys.q: place a premium on the ignorance of the law
keys.w: Walsh J, warning against a knowledge-based test

later: The 'deliberate and conscious' debate continued. Kenny [1990] adopted Walsh J's act-based reading, and JC [2015] went back to a knowledge-based test, with Hardiman J's dissent in JC echoing Walsh J's warning about rewarding ignorance of the law.

Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 (and later powers) created statutory detention for questioning. When those periods end, Shaw's rule applies: charge and bring the person to court, or release them.

DPP v Hoey [1987] IR 637: asking a suspect whether gardaí would have to approach his family about items found in the house was an inducement. The admission wasn't shown to be voluntary and the conviction was set aside.
People (DPP) v Doyle [2015] IECA 109: the Court of Appeal applied the Shaw principles and found the admissions voluntary, with no oppression and no breach of fundamental fairness.
job: Never arrest just to question. Unless a statute gives you a detention power (e.g. s.4 CJA 1984), the person must be brought before a court or released at the earliest reasonable opportunity.
When the statutory detention period ends, charge and bring them to court, or release them. Don't hold on informally.
Saving a life can justify extraordinary steps, but record exactly what you believed, why, and who decided. Shaw is a rare exception, not a licence.
Keep interviews free of threats, promises and pressure: no 'it'll go easier for you', no hints about family or bail. Even an innocent-sounding question can be an inducement (Hoey).
Oppression covers more than threats: long sessions, tiredness, no breaks, food or rest. Follow the custody regulations and record every break.
The judge can exclude even a voluntary statement as unfair, so follow the Judges' Rules and the custody regulations to the letter.
People (DPP) v Shaw.law: Yes. Shaw is still cited on voluntariness and fundamental fairness, and for the principle that when constitutional rights conflict, the higher one prevails. Its 'deliberate and conscious' discussion has been overtaken, first by Kenny and then by JC.

bg: In the early hours of 21 April 2014 the accused was stopped after driving at 80 km/h in a 50 km/h zone and arrested on suspicion of drink driving. At Store Street Garda Station he gave breath specimens on the evidential breath-testing machine.
The machine printed the statement of the result (the s.13 statement) in English only. The 2011 Regulations prescribed a single form with Irish and English versions.

He was charged under s.4(4) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 (breath alcohol over 22 mg per 100 ml). The District Court and High Court held the statement wasn't 'duly completed', which halted the prosecution. The Court of Appeal disagreed. About 1,000 other drink-driving prosecutions were on hold awaiting the outcome.
DPP v Avadenei.q: Is a statement that leaves out the Irish-language version required by the prescribed form still evidence? Or does any departure from the prescribed form make it inadmissible?
dec: On 20 December 2017 a unanimous five-judge Supreme Court (judgment of O'Malley J) dismissed his appeal. The statement was admissible.

Read literally, the Regulations did require one bilingual form, so the English-only printout didn't comply. But s.12 of the Interpretation Act 2005 provides that deviations from a prescribed form which don't materially affect its substance, and aren't calculated to mislead, don't invalidate it.
The substance of the form, meaning every piece of information it had to contain, was there. It wasn't misleading, confusing or unfair, and admitting it breached no right of the accused.

More broadly, whether a procedural error matters depends on its actual effect. Where it causes the accused no unfairness, prejudice or detriment, the evidence is admissible on the ordinary criminal standards. The Court didn't decide any constitutional question about entitlements to Irish-language documents.

keys.q: do not materially affect the substance and are not calculated to mislead
keys.w: s.12 Interpretation Act 2005 — the test applied by O'Malley J

later: DPP v Hodgins [2024] IESC 36 (O'Malley J): the driver signed the s.13 statement before the garda. That was not a mere matter of form. The garda must sign first, because the driver's duty to sign (enforced by an offence) only arises after that. The statement wasn't duly completed and was inadmissible. The Court distinguished Avadenei and declined to overrule DPP v Freeman.

In Hodgins, O'Malley J placed the error in one of the categories of procedural defect identified in Avadenei: procedures followed wrongly, so the document doesn't prove what it was meant to prove. Defects of form can be saved; errors in the statutory procedure itself usually can't.
job: Check the statement before handing it over: the right person, date, times and readings, and every required detail.
The garda signs first, then offers it to the driver to sign. Never the other way round (Hodgins).
Follow the s.13 procedure exactly (the statements, the signatures, the driver's copy) and record each step in your notebook.
Minor departures in a form's layout can be saved by s.12. Wrong content or the wrong procedure can't.
If the printout or form looks wrong, note it and tell your sergeant. Don't 'fix' it by hand.
DPP v Avadenei.law: Yes. Avadenei is the leading case on form defects in breath statements and on s.12 of the Interpretation Act 2005. But read it with Hodgins (2024): errors in the statutory procedure itself, such as the signing order, are fatal.

bg: On 20 September 1959 two boys aged about five were led away across a field and assaulted. The man was a stranger to the boys and to every witness.

The case turned on visual identification. A 12-year-old boy said he saw the accused at about 7.45 p.m. walking across the field holding each child by the hand, and he picked him out at a parade and again in court. Another witness had seen a man near the field shortly before. A local man who chased someone away later glimpsed a man's face in car headlights at about four yards. One of the two boys failed to pick the accused out at a parade but claimed to identify him at the retrial.
The witnesses' descriptions of the man's clothing didn't match. The accused was convicted at a retrial and appealed, challenging how the judge had directed the jury on the identification evidence.
People (AG) v Casey (No 2).q: When a conviction depends on eyewitness identification, what must the jury be told about the risk of honest mistakes?
dec: On 21 December 1963 the Supreme Court (judgment of Kingsmill Moore J) allowed the appeal and ordered a new trial.

Experience shows that honest, confident witnesses who had a fair chance to observe can still be wrong, and juries may not appreciate that danger. So where the verdict depends substantially on the correctness of a visual identification, the judge must give a general warning: the jury should be especially cautious before accepting it as correct.

The warning must explain why. There have been cases where responsible witnesses, whose honesty wasn't in question and whose opportunity to observe was adequate, made positive identifications that turned out to be wrong. Mistakes can happen even where two or more witnesses identify the accused. Only if, having taken all this into account, the jury is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the identification is correct should they rely on it.

keys.q: especially cautious before accepting such evidence of identification as correct
keys.w: Kingsmill Moore J — the core of the Casey warning

keys.q: mistakes can occur where two or more witnesses have made positive identifications
keys.w: Kingsmill Moore J

keys.q: may not be fully aware of the dangers involved in visual identification
keys.w: Kingsmill Moore J, on why juries need the warning

later: People v Stafford (Court of Criminal Appeal, 1981): leaving out the warning was a misdirection even though the witness knew the accused beforehand, and a retrial was ordered. DPP v O'Donovan (2004): the Casey warning applies to recognition as well as to identifying a stranger.
DPP v Mahon (CCA, 1990) and DPP v Barnwell (Central Criminal Court, 1997) are typical of how judges still charge juries in Casey's terms.

People (AG) v Martin [1956] IR 22: there is no fixed rule that an identification parade must be held; each case turns on its own circumstances. In practice a properly run formal procedure carries far more weight than a first identification in court.
R v Turnbull (England, 1976) later set out a more detailed checklist. Irish courts treat it as persuasive, but Casey remains the governing Irish authority.
job: Take the first description in detail before any identification procedure (height, build, age, clothing, hair, marks, voice) and record it word for word. Every later identification is measured against it.
Record the conditions: how long they saw the person, the distance, the light, any obstructions, whether they knew the person, any reason to remember, and how long before they told gardaí.
Never show a witness a single photo or the suspect alone, and keep witnesses apart. Use a formal identification procedure run by a member not involved in the investigation.
Several witnesses agreeing isn't enough on its own; Casey warns they can all be wrong. Look for independent support such as CCTV, phone data, forensics or property.
Recognition ('I know him from school') still needs the warning (Stafford). Record how well and how recently the witness knew the person.
Record any failure to identify, or any identification of someone else. It must be disclosed.
People (AG) v Casey (No 2).law: Yes. Casey (No 2) is still the leading Irish authority. The warning is given in every case that turns substantially on visual identification, including recognition.

bg: Four appeals were heard together by a five-judge English Court of Appeal, all turning on disputed visual identification: Turnbull and Camelo (conspiracy to burgle), Whitby (robbery) and Roberts (unlawful wounding).
There was growing concern in England about wrongful convictions based on mistaken identification, and the Court set out to give trial judges clear, general guidance.
R v Turnbull.q: How should a judge direct a jury where the case depends wholly or substantially on disputed identification? And when should such a case be stopped altogether?
dec: Judgment of Lord Widgery CJ (with Roskill and Lawton LJJ, Cusack and May JJ), 9 July 1976.

The judge must warn the jury of the special need for caution before convicting on identification evidence, and explain why: a mistaken witness can be a convincing one, and several such witnesses can all be mistaken. No particular form of words is required.

The jury should examine closely how each identification came to be made: how long the witness had the accused under observation, the distance, the light, whether the view was impeded, whether the witness had seen the accused before and how often, any special reason for remembering, how long it was before the identification to police, and any material difference between the first description and the accused's actual appearance. The judge should remind them of any specific weaknesses.
Recognising someone you know is more reliable than identifying a stranger, but mistakes in recognising relatives and friends do happen.

Where the identification is of good quality, it can go to the jury, with the warning, even without supporting evidence. Where it is poor, such as a fleeting glance or a longer look in difficult conditions, the judge should withdraw the case unless other evidence supports it. That support needn't be corroboration in the technical sense; odd coincidences can count (R v Long).

keys.q: the special need for caution
keys.w: Lord Widgery CJ

keys.q: a mistaken witness can be a convincing one
keys.w: Lord Widgery CJ

keys.q: a fleeting glance
keys.w: Lord Widgery CJ — his example of poor-quality identification

later: Still the foundation of identification directions in England and Wales and across the common law world. The Privy Council applied it in France and Vassell v The Queen [2012] UKPC 28.
In Ireland it is persuasive only, as Casey (No 2) [1963] governs, but its checklist underpins Garda training, including the ADVOKATE mnemonic.
job: Cover ADVOKATE in every identifying witness's statement: Amount of time, Distance, Visibility, Obstructions, Known or seen before, Any reason to remember, Time lapse, Errors (differences from the first description).
Get the first description down before any identification procedure. It's the benchmark the court will use for 'material discrepancy'.
If all you have is a fleeting glance, look for support (CCTV, forensics, phone, property) from the start. Without it the case may be withdrawn.
For recognition, record how long the witness has known the person, how often they see them, when they last saw them, and what they recognised (face, walk, voice).
Record weaknesses honestly. The defence will find them anyway, and the judge has to point them out.
R v Turnbull.law: Yes in England and Wales, where it's still applied every day. In Ireland it's persuasive only, since Casey (No 2) governs, but its checklist is the best guide to a strong identification statement.

bg: In March 2002 gardaí took fingerprints from a 15-year-old and kept them on record. They were said to have been given with consent, but there was no evidence of how they were taken.

In 2003 a house was burgled and prints were lifted from broken window glass. A detective received confidential information that they matched the prints on record. Under cross-examination he accepted that he didn't know how the match was made, or whether the record prints had been lawfully taken and kept under s.8 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, which required destruction in some circumstances.
In September 2003 the accused was arrested on suspicion of burglary, with the match as the only basis, and fresh prints were taken in custody. Those fresh prints were the evidence relied on.

The District Court stated a case. The defence argued that unless the prosecution could prove the record prints were lawfully held, the arrest was unlawful and the custody prints had to be excluded under Kenny. In the High Court, Charleton J sharply criticised the Kenny rule but held the prints admissible.
DPP (Walsh) v Cash.q: Must the prosecution prove that the information that gave the gardaí their suspicion was lawfully obtained? And does an arrest founded on unlawfully kept information make the evidence gathered after it inadmissible?
dec: On 18 January 2010 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal (Fennelly J, with Murray CJ, Geoghegan, Macken and Finnegan JJ; Hardiman J separately), and the case went back to the District Court.

The lawfulness of an arrest and the admissibility of evidence at trial are different questions, normally decided in different settings. It has never been held that the suspicion behind an arrest must rest on evidence that would be admissible at trial.

The accused hadn't shown that the prosecution must prove the lawful origin of the material the gardaí relied on for the arrest, or that it was obtained in breach of a constitutional right. Stretching Kenny to cover the information behind an arrest would blur the line between arrest and trial.
There was no proper evidence of how the 2002 prints were taken or kept, so the Court didn't need to decide the DPP's request to review Kenny.

keys.q: lawful provenance of evidence used to ground a suspicion
keys.w: Fennelly J — what the exclusionary rule is not concerned with

keys.q: different matters which will normally be considered in distinct contexts
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the lawfulness of an arrest and admissibility at trial

keys.q: blur the distinction between the arrest and the trial
keys.w: Fennelly J

later: Charleton J's High Court criticism of Kenny ([2007] IEHC 108) fed the debate that ended with JC [2015] IESC 31 overruling Kenny.
The rules on keeping and destroying prints and other identifying records were recast by the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014.
job: Your suspicion can rest on intelligence, hearsay or a database hit; it doesn't have to be admissible evidence. But you must be able to say what it was and why it was reasonable.
Know where your information came from. In Cash the arresting detective couldn't say how the match was made or whether the record prints were lawfully held, and that is what opened the challenge.
Follow the retention and destruction rules for prints, photos and samples (the 2014 DNA Act). Records kept unlawfully invite exactly this attack.
After arrest, take fresh prints or samples under the proper power. Evidence gathered lawfully after the arrest stands on its own footing.
Note the grounds for your suspicion in your notebook at the time of the arrest.
DPP (Walsh) v Cash.law: Yes. Cash is still cited for the difference between arrest and trial, and for the point that reasonable suspicion needn't rest on admissible evidence. The exclusionary rule behind the case has changed since JC (2015).

bg: A man who had gone missing in 2011 was found dead on the accused's land in April 2013.

Gardaí then got a District Court warrant to search the accused's home. The sworn information listed physical items (the dead man's clothing, keys and phone, and the weapon) and said nothing about computers. Gardaí intended to seize and examine the family computer, but they didn't tell the judge.

Forensic examination of the seized computer found internet searches on topics such as human decomposition, which were used at his murder trial. He was convicted. The trial judge and the Court of Appeal upheld the warrant, although the Court of Appeal called the omission 'certainly sub-optimal'.
People (DPP) v Quirke.q: Does a warrant to search a home for physical items let gardaí seize a computer found there and search its digital contents?
dec: In March 2023 a seven-judge Supreme Court (judgment of Charleton J) held that seizing the computer to search its contents was unlawful, though the warrant was otherwise valid.

A computer isn't a separate 'place' for warrant purposes: s.6 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006 defines a place as a physical location. A device found in the place can be seized and examined physically. But searching its contents goes into a different and far bigger space, a portal into the person's digital life, where the privacy interests are much stronger than for almost any physical object.

So the issuing judge must be told that gardaí intend to seize and search devices, and on what basis, so the judge can weigh the privacy intrusion and decide whether to authorise it. A fair summary of the facts and grounds is required. Here the judge was never asked.
The Court then heard further argument on what followed from that (Quirke No 2).

keys.q: portal into the digital world
keys.w: Supreme Court, describing a computer

keys.q: certainly sub-optimal
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on not telling the judge about the computers

keys.q: due to honest inadvertence
keys.w: Supreme Court (Quirke No 2), on the warrant error

later: Quirke (No 2) [2023] IESC 20 (28 July 2023, Charleton J): applying JC, the computer evidence was still admissible. The error was honest inadvertence, and the requirement for specific authority to search devices was a new development in the law on digital privacy, not settled law in 2013. The conviction was affirmed and no retrial ordered.

Poptoshev v DPP [2025] IESC 47 (Charleton J; in this app): a 2024 warrant expressly listed electronic devices and items held by electronic means, and the District Court judge was satisfied, following Quirke, that there were grounds to search the digital space as well as the physical one, so seizing and searching the devices was reasonable. The Court also upheld s.49 of the Theft and Fraud Act 2001 (refusing to give passwords), subject to the safeguard that compelled evidence can't be used against the suspect.

The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 provides for warrants tailored to seizing and searching electronic devices, a procedure for examining devices seized without prior judicial approval, and a process for privileged material. It was still before the Oireachtas in mid-2026.
job: If you may seize phones, laptops or other devices and search their contents, say so expressly in the sworn information, and explain what you expect to find and why it's likely to be on the device.
Ask for the warrant to cover the digital search, not just the physical items. A general 'any other evidence' clause isn't enough.
If you find devices the warrant didn't anticipate, secure them, then get specific authority before searching the contents.
Record what was seized, where, its state (on or off, locked) and continuity, and don't browse it at the scene unless authorised and necessary.
Where a statutory power lets you require passwords (as under the Theft and Fraud Act 2001 in Poptoshev), make the requirement clearly and record the request and the answer word for word.
People (DPP) v Quirke.law: Yes. Quirke is the leading authority on searching devices under a warrant, and Poptoshev (2025) shows a warrant drafted the Quirke way. Watch the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026.

bg: In August 1974 four men raided a house in south Dublin to rob it. One occupant was struck on the head with an object, and a fingerprint was later found on it. Gardaí believed the print was the accused's.

In January 1975 a detective sergeant arrested him in a pub on Thomas Street on suspicion of the robbery. Because of the crowd he didn't give the reason there. He told him why, and cautioned him, shortly after they reached Store Street Garda Station.

Within about an hour the accused was asked about fingerprints. He didn't object and they were taken, and when his solicitor arrived he signed a consent form. He was then held overnight without charge. A habeas corpus order was granted, and he was charged and later convicted, with the fingerprint as the only evidence against him.
People (DPP) v Walsh.q: Was the arrest lawful when the reason wasn't given at the scene? Could he lawfully be held at the station without being charged? And did any of that taint the fingerprint evidence?
dec: Supreme Court, 17 January 1980: judgment of O'Higgins CJ (Kenny J agreeing), with a separate judgment from Walsh J.
A garda may arrest without a warrant on reasonable suspicion of a felony, even if it turns out no felony was committed. This arrest was lawful.
A short delay in giving the reason, explained by the circumstances (a crowded pub), didn't make the arrest unlawful. He was told soon after reaching the station.

There's no such thing as holding someone for questioning. After an arrest a person may be detained only under a court order, or for the purpose of charging them and bringing them before a court. Any other purpose is unknown to the law.
The time allowed for that is what is reasonably needed: the gardaí must act with reasonable expedition, but instant action isn't required.

keys.q: Any other purpose is unknown to the law
keys.w: O'Higgins CJ, on detention after arrest

keys.q: Reasonable expedition is required but more than this cannot be demanded
keys.w: People (DPP) v Walsh, as applied in DPP v Finn (2003)

later: Statute later created detention for questioning: s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 for serious arrestable offences, and other statutes (such as the drug-trafficking and serious-offence regimes) with their own time limits and safeguards. Outside those powers, Walsh still applies.
DPP v McCormack [1999] 4 IR 158: an arrest isn't valid if the person isn't expressly told they're under arrest.
DPP v Finn [2003] IESC 11 and Brehon v DPP [2019] IEHC 63 apply Walsh's 'reasonable expedition' principle to drink-driving procedures at the station.
job: Tell the person, in words, that they're under arrest and why. If the scene makes that impractical (a crowd, violence), tell them as soon as you can and note why you waited.
Arrest isn't for questioning. Unless you're using a statutory detention power (e.g. s.4 CJA 1984), get them charged and before a court with reasonable expedition, or release them.
For prints or samples, use the statutory power (now under the 2014 DNA Act) or properly recorded consent, and note which.
Every period in custody must be justified, so record times and reasons in the custody record.
People (DPP) v Walsh.law: Yes. Walsh is still the leading statement that there is no common-law power to detain for questioning; that exists only under statute. Its 'reasonable expedition' principle is applied every day (Finn; Brehon).

bg: A man was arrested on a Sunday afternoon on suspicion of murder, connected with a robbery, and detained under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984. Questioning began at about 3.24 p.m.

During questioning he asked for a solicitor. Gardaí tried several solicitors, which was difficult on a Sunday with a big local sporting event on. Questioning continued until 6.45 p.m., and the solicitor who agreed to come arrived at 8.33 p.m.

His incriminating statements came after the solicitor's visit: between 9.40 and 11.05 p.m. that night, and the next morning. He was convicted of murder in the Central Criminal Court. The Court of Criminal Appeal dismissed his appeal but certified a point of law.
People (DPP) v Buck.q: Is it a conscious and deliberate breach of the right of access to a solicitor to keep questioning a detainee for a substantial period after he asks for one but before the solicitor arrives? And does that taint statements made later, after the solicitor's visit?
dec: Supreme Court, 17 April 2002 (Keane CJ; Denham, Murray, McGuinness and Hardiman JJ agreeing): appeal dismissed, and the statements were admissible.

Where a detainee asks for a solicitor and gardaí make genuine (bona fide) attempts to get one, they weren't obliged at that time to stop questioning until the solicitor arrived. Whether anything said was admissible was for the trial judge to decide.
The trial judge was entitled to find no breach of the right of access. And the admissions came after the solicitor had been, so nothing linked the earlier questioning to the statements relied on.
later: Overtaken by Gormley [2014] IESC 17: once a detainee asks for a lawyer, questioning must wait until advice has been received, except in wholly exceptional circumstances.

Buck then tried to reopen his conviction relying on Gormley. The Court of Appeal ([2015] IECA 344) held that a later court ruling isn't a 'newly discovered fact'. The High Court (McDermott J, 2016) refused an Article 40 inquiry. The Supreme Court ([2020] IESC 16, Charleton J) struck out his miscarriage-of-justice application on the same basis.
So Gormley doesn't reopen old convictions. It changed the rules for interviews from then on.
job: Buck's approach of carrying on while you try to get a solicitor is no longer lawful practice. Since Gormley: once advice is requested, stop questioning until it has been received.
Make and record real efforts to reach the solicitor: names, numbers, times, outcomes. Offer another solicitor if the first choice can't be reached (Garda Code of Practice).
Weekends and big events are no excuse for skipped steps, but documented genuine efforts protect the case.
People (DPP) v Buck.law: No, on its main point: Gormley (2014) replaced it, and questioning must now wait for requested legal advice. Buck is still cited for the trial judge's discretion and the need for a causal link between breach and statement, and for the rule that a later change in the law doesn't reopen a concluded conviction.
