bg: The accused was detained under a statutory power that allowed him to be held for a fixed period. He was kept beyond the end of that period, and he made a confession during the extra time.
The gardaí believed they were acting for good reasons, to get a confession and secure a conviction, but two senior officers must have known the lawful period had run out.
People (DPP) v Madden.q: Is a confession admissible if it was made while the suspect was being held after the lawful detention period had expired, even though the gardaí acted with good intentions?
dec: The Court of Criminal Appeal excluded the confession.
Holding him beyond the statutory period breached his constitutional right to liberty. Because senior gardaí must have known the time was up, the breach was deliberate and conscious.
Good motives didn't save it: evidence can be excluded without any bad faith (mala fides) on the gardaí's part.
The Court also held that a detained person has a right of reasonable access to his legal advisers, and that refusing that access would make the detention itself unlawful.

keys.q: has got a right of reasonable access to his legal advisers
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (as quoted by the Supreme Court in Doyle, 2017)

later: People (DPP) v Healy [1990] 2 IR 73 (Supreme Court, Finlay CJ) held that the right of reasonable access to a solicitor is constitutional in origin. Gormley (2014) then required questioning to wait for advice once it is requested.

The test for 'deliberate and conscious' has moved on: Kenny looked at the act, and JC (2015) looks at knowledge. But holding someone past the lawful period, knowing the time is up, is still a knowing breach under JC.
Detention periods, extensions and rest periods are now set out in statute (e.g. s.4 Criminal Justice Act 1984, s.30 Offences Against the State Act 1939) and recorded in the custody record.
job: Know exactly when the detention period and any extension end. Write it on the custody record and watch the clock.
When time is up, release or charge. Don't 'just finish the statement': anything said after expiry is at serious risk.
Extensions must be authorised before the period expires, by the right rank and on the right grounds.
Give reasonable access to a solicitor throughout. Refusing it can make the whole detention unlawful.
People (DPP) v Madden.law: Yes, in principle: evidence obtained during detention known to be unlawful is excluded, whatever the motive, and that is still a deliberate and conscious breach under JC. The wording of the test is now as restated in JC (2015).

bg: At 11.25 p.m. on 9 June 2000 a driver was arrested for drink driving under s.49(8) of the Road Traffic Acts. He reached Dún Laoghaire Garda Station at 11.40 p.m. and was in an interview room by 11.44 p.m.

A garda kept him under observation for 20 minutes, saying that guidelines required this before a breath test so that he took nothing by mouth. At 12.07 a.m. he was required to give two breath specimens. He refused at 12.08 a.m. and was charged with refusing.

About 27 minutes had passed between arrival and the requirement. Nothing prevented the requirement being made on arrival, and no evidence was given explaining why the observation was needed. The Circuit Court stated a case for the Supreme Court.
DPP v Finn.q: Once a driver is lawfully arrested and brought to the station, how long can gardaí take before starting the breath procedure? And what happens if a delay isn't explained?
dec: Supreme Court, 19 February 2003 (Murray J; McGuinness, Hardiman, Geoghegan and Fennelly JJ): he was not in lawful detention when the requirement was made.

The detention was lawful on arrival; the question was whether what happened at the station made it unlawful later. Where the statute sets no specific time limit, the principle from Dunne v Clinton and Walsh applies. Gardaí get a reasonable period to carry out the procedure and must act with reasonable expedition, but any interval has to be justified.
Here no reason for the 20-minute wait was proved, so it couldn't be shown to be reasonable. The Court accepted that, on different evidence, a 20-minute observation period might well be justified.
The DPP's argument that the three-hour window for testing covered the delay was rejected.

keys.q: Reasonable expedition is required but more than this cannot be demanded
keys.w: People (DPP) v Walsh, applied in Finn

later: DPP (Curran) v Foley [2006] IEHC 11 (O'Neill J): a 20-minute observation needed to get a valid breath sample was part of the detention following arrest, and no extra caution was needed at its start.

DPP v Stack and Foley [2016] IEHC 159 (Barrett J): uncontradicted evidence that the Medical Bureau of Road Safety trains gardaí to observe for 20 minutes before an Evidenzer test, to rule out mouth alcohol, justified the wait. It didn't make the detention unlawful.

Brehon v DPP [2019] IEHC 63 (Murphy J): a two-hour wait for a doctor delayed by an emergency call-out was reasonable, and gardaí could rely on the doctor service's explanation. The three hours is a backstop, not an entitlement, and leaving someone waiting for no reason could still be unlawful.
job: Start the station procedure promptly and write down every step with times: arrival, rights, observation start and end, requirement, result.
If you observe for 20 minutes before an evidential breath test, say why in evidence: MBRS training to exclude mouth alcohol, and that you watched continuously.
Waiting for a doctor? Record who you called, when, what they said, and every follow-up call.
Never leave a detainee waiting without a reason. Unexplained gaps can make the detention unlawful and sink the case.
DPP v Finn.law: Yes. Finn is still the authority that every delay after arrest must be justified by evidence. Foley, Stack and Brehon show what that justification looks like.

bg: In September 1975 a husband and wife took part in an armed robbery of a bank in Killester, Dublin. An off-duty garda in plain clothes, who was out driving with his family, followed the getaway car and then chased the robbers on foot. He was shot dead.

They were tried in the Special Criminal Court for capital murder, which under the Criminal Justice Act 1964 meant the murder of a garda acting in the course of his duty and still carried the death penalty. In June 1976 both were convicted and sentenced to death.
The Supreme Court certified a point of law: did the prosecution have to prove that the accused knew the victim was a garda acting in the course of his duty?
People (DPP) v Murray.q: For the capital murder of a garda, what did the accused have to know or foresee about who the victim was? And what does 'recklessness' mean in Irish criminal law?
dec: In 1977 the Supreme Court held that the garda was acting in the course of his duty even though he was off duty.

But capital murder needed a guilty mind as to that extra element too. The accused had to know the victim was a garda acting in the course of his duty, or be reckless about it, and the Special Criminal Court had never examined that.

The Court gave recklessness a subjective meaning. Henchy J adopted the definition in the US Model Penal Code: a person is reckless if they consciously disregard a substantial and unjustifiable risk, where disregarding it is a gross departure from what a law-abiding person would do in their situation. It turns on the accused's own awareness, not on what a reasonable person would have realised.
The husband's conviction was replaced with murder. The wife was retried and convicted of murder. Both death sentences were commuted to life imprisonment.
later: Still treated as the leading Irish authority on recklessness, for example in Phelan v Ireland (High Court, 2024).
People (DPP) v Cagney and McGrath [2007] IESC 46 applied the subjective test: the jury must be told the accused had to be aware of the risk.
The Criminal Justice Act 1990 abolished the death penalty. Murder of a garda acting in the course of duty now carries life imprisonment with a minimum of 40 years to be served.
job: Where an offence turns on what the suspect knew or foresaw (that the victim was a garda, or that there was a risk of serious harm), ask directly in interview: 'Did you know he was a garda?' 'Did you realise there was a risk that…?'
If you have to act off duty, identify yourself clearly as a garda, both for safety and because offences against gardaí can turn on whether the suspect knew.
Recklessness is about what the suspect actually realised, so record their own words about what they saw, knew and thought.
People (DPP) v Murray.law: Yes. Murray is still the leading Irish authority on recklessness: the subjective test of consciously disregarding a substantial and unjustifiable risk. Capital murder itself no longer exists.

bg: A man was arrested at 1 p.m. on 3 March 1999 under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 and detained at Pearse Street Garda Station.

At 3.40 p.m. he asked for a solicitor without naming one. Gardaí suggested a busy sole practitioner based in Tallaght, who didn't arrive until 8.22 p.m., and he was questioned at least twice in the meantime. After a 30-minute consultation, interviews continued until 11.25 p.m.

The trial judge found that the gardaí must have known that choosing that solicitor would mean an inevitable delay, which was a conscious and deliberate breach of the right of access. Statements made before the solicitor arrived were excluded. Statements made afterwards were admitted, and he was convicted.
People (DPP) v O'Brien (2005).q: Where gardaí consciously and deliberately deprive a detainee of access to a solicitor, must every statement made during the detention be excluded, or only those made before access was given?
dec: Supreme Court, 5 May 2005 (judgment of McCracken J): appeal dismissed.
A conscious and deliberate denial of reasonable access to a solicitor makes the detention unlawful while it continues, and statements taken during that period are inadmissible.
Once genuine access is given, the breach ends. Statements made afterwards that aren't causally linked to the earlier breach can be admitted, so the later statements here stood.
Deliberately calling a solicitor who is likely to take a long time to arrive can itself amount to a denial of access.

keys.q: a somewhat doubtful proposition
keys.w: McCracken J, on requiring a causal link while the breach is still going on

later: The Garda Code of Practice on Access to a Solicitor (2015) builds this in: deliberately contacting a solicitor who is likely to take a long time to arrive may make the detention unlawful.
Applied in DPP v Ryan [2011] IECCA 6.
Since Gormley (2014), questioning must in any event wait until requested advice has been received.
job: If the person has no solicitor, give them the list and let them choose. Never steer them to someone you know is slow or far away.
Record every call: number, time and outcome. If the solicitor can't come promptly, tell the detainee and offer another.
Don't question while access is being frustrated. Anything said is likely to be excluded, and the detention itself may be unlawful for that period.
Once they've had advice, later interviews can stand on their own, so fix a problem promptly rather than carrying on.
People (DPP) v O'Brien (2005).law: Yes. O'Brien is still good law on what follows from denying access: the detention is unlawful while the denial lasts, and later statements are judged on whether they are causally linked to it. The Garda Code reflects it.

bg: A 19-year-old died after being punched by Cagney, then 17. He fell and hit his head. The prosecution said McGrath had told Cagney to hit him. Cagney said he acted in self-defence.

Both were charged with manslaughter and with endangerment under s.13 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997 (intentionally or recklessly engaging in conduct that creates a substantial risk of death or serious harm). The jury acquitted both of manslaughter and, by 10–2, convicted both of endangerment. Each was sentenced to 15 months.
People (DPP) v Cagney and McGrath.q: Was endangerment properly left to the jury as an alternative to manslaughter? And what did the jury need to be told about recklessness?
dec: Supreme Court, 25 October 2007 (judgment of Hardiman J, with Murray CJ, Geoghegan, Fennelly and Kearns JJ): both convictions were quashed, with no retrial.
Endangerment had gone to the jury as an alternative to manslaughter with no explanation of how the two related.

Worse, the jury was never told what recklessness requires: proof that each accused actually adverted to (was aware of) the serious risk. Neither the prosecution nor the judge explained this, so the jury never considered each accused's own state of mind. The Court called that a grave defect affecting both accused.

keys.q: grave defect in the trial affecting both defendants
keys.w: Hardiman J

later: Confirms that recklessness in Irish criminal law is subjective, following People (DPP) v Murray [1977].
Where endangerment is offered as an alternative to a homicide count, the jury must be told how the two relate and what mental element each needs.
job: Recklessness is proved from what the suspect actually realised, not from what a reasonable person would have seen. Ask in interview: 'Did you realise there was a risk that…?'
Record the suspect's own account of what they saw, knew and intended at the moment of the act.
In one-punch cases, gather evidence of the circumstances that show awareness of the risk: the surface (concrete, kerb), the victim's state (drunk, defenceless), any warning given, and the force used.
People (DPP) v Cagney and McGrath.law: Yes. Cagney and McGrath is still cited on the subjective test of recklessness and on how alternative counts must be explained to a jury.

bg: The accused had met the deceased in prison and later moved into his flat in Dublin. The deceased drank heavily and became aggressive when drunk. On the night, after a day's heavy drinking, the accused came back late.
He said the deceased attacked him with a hammer. He took it from him and struck him, then, in a rage, struck him several more times, killing him.

The trial judge, relying on the English case Holmes v DPP, told the jury that provocation had to leave the accused unable to form an intention to kill or cause serious injury. He was convicted of murder.
People (DPP) v MacEoin.q: What is the test for provocation in Irish law? And should the jury be told that provocation must prevent the accused from forming an intention to kill?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 17 April 1978 (Finlay P, Kenny and McMahon JJ; judgment of Kenny J): a new trial was ordered.

The direction was wrong. Provocation doesn't usually stop someone forming an intention to kill; it is usually what causes that intention. Treating it as cancelling out intent confuses cause and result.

The Court moved Irish law from the objective 'reasonable man' test to a subjective one. The question is whether the provocation actually caused this accused, with his own temperament, character and circumstances, a sudden and complete loss of self-control. If there's evidence of that, the judge must leave provocation to the jury.
Provocation is a partial defence: if it succeeds, murder is reduced to manslaughter.

keys.q: a hot-tempered man may react violently to an insult
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on why the test looks at the accused himself

later: For decades Ireland's test was described as uniquely subjective in the common law world, though trial judges sometimes slipped back into requiring proportionate force.

DPP v McNamara (Supreme Court, 2020, Charleton J): MacEoin isn't purely subjective, and the trial judge has a gatekeeping role. There must be a total loss of control, not just losing one's temper. The provocation must be serious, not a mere insult, and can't be put down to intoxication. The reaction is measured against a sober person of reasonable firmness who shares some of the accused's characteristics. Gross disproportion (a sawn-off shotgun at close range) defeated the plea.
job: In any killing where the suspect says they 'lost it', record exactly what they say triggered it, what happened in what order, and how long it took. It goes straight to provocation.
Gather evidence of drink and drugs (provocation can't rest on intoxication) and of any time to cool down.
Record the number of blows, the weapon and the sequence. Disproportion, or a pause between blows, undermines a claimed total loss of control.
People (DPP) v MacEoin.law: Partly. MacEoin is still the starting point, but in McNamara (2020) the Supreme Court reshaped the test into a mixed one, with a gatekeeping role for the judge. Read the two together.

bg: On 12 March 1986 an 18-year-old was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of unlawful possession of firearms, connected with an attempted armed robbery in Dublin the previous month. He was questioned for several hours at Finglas Garda Station.

At about 3.40 p.m. he said he would tell the truth about the robbery and began a written statement. At 4.00 p.m. a solicitor retained by his family arrived and asked to see him. He was told to wait: the garda in charge thought it would be bad manners to interrupt the interview. The solicitor wasn't let in until 4.34 p.m., just after the statement was signed at 4.30 p.m.

He was charged with attempted murder, shooting with intent and robbery, and the statement was the only evidence. The trial judge (Egan J) found he had been denied access to his solicitor without excuse. Because the judge couldn't be satisfied the admissions were made before that denial, he excluded the statement and directed an acquittal. The DPP appealed.
People (DPP) v Healy.q: Is reasonable access to a solicitor in custody a constitutional right? And does it apply where the detainee's family, rather than the detainee, sent the solicitor?
dec: Supreme Court, 1990 (Finlay CJ; Walsh, Griffin, Hederman and McCarthy JJ): appeal dismissed, and the acquittal stood.

Finlay CJ held that the right of reasonable access to a solicitor is constitutional in origin, not just a matter of statute or regulations. Its purpose is to give a detainee independent advice, so they understand their rights and can decide freely how to respond to questioning, on a more equal footing with the interrogators.

When a solicitor arrives, the detainee must be told at once and, unless there's a valid reason (judged objectively and in the detainee's interests), must get immediate access if they want it. It makes no difference whether the detainee asked for the solicitor or someone acting in good faith for them, such as family, did.

Keeping the solicitor out was a deliberate and conscious act. What mattered was the gardaí's act, not their motives or whether they knew it was unconstitutional, so admissions made after it were inadmissible. As the trial judge couldn't be sure the admissions came before the solicitor arrived, the exclusion stood.
Griffin J reached the same result through the constitutional guarantee of fair procedures.

keys.q: the undoubted right of reasonable access to a solicitor
keys.w: Finlay CJ

keys.q: must be deemed to be constitutional in its origin
keys.w: Finlay CJ

keys.q: bad manners
keys.w: The garda in charge, on why he didn't interrupt the interview

later: Healy is the foundation for Buck (2002), O'Brien (2005), Gormley (2014) and Doyle (2017). Gormley added that questioning must wait until requested advice has been received.

Its act-based reading of 'deliberate and conscious' followed Kenny and has since been replaced by the knowledge-based test in JC (2015). Deliberately keeping a solicitor out would still be a knowing breach.
The Garda Code of Practice on Access to a Solicitor (2015) builds on it.
job: If a solicitor arrives or rings for a detainee, tell the detainee straight away and arrange a private consultation if they want one, even in the middle of an interview or statement.
It doesn't matter who sent the solicitor (family, a friend). If they're acting in good faith for the detainee, treat it the same way.
Never keep a solicitor waiting so you can finish a statement. Record the arrival time, when the detainee was told, and when the consultation started.
People (DPP) v Healy.law: Yes. Healy is the foundation of the constitutional right of access to a solicitor in custody.

src.t: vLex Ireland — People (DPP) v Healy [1990] 2 IR 73
People (DPP) v Doyle [2017] IESC 1 — Supreme Court judgment (reviews Healy)

bg: The accused was convicted in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court of burglary (a video recorder and a games console taken from a house) and of taking a car from the same house. He was sentenced to three years.

The only evidence was a signed, confession-type statement made while he was detained under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984. For most of the interview only one garda was present. A second joined near the end, while the final part was dictated, read over and signed.
He appealed on several grounds, including the judge's warning under s.10 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993 about the confession not being corroborated.
People (DPP) v Connolly.q: What must a judge tell the jury when a conviction may rest on an uncorroborated confession? And does questioning by a single garda make a statement unfair?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 7 May 2002 (Hardiman J, with Lavan and O'Sullivan JJ): conviction quashed and a retrial ordered.

Where a confession isn't corroborated, s.10 requires the judge to tell the jury to have 'due regard' to the absence of corroboration. No particular words are needed, but 'due regard' is an objective standard of attention and isn't self-explanatory. It must be explained, not just recited: what corroboration is, where the prosecution case stands on it, and often why corroboration matters especially with confessions.
The judge's phrase 'something you should bear in mind' was too vague, and weaker than the statute requires.
The custody regulations limit the maximum number of gardaí present at an interview, not the minimum, so questioning by one garda wasn't unlawful. It went only to reliability.
A judge may fairly comment on the accused not giving evidence, and what counsel says isn't evidence.
Hardiman J added that it might soon be argued that, without extraordinary circumstances, statements that weren't audio-visually recorded shouldn't be admitted.

keys.q: something you should bear in mind
keys.w: The trial judge's wording, held too weak to meet s.10

later: Still cited for how the s.10 corroboration warning must be given.
Video-recording of interviews is now routine, and the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would require electronic recording of interviews by statute.
job: If your case rests on an admission, look for independent corroboration from the start: property, CCTV, forensics, phone data, details only the offender would know.
Record every interview electronically and have two members present where possible. A one-garda interview isn't unlawful, but it invites attacks on reliability.
Note the details in an admission that can be checked, then check them and record the result.
People (DPP) v Connolly.law: Yes. Connolly is still cited on the s.10 corroboration warning.

bg: A garda got a s.26 Misuse of Drugs Act warrant from a peace commissioner. The address on the warrant left out one word of the real street name, so it described an address that didn't exist.
Gardaí searched the intended premises and found heroin (diamorphine) worth about €300,000.

The trial judge held the warrant invalid because of the wrong address and dismissed the charges. He felt bound by earlier authority, while calling the exclusionary rule a nonsense. The DPP appealed under s.4(7) of the Criminal Procedure Act 1967 (inserted in 1999).
People (DPP) v Mallon.q: Does a mistake in the address on a search warrant make it invalid, and the search unconstitutional, when there's no doubt which premises were meant?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 3 March 2011 (O'Donnell J, with Gilligan and O'Keeffe JJ): appeal allowed and the dismissal overturned.

A mere error doesn't invalidate a warrant, especially one not likely to mislead. The cases where warrants had been held invalid involved either no jurisdiction to issue them (a statutory precondition wasn't met), or a warrant showing on its face that the preconditions weren't satisfied.

Where the content of a warrant is challenged, the court asks whether the error is fundamental: is it a mere misdescription, and could it mislead? Here the address on the warrant didn't exist, so the only realistic target was the intended premises, and nobody was misled.
The trial judge had misread the case law. DPP v Balfe, which allows for minor errors, had not been overruled and was binding.
O'Donnell J also criticised the logic of the strict Kenny exclusionary rule, a critique the Supreme Court took up four years later in JC.

keys.q: a mere error will not invalidate a warrant
keys.w: O'Donnell J

later: People (DPP) v JC [2015] IESC 31: O'Donnell J, by then in the Supreme Court, was in the majority that overruled Kenny, calling it plainly wrong.
The Law Reform Commission's 2015 Report on Search Warrants reviewed Mallon among the misdescription cases.
Read with Damache and JC. Errors on the face of a warrant are judged by whether they're fundamental and could mislead, while constitutional breaches in obtaining evidence are judged under JC.
job: Get the address exactly right. Check it against the Eircode and other records, or with a site visit, and describe the premises (type of house, door colour, location) in the information.
If you spot an error before you execute the warrant, go back for a corrected one rather than relying on Mallon.
Record how you identified the premises on the day. That's what saves a misdescribed warrant.
People (DPP) v Mallon.law: Yes. Mallon is the leading authority on misdescription in warrants: a minor error that doesn't mislead won't by itself invalidate the warrant.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Mallon [2011] IECCA 29
D. Clooney, The Exclusionary Rule in Ireland (UCC CCJHR Working Paper 22, 2023)

bg: In 2001 a 17-year-old in Turkey was arrested by anti-terrorism police on suspicion of taking part in an unlawful demonstration and hanging an illegal banner.

Turkish law then didn't allow a lawyer during police questioning for that kind of offence. Questioned without one, he signed a statement admitting his involvement. He later withdrew it before a prosecutor and a judge, saying he had been ill-treated, though medical reports found no signs of it.
He got access to a lawyer only after he was remanded in custody. He was convicted, partly on the police statement, and his appeals in Turkey failed.
Salduz v Turkey.q: Does a fair trial require access to a lawyer at the first police interrogation? And can a court fairly convict on statements made without one?
dec: Grand Chamber, 27 November 2008: violation of Article 6(3)(c) together with Article 6(1).

Article 6 applies before trial, because what happens at the investigation stage, especially in interviews, sets the framework for the trial. The rights must be practical and effective, not theoretical.

So access to a lawyer should be given from the first police interrogation, unless there are compelling reasons to restrict it in the particular case. Even then, a restriction mustn't unduly prejudice the defence, and the defence is irretrievably prejudiced when statements made in police interrogation without a lawyer are used to convict.
Here the restriction was systematic (it was set by law), he was a minor, and his statement was used to convict him. The later trial couldn't cure that.

keys.q: access to a lawyer should be provided as from the first interrogation
keys.w: Grand Chamber

keys.q: irretrievably prejudiced
keys.w: Grand Chamber, on using statements made without a lawyer to convict

keys.q: one of the fundamental features of a fair trial
keys.w: Grand Chamber, on legal assistance

later: Dayanan v Turkey (2009): a systematic restriction breached Article 6 even though the suspect stayed silent.

Ibrahim and Others v UK (Grand Chamber, 2016) uses a two-part approach: were there compelling reasons for the restriction, and were the proceedings as a whole fair? An urgent need to prevent further suicide attacks justified temporary delays for three of the applicants. For the fourth there were no compelling reasons and he hadn't been cautioned, and there was a violation.
Beuze v Belgium (Grand Chamber, 2018) and Doyle v Ireland (2019): without compelling reasons, the overall fairness of the trial gets very strict scrutiny. In Doyle the Irish trial survived it.
In Irish law, Gormley (2014) drew on Salduz to require that questioning wait for requested legal advice.
job: Don't question a detainee who has asked for a lawyer until they've had advice. Irish law (Gormley) and Strasbourg agree on this.
Any restriction needs compelling reasons specific to that person (e.g. an imminent risk to life), recorded at the time so they can be reviewed. Never apply a blanket practice.
With juveniles take extra care: make sure they understand their rights, follow the Children Act 2001 safeguards (a parent or guardian informed and present), and never accept a vague 'waiver'.
A waiver must be clear and fully informed. Record it, and re-confirm it at the start of each interview.
Salduz v Turkey.law: Yes, as refined by Ibrahim (2016) and Beuze (2018): access from the first interrogation, restrictions only for compelling reasons, and a test of overall fairness wherever access was restricted.

bg: A woman was found dead in the top flat of a house. The accused, a soldier who was decorating the house and had a key, found the body on a Sunday.

He gave a detailed witness statement at Irishtown Garda Station from about 4 to 7 p.m. The gardaí had no suspicion of him then, but he wasn't sent home. He was questioned almost continuously through the night and into Monday morning, without sleep or rest. At 10 a.m. he was moved to Donnybrook station, where the questioning continued.

His wife came to the station but was kept in another room and not allowed to see him, and seven calls from his wife, friends and family were never passed on. He said he asked repeatedly to leave; the gardaí said he was there as a free agent. He was formally arrested around noon, made an oral admission at about 2 p.m., slept for a few hours, and gave a written confession at 6 p.m.
The statements were the only evidence against him. The trial judge held them voluntary because there were no threats or promises, and the jury convicted.
People (DPP) v Lynch.q: Can a statement be admitted where the person was kept at the station for many hours, without sleep or contact with family, before being arrested, even if no threat or promise was made?
dec: Supreme Court, 1982 (O'Higgins CJ, Walsh and Kenny JJ): the conviction was quashed and a verdict of not guilty entered.

O'Higgins CJ said he had spent about 22 hours in garda stations before his first admission, and was formally under arrest for only the last two. He was deprived of sleep, cut off from his family, in strange surroundings and constantly watched, and those conditions were oppressive enough to rebut the claim that his admissions were voluntary. Untrue details in the admissions, apparently drawn from a newspaper, added to the doubt. Without the admissions there was no case.

Walsh J said his constitutional rights had been violated. Under O'Brien, evidence obtained by a deliberate and conscious violation must be excluded, and the trial judge had no real discretion. Being voluntary isn't enough on its own. A person kept at a station may reasonably assume he isn't free to leave until he is told he is.
Kenny J would have excluded the statements in the trial judge's general discretion because the circumstances were oppressive.

keys.q: sufficiently oppressive to rebut the claim
keys.w: O'Higgins CJ, on the conditions of questioning

keys.q: not free to leave until he is so told
keys.w: Walsh J, on people 'helping' at a station

keys.q: the fruits of that violation must be excluded from evidence
keys.w: Walsh J

later: Lynch effectively ended the practice of inviting people in to 'help with inquiries' and holding them informally, which Dunne v Clinton had condemned as far back as 1930.

Custody is now governed by statutory detention powers (e.g. s.4 Criminal Justice Act 1984) and the Custody Regulations 1987, which control how long interviews last, rest periods and questioning at night.
Voluntariness and fairness are judged on the Shaw principles, and exclusion for constitutional breaches now runs through JC (2015).
job: If someone attends 'voluntarily', tell them clearly that they're free to leave at any time, and record that you told them. If you wouldn't let them go, arrest them properly.
Once you would stop someone leaving, they're in custody: arrest, caution, notice of rights, custody record.
Give rest, food and breaks, and record them. The Custody Regulations limit how long interviews last and questioning at night.
Pass on calls and visits from family and solicitors, and record what you did.
Check the details in an admission against independent facts. Details that match the newspapers but not the scene are a warning sign.
People (DPP) v Lynch.law: Yes. Lynch is still the leading authority on oppressive questioning and on 'voluntary' attendance at a station. Its exclusion analysis now runs through the Shaw voluntariness principles and JC.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Conroy (describes Lynch)
K. Sweeney, The Changing Nature of Police Interviewing in Ireland

bg: Three men robbed a building society and the security camera filmed it. Stills from the film were put in evidence, and the prosecution said two of the men were the accused and a co-accused.
No witness said they recognised either man. The case rested on the footage and stills, and on hair-sample evidence said to match.

He was convicted of robbery in the Circuit Criminal Court. He appealed on the grounds that the judge hadn't properly directed the jury on using the video to identify him, and that the hair evidence shouldn't have been admitted without evidence of how conclusive the test was.
People (DPP) v Maguire.q: Can a jury itself identify an accused from CCTV footage and stills? And what warnings and explanations must the judge give?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 7 April 1995 (O'Flaherty, Barron and Flood JJ): the conviction was quashed and a retrial ordered.

Security-camera footage and stills of a crime are admissible, and the jury may compare them with the accused and decide for themselves whether it's him. In doing that they aren't acting as experts. They're doing what people do every day when they recognise someone in a photograph (following the English case R v Dodson).

But the usual identification warnings must be given. A jury should form its own view of identity from footage only where there's no independent identification evidence, and should then weigh it with the rest of the case. Relying on video alone, with no supporting evidence, is unsatisfactory, though it can still go to the jury if nothing else exists.
Where hair samples match but the match isn't conclusive, evidence must explain why, so the jury understands what it's worth.
Footage can also be used to show whether a witness had a fair chance to identify someone, or to explain why they couldn't.
later: Still cited on identification from CCTV. Read it with Casey (No 2) on the warning, and with Braddish and Dunne on seeking out and keeping the footage.
Where a garda or other witness who knows the accused recognises them on footage, that is recognition evidence, and the Casey warning applies to it too (Stafford; O'Donovan).
job: Seize the original footage and make a full working copy. Produce stills from it with continuity, and keep the footage they came from.
Record the system's time offset, where each camera is and what it views, and the image quality.

If you recognise someone on CCTV, write down straight away how you know them (how long, how often, when you last saw them) and what you recognised. Your evidence will be tested like any identification.
Look for supporting evidence (clothing seized, phone location, forensics), because a case resting on footage alone is weak.
For forensic comparisons (hair, DNA, fibres), get the scientist to explain how strong the match is.
People (DPP) v Maguire.law: Yes. Maguire is still cited on CCTV identification: the footage is admissible and the jury can identify from it, but with warnings, and ideally with supporting evidence.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Maguire [1995] 2 IR 286
vLex Ireland — People v Stafford (CCA; recognition and the Casey warning)

bg: In November 1984 three intruders broke into a house in Co. Cork, seriously assaulted two elderly brothers, one of them fatally, and damaged furniture.

Gardaí suspected the two accused and arrested them under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of malicious damage, a scheduled offence. Their evidence was that the aim was to question them about the killing and related matters. In custody both made written admissions, and the case depended on them.

The trial judge accepted that the gardaí genuinely suspected malicious damage. But he held the arrests unlawful because, as he read s.30, it required a connection with subversive activity, and the damage had none. He excluded the statements and directed acquittals. The DPP appealed on the point of law.
People (DPP) v Quilligan.q: Is s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act limited to offences connected with subversive activity, or does a genuine suspicion of any scheduled offence justify arrest?
dec: Supreme Court, 25 July 1986 (Walsh J, with Hederman J): s.30 isn't limited to subversive offences.

Neither s.30 nor s.36 requires the scheduled offence to be connected with subversion. A genuine (bona fide) suspicion of a scheduled offence, here malicious damage, is enough for a lawful s.30 arrest.
The Act's long title, which refers to subversive activities, couldn't cut down the clear words of the section. Where the wording is unambiguous, its ordinary meaning applies.
The Central Criminal Court's ruling was disapproved.
later: Followed in People (DPP) v Howley [1989] ILRM 629.
People (DPP) v Quilligan and O'Reilly (No 3) [1993] 2 IR 305: the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of s.30.
People (DPP) v Braney [2021] IESC 7: s.30 detention was upheld again.
job: A s.30 arrest needs a genuine suspicion of a scheduled offence (e.g. firearms, explosives, malicious damage, membership of an unlawful organisation). Record the specific grounds for that suspicion.
Don't use a scheduled offence as a pretext with no real suspicion behind it. The suspicion must be genuine.

Know the s.30 time limits: 24 hours, extendable by a chief superintendent for another 24, and by a District Court judge for a further 24. Make sure each extension is in place before the current period ends.
People (DPP) v Quilligan.law: Yes. Quilligan is still the authority that s.30 applies to any scheduled offence on a genuine suspicion, not only to subversive crime.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Quilligan and O'Reilly [1986] IR 495
vLex Ireland — DPP v Quilligan (No. 3)

bg: On 8 October 2002, in heavy rain near Tullow, Co. Carlow, a lorry was involved in a fatal collision. The driver was charged with dangerous driving causing death and several summary offences.

The prosecution case was that the lorry's tyres were excessively and illegally worn and had caused the crash. Gardaí examined the lorry forensically at the time and then disposed of the physical evidence.

After the prosecution disclosed its case, the driver asked for the evidence to be inspected by his own engineer. In October 2004 he learned it was gone. He sought judicial review in December 2004, and the High Court stopped the prosecution.
Ludlow v DPP.q: Can a trial go ahead where gardaí have disposed of the key physical evidence before the defence could examine it? And are a garda report and photographs enough?
dec: Supreme Court, 31 July 2008 (Hardiman J, with Murray CJ and Denham J): the DPP's appeal was dismissed, and the prosecution stayed stopped.
Gardaí must take and keep evidence that could affect guilt or innocence. The duty is especially strong where the evidence is technical and indirect, as here, where the tyres were the whole case.

The duty can't be defined precisely. It depends on the circumstances, is applied fairly and reasonably, and doesn't require a disproportionate use of manpower and resources. For large items like vehicles, a forensic report may sometimes be a reasonable alternative to keeping the item, but the accused should generally get the chance to examine it.

Why the evidence was destroyed is background, not decisive. The test is whether there's a real risk of an unfair trial that can't be avoided. Photographs and garda statements were no substitute for the defence examining the tyres themselves.
Seeking judicial review about three months after finding out was prompt enough.
later: Savage v DPP [2008] IESC 39, decided the same month, went the other way: the destroyed car had been examined and reports existed, so the trial could go ahead. Best practice is to notify the accused before destroying evidence.

Wall v DPP [2013] IESC 56: the trial judge is now the main safeguard, and stopping a trial is rare. Ludlow shows the kind of case where it can still be justified: the missing item is the core of a technical case.
job: In fatal and serious collisions, treat the vehicle and key parts (tyres, brakes) as exhibits. Secure them, photograph and examine them, and keep them until the case is over or the defence has had the chance to inspect.
Before releasing or disposing of any vehicle or bulky exhibit, notify the suspect or their solicitor in writing, give them a reasonable chance to examine it, and record the response.
If storing the whole item is impossible, keep the critical components (e.g. the tyres) along with a full forensic report with measurements and photos.
Log every retention and disposal decision, with who authorised it.
Ludlow v DPP.law: Yes. Ludlow is the leading example of when missing evidence can still justify stopping a trial. Read it with Savage and Wall.

src.t: vLex Ireland — Ludlow v DPP [2008] IESC 54
vLex Ireland — Savage v DPP [2008] IESC 39
vLex Ireland — Wall v DPP [2013] IESC 56

bg: A teacher at a London school became obsessed with one of his pupils. Over many months there were incidents and warning signs that came to the attention of the school and the police.
In 1988 the teacher shot the pupil's father dead and wounded the pupil.

The family sued the police for negligence. The English courts struck the claim out, applying Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire (police owe no duty of care to individual victims when investigating crime). The family complained to Strasbourg under Articles 2, 6 and 8.
Osman v United Kingdom.q: When must the police act to protect someone whose life is threatened by another person? And could the police be given blanket immunity from negligence claims?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 28 October 1998: no violation of Article 2 (or 8), but a violation of Article 6.

Article 2 includes a positive obligation. Where the authorities know, or ought to know, of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual from the criminal acts of another, they must take the reasonable measures within the scope of their powers that might be expected to avoid that risk.

The obligation mustn't impose an impossible or disproportionate burden. Police have to make choices about priorities and resources, and must respect due process and other people's rights (for example, no arrest without grounds).
On the facts, it wasn't shown that the police knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to the family's lives, so there was no breach of Article 2.
But using the police immunity rule from Hill as a blanket bar to the negligence claim, without weighing the competing interests, breached the right of access to a court under Article 6.

keys.q: real and immediate risk
keys.w: European Court of Human Rights — the core of the Osman test

keys.q: an impossible or disproportionate burden
keys.w: European Court of Human Rights, on the limits of the duty

later: The case gave rise to formal threat-to-life warnings, often called Osman warnings. In Ireland these are delivered in person as a Garda Information Message (GIM), with a leaflet on basic security.

Van Colle v UK (2012): threats and intimidation against a prosecution witness, who was later shot dead, did not meet the Osman threshold. The police didn't know, and ought not to have known, of a real and immediate risk to his life.
Opuz v Turkey (2009) applied the Osman duty to domestic violence, and found violations.
job: If you get information that someone's life is at real and immediate risk from an identified person, act on it: record it, escalate it to your sergeant or inspector, and follow the threat-to-life procedure.
Where a threat-to-life warning is required, deliver it in person and record when you gave it, what you said and how they responded.
Consider every measure within your powers: arrest if grounds exist, searches, objecting to bail, supporting safety or protection orders, patrols, liaison with other units.
Record your decisions and the reasons for them. The test is what you knew or ought to have known, and whether your response was reasonable.
Osman v United Kingdom.law: Yes. Osman sets the test for the State's duty to protect life from other people. It is applied across Europe, including in domestic violence (Opuz) and witness-intimidation (Van Colle) cases.

Human Rights Law Centre — Scope of the obligation to protect life (Van Colle, applying Osman)
Wikipedia — Garda Information Message

bg: Over several years the applicant and her mother suffered repeated violence from the applicant's husband: assaults causing serious injury, death threats, harassment, and attempts to kill them, including driving a car into them.
They reported it to the authorities many times. Several prosecutions were dropped after the women withdrew their complaints, and on one occasion he was only fined.
In March 2002 he shot and killed the applicant's mother. He was convicted of murder but released pending his appeal, after which he threatened the applicant again.
Opuz v Turkey.q: Did the State do enough to protect the women from a known and escalating risk? And was its passivity discrimination against women?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 9 June 2009: violations of Article 2 (the mother's death), Article 3 (the applicant's ill-treatment) and Article 14 (discrimination).

Article 2: given his history of escalating violence and threats, a lethal attack was foreseeable. The authorities had to act with due diligence, and they failed to. Given how serious the violence was, the legal framework should have allowed prosecutions to continue despite the withdrawn complaints.
Article 3: the response to the applicant's injuries and the threats against her was manifestly inadequate. The Court criticised the rule that ended proceedings when a complaint was withdrawn.

Article 14: domestic violence in Turkey mainly affected women, and the authorities' general passivity amounted to discrimination. The Court pointed to how women were treated when they reported violence, the reluctance of the courts to protect them, and the law's weak deterrent effect. Gender-based violence is a form of discrimination against women.

keys.q: gender-based violence which is a form of discrimination against women
keys.w: European Court of Human Rights

later: Opuz is the leading Strasbourg case on the State's duties in domestic violence. It fed into the Council of Europe's Istanbul Convention (2011), which Ireland ratified in 2019.
In Ireland, the Domestic Violence Act 2018 created the offence of coercive control and strengthened safety and protection orders.
job: Treat each domestic violence report as part of a pattern. Check PULSE history, earlier incidents, threats, weapons and escalation.

A withdrawn complaint doesn't end your duty. In serious cases, ask whether the prosecution can go ahead on other evidence: 999 recordings, photos of injuries, medical evidence, independent witnesses, admissions.
Record the risk factors and the safety measures you took or offered: arrest, objecting to bail, safety or protection orders, referral to support services.
Act on threats to kill (the Osman duty) and escalate them.
Opuz v Turkey.law: Yes. Opuz is the leading case on the State's positive duties in domestic violence, and on domestic violence as discrimination against women.

src.t: Human Rights Law Centre — Opuz v Turkey summary
Council of Europe — Press release on Opuz v Turkey
Equal Rights Trust — Turkey's passive response to domestic violence violates non-discrimination

bg: A man was convicted of murder in 2015, partly on mobile phone traffic and location data that phone companies had retained under the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011 and that gardaí had accessed.

The 2011 Act required general retention of every user's traffic and location data. Access requests were dealt with inside An Garda Síochána by a senior officer, with no prior review by a court or independent body.
He brought civil proceedings challenging the 2011 Act. The High Court found part of it inconsistent with EU law, and the Supreme Court referred questions to the Court of Justice of the EU.
GD v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána.q: Can national law require general retention of everyone's traffic and location data to fight serious crime? And who must authorise police access to that data?
dec: Court of Justice of the EU (Grand Chamber), 5 April 2022.

EU law (the ePrivacy Directive, read with the Charter rights to privacy and data protection) precludes general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data to fight serious crime. Serious crime can't be treated like a threat to national security.

What is allowed: targeted retention (by category of person or by area), general retention of IP addresses and of basic identity data, and expedited ('quick freeze') preservation of data for a specific investigation.

Access must be subject to prior review by a court or an independent administrative body. A police officer doesn't qualify, even with a semi-autonomous unit behind him and judicial review available afterwards.

A national court can't limit the time effects of a declaration of invalidity it is obliged to make. Whether evidence obtained this way is admissible at trial is a matter for national law, subject to the EU principles of equivalence and effectiveness.

keys.q: general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data
keys.w: CJEU — what EU law rules out for fighting serious crime

keys.q: The admissibility of such evidence is a matter for national law
keys.w: CJEU

later: The Communications (Retention of Data) (Amendment) Act 2022 (signed 21 July 2022) followed. General retention is now possible only on a High Court order on State-security grounds. Preservation ('quick freeze') and production orders, and disclosure of traffic, location and internet-source data, need an order from a District Court judge. Basic user data can be disclosed without one.

DPP v Smyth [2024] IESC 22 and DPP v Dwyer [2024] IESC 39: data obtained under the 2011 Act was still admissible under JC, because the gardaí had relied on an Act in force and its invalidity was a later legal development.
The CJEU's Landeck judgment (2024) extended prior-review requirements to accessing data on seized phones, and the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 responds to it.
job: For phone traffic and location data, use the 2022 Act procedures: a District Court order for disclosure. Know your local procedure for urgent applications, and record why the matter was urgent.
Ask for preservation ('quick freeze') early, before the data is deleted.
Basic subscriber or user data doesn't need a court order, but keep the request proportionate and recorded.
For phones you seize, get specific authority to search the contents (Quirke).
GD v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána.law: Yes. GD is the governing EU law on data retention and access, and Irish law now follows it through the 2022 Amendment Act. Evidence gathered under the old 2011 Act has been admitted under JC (Smyth; Dwyer).

bg: Gardaí searched a house under a search warrant that described the premises incorrectly: the wrong address had been written on it. Stolen goods were found and the accused were convicted.

On appeal they argued that the evidence came from a direct violation of Article 40.5 of the Constitution (the dwelling is inviolable and may not be forcibly entered except in accordance with law), so it had to be excluded.
People (AG) v O'Brien.q: Is evidence obtained under an invalid search warrant admissible? And is there a difference between evidence obtained illegally and evidence obtained in breach of constitutional rights?
dec: Supreme Court, 1965: appeal dismissed, and the evidence was admissible. Kingsmill Moore J gave the majority judgment (Lavery and Budd JJ agreeing). Walsh J (Ó Dálaigh CJ agreeing) gave a judgment that became the foundation of the Irish exclusionary rule.

Evidence obtained illegally isn't automatically excluded. The trial judge has a discretion, weighing the public interest in convicting criminals against the public interest in the State not benefiting from unlawful conduct.

Walsh J set a stricter rule for constitutional rights. Evidence obtained by a deliberate and conscious violation of constitutional rights must be excluded unless there are extraordinary excusing circumstances, such as the imminent destruction of vital evidence, the need to rescue a victim in peril, or a search incidental to a lawful arrest.
Here the error in the warrant was an oversight, not a deliberate and conscious violation, so the evidence stood.

keys.q: the imminent destruction of vital evidence
keys.w: Walsh J — an extraordinary excusing circumstance

keys.q: the need to rescue a victim in peril
keys.w: Walsh J — another

later: Shaw (1980) and Kenny (1990) argued over what 'deliberate and conscious' meant, and Kenny made the rule close to absolute.

JC (2015) restated the test. Knowing breaches lead to exclusion, and so, in practice, do reckless or grossly negligent ones. Inadvertent breaches can be saved, and the prosecution must prove which kind it was.
O'Brien's discretion for evidence that is illegal but not unconstitutional still applies.
Mallon (2011) applied similar thinking to misdescribed warrants: a mere error that doesn't mislead won't invalidate a warrant.
job: Check every warrant before you use it: address, name, statutory power, date, signature. Mistakes you could have caught invite exclusion arguments.
Not every illegality is a constitutional breach. Illegality goes to the judge's discretion; breaches of constitutional rights (the home, liberty, solicitor access, privacy) are judged under JC.
If you enter urgently to save a life or stop vital evidence being destroyed, record exactly why it couldn't wait.
People (AG) v O'Brien.law: Yes, as the root of Irish exclusion law. Its discretion for illegally obtained evidence still applies, and the constitutional test is now as restated in JC (2015).

bg: The plaintiff was charged under s.8 of the Forgery Act 1913 with possessing 2,000 forged US $100 notes at a Dublin hotel on 4 May 1994.

He challenged ss.18 and 19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984. These allow a court to draw inferences when an arrested person fails or refuses to account for an object, substance or mark (s.18), or for their presence at a place (s.19). He said they breached the right to silence, the presumption of innocence and the right to a fair trial. The High Court (Murphy J, 1995) rejected the challenge.
Rock v Ireland.q: Can the State allow courts to draw inferences from a suspect's failure to account for incriminating objects, or for being at a scene, without breaching the right to silence?
dec: Supreme Court, 19 November 1997 (Hamilton CJ; O'Flaherty, Denham, Barrington and Keane JJ): the sections are constitutional.

Starting from the presumption that legislation is constitutional, the Court weighed the restriction on the right to silence against the State's duty to investigate and prosecute crime, and found it proportionate, mainly because of the safeguards written into the sections.

Those safeguards were central. The court may draw only such inferences as appear proper. No one can be convicted solely on an inference. And the inference is available only if the suspect was told in ordinary language what the effect of failing to account might be.

keys.q: such inferences as appear proper
keys.w: ss.18–19 Criminal Justice Act 1984 — the safeguard the Court relied on

later: The Criminal Justice Act 2007 substituted ss.18 and 19 and added s.19A (failure to mention facts later relied on). An inference now needs all of the following: the suspect was told in ordinary language what the effect of not answering might be; they had a reasonable opportunity to consult a solicitor; and the questioning was electronically recorded, unless they agreed in writing to it not being recorded. No one can be convicted solely or mainly on an inference.
After the Omagh bombing, the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1998 added inference provisions for membership offences.
job: Before you invoke s.18, 19 or 19A, tell the suspect in ordinary language (using the standard wording) what the effect of not answering may be, make sure they've had a reasonable opportunity to consult a solicitor, and make sure the interview is electronically recorded.
Put the specific object, mark or presence to them, and tell them why you believe it's linked to the offence. The section requires you to say so.
Record their answer, or their silence, exactly. An inference can support a case but can never prove it on its own, so keep building the rest of the evidence.
Rock v Ireland.law: Yes. Rock is still the foundation for the inference provisions. The current conditions are in the 2007 versions of ss.18, 19 and 19A.

bg: The accused was arrested at home on 8 December 1996 in a murder investigation and detained at Lucan Garda Station under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984.

The interviews weren't audio-visually recorded, and the written records were grossly deficient. Most seriously, no record at all was made of one entire interview, in which he consistently denied involvement. The trial judge found several breaches of the Custody Regulations but still admitted his statements, and he was convicted of murder.
The Court of Criminal Appeal deplored the breaches but held they weren't material. It refused leave to appeal but certified a point of law for the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Diver.q: Should statements be admitted where there were serious breaches of the Custody Regulations in recording interviews?
dec: Supreme Court, 29 July 2005 (Hardiman J; Murray CJ, Denham, Fennelly and McCracken JJ): the conviction was quashed and a retrial ordered.

The breaches couldn't be treated as trivial or inconsequential: they were grave, obvious and deliberate. Not recording a whole interview in which the suspect denied involvement meant the jury never saw an important part of the picture.
The case turned on narrow issues, and the Court couldn't be sure the verdict would have been the same without the statements.
Under s.7(3) of the 1984 Act a breach of the regulations doesn't automatically make evidence inadmissible, but serious breaches like these must weigh heavily when the judge decides admissibility.

keys.q: grave, obvious and deliberate
keys.w: Supreme Court (Hardiman J), on the breaches

keys.q: grossly deficient
keys.w: Describing the written interview records

later: He was acquitted at the retrial in 2006.
Electronic recording of interviews is now routine, and the inference provisions (ss.18, 19 and 19A) depend on it unless the suspect agrees in writing to no recording.
The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would put electronic recording of interviews on a statutory footing.
job: Record every interview, on video and in notes, including the ones where the suspect denies everything. A missing record of a denial does more damage than having no admission.
Fill in the custody record as you go: every interview start and finish, breaks, visits, calls and requests.
If you notice a breach, such as a missed note or a late entry, record it honestly and tell the member in charge. Hiding it turns a minor breach into a deliberate one.
People (DPP) v Diver.law: Yes. Diver is the leading authority that grave, deliberate breaches of the Custody Regulations can lead to exclusion, despite s.7(3).

bg: Gardaí investigating a fatal assault entered the home of one of the accused relying on a search warrant, and arrested him inside.
The warrant was later found to be invalid. He was detained and made admissions that were used at his trial.
People (DPP) v Laide and Ryan.q: If gardaí enter a home on a bad warrant and arrest someone inside, is the arrest lawful? And what happens to admissions made in the detention that follows?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 24 February 2005 (McCracken J).
The prosecution bears the onus of proving that entry into a dwelling was lawful.

The gardaí believed they were lawfully in the house, but their entry was deliberate, and on an invalid warrant it breached the constitutional inviolability of the dwelling. An arrest made inside, while they were there unlawfully, was itself unlawful.
Applying Kenny, statements made during the detention that followed had to be excluded, absent extraordinary excusing circumstances, and that accused's appeal was allowed.
later: Decided under Kenny. Under JC (2015) the outcome would turn on whether the breach was knowing or inadvertent, so gardaí relying on a warrant they genuinely believed valid might now be treated differently.

DPP v Barry O'Brien (Court of Criminal Appeal, 2012): after Damache, gardaí who had entered a home under a s.29 warrant were treated as trespassers, and an arrest made inside was unlawful. The conviction was quashed.
job: Before you enter a home, know your power: a valid warrant, a statutory power of entry, an occupier's consent, or a genuine emergency such as saving life. Write down which one you relied on.
Check the warrant is valid before you go in: issuer, power, address, date. An arrest made inside on a bad warrant can be unlawful.
If in doubt, arrest outside the dwelling, or make sure you have a separate lawful basis for entry.
The prosecution has to prove lawful entry, so record how you got in, who let you in, what was said, and the time.
People (DPP) v Laide and Ryan.law: Partly. The principles still stand: the State must prove lawful entry, and an arrest made inside after an unlawful entry is unlawful. Whether evidence is excluded now depends on JC.

src.t: Y. Daly, Judicial Oversight of Policing (DCU)
CaseMine — DPP v Barry O'Brien (CCA 2012), citing Laide

bg: After the Omagh bombing in August 1998, the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1998 allowed inferences to be drawn from a suspect's failure to answer material questions in membership cases.

On 30 September 1998 the applicant was arrested at home under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of membership of an unlawful organisation, and taken to Carrickmacross Garda Station.

His solicitor advised him by phone, then faxed the superintendent. He asked for particulars of the allegations and offered to have the interviews video-recorded, or failing that asked for full interview notes before the detention ended. No notes had been taken at the early interviews, and access to the later notes was refused. The High Court ordered his release under Article 40.4.
Lavery v Member in Charge, Carrickmacros.q: Does reasonable access to a solicitor entitle the solicitor to particulars, interview notes and progress reports during the detention? And does refusing them make the detention unlawful?
dec: Supreme Court, 23 February 1999 (O'Flaherty J; Hamilton CJ, Barrington, Keane and Murphy JJ): the release order was reversed, and the detention was lawful.

Gardaí may conduct interviews as they judge appropriate, provided they act reasonably. The solicitor wasn't entitled to regular updates and running accounts of the investigation, and had no right to attend the interviews.

Whether the interview notes were adequate was a matter for any later trial, not for whether the detention was lawful. It was odd that the suspect could see the notes while his solicitor couldn't, but that didn't make the detention unlawful. If he was charged, he would be entitled to all the relevant documents.

keys.q: not entitled to regular updates and running accounts
keys.w: Supreme Court (O'Flaherty J), on the solicitor's requests

later: Doyle [2017] confirmed there is no constitutional right to a solicitor's presence, but since 2014 solicitors may attend interviews on request (DPP direction; Garda Code 2015).
The Garda Code of Practice (2015) cites Lavery: interview notes don't have to be disclosed during custody.
Interviews are now routinely recorded electronically, and the inference provisions generally require it.
job: You don't have to give a solicitor running updates or your interview notes during the detention, but be courteous, and record their requests and your answers.
Allow the solicitor to attend interviews when asked (Garda Code), and facilitate consultations.
Take full notes of every interview as it happens. Their adequacy will be tested at trial, even though it doesn't affect whether the detention is lawful.
Lavery v Member in Charge, Carrickmacros.law: Yes, on notes and updates. On solicitors attending interviews, it has been overtaken in practice by the 2014 DPP direction and the 2015 Garda Code.

bg: In the early hours of 28 February 1984 a driver failed to stop at a Garda checkpoint in Rathgar, Dublin, and drove dangerously. Gardaí pursued him for about 45 minutes. He rammed a patrol car and was followed to a house in Terenure.
Gardaí twice asked to enter the house. An occupant refused both times and told them to leave. That occupant was then arrested for assaulting a garda and put in a patrol car.
An inspector knocked on the open front door and asked if anyone was inside. A male voice answered 'Yes, in here'. Gardaí went in and arrested the driver inside for road traffic offences.
The District Justice found there had been no invitation to enter and stated a case. The High Court held that the arrest was lawful.
DPP v Gaffney.q: Can gardaí go into a dwelling without a warrant to make an arrest, after entry has been refused, on the strength of a reply from inside?
dec: Supreme Court, 23 February 1987 (Walsh J, with Finlay CJ and Hederman J; Henchy and McCarthy JJ also sat): the High Court was reversed. The entry breached Article 40.5 and the arrest was unlawful.
The dwelling is inviolable and may not be forcibly entered except in accordance with law. A statutory power of arrest doesn't, by itself, give a power to enter a home to use it.
After two express refusals, 'Yes, in here' couldn't be read as an invitation to come in. The absence of a fresh refusal can't be treated as implied permission to enter.

keys.q: Yes, in here
keys.w: The reply from inside, held not to be an invitation

later: Relied on in DPP v Cullen [2014] IESC 7.

Statute now fills part of the gap. Section 6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997 allows entry, with reasonable force if needed, to arrest for an arrestable offence. Entering a dwelling without a warrant needs one of the following: an occupier's consent; the person was seen in or entering it; reasonable cause to suspect they would abscond, obstruct justice or commit an arrestable offence before a warrant could be obtained; or they ordinarily live there.
Section 7 of the Road Traffic Act 2010 allows entry without a warrant to the curtilage of a dwelling, but not the dwelling itself, for drink- and drug-driving arrests and requirements.

Rozmyslowicz [2018] IECA 289 (Hogan J): s.6 entry to execute an arrest warrant needs reasonable cause to suspect the person is inside. It 'does not empower a purely warrantless search for no reason'. Damages were awarded for an unlawful forced entry.
Delaney (1997): entering to protect life is different. A genuine belief that entry is needed to save life or limb justifies it.
job: A power of arrest isn't a power of entry. Before you go into a home, identify your entry power: a warrant, s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997 (an arrestable offence plus one of its conditions), another statute, consent, or protection of life.
Consent must be real and given by someone entitled to give it. Record who gave it, what was said and when. A refusal stands until it's clearly withdrawn.
If a road traffic suspect gets home, you may arrest on the driveway or curtilage (s.7 RTA 2010) but not inside, unless another power applies.
Note exactly how and why you entered. The prosecution has to prove the entry was lawful.
DPP v Gaffney.law: Yes. Gaffney is still the leading case that a power of arrest doesn't carry a power to enter a home. Statute now provides specific entry powers.

src.t: Revised Acts — Criminal Law Act 1997, s.6
Revised Acts — Road Traffic Act 2010, s.7
Irish Legal News — Gardaí lacked reasonable grounds to force entry without warrant (Rozmyslowicz, 2018)

bg: Gardaí followed a speeding car and saw it turn into the driveway of the driver's home. The driver gave his name and the garda smelt alcohol.
When the garda said he was arresting him, the driver said the garda was a trespasser on private property and told him to leave. The garda took hold of his arm and arrested him anyway.
At the station he opted for a urine test but didn't provide a sample, and he was charged with failing to comply (s.13(3) Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 1978).
DPP v McCreesh.q: Could the garda lawfully arrest him on his own driveway after being told to leave?
dec: Supreme Court, 7 March 1991 (Hederman J; Griffin J agreeing with further remarks; McCarthy J): the arrest was unlawful.

Once the owner told the garda to leave, the garda was a trespasser. The drink-driving arrest power gave no authority to enter or stay on private property against the owner's will. A lawful arrest was an essential ingredient of the charge of failing to give a specimen, so the charge failed.

Griffin J pointed out that, under the law as it then stood, a driver who reached his own premises before the gardaí caught up couldn't be arrested there. England had changed its law to give an express power of entry, and that was a matter for the Oireachtas.

keys.q: cannot be exercised if a driver succeeds in reaching his own premises
keys.w: Griffin J, on the law as it then stood

later: DPP v Forbes [1994] distinguished it: where nobody has withdrawn permission, gardaí have implied authority to come onto a driveway to enforce the law.

The gap is now filled by s.7 of the Road Traffic Act 2010. Gardaí may enter without a warrant, with reasonable force if needed, any place including the curtilage of a dwelling, but not the dwelling itself, to arrest under ss.4(8), 5(10) or 6(4) or to make requirements under ss.9 and 10.
job: Under s.7 RTA 2010 you can now follow a suspected drink or drug driver onto a driveway or yard and arrest them there, even if you're told to leave, but not into the house.
If they get inside the dwelling, you need a separate lawful basis: consent, a warrant, another statutory power, or protection of life.
Record exactly where the arrest happened (public road, driveway, inside) and what was said about permission.
DPP v McCreesh.law: Overtaken by statute for road traffic arrests (s.7 RTA 2010), but still good law on trespass and implied permission generally.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v McCreesh [1992] 2 IR 239
Revised Acts — Road Traffic Act 2010, s.7 (power of entry)

bg: Late at night a motorist parked at a bridge in Ballymahon drove off when a patrol car approached. He turned up a side road and into the driveway of a private house, and stopped.
A garda followed on foot, caught him as he tried to run, smelt alcohol and arrested him under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 at 1.05 a.m. He didn't own or live in the house.
He was convicted in the District Court. On appeal the Circuit Court stated a case: was an arrest on private property he didn't own or occupy unlawful?
DPP v Forbes.q: Can gardaí go onto the driveway of a private house to arrest a suspected drink driver when nobody has given, or refused, permission?
dec: Supreme Court, 26 May 1993 (O'Flaherty J; Finlay CJ, Egan, Blayney and Denham JJ): the arrest was lawful.
A householder is taken to give gardaí implied authority to come onto the forecourt or driveway of the house to enforce the law or prevent a breach of it, so the gardaí weren't trespassers.
McCreesh was different because there the owner expressly withdrew permission. The implied authority doesn't extend into the dwelling itself.
later: The Law Reform Commission relied on Forbes for the distinction between the dwelling and its forecourt. In DPP v Delaney (High Court, 2003) a forced entry into a house to arrest a driver was unlawful, though an arrest on the curtilage would have been fine.
Now supplemented by s.7 of the Road Traffic Act 2010, an express power to enter the curtilage for drink- and drug-driving arrests, even against the owner's wishes.
job: You can generally go onto a driveway or forecourt to enforce the law. If you've been told to leave, rely on s.7 RTA 2010 for drink or drug driving, or on another power.
The front door, the hallway and everything inside are the dwelling. Implied authority stops at the door.
DPP v Forbes.law: Yes, for the implied-authority principle. Section 7 of the RTA 2010 now adds an express curtilage power for drink- and drug-driving.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Forbes [1994] 2 IR 542
Revised Acts — Road Traffic Act 2010, s.7 (power of entry)

bg: A sergeant and nine gardaí attended a disturbance where a crowd, some carrying sticks, was threatening to burn down a flat.
Through a window the sergeant saw five people barricaded inside and armed, and they told him not to come in. Two women said there were children inside.

Believing he could enter for the children's safety and the occupants' own protection, he went in with five gardaí. Four children were found unharmed upstairs. The five were arrested and charged with offences including provoking a breach of the peace, producing an article capable of causing serious injury, and assaulting a garda.

In the District Court the defence argued the entry was illegal and breached the occupiers' constitutional rights, and a case was stated. The High Court (Morris J) held that the entry could be justified if the gardaí could presume consent or there was a real danger to life.
DPP v Delaney.q: Can gardaí enter a dwelling without a warrant or consent to protect life? And does an unlawful entry or arrest defeat charges like assaulting a garda?
dec: Supreme Court, 27 November 1997 (O'Flaherty, Keane and Murphy JJ): appeal dismissed.
If the sergeant acted in good faith, believing entry was needed to safeguard life and limb, there was no breach of the Constitution. Protecting life outranks the inviolability of the home.
Whether an arrest was lawful matters only where a valid arrest is an essential element of the charge, as in drink-driving procedures. None of these charges required proof of a lawful arrest.
later: Current Garda guidance, including the guidance on missing persons, relies on Delaney as the basis for entering without a warrant to protect life.
Consistent with Shaw (1980): when constitutional rights conflict, the right to life prevails.
Rozmyslowicz [2018] IECA 289 is the contrast: a forced entry to look for a wanted man, without reasonable cause to believe he was there, was unlawful. The belief must be genuine and well grounded.
job: You may enter a home without a warrant or consent if you genuinely believe it's necessary to protect life or prevent serious injury. Record exactly what you saw, heard and were told, and why it couldn't wait.
Once the risk is dealt with, the justification ends. Don't search beyond what protecting life required.
Charges like assaulting a garda don't depend on the lawfulness of an arrest, but drink-driving procedures do. Get the arrest right.
DPP v Delaney.law: Yes. Delaney is still the authority for entering a home without a warrant to protect life and limb.
