bg: At about 12.45 a.m. a garda stopped a car. She noticed slurred speech and a strong smell of alcohol, and required a roadside breath test, which was positive.
She formed the opinion he was unfit to drive and, by her account, arrested him at 12.50 a.m. under s.49(8) of the Road Traffic Act 1961. A later blood test showed 235 mg per 100 ml.

The District Judge found that she never told him he was under arrest, or under what power, and dismissed the drink-driving charge. The DPP appealed by case stated, relying partly on Christie v Leachinsky: he must have known why.
DPP v McCormack.q: Is an arrest valid if the person is never told they're under arrest? And must the garda cite the statutory section?
dec: High Court, 8 July 1999 (McGuinness J): the dismissal was upheld.
Where the reason for the arrest is obvious to the person (here, a positive breath test and the garda's stated opinion), the garda needn't cite the section.

But the person must be told they're under arrest, meaning they're no longer at liberty. He was never told that, so the arrest was invalid, and everything that followed (the station procedure, the blood sample) was tainted.
later: Consistent with Christie v Leachinsky (1947), People v Walsh (1980) and DPP v Mooney (1992), where 'arrested for drunken driving' was enough.
A valid arrest is an essential step in drink-driving prosecutions, so the wording of the arrest is a common defence target (see Delaney (1997) on when a lawful arrest matters).
job: Say the words, e.g. 'I am arresting you under section … for …'. The fact of arrest must be clear, and give the reason in plain language.
Make the custody obvious (a hand on the arm, for instance), and record the exact words used and the time in your notebook.
If the person is drunk or confused, repeat it and record how they responded.
DPP v McCormack.law: Yes. McCormack is applied consistently: tell the person they're under arrest. Citing the section is optional if the reason is obvious.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v McCormack [1999] IEHC 13 (McGuinness J, 8 July 1999)

bg: On 21 September 2007, at about 10.30 p.m., a sergeant stopped a driver in Clonee after noticing erratic driving. The driver gave a roadside breath sample without objection, and it indicated alcohol over the limit.
He was arrested, handcuffed and taken to Blanchardstown Garda Station, where two breath specimens showed 71 micrograms per 100 ml.

Under cross-examination the sergeant accepted that the driver had been obliging, and that he had handcuffed him as a matter of personal policy, not because he thought it was necessary. The Circuit Court stated a case for the Supreme Court.
DPP v Cullen (2014).q: Does handcuffing a cooperative person under a blanket personal policy make the arrest and detention unlawful?
dec: Supreme Court, 18 February 2014 (Fennelly J, with Hardiman J; Clarke J dissenting in part).

A garda making an arrest may use only such force as is reasonable in the circumstances. Handcuffing can be justified, and gardaí have a generous margin of judgment, but handcuffing without any consideration of the person's behaviour and the circumstances is unlawful.
Here the driver hadn't resisted and was cordial and sensible, and the handcuffs were applied purely as a personal blanket policy, so the arrest was unlawful.
Clarke J disagreed in part. Unlawful handcuffing affects the manner of the arrest, not the arrest itself, so it needn't make the arrest or the custody unlawful.

keys.q: only use such force as is reasonable in the circumstances
keys.w: Fennelly J

keys.q: the manner of the arrest, not the arrest itself
keys.w: Clarke J (dissenting in part)

later: Pires, Corrigan and Gannon v DPP [2018] IESC 51 (Dunne J, five judges): a District Judge who acquitted three compliant drink drivers because the handcuffing wasn't objectively justified had misread Cullen. A garda may handcuff where they genuinely believe it's necessary, and Cullen allows considerable scope in judging that.
So the rule is a genuine assessment of the individual case: not a blanket policy, and not an after-the-event test of objective necessity.
job: Never handcuff 'as standard'. Decide each time, weighing behaviour, threats, intoxication, flight risk, size and numbers, the location, your own safety, and risks during transport.
Record your reasons for handcuffing, or for not handcuffing, in your notebook at the time. The court will look for a genuine individual assessment.
If the person is fully compliant and nothing suggests a risk, consider not handcuffing, or be ready to explain why you still judged it necessary.
DPP v Cullen (2014).law: Yes, as clarified by Pires (2018): handcuffing is lawful where the garda genuinely judges it necessary in the individual case.

AGSI — Gardaí have 'measure of latitude' when using handcuffs

bg: At a Garda checkpoint a driver gave an oral fluid (saliva) specimen for drug testing. Gardaí told him he might have to wait up to an hour for the result.

The result came in under 20 minutes and indicated cannabis. He was arrested, and a blood sample taken at the station showed cannabis and cocaine above the concentrations set in the schedule (s.4(1A) Road Traffic Act 2010).
The High Court (Simons J) held that the 2010 Act gave gardaí no power to make a driver wait at the checkpoint for the apparatus to finish, and declined to imply one.
DPP v O'Flaherty.q: Must a driver who gives a roadside drug specimen wait for the result? And does a garda need a separate power to hold them while it's processed?
dec: Supreme Court, November 2024 (O'Malley J): the DPP's appeal was allowed.

Read with the whole scheme of s.10 of the 2010 Act (checkpoints, and specimens without suspicion), using the apparatus 'for indicating the presence of drugs' means using it until it gives a result. The use isn't over until the result is available, so the requirement itself obliges the driver to wait. No separate implied power to detain was needed.
A positive roadside result has an obvious purpose: it grounds an arrest so that a blood sample can be taken at the station by a doctor or nurse for the concentration offence.
Telling the driver he might have to wait an hour was an error of law. Whether it made any difference, when the actual wait was under 20 minutes, was left to the District Court.

keys.q: for indicating the presence of drugs
keys.w: The statutory wording O'Malley J relied on

later: Section 13 of the Road Traffic Act 2024 has since amended the law on waiting for roadside drug-test results. Check the current wording of s.10 and its time limit.
Finn (2003) and Brehon (2019) apply a similar idea: procedures must be carried out with reasonable expedition, and unexplained delay is fatal.
job: Tell the driver they must stay until the result is available. Don't overstate the time ('an hour'); state the correct statutory position.
Record the time the specimen was taken, the time and content of the result, and the device ID.
On a positive result, arrest and bring them to the station promptly for the blood sample by a doctor or nurse.
DPP v O'Flaherty.law: Yes, and the 2024 Act amendment now deals with waiting expressly.

bg: A young Dublin man was charged with begging under s.3 of the Vagrancy (Ireland) Act 1847, which made it an offence to beg or gather alms in any public place, punishable by up to a month in prison. The Act dated from the Great Famine.
He challenged the section as unconstitutional.
Dillon v DPP.q: Can the State make all begging in any public place a criminal offence?
dec: High Court, 2007 (de Valera J): s.3 was unconstitutional, and the prosecution couldn't proceed.
A blanket ban on begging, in any public place and in all circumstances, interfered with the constitutional rights to freedom of expression and to communicate with others.
An argument that the section discriminated between rich and poor was rejected.
later: The Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 2011 replaced it with targeted measures: an offence of begging while harassing, intimidating, assaulting, threatening or obstructing people (s.2), a garda direction power (s.3), arrest powers, and offences of organising begging or living off its proceeds.
IHREC has argued that the State's response to begging should be services and supports rather than criminal law.
job: Begging itself isn't an offence. Act under the 2011 Act only where its conditions are met.

Under s.3 you may direct a person to stop begging and leave the area peaceably where you reasonably believe they're committing a s.2 offence or causing reasonable fear for safety, property or the peace. The power also applies where they're begging at or near a dwelling entrance, an ATM, a vending machine or a night safe; at a business entrance where you believe the public are being deterred; or in a private place.
You must clearly warn them that failing to comply is an offence. Record the warning word for word.
Watch for organised begging and exploitation, and consider trafficking indicators and safeguarding, especially where children are involved.
Dillon v DPP.law: Yes. Dillon struck down the 1847 offence. Begging is now regulated only by the targeted offences and powers in the 2011 Act.

bg: Gardaí found firearms and ammunition under a bed in a house in Dublin where the accused lived. He fled, surrendered about three months later, and was detained under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939.

During questioning, a detective inspector asked him, in effect, whether gardaí would have to go to his family to see whether one of them would take responsibility for what was found. Immediately afterwards he made a statement accepting responsibility.
The statement was the only evidence against him, and the Special Criminal Court convicted him of possessing firearms and ammunition.
People (DPP) v Hoey.q: Was a question that suggested his family would otherwise be pursued an inducement that made his statement involuntary? And whose view counts: what the garda meant, or how it came across?
dec: Supreme Court, 1987 (Walsh, Henchy, Griffin, Hederman and McCarthy JJ): the appeal was allowed and the conviction quashed.

The prosecution must prove that a statement was voluntary. The test is objective: was the question calculated to produce an admission through fear of prejudice or hope of advantage? What the questioner intended is irrelevant. What matters is the effect of the words.

The question conveyed that his family wouldn't be questioned if he admitted responsibility. In the circumstances that was an improper inducement that produced the confession, so the statement should not have been admitted.
later: Still the leading Irish authority on threats and inducements in interview. Read it with Shaw (1980) on voluntariness and fairness, and Lynch (1982) on oppression.
Interviews are now video-recorded, so the exact words used, and how they could have been understood, are there for the court to see.
job: Never suggest consequences for family, partners or friends depending on whether the suspect admits something, even as a 'genuine' question.
No promises or hints about bail, charges, sentence, release, or 'it'll go easier for you'.
If the suspect raises a deal or asks what will happen to family members, don't bargain. Explain that you can't make promises, and note the exchange.
Remember the test is how your words would come across to the suspect, not what you meant by them.
People (DPP) v Hoey.law: Yes. Hoey is still the leading authority on inducements: the test is objective, and the prosecution must prove voluntariness.

bg: In October 1996 a leather jacket was stolen from a shop in Balbriggan, Co. Dublin. The shop owner was the only identifying witness.

Days later, at Balbriggan District Court, a garda asked her to look around a courtroom holding about ten women, and she picked out the accused. No formal identification parade was held, and no reason was given for not holding one. At trial she identified the accused again in court.
The accused was convicted of larceny in the Circuit Criminal Court and sentenced to six weeks.
People (DPP) v Lee.q: Is an informal identification in a courtroom, without a formal parade, safe to rely on? And what must the judge tell the jury about it?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 20 July 2004 (Murray J, with Lavan and O'Caoimh JJ): conviction and sentence quashed as unsafe.

There were serious frailties in the informal identification. The accused had been a suspect from very soon after the offence, so this was a classic case in which a formal identification parade should have been held.

The judge's warning met the general minimum but wasn't adapted to the facts. He didn't mention that no parade was held, or the make-up of the women in the courtroom, about whom the prosecution had no evidence.
Defence counsel's failure to ask the judge to correct the charge didn't stop the Court quashing an unsafe conviction.

keys.q: a classic case in which a formal identification parade should have been held
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (Murray J)

later: Cited on informal identification in later cases, for example DPP v Mekonnen (2011).

Read with Casey (No 2) on the warning, and with Martin (1956): there's no absolute rule requiring a parade, but where there's a known suspect and a parade is practicable, leaving it out is very hard to defend.
job: If you have a suspect and a witness who might identify them, arrange a formal identification procedure. Don't set up informal 'have a look around' identifications.
If a formal parade isn't possible (the suspect refuses, or no suitable volunteers), record why, and what alternative was used.
Keep a record of the composition of any procedure: who stood in it, ages, appearance, clothing.
Avoid first identifications in court or in the street, and never point the suspect out to a witness.
People (DPP) v Lee.law: Yes. Lee is still cited for the rule that, with a known suspect, a formal identification procedure should be used, and that the warning must deal with any weaknesses.

bg: The applicant and a companion arrived at Manchester from Pakistan. The companion was found with heroin worth about £100,000. The applicant had none on him and was released.

Police later secretly installed a listening device in the house of a friend of the applicant, whom they suspected of dealing drugs. It recorded the applicant saying he had taken part in the importation. At the time no statute governed police use of such devices; only non-binding Home Office guidelines existed.

The trial judge admitted the recording, which was the only evidence. The applicant then pleaded guilty and was jailed for three years. The Court of Appeal and the House of Lords upheld the admission of the evidence.
Khan v United Kingdom.q: Is a trial unfair if it relies on a recording obtained by covert surveillance that breached the right to privacy?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 12 May 2000: violations of Articles 8 and 13, but not of Article 6.

Article 8: no domestic law regulated covert listening devices at the time, so the interference wasn't 'in accordance with the law'. The law must be clear enough to show when covert surveillance may be used.

Article 6 doesn't lay down rules on the admissibility of evidence; that is for national law. The question is whether the proceedings as a whole, including how the evidence was obtained, were fair. The applicant could challenge the recording at every level, the domestic courts could have excluded it if it made the trial unfair, the admissions were voluntary, and the recording's reliability wasn't in doubt.
Article 13: the police complaints system lacked independence, so there was no effective remedy for the privacy breach.

keys.q: sufficiently clear in its terms
keys.w: European Court of Human Rights, on the law that must govern covert surveillance

later: Followed in Allan v UK (2002), where a primed informant in custody made the trial unfair, and in Bykov v Russia (Grand Chamber, 2009), where a recording of a suspect at liberty did not.

In Ireland, covert surveillance devices now need authority under the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009: a District Court authorisation, or in urgency a superior officer's approval for up to 72 hours.
In Irish courts, admissibility is governed by JC (2015) for constitutional breaches and by O'Brien's discretion for other illegality.
job: Don't record anyone covertly without lawful authority. Get it under the 2009 Act, and follow the authorisation and its conditions to the letter.
Keep the original recordings, logs and continuity. Reliability is part of the fairness test.
Overheard remarks in public, or with consent, are different from planted devices, but if in doubt, take advice before relying on them.
Khan v United Kingdom.law: Yes. Khan is the leading Strasbourg case on surveillance evidence. A privacy breach doesn't automatically make a trial unfair, but the surveillance needs a clear legal basis.

bg: The Special Criminal Court convicted the accused of drug offences (importation and possession for sale or supply), and acquitted him of other charges before it.

The drugs case relied on three accomplices who had entered the State's Witness Protection Programme. The defence argued that the witnesses depended financially on the State and had tailored their evidence to please the authorities.

The Court of Criminal Appeal refused leave but certified two points of law: when evidence from protected witnesses is inadmissible or unfair, and what corroboration is needed for accomplices in the programme.
People (DPP) v Gilligan.q: Can a court convict on the evidence of accomplices in the Witness Protection Programme? And what safeguards apply?
dec: Supreme Court, 23 November 2005 (Denham J; McGuinness, Geoghegan, Fennelly and Macken JJ): appeal dismissed, unanimously.
The State is entitled to run a witness protection programme, which reflects the reality of gangs and drug trafficking, but the courts must ensure a fair trial.

Evidence from a protected witness who is an accomplice is treated as accomplice evidence. There's no rule that it must be rejected without corroboration, but the trier of fact must be warned that it is dangerous to convict on it without corroboration.
The Special Criminal Court had seen the witnesses, assessed their reliability and acted only on corroborated evidence. The ordinary admissibility rules applied, and it didn't err.

The Court endorsed the trial court's criticism of shortcomings in Garda handling, such as meetings with witnesses that weren't recorded. Those shortcomings compromised parts of the evidence but didn't undermine the whole process.

keys.q: no special rules of evidence apply
keys.w: Denham J, on evidence from protected witnesses

later: Still the current law on accomplice and protected-witness evidence: admissible, but with a corroboration warning, and examined with care.
Commentators argue for statutory regulation of the programme and fuller jury warnings about the benefits protected witnesses receive.
job: Record every contact with a cooperating or protected witness: meetings, calls, payments, benefits, promises asked for. Unrecorded meetings were criticised here.
Disclose all benefits and inducements through the proper channels. The defence will probe them, and they go to credibility.
Look for independent corroboration of everything an accomplice says, such as phone data, CCTV, financial records and seizures. The courts will want it.
People (DPP) v Gilligan.law: Yes. Gilligan is the leading authority that evidence from protected witnesses is treated as accomplice evidence: admissible, but with a corroboration warning.

Decisis — Does evidence from a witness in the witness protection programme abridge the rights of the accused?

bg: At about 12.30 a.m. on 14 November 1991 a garda on checkpoint duty on Cathal Brugha Street, Dublin, signalled a passing car to stop. Nothing suggests he suspected that driver of anything beforehand.

He smelt alcohol on the driver's breath and noticed slurred speech, and when the driver got out he was very unsteady. The garda arrested him for drunken driving (s.49(6) Road Traffic Acts), and a urine sample was over the limit.
The District Judge stated a case: can a garda with no suspicion of any offence stop a driver, and if so, is the evidence admissible? The High Court (Carney J) answered yes to both.
DPP (Stratford) v Fagan.q: Do gardaí have power to stop vehicles at random, with no suspicion of any offence by that driver?
dec: Supreme Court, 22 June 1994 (Finlay CJ, O'Flaherty, Egan, Blayney and Denham JJ): appeal dismissed. The stop was lawful and the evidence admissible.

Gardaí have a common-law power to stop vehicles to detect or prevent crime. Finlay CJ saw no logical difference between the stops already accepted and a road-check at a particular time and place aimed at finding drunk drivers.
Statutory stopping powers, such as the driver's duty under s.109 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 to stop when required, don't displace the common-law power.

The power must be used in good faith (bona fide). An arbitrary, capricious or improper use would be wholly illegal, and a stopped motorist may ask why they've been stopped. A night checkpoint near closing pubs is on its face aimed at detecting drink drivers. A general suspicion is enough; there need be no suspicion of the particular driver.

keys.q: a proper exercise of the common law duties
keys.w: Finlay CJ, on a road-check to detect drunk drivers

later: Mandatory alcohol and drug testing checkpoints are now statutory (s.10 Road Traffic Act 2010, rewritten in 2016). An inspector or higher must authorise them in writing, specifying the date, place and hours.
DPP v Gregory [2015] IEHC 706: one written authorisation can cover several checkpoints if each one is clearly identified.
DPP v O'Flaherty [2024] IESC 54: drivers at a checkpoint must wait for the result of a roadside drug test.
job: You can stop a vehicle without suspecting that driver of anything, but only for a genuine policing purpose such as detecting or preventing crime or road safety. Never for a personal or improper reason.
If the driver asks why they've been stopped, tell them.
For a MAT checkpoint (testing everyone), make sure there's a valid written authorisation from an inspector or above covering the place, date and hours, and that you're operating within it.
Note the reason for any stop, and what you then observed, in your notebook.
DPP (Stratford) v Fagan.law: Yes. Fagan is still the leading authority on the common-law power to stop vehicles in good faith. Mandatory testing checkpoints are statutory.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP (Stratford) v Fagan [1994] 3 IR 265

bg: The plaintiff was convicted in the District Court of loitering with intent to commit a felony as a 'suspected person', and of possessing housebreaking implements, under s.4 of the Vagrancy Act 1824 (extended to Ireland in 1871).

The offence allowed a 'suspected person or reputed thief' found frequenting certain places with intent to commit a felony to be convicted. He challenged it as unconstitutional, and the High Court (McWilliam J) found in his favour. The State appealed.
King v Attorney General.q: Is it constitutional to make it a crime for someone labelled a 'suspected person or reputed thief' to loiter with intent?
dec: Supreme Court, 1981 (O'Higgins CJ, Henchy, Griffin, Kenny and Parke JJ): the 'suspected person or reputed thief' loitering offence was unconstitutional, and the State's appeal was dismissed.

It was inconsistent with the right to a trial in due course of law (Article 38.1), liberty in accordance with law (Article 40.4.1), equality before the law (Article 40.1) and the State's duty to vindicate personal rights (Article 40.3). So it didn't survive the coming into force of the Constitution (Article 50.1).
The core problem was that its ingredients were so vague and arbitrary that ordinary lawful conduct could be made criminal at official discretion, and they were very hard for an accused to rebut.
O'Higgins CJ dissented on whether the Court should instead cut the offending words out of the section.
His convictions were declared invalid.
later: Still the leading authority on unconstitutionally vague offences. In Tallon v DPP (Court of Appeal, 2023) the same legal-certainty principle was applied to an individual civil order.
Street offences are now found in specific statutes, such as the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 (e.g. s.8 failure to comply with a garda direction; s.13 trespass).
job: There's no offence of being a 'suspected person'. Act on specific conduct and specific powers, such as s.8 Public Order Act directions, s.13 trespass, possession of articles, or attempts.
When you use a direction power, say clearly what the person must do and that failing to comply is an offence, and record your words.
Write down the specific behaviour that grounded your action, not the person's reputation or record.
King v Attorney General.law: Yes. King is still the leading Irish case that criminal offences must be clear enough for people to know what's forbidden.

Law Reform Commission — Report on Vagrancy and Related Matters

bg: Between June and August 2020 a street preacher spoke publicly, often amplified, in Wexford town. Gardaí treated it as anti-social behaviour and gave him five behaviour warnings.

On 31 August 2020 the District Court made a civil order under s.115 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006. It banned him from public speaking and recording anywhere in Wexford town and its environs, at any time, for two years.

On 7 October 2020 he was arrested for breaching the order after singing through a loudspeaker. The arresting garda accepted the singing wasn't anti-social or abusive. He was convicted of breaching the order (and of public order offences over signs) and sentenced to eight months' imprisonment.
Tallon v DPP.q: Can a behaviour order backed by criminal penalties ban public speaking across a whole town? And how precise must such an order be?
dec: High Court, 31 May 2022 (Phelan J): the order and the breach convictions were quashed. The ban was overly broad and impermissibly vague, went beyond conduct shown to be anti-social, and was a disproportionate interference with freedom of expression.
Court of Appeal, 25 May 2023 (Edwards, McCarthy and Donnelly JJ): the State's and the DPP's appeals were dismissed.

An order that creates criminal liability for one individual must be strictly construed, with any ambiguity resolved in that person's favour. This order was unclear about the boundaries of the area, whether speech indoors was covered, what 'public speaking' meant, what 'recording' covered, and whether broadcasting on social media was included.

He didn't have to risk arrest by breaching the order, or seek a variation, before challenging it. Civil orders under the 2006 Act aren't automatically stayed, and the State is responsible for keeping them within jurisdiction.

keys.q: overly broad and impermissibly vague
keys.w: Phelan J (High Court), on the order

later: Applies the legal-certainty principle from King v Attorney General (1981) to individual orders.
The Court of Appeal didn't decide whether s.115 itself is constitutional; it was presumed to be.
job: When gathering evidence for a behaviour order, record specific anti-social conduct: dates, times, what was said or done, and its effect on others. Don't just record that the person is a nuisance.
Behaviour warnings must describe the conduct and what's required. Keep copies.
Before arresting for a breach, read the exact terms of the order. If the conduct isn't clearly covered, don't stretch it.
Preaching, protest and street speech are protected. Act on noise, obstruction, threats or harassment under specific powers.
Tallon v DPP.law: Yes. Tallon (Court of Appeal, 2023) is good law: civil orders backed by criminal penalties must be precise and proportionate.

src.t: Columbia Global Freedom of Expression — Tallon v DPP
Court of Appeal judgment — Tallon v DPP [2023] IECA 125

bg: On 3 August 1986 a peace commissioner issued a search warrant under s.26 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 for a house in Tallaght. The garda's sworn information was about suspected cannabis cultivation, and the warrant authorised a search for controlled drugs.

The applicant was visiting the house during the search. Heroin was found, and he had plastic bags in his pocket. He was arrested, charged and sent for trial, and he applied to the High Court to quash the warrant.
Byrne v Grey.q: Is a s.26 warrant valid if the issuer simply relies on the garda's sworn belief, without being satisfied personally that reasonable grounds exist?
dec: High Court, 9 October 1987 (Hamilton P).

Section 26(1) requires the issuer to be satisfied, on the information given on oath, that there are reasonable grounds for suspicion. It isn't enough that the garda swears he has reasonable grounds: the issuer must be satisfied. The peace commissioner wasn't shown to have been, so the warrant was issued without jurisdiction.
But the court refused to quash it. The warrant had been executed and was spent, and whether the evidence was admissible was a matter for the trial court.
Challenges to s.26 under Article 40.5 (the dwelling) and Article 34 (the administration of justice) failed. Signing a warrant wasn't administering justice.

keys.q: is satisfied by information on oath
keys.w: s.26(1) Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 — the condition the issuer must meet

later: Its reasoning underpinned the invalid warrant in People (DPP) v Kenny (1990), where the evidence was excluded.
Damache (2012) added that the issuer must also be independent of the investigation.
Statutes and warrant forms now expect the grounds to be set out in the information so that the issuing judge can assess them.
job: In your information, set out the facts behind your suspicion, not just 'I have reasonable grounds'. The judge must be able to assess them independently.
Make sure the information and the warrant match: the offence, the drugs and the premises.
Expect questions from the judge, answer them on oath, and note what was asked.
Byrne v Grey.law: Yes. Byrne v Grey is still routinely cited: the person issuing a warrant must personally be satisfied on the sworn information.

src.t: vLex Ireland — Byrne v Grey [1988] IR 31
Revised Acts — Misuse of Drugs Act 1977, s.26

bg: On 20 August 2022 the accused was arrested at a mandatory checkpoint after failing to provide a breath specimen. At 12.37 a.m. a blood sample was taken at a garda station and divided into two sealed, numbered containers.
One container was given to him. The other was posted to the Medical Bureau of Road Safety (MBRS) on 22 August, and on 29 August the MBRS issued a certificate showing 126 mg per 100 ml.

He was convicted in the District Court. His defence argued the result was inadmissible because there was no evidence of how the specimen was stored between sealing and posting. On 31 July 2025 the High Court (Phelan J) agreed: the statutory presumptions didn't cover that gap, so chain of custody had to be proved, and she quashed the conviction.
Ratinskis v DPP.q: Must the prosecution prove an unbroken chain of custody for a blood specimen, including where it was kept before posting, for the MBRS certificate to be admissible?
dec: Supreme Court, 11 June 2026: the High Court was reversed. Because of its importance to prosecutions nationally, the case went straight to the Supreme Court, bypassing the Court of Appeal.
The real evidence in the case is the certificate of analysis, not the specimen itself.
No general rule of criminal evidence requires absolute proof of chain of custody, so a gap doesn't automatically make the certificate inadmissible.
The prosecution doesn't have to rule out every hypothetical possibility of interference with the specimen. The Road Traffic Act 2010 doesn't require that.

keys.q: does not necessarily render the certificate inadmissible
keys.w: Supreme Court, on a gap in chain of custody (as reported in the Law Society Gazette)

later: The ruling ended months of adjourned drink- and drug-driving prosecutions around the country, many of which involved specimens sent by post from outside Dublin.
job: Even though a perfect chain of custody isn't required, keep one anyway. Record who sealed the containers, the numbers, where the specimen was kept and by whom, and when and how it was posted.
Give the driver their container and record that you did.
Post specimens promptly and keep the proof of posting.
A good record makes any defence point about interference easy to answer.
Ratinskis v DPP.law: Yes. Ratinskis (Supreme Court, June 2026) is now the leading authority: the MBRS certificate is the evidence, and no absolute chain-of-custody proof is required.

src.t: Law Society Gazette — Supreme Court ruling ends drink-driving doubts (July 2026)
RTÉ News — Ruling that cast doubt on drink-driving cases overturned (11 June 2026)

bg: Shortly before 4 a.m. on 10 May 2020 a garda patrol followed a car being driven erratically. The garda smelt alcohol on the driver's breath and noticed slurred speech. After caution, the driver admitted drinking earlier that evening.
He failed a roadside breath test and was arrested under s.4(8) of the Road Traffic Act 2010. Evidential samples later read 63 micrograms per 100 ml.

The garda said that before the roadside test he had only formed the view that the driver had taken an intoxicant, and that he understood a 'Fail' showed alcohol was present but not how much. The District Judge held the required opinion couldn't have been formed, so the arrest wasn't shown to be lawful, and she stated a case.
DPP v Flanagan.q: Is an arrest for drink driving unlawful because the garda misunderstood what a roadside 'Fail' result shows?
dec: High Court, November 2023 (Phelan J): the arrest was lawful, and the case went back for the prosecution to proceed.
The threshold for forming the opinion needed to arrest is low. Under DPP v McGovern [2019] IECA 293, a 'Fail' result alone can ground a reasonable opinion.
Here the 'Fail' was backed up by erratic driving, slurred speech and an admission of drinking, which was stronger than in McGovern.

The District Judge's doubt came from her own view of what the device shows, which wasn't in evidence. The garda's misunderstanding didn't make his opinion unreasonable, and with no challenge to his good faith she couldn't find that the opinion was one that couldn't reasonably be formed.
later: Applies DPP v McGovern [2019] IECA 293 and is current law on the 'opinion' needed for a drink-driving arrest.
job: Record every indicator before arrest: the driving, smell, speech, eyes, balance, admissions, and the roadside result.
In evidence, say plainly that you formed the opinion the person had committed the offence (under s.4 or s.5), and give the grounds.
Don't speculate in the box about what the device does or doesn't measure. Stick to what you observed and the result displayed.
DPP v Flanagan.law: Yes. Flanagan (2023) is current: the threshold for the opinion is low, and a 'Fail' with other indicators is ample.

src.t: Irish Legal News — Garda opinion reasonably formed despite misunderstanding breathalyser result (Nov 2023)

bg: On 7 May 2021 a driver was stopped at a checkpoint with no visible tax or insurance disc. Gardaí noticed a strong smell of cannabis and found cannabis in the car. Based on his demeanour and the smell, they formed the view that he was under the influence of an intoxicant, and a roadside saliva test (s.9A) was positive.

The garda told him he was suspected of being under the influence to the extent of being incapable of proper control (a s.4(1) offence), and arrested him. A blood sample taken under s.13B confirmed cannabis.

He was prosecuted for the separate offence of having a specified drug in his blood above the set level (s.4(1A)). The Circuit Court held that the garda's evidence couldn't have excluded s.4(1A), and convicted him.
McGuinness v DPP.q: Can a garda's opinion about one drug-driving offence (impairment) stand in for the opinion the law requires before taking blood for the separate concentration offence?
dec: High Court, May 2024 (Bolger J): the conviction was quashed.
Section 4(1A), added in 2016, is a distinct offence based on the concentration of a drug in the blood within three hours of driving. It isn't a sub-part of s.4(1).

Section 13B allows a blood sample to be required only where the garda is of the opinion that a s.4(1A) or s.5(1A) offence has been committed. That is mandatory, and because the power is penal and significant it must be strictly construed.

The question is whether the garda actually formed that opinion, not whether they could have. It can't be inferred from an opinion about a different offence, so the garda had no power to require the blood sample.
later: Read with Flanagan (2023): the threshold for an opinion is low, but it must be the right opinion for the offence and the power you are using.
job: Know which drug-driving offence you suspect: impairment (s.4(1)/5(1)) or concentration (s.4(1A)/5(1A)). They're different.
Before requiring blood under s.13B, form and record the opinion that a s.4(1A) or s.5(1A) offence has been committed, and say so in evidence.
If you suspect both, record both opinions and the grounds for each.
McGuinness v DPP.law: Yes. McGuinness (2024) is current High Court authority. Where a power depends on a specific opinion, it must actually be formed, and it can't be implied.

src.t: Irish Legal News — Drug driving conviction quashed following misinterpretation of Road Traffic Act 2010 (May 2024)

bg: A driver was charged with drink driving after being stopped at a Mandatory Alcohol Testing (MAT) checkpoint in the Bray area.

The inspector's written authorisation covered checkpoints at 14 locations over seven days (24 to 30 March 2014), at set 45-minute intervals. One 'location' was a stretch of road over a kilometre long.
The District Judge referred two questions: can one written authorisation cover several times and places, and can a road over a kilometre long be a 'location'?
DPP v Gregory.q: Is a single MAT authorisation covering many checkpoints over a week valid? And how specific must a 'location' be?
dec: High Court, November 2015 (Barrett J).

Under the Interpretation Act 2005 the singular includes the plural, so one written authorisation can cover several checkpoints, provided each is clearly identified in writing by place, date and time. This one wasn't a free-wheeling authority, because it specified the dates, locations and intervals.

A road over a kilometre long isn't necessarily too large to be a 'location', and gardaí get some latitude in choosing suitable sites. Whether this road was specific enough was for the District Judge to decide.

keys.q: free-wheeling
keys.w: High Court, describing what a valid authorisation must not be

later: Section 10 of the Road Traffic Act 2010 was rewritten in 2016, but a written authorisation from an inspector or above, specifying date, location and hours, is still required.
Fagan (1994) is the common-law basis for non-MAT stops.
job: Before you operate a MAT checkpoint, see the written authorisation and check that your place, date and time fall within it.
Set up at the specified location, not 'nearby', and record the time you started and finished.
Keep a copy of the authorisation with the case file, because it will be proved in court.
DPP v Gregory.law: Yes. Gregory is still good law on MAT authorisations under s.10 (as rewritten in 2016).

src.t: Irish Legal News — Authorisation of drink-driving checkpoints at multiple locations held legal (Nov 2015)
vLex Ireland — DPP (Garda Hegarty) v Gregory

bg: Gardaí were called to a disturbance at a flat. They found a man who was agitated, a broken window, and knives lying about.

After he spat at a garda at the door, they went in without a warrant or consent and arrested him for breach of the peace. He resisted, and the District Court convicted him of obstructing a peace officer (and of assault), holding that gardaí had a common-law power to enter a home to arrest for a breach of the peace.
A case was stated to the High Court.
DPP v O'Brien (2021).q: Does the common-law power to arrest for a breach of the peace include a power to enter a dwelling to make that arrest?
dec: High Court ([2020] IEHC 110): gardaí did not have a common-law power to enter his dwelling to arrest him for breach of the peace, and the District Judge was wrong to find a case to answer on the obstruction charge.
No attempt was made to justify the entry under s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997.

Apart from cases where life is in imminent danger, the only restrictions on the constitutional inviolability of the dwelling (Article 40.5) are those set out in statute. Entry is lawful with consent, or where the situation demands it, such as a real risk to life and limb (Delaney).
Court of Appeal ([2021] IECA 290): the DPP's appeal was dismissed. Because the entry was unlawful, the obstruction conviction couldn't stand.

keys.q: did not enjoy a common law power to enter the dwelling
keys.w: High Court, on arrest for breach of the peace

later: Continues the line from Gaffney (1987): a power of arrest isn't a power of entry.
Read with Delaney (1997), which allows entry to protect life and limb, and with s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997, which allows entry for arrestable offences on conditions.
job: Breach of the peace at someone's door isn't, on its own, a power to go in. Arrest outside, get consent, or identify another power.
If there's a genuine risk to life or limb inside (weapons, threats, someone injured or in danger), you can enter to protect life. Record exactly what you saw and heard, and why it couldn't wait.

If the person has committed an arrestable offence (e.g. assault causing harm, criminal damage), consider s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997 and its conditions, such as having seen the person in or entering the dwelling.
Obstruction and resisting charges depend on you acting lawfully, so get the entry right first.
DPP v O'Brien (2021).law: Yes. The Court of Appeal (2021) confirmed that there is no common-law power to enter a home to arrest for breach of the peace; entry needs consent, a statute, or an emergency involving life and limb.

src.t: Decisis — gardaí did not enjoy common law power to enter the dwelling to arrest for breach of the peace
Revised Acts — Criminal Law Act 1997, s.6

bg: A driver was arrested for drink driving and brought to Blanchardstown Garda Station on 9 June 2007. His notice of rights was read to him.

Shortly after the garda required two breath specimens, he asked to speak to his solicitor. She refused, believing that stopping the procedure midway would prevent her from making the requirement again. The State later conceded she was wrong about that.

He was charged with refusing to provide the specimens. The District Judge found an immediate request for a solicitor had been refused because of that mistaken belief, held his right of reasonable access had been breached, and dismissed the charge.
DPP v McCrea (2010).q: Does the right of reasonable access to a solicitor apply in a drink-driving detention at the station? And what happens if it's refused because of a garda's mistake about the law?
dec: Supreme Court, 9 December 2010 (Hardiman J; Murray CJ, Fennelly, Macken and Finnegan JJ): the DPP's appeal was dismissed.

The right of a person in custody to consult a solicitor is constitutional in nature, and it applies in road traffic detentions too. He had been told on arrival, as the regulations require, that he could consult a solicitor at any time.
Refusing any access because of a mistaken view of the law was a denial of reasonable access. On the facts she found, the District Judge was entitled to dismiss the charge.

keys.q: a right of a constitutional nature
keys.w: Supreme Court, on consulting a solicitor in custody

later: Applies Healy (1990) to drink-driving detentions. Note the tension with the time-sensitive nature of breath testing: the right is to reasonable access, which doesn't necessarily mean waiting indefinitely, but an outright refusal based on a mistake is fatal.
Commentators read McCrea as protecting real evidence obtained through statutory procedures, not just admissions.
job: If a drink-driving detainee asks for a solicitor, don't refuse. Facilitate a prompt phone consultation, and record the request, the call and the times.
Making a breath requirement and then pausing for a short consultation is lawful. Don't refuse access on the belief that you'd lose the ability to repeat the requirement.
If the solicitor can't be reached quickly, record your genuine attempts. The right is to reasonable access, not to an indefinite delay.
DPP v McCrea (2010).law: Yes. McCrea is still the authority that the right to consult a solicitor applies in road traffic detentions, and that refusing it outright can defeat the prosecution.

bg: On 2 February 2019 a driver was involved in a single-vehicle collision in Co. Wicklow. In the ambulance he agreed to give a breath sample but didn't provide one.

He was taken to St Vincent's Hospital, Dublin. The garda cautioned him but didn't arrest him. She got permission for a blood sample from a doctor she believed was the 'doctor in charge', but in cross-examination she couldn't say whether that doctor was treating him or had any role in his care.
The sample showed 203 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood, and he was convicted in the District Court. A case was stated to the High Court.
DPP v Cullen (2021).q: When a driver is in hospital, whose permission does the garda need before requiring a blood specimen?
dec: High Court, March 2021 (Simons J): the conviction was reversed.

Section 14 of the Road Traffic Act 2010 requires permission from the doctor treating the person. That means a doctor who has had actual involvement in the patient's treatment and care, not any senior or available doctor, and not a 'doctor in charge' with no role in that patient's care.
As no treating doctor was consulted, the specimen wasn't lawfully obtained and was inadmissible.

keys.q: a doctor treating the person
keys.w: s.14 Road Traffic Act 2010 — the doctor whose permission is needed

later: Current High Court law on hospital blood specimens.
It sits with the Road Traffic Act's strict approach to statutory procedures in drink and drug driving (e.g. Hodgins, 2024, on signing order).
job: In hospital, identify the doctor actually treating the driver (name, role, what they're doing for the patient) and ask that doctor's permission. Record it.
If the treating doctor refuses because of the patient's condition, record that and the reason.
Don't rely on a 'doctor in charge' of the department who has no involvement in the patient's care.
DPP v Cullen (2021).law: Yes. Cullen (2021) is current: permission must come from a doctor actually involved in treating the person.

bg: In a rape investigation a foreign national was questioned twice with an interpreter. Both interviews were video-recorded and written down.

As the first interview was ending, a solicitor arrived and he said he wanted to see the solicitor. Gardaí asked one more question, read the record back with translation, let him make one change and got his signature, all before he was allowed to see the solicitor. No explanation was given for the delay.
The trial judge excluded the second interview entirely but admitted the first. He was convicted in the Central Criminal Court, and the Court of Criminal Appeal certified a point of law.
People (DPP) v A.D..q: If the right of access to a solicitor is deliberately breached part-way through an interview, must everything said in that interview be excluded, including what was said before the breach?
dec: Supreme Court, 24 May 2012 (Clarke J; Denham CJ, Hardiman, Fennelly and McKechnie JJ): appeal dismissed.
The custody became unlawful from the moment of the conscious and deliberate breach, so what came after was affected.
But automatically excluding everything said earlier, while he was lawfully in custody, would be an excessive exclusionary rule, not justified by any need to deter improper police conduct.
The earlier part is excluded only if there's a sufficient connection (nexus) between the lawful and unlawful parts to taint it.

keys.q: sufficient nexus
keys.w: Clarke J — what must link the lawful and unlawful parts before both are excluded

later: Read with O'Brien (2005): a denial of access makes the detention unlawful while it lasts, and later statements are judged on whether they're causally linked to it.
Since Gormley (2014), questioning should stop as soon as advice is requested. In A.D. even one more question and a read-back were enough to create a breach.
job: The moment a detainee asks for a solicitor, or one arrives and the detainee wants to see them, stop. No 'one more question', and no reading back and signing first.
Let them consult, then resume. Read back and sign afterwards if needed.
Record the time of the request or arrival, and when the consultation began.
People (DPP) v A.D..law: Yes. A.D. is still the authority that a deliberate breach taints the custody from that point on, and earlier statements are excluded only if they are sufficiently connected to it.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v A.D. [2012] IESC 33

bg: In 2010 a man was shot dead in north Dublin by a lone gunman, who dropped several items as he fled. A revolver, gloves, a baseball cap and a hoodie were later found nearby.

The accused was arrested on suspicion of murder and refused to give a bodily sample. Gardaí instead collected cigarette butts he discarded while in custody. His DNA from them matched DNA on the gun, a glove, the cap and the hoodie.

Gardaí had a statutory power to take a mouth swab without consent but apparently weren't aware of it. There was no other evidence linking him to the killing. He was convicted of murder, and the Court of Criminal Appeal certified a point of law.
People (DPP) v Wilson (2017).q: Did collecting DNA from items a detainee discarded in custody breach his right to privacy? And can DNA alone prove identity beyond reasonable doubt without a special jury warning?
dec: Supreme Court, July 2017 (joint judgment of Clarke, Dunne and O'Malley JJ): appeal dismissed.

The right to privacy covers the intimate information in DNA, but it isn't absolute and can be outweighed by the public good. A person at liberty couldn't complain about items he threw away being collected, and the same procedure can't breach the rights of a detained person.
Not using force to take a statutory sample didn't make collecting the discarded items unlawful.

DNA evidence can be robust enough on its own. The theoretical chance of two unconnected people sharing a profile was acknowledged, but the items were quickly secured, with no sign of contamination or degradation.
No special warning is required where identity rests only on DNA profiling, though the Court gave general guidance on how judges might direct juries in such cases.

keys.q: the man's right to privacy had not been breached
keys.w: Supreme Court (as reported by Irish Legal News)

later: Sampling of detained persons is now governed by the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014. Use its powers rather than workarounds where they apply.
Read with Boyce (2008) on consent samples and McDonald (2022) on consent after a phone consultation with a solicitor.
job: Items a detainee voluntarily discards (cups, cigarette ends, tissues) can be lawfully collected. Seize them properly, with gloves, bagging, labelling and continuity.
Know your statutory sampling powers under the 2014 Act. If the person refuses, use the proper procedure rather than relying on luck.
Secure scene exhibits quickly and document their packaging and storage. Contamination arguments are the main attack on DNA.
People (DPP) v Wilson (2017).law: Yes. Wilson is still the authority on DNA from discarded items, and on DNA being sufficient on its own without a mandatory warning.

bg: While lawfully detained under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, a man gave gardaí blood samples voluntarily. DNA from them was used to convict him of sexual offences including rape.
Gardaí didn't use the procedures in the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence) Act 1990. They relied on a common-law power to take a sample with consent.
The Court of Criminal Appeal certified the question: can a garda take a blood sample from a detained person who voluntarily agrees, without using the 1990 Act?
People (DPP) v Boyce.q: Could gardaí take a blood sample from a detainee with his consent, outside the statutory scheme?
dec: Supreme Court, 18 November 2008 (Denham J giving the lead judgment; Finnegan J concurring; Fennelly J dissenting): appeal dismissed.
Section 2(11) of the 1990 Act said its powers were without prejudice to any other powers of gardaí. That preserved the existing common-law power to take a sample with free and voluntary consent.
Fennelly J would have held that the statutory procedures had to be followed, so the sample was unlawfully taken.

keys.q: without prejudice to any other powers
keys.w: s.2(11) of the 1990 Act — the words the majority relied on

later: Effectively superseded for detained persons. Section 26 of the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014 bars gardaí from taking forensic samples from a detained person except in accordance with that Act.
DPP v McDonald [2022] IESC 29 later upheld a consent sample from a detainee who had had a short phone consultation with his solicitor.
job: For detained persons, take samples under the 2014 Act and follow its procedures, rather than relying on 'consent' outside it.
Where consent is part of the procedure, make sure it's genuinely free and informed, that the person has had the chance of legal advice, and that it's recorded in writing.
People (DPP) v Boyce.law: Largely overtaken by the 2014 Act for detained persons. Boyce is still cited on consent and on how statutes preserve existing powers.

vLex Ireland — DPP v McDonald [2022] IESC 29

bg: A s.26 Misuse of Drugs Act warrant dated 11 November 1996 was signed by a peace commissioner. The words 'Judge of the District Court' were struck out and 'Peace Commissioner' written in. The form was headed 'The District Court' and didn't state the county she was appointed for.
She had in fact been properly appointed in 1981 for Dublin and the adjoining counties.

At the accused's trial for drugs offences in the Dublin Circuit Court in 1998, the judge held the warrant void, excluded much of the evidence and directed acquittals. The DPP referred the point of law to the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Edgeworth.q: Is a warrant void because it doesn't state the peace commissioner's area, or because it is headed 'The District Court'?
dec: Supreme Court, 29 March 2001 (Hardiman J; Keane CJ, Denham, Murphy and Murray JJ): neither defect invalidated the warrant.
Section 26 didn't require the peace commissioner's area to be stated on the face of the warrant.
The wrong heading was a mere error, not a breach of any statutory condition for issuing the warrant. The signatory was properly appointed and was the right person to apply to.
later: Mallon [2011] IECCA 29 discussed it, noting that the Edgeworth court hadn't been referred to Balfe, which was still binding, and set out the modern test: a mere error that doesn't mislead won't invalidate a warrant.
Contrast Byrne v Grey (1987) and Kenny (1990): defects in the issuer's satisfaction or jurisdiction are fatal, but clerical errors on the form usually aren't.
job: Use the correct, current warrant form, and check the issuer's details, title and area.
A clerical slip on the form is usually survivable. Defects in the grounds, the jurisdiction or the issuer's satisfaction are not.
If you notice a form error before executing the warrant, get it corrected.
People (DPP) v Edgeworth.law: Yes. Edgeworth is still good law on form errors in warrants, and is read with Mallon (2011).

bg: The accused was charged with taking a car without the owner's consent and with dangerous driving causing serious injury to his passenger, who later died.
The car was inspected on 13 June 2001 and reports were made. Gardaí then destroyed it on 25 July 2001.
He sought to stop the trial on the basis that, without the car, he couldn't get a fair trial. The High Court (Quirke J) refused.
Savage v DPP.q: Must a trial be stopped where gardaí destroyed a vehicle after it had been examined, so the defence can't inspect it?
dec: Supreme Court, 3 July 2008 (Denham J, with Hardiman and Fennelly JJ): appeal dismissed, and the trial could proceed.
The accused bears the onus of showing a real and serious risk that he can't get a fair trial.
Here the inspection reports were available and could be examined, and he could still raise the car's condition in his defence. He hadn't shown a real and serious risk of an unfair trial.
The Court added that it would be best practice for gardaí to notify an accused before destroying such a vehicle.

keys.q: real or serious risk
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the test for stopping a trial over missing evidence

later: Decided the same month as Ludlow v DPP [2008] IESC 54, where the trial was stopped because the tyres, the core of a technical case, were gone and photographs were no substitute.
Wall v DPP [2013] IESC 56 confirmed that stopping a trial is exceptional, and that the trial judge is the main safeguard.
job: Before destroying or releasing a vehicle or any bulky exhibit, notify the suspect or their solicitor in writing and give them a reasonable chance to inspect it.
Keep full examination reports, measurements and photographs. They're what saved this prosecution.
Record who authorised disposal, and when.
Savage v DPP.law: Yes. Savage is part of the 2008 line making it exceptional to stop a trial over missing evidence.

src.t: vLex Ireland — Savage v DPP [2008] IESC 39
vLex Ireland — Ludlow v DPP [2008] IESC 54

bg: In May 2017 a man was shot at a Dublin petrol station and survived a serious head injury. Witnesses and CCTV identified the accused as the gunman.

He was convicted of attempted murder by the Special Criminal Court. The prosecution relied partly on traffic and location data for a SIM card attributed to him, which phone companies had retained under s.3 of the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011.

The CJEU later held, in GD v Commissioner (2022), that general and indiscriminate retention of such data for fighting serious crime is contrary to EU law. A related appeal (McAreavey), involving a number that had contacted his, was heard with it.
People (DPP) v Smyth (2024).q: Does the JC test apply where evidence was obtained in breach of EU Charter rights, or does EU law require it to be excluded automatically?
dec: Supreme Court, June 2024 (seven judges; majority judgment of Collins J): appeal dismissed. The data had been properly admitted.
Admissibility is a matter for Irish law, subject to the EU principles of equivalence and effectiveness. EU law doesn't require automatic exclusion; the CJEU confirmed this in Prokuratuur.
The JC test applies to breaches of Charter rights. A less demanding test would give Charter rights a lower status than constitutional rights.
Accessing the data was a breach of privacy, but it wasn't deliberate or conscious. Gardaí relied on an Act on the statute book, and the breach arose from a later legal development.

The JC 'backstop' (evidence that could never be lawfully obtained) is narrow. It covers things like privileged material, or evidence obtained by oppression or torture, not ordinary data. The seriousness of the offence, the targeted access and the undisputed reliability of the data all weighed against exclusion.
An accused doesn't have to admit owning a phone in order to challenge the evidence about it. The burden stays on the DPP.
later: DPP v McAreavey [2024] IESC 23: the data was also admissible there, though that conviction was quashed on other grounds.
DPP v Dwyer [2024] IESC 39 followed Smyth.
Data retention and access are now governed by the Communications (Retention of Data) (Amendment) Act 2022, with court orders required.
job: Evidence obtained in good faith under the law as it stood will usually survive a later change in the law. Following current law and procedure is what protects it.
For phone data today, use the 2022 Act procedures (District Court orders). Don't rely on old practices.
Build attribution evidence linking a person to a phone (top-ups, contacts, location matches, the handset found on them). It's often what decides these cases.
People (DPP) v Smyth (2024).law: Yes. Smyth is the leading authority that JC governs evidence obtained in breach of EU Charter rights.

src.t: Irish Legal News — Supreme Court: appeal on admissibility of phone traffic and location data dismissed (June 2024)

bg: The accused was convicted of murder in 2015. The case relied partly on mobile phone traffic and location data retained and accessed under the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011.

He challenged the 2011 Act in civil proceedings. The High Court made a declaration in 2018, the Supreme Court referred questions to the CJEU, and the CJEU ruled in 2022 (GD v Commissioner) that the general retention regime breached EU law.
The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal against conviction in 2023, and he appealed to the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Dwyer (2024).q: After the CJEU ruling, should the phone data have been excluded at his trial?
dec: Supreme Court, July 2024 (Collins J, with a concurring judgment from Hogan J): appeal dismissed.
Evidence obtained in breach of the Constitution or the EU Charter isn't automatically excluded. Admissibility is decided under JC.
An absolute exclusionary rule would exact too high a price from the administration of justice.
In any event, the other evidence linking him to the phones was overwhelming and unanswerable, so even if the data had been inadmissible there was no miscarriage of justice, and the proviso applied.
Hogan J, who had dissented in Smyth, followed it as binding precedent.

keys.q: too high a price
keys.w: Collins J, on an absolute exclusionary rule

keys.q: overwhelming and unanswerable
keys.w: Collins J, on the other evidence linking him to the phones

later: Ends the long litigation over the 2011 Act's data in this case. Read with Smyth (2024) and GD v Commissioner (CJEU, 2022).
The 2022 Amendment Act now requires court orders for access to retained data.
job: Build independent evidence around any phone data, such as attribution, witnesses, CCTV and seized items, so the case doesn't stand or fall on one data source.
Use the current 2022 Act procedures for phone data.
People (DPP) v Dwyer (2024).law: Yes. Dwyer confirms that the JC test (not automatic exclusion) applies to data obtained under the invalid 2011 regime.

bg: In March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled (Quirke No 1) that seizing a family computer to search its digital contents was unlawful, because the District Court judge who issued the warrant hadn't been told devices would be seized and searched.
The Court then heard argument on what followed: should the computer evidence (internet searches used at the murder trial) have been excluded, and could the conviction stand?
People (DPP) v Quirke (No 2).q: Is digital evidence obtained without specific authority to search a computer admissible under JC, where the requirement was only established after the search?
dec: Supreme Court, 28 July 2023 (Charleton J; seven judges): conviction affirmed, with no retrial.
Applying JC, the warrant error was due to honest inadvertence. The trial judge had found no dishonesty, and the gardaí had followed the law as it then appeared.
The illegality came from a new legal development on digital privacy, declared in Quirke No 1, which post-dated the 2013 search. That is the kind of later legal development JC treats as excusing.

keys.q: due to honest inadvertence
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the warrant error

later: Cited in Smyth (2024) on applying JC.

Now that Quirke No 1 has settled the law, a failure to seek authority for a digital search would be much harder to call inadvertent. Poptoshev v DPP [2025] IESC 47 (in this app) shows the right way to draft the warrant.
job: After Quirke, there's no excuse for not telling the judge you intend to seize and search devices. Put it in the sworn information.
Honest mistakes about unsettled law are excused, but ignoring settled law won't be.
People (DPP) v Quirke (No 2).law: Yes. Quirke (No 2) is the leading example of applying JC to digital evidence.

src.t: Echo (Press Association) — Supreme Court dismisses Quirke's appeal over murder conviction (28 July 2023)

bg: Three men were arrested separately for drink-driving offences under the Road Traffic Act 2010 and handcuffed, although each was described as compliant and not aggressive.
Applying Cullen (2014), the District Judge held each arrest unlawful because the handcuffing hadn't been shown to be objectively reasonable, and acquitted all three.

The High Court (Barrett J, 2015) set out fourteen principles from Cullen and held the District Judge had erred. The Court of Appeal (Mahon J, 2016) said the test is subjective: did the garda genuinely judge handcuffs necessary?
Pires v DPP.q: Must handcuffing on arrest be objectively justified, or is a garda's genuine, good-faith judgment enough?
dec: Supreme Court, October 2018 (Dunne J; five judges): the appeals were dismissed, and the arrests were lawful.
The District Judge's approach seemed to fly in the face of the principles made clear in Cullen.
A garda may handcuff an arrested person where they genuinely believe it's necessary, and Cullen gives considerable scope in judging what's reasonable.
Cullen condemns only automatic handcuffing applied without any thought to the circumstances.

keys.q: genuinely believes that it is necessary to do so
keys.w: Dunne J, on when handcuffing is lawful

keys.q: considerable scope
keys.w: Dunne J, on the latitude Cullen gives gardaí

later: The current leading authority on handcuffing on arrest, explaining DPP v Cullen [2014] IESC 7.
job: Make a genuine decision every time. Consider behaviour, intoxication, threats, flight risk, transport and your own safety.
Note your reasons in your notebook. A recorded, genuine judgment is what the courts protect.
Never handcuff 'as standard'. That's still unlawful under Cullen.
Pires v DPP.law: Yes. Pires (2018) is the current leading authority: a garda's genuine judgment, made in good faith, justifies handcuffing.

bg: On 21 July 2005 four bombs were planted on the London transport system but failed to explode, and the bombers fled.

Three of the applicants were arrested on suspicion of detonating bombs. Police questioned them in urgent 'safety interviews' before they had access to a lawyer, under a legislative framework for such interviews. They were convicted of conspiracy to murder.

The fourth applicant was first interviewed as a witness. When it emerged that he had helped one of the bombers after the attack, he should have been cautioned and offered legal advice under the code of practice, but he wasn't. He went on to give a written statement and was later convicted of assisting the bomber and failing to disclose information.
Ibrahim and Others v United Kingdom.q: When can police delay a suspect's access to a lawyer? And when does that make the trial unfair?
dec: Grand Chamber, 13 September 2016: no violation for the first three applicants (15–2), and a violation for the fourth (11–6).

The first question is whether there were compelling reasons to restrict access. Restrictions are allowed only in exceptional circumstances, must be temporary, and must rest on an individual assessment of the particular case. An urgent need to avert serious harm to life, liberty or physical integrity can be a compelling reason.

The second question is whether the proceedings as a whole were fair. Without compelling reasons, the court applies very strict scrutiny and the government must show the trial was still fair. Relevant matters include whether the suspect was vulnerable, the legal framework and whether the restriction can be reviewed, whether the statements could be challenged, how reliable they were and how they were obtained, how central they were to the case, the other evidence, how the jury was directed, and the public interest.

For the first three, there was an urgent need to prevent further suicide attacks, the safety interviews followed a legal framework that the courts reviewed, the statements could be challenged, and there was significant other evidence.

For the fourth, there was no compelling reason and no legal basis for skipping the caution. He was misled about his fundamental procedural rights, the decision wasn't recorded or reviewable, and the government couldn't show the trial was fair.

keys.q: misled as to his fundamental procedural rights during questioning
keys.w: Grand Chamber, on the fourth applicant

keys.q: very strict scrutiny
keys.w: Grand Chamber, where there were no compelling reasons

later: Beuze v Belgium (Grand Chamber, 2018) applied the same overall-fairness approach and found a violation.
Doyle v Ireland (2019) applied it to Irish practice on solicitors in interviews: no compelling reasons, very strict scrutiny, but the trial was still fair.
In Irish law Gormley (2014) is stricter: questioning must wait for requested legal advice, except in wholly exceptional circumstances such as an imminent risk to life.
job: If a witness starts incriminating themselves, stop. Caution them, offer legal advice, and treat them as a suspect from then on.

Any decision to question before legal advice, which in Ireland is only for a wholly exceptional threat to life, must be recorded with the reasons, the authorising rank and the time, so it can be reviewed.
Keep 'safety' questions narrowly focused on the urgent risk (e.g. where is the device, who else is involved) and stop once that risk has been dealt with.
Ibrahim and Others v United Kingdom.law: Yes. Ibrahim sets the current Strasbourg two-stage test, and Irish practice under Gormley is at least as protective.

bg: After a felony, a Civic Guard asked two men he suspected of being involved to come to the barracks. They went voluntarily.
At the barracks they were questioned by the chief superintendent and held while inquiries continued, without being charged or brought before a peace commissioner. They later sued for damages.
Dunne v Clinton.q: Can the police hold suspects at a station for questioning, on the footing that they came voluntarily or are merely 'detained', without arresting and charging them?
dec: High Court of the Irish Free State, 28 May 1930 (Hanna J).

The Court condemned the practice of holding suspects at a barracks for inquiries under the label of voluntary attendance or 'detention'. A person held by the police against their will is, in law, under arrest.
Once someone is detained, they must be brought before a peace commissioner (now a judge) as soon as can reasonably be done. Detention can't be prolonged for another purpose, such as questioning.
later: The Supreme Court in People (DPP) v Walsh (1980) called it the leading authority on arrest at common law. Shaw (1980) relied on it for the duty to bring a detained person before a court as soon as reasonably possible.
Lynch (1982) and later cases attacked the same 'helping with inquiries' practice, which continued for decades afterwards.
Statutory detention for questioning now exists (s.4 Criminal Justice Act 1984; s.30 Offences Against the State Act 1939, and others). Outside those powers, Dunne v Clinton still applies.
Applied in Brehon v DPP (2019) on the time taken for road traffic procedures.
job: There's no halfway house. Either the person is free to go, and knows it, or they're under arrest, with all the safeguards that follow.
If you use a statutory detention power, follow its time limits. If not, charge or release with reasonable expedition.
With 'voluntary' attendees, say clearly that they can leave, and record that you did.
Dunne v Clinton.law: Yes. Dunne v Clinton is still foundational on arrest and detention at common law, alongside Walsh (1980) and Lynch (1982).

bg: A driver gave two breath specimens on an evidential breath-testing machine and was convicted of drink driving.

The machine-printed statements were signed in the wrong order: he signed first and the garda signed afterwards. Section 13 of the Road Traffic Act 2010 and the 2015 Regulations require the garda to sign first.
In DPP v Freeman (an ex tempore Supreme Court ruling of 25 March 2014), the same reversed order had made the statement inadmissible. The DPP asked the Supreme Court to overrule Freeman.
DPP v Hodgins.q: Does signing the breath statement in the wrong order make it inadmissible? And should Freeman be overruled?
dec: Supreme Court, July 2024 (O'Malley J): the appeal was dismissed and Freeman was not overruled.

The garda's signature is what makes the document admissible as proof of its contents. The garda certifies the identifying details and that the machine produced the statement after analysing the specimen. The driver signs only to acknowledge receipt, and the driver's duty to sign, enforced by an offence of refusing, only arises once the garda has signed.

O'Malley J accepted it was arguable that, where both did sign, the order shouldn't affect admissibility. But Freeman could be overruled only if it was 'clearly wrong' (the Mogul test), and on identical facts it wasn't, so the Court was bound by it.
Avadenei (2017) was distinguished. That case concerned a defective printed form (a missing Irish version), not a garda's error in the statutory procedure.
She described Freeman as being at the far end of the spectrum of insistence on the letter of the law, and said it shouldn't be extended by analogy to different facts or legislation.

keys.q: the far end of the spectrum of insistence on the letter
keys.w: O'Malley J, describing Freeman

later: The settled rule: the garda signs first, and a reversed signing order makes the s.13 statement inadmissible.
Contrast Avadenei (2017), where a defect in the form was saved by s.12 of the Interpretation Act 2005, and Ratinskis (2026), where no absolute chain of custody is required for blood specimens.
job: Follow the order every time: the statements print, you sign, then you offer them to the driver to sign and give them their copy.
If the driver refuses to sign after you've signed, record it. That's a separate offence, but only if you signed first.
Check the signatures before you hand anything over. A reversed order can't be fixed afterwards.
DPP v Hodgins.law: Yes. Hodgins (2024) confirms Freeman: the garda must sign the breath statement first, or it's inadmissible.

bg: A driver was arrested without a warrant under s.49(6) of the Road Traffic Act 1961. The garda told him he was being 'arrested for drunken driving' rather than citing the exact statutory offence under s.49(2) or (3).
The District Court dismissed the summons, and the DPP appealed by case stated.
DPP v Mooney.q: Does an arrest fail because the garda described the reason in everyday words ('drunken driving') rather than the precise statutory offence?
dec: High Court (Blayney J), reported [1992] 1 IR 548: the arrest wasn't invalidated by the reason being given as 'drunken driving'.
Applying Christie v Leachinsky and People v Walsh, no technical or precise language is needed when arresting someone. It's enough that the person understands why they're being arrested.
The court also doubted, without deciding, whether an arrest would be invalid where no reason at all was given but the circumstances (such as a positive roadside breath test) made the reason obvious.

keys.q: arrested for drunken driving
keys.w: The words used, held sufficient

later: Consistent with McCormack (1999): the section needn't be cited where the reason is obvious, but the fact of arrest must always be communicated.
Later cases cite Mooney for the point that the substance, not the form of words, is what counts when giving the reason for an arrest.
job: Plain words are fine ('for drink driving', 'for the theft of that phone'), as long as the person understands why.
Always make the fact of arrest itself clear (McCormack). The reason can be in ordinary language.
Record your exact words and the time in your notebook.
DPP v Mooney.law: Yes. Mooney is still good law: everyday language is enough when giving the reason for an arrest.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Mooney [1992] 1 IR 548

bg: On 20 February 2006 a garda on patrol in Clondalkin stopped a car carrying the accused. He said there was a drugs problem in the Neilstown area, and he searched the car under the Misuse of Drugs Act.
The accused gave his name and address and didn't object. The garda found a knife, and the accused was charged under s.9(1) of the Firearms and Offensive Weapons Act 1990.
The District Judge held that the area's drugs problem was enough to justify the search, convicted him and sentenced him to two months. A case was stated to the High Court.
DPP (Garda O'Higgins) v Farrell.q: Does a general drugs problem in an area give a garda reasonable cause to search a particular person under s.23 of the Misuse of Drugs Act? And must the person be told why they are being searched?
dec: High Court, 16 July 2009 (Clark J): the search was unlawful.
At common law gardaí may stop cars without specific suspicion to detect or prevent crime (Fagan). But without consent, that doesn't give a right to search.

A s.23 search requires reasonable cause to suspect that this particular person has a controlled drug. General knowledge of drug activity in the area can't stand in for suspicion about the individual, and that reasonable cause was missing here.
The person is entitled to be told the reason for the search, and there was no evidence he was. The garda doesn't have to cite the statutory section.

keys.q: Reasonable cause for suspecting that the accused was in possession
keys.w: High Court, on what s.23 requires (and what was missing)

later: Stop and search powers are being placed on a fuller statutory footing. The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 provides a power to stop and search on reasonable suspicion, with a formal record of every search.
Contrast DPP v O'Brien (2018) [2018] IECA 166, where there was specific suspicion (two men counting cash in a car) and detention for a s.23 search was upheld.
job: Before a s.23 search, be able to say what made you suspect this person: behaviour, a smell, items seen, intelligence about them, a hand-to-hand exchange. 'It's a drugs area' isn't enough.
Tell the person why you're searching them. You don't need to cite the section, but give the reason in plain words.
Record your grounds in your notebook at the time, and record what was found and where.
If you're relying on consent, make sure it's real, and record how it was given.
DPP (Garda O'Higgins) v Farrell.law: Yes. Farrell is still the authority that a s.23 search needs suspicion about the individual, not just the area.
