bg: Protesters at an Irish Water installation in Dún Laoghaire stood on the road in front of a truck, blocking it and forcing traffic into the other lane.

A sergeant gave them directions under s.8 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994. They were charged with obstruction (s.9), failing to comply with a direction (s.8), and a name-and-address offence (s.24).

The District Court dismissed the charges and stated a case. The High Court held there was inadequate evidence that each protester was acting without lawful authority or reasonable excuse for the obstruction charge, but that the sergeant's belief that an offence was being committed was reasonable. The matter went to the Court of Appeal.
DPP v Kelly (2018).q: What must a garda have in mind to give a valid s.8 direction? Must they first consider whether the protesters had a lawful authority or reasonable excuse?
dec: Court of Appeal, 2018 (Birmingham P).
A valid s.8 direction requires the garda to suspect, with reasonable cause, that the person is committing one of the offences listed in s.8, here obstruction under s.9.

The garda doesn't have to expressly address whether the person has lawful authority or a reasonable excuse before giving the direction. A reasonable suspicion that the listed offence is being committed is enough.
later: Read with Tallon (2023) and Dillon (2007) on expression and protest: act on obstruction, threats and disorder, not on the message.
Later protest cases (e.g. one involving an obstructed ambassador) turn on whether the obstruction was 'without lawful authority or reasonable excuse', which is a matter for proof at trial.
job: Before giving a s.8 direction, identify the listed offence you suspect (e.g. obstruction under s.9, or threatening behaviour) and the facts that make your suspicion reasonable.
Give the direction clearly: what to do (e.g. move to the footpath) and that failing to comply is an offence. Record your exact words.
Protest is lawful. Focus on obstruction of traffic or people, threats and breach of the peace, and record their effect.
DPP v Kelly (2018).law: Yes. Kelly is current Court of Appeal authority on the threshold for s.8 directions.

bg: A man wanted in Australia was arrested at about 2 p.m. on 25 October 1984 under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939, supposedly on suspicion of a firearms offence.

Shortly before, the Government had made an order applying Part II of the Extradition Act 1965 to Australia from that day. While he was in custody a provisional extradition warrant was issued, and after a High Court hearing he was arrested on it outside the Four Courts.

The High Court (Egan J) found the arresting garda couldn't have had a genuine suspicion of a firearms offence. The real object was to hold him until the extradition warrant was ready, a deliberate and conscious violation of his constitutional rights. Egan J held the later detention was tainted and ordered his release.
State (Trimbole) v Governor of Mountjoy.q: Can a power of arrest be used for a different purpose from the one it was given for, here to hold someone until extradition papers were ready? And can the State keep the benefit?
dec: Supreme Court, 26 March 1985: appeal dismissed, and his release was upheld.

Courts have an inherent jurisdiction and a positive duty to protect constitutional rights, to restore the person as far as possible, and to make sure that State agents who deliberately violate rights don't get the planned results of that invasion.
Courts also have a direct duty to prevent abuse of their own process, so the extradition detention that followed the abuse couldn't stand.

keys.q: deliberate and conscious violation of constitutional rights
keys.w: Egan J (High Court), on the s.30 arrest

later: Still cited on the misuse of arrest powers for ulterior purposes. Read with Quilligan (1986) and Howley (1989): a s.30 arrest must rest on a genuine suspicion of the scheduled offence, though other offences may also be investigated.
Under JC (2015) a knowing misuse of an arrest power is the clearest kind of deliberate and conscious breach.
job: Only use an arrest power for its proper purpose, on a genuine suspicion of that offence. Never use it as a holding device for something else (extradition, immigration, another inquiry).
If you need someone held for a different process, use the power designed for it, such as an extradition warrant, a European Arrest Warrant or an immigration power, and wait for it if necessary.
Record the genuine grounds for every arrest.
State (Trimbole) v Governor of Mountjoy.law: Yes. Trimbole is still the leading authority that misusing an arrest power for an ulterior purpose is a deliberate breach of rights, and the courts won't let the State benefit from it.

bg: The applicant was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of membership of an unlawful organisation. A chief superintendent extended his detention by 24 hours under s.30(3).
In May 2018 the Special Criminal Court convicted him of IRA membership and jailed him for four and a half years.

He challenged the s.30 extension regime. He argued it was unequal compared with the Criminal Justice Act 1984 (where the arresting officer must also form the view that detention is necessary), that only a judge or an uninvolved officer should be able to extend detention, and that Quilligan (No 3) [1993], which upheld s.30, should be revisited.
Braney v Special Criminal Court.q: Is s.30 detention, with extensions by a chief superintendent, constitutional when other detention regimes have different safeguards?
dec: Supreme Court, February 2021 (Charleton J for the Court): appeal dismissed, and s.30(3) upheld.
Every detention under any criminal statute carries a basic floor of rights. Above all, the garda must reasonably suspect the person of an arrestable offence, and that applies under the 1939 Act too.

The Oireachtas may legitimately treat terrorist and organised-crime offences differently from general offences. Different detention periods and procedures are constitutional provided the floor of rights is respected.
The search-warrant analogy (Damache) failed. A search is a one-off event that requires rights to be front-loaded, while detention is ongoing and needs a floor of rights, not identical procedures.
There was no sufficient basis to revisit Quilligan (No 3).

keys.q: floor of rights
keys.w: Charleton J, on what every detention regime must respect

keys.q: front-loading of rights
keys.w: Charleton J, on why search warrants are different

later: Confirms that the different statutory detention regimes (s.4 CJA 1984, s.30 OASA 1939, drug trafficking and serious-offence regimes) can coexist, each with its own time limits and authorisation rules.
job: Know which detention regime you're using and its rules: who may authorise an extension, on what grounds, and for how long.
Whatever the regime, the floor applies: a genuine, reasonable suspicion at arrest, the custody regulations, access to a solicitor, and recorded reasons for each extension.
Extensions must be in place before the current period expires. Record who authorised them, when, and why.
Braney v Special Criminal Court.law: Yes. Braney (2021) is the current Supreme Court authority upholding s.30 extensions.

bg: A body was found in a lake. Gardaí suspected the accused, and had questioned him about the death twice before; he denied involvement.

About two weeks later he was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of maiming cattle, a scheduled offence. During the first 24 hours he was questioned about the cattle and about the death.

A chief superintendent extended the detention by 24 hours without knowing that gardaí also wanted to question him about the death. Shortly after the first 24 hours, the accused made a statement admitting the killing, and he was convicted of murder in 1986.
People (DPP) v Howley.q: Is a s.30 arrest lawful if investigating the scheduled offence wasn't the main motive? And can gardaí question about other offences during s.30 detention?
dec: Supreme Court, 29 July 1988 (Walsh J, with Henchy and Griffin JJ): the appeal was dismissed.

The arrest was lawful because it rested on a genuine suspicion of a scheduled offence. The prosecution didn't have to prove that investigating the cattle maiming was the predominant or primary motive.

The extension was lawful too. The genuine suspicion still existed when it was authorised, and the chief superintendent's lack of knowledge about the murder inquiry didn't make the continued detention unlawful.
Questioning about other offences during a lawful detention wasn't in itself unlawful.
later: Follows Quilligan (1986). Contrast Trimbole (1985), where there was no genuine suspicion at all and the arrest was a device.
Questioning about other offences during s.30 detention is now governed by statute: s.30(3A), inserted in 2009, which the Supreme Court has applied strictly.
job: A s.30 arrest needs a genuine, reasonable suspicion of the scheduled offence you name. Record the grounds for that offence specifically.
If you intend to question about other offences, check the current rules in s.30(3A) first, and make sure the officer authorising an extension has full and accurate information.
Never use a minor scheduled offence as a pretext without a genuine suspicion of it (Trimbole).
People (DPP) v Howley.law: Partly. Howley's core point still stands: a genuine suspicion of the scheduled offence is required, but the motive needn't be the main one. Questioning about other offences is now regulated by s.30(3A).

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Howley [1989] ILRM 629

bg: A driver seen driving erratically in Drogheda was arrested at about 4 a.m. At the station the breath-testing apparatus was locked away and its key couldn't be found.
A doctor was called at 5.35 a.m. and said he'd be there in five minutes, but arrived at 6.30 a.m. The driver refused to give a blood or urine sample.

He was convicted in the Circuit Court of failing to provide a specimen and of dangerous driving, fined and disqualified for six years. He argued that the delay made his detention unlawful, and that everything after it had to be excluded.
Brassil v DPP.q: Does a delay at the station, here waiting for a doctor because the breath machine couldn't be used, make the detention unlawful?
dec: High Court, 3 July 2020 (Gearty J): judicial review was refused, mainly on procedural grounds (delay and deficiencies in the application). The substantive claim was described as extremely weak.
Court of Appeal, 2021 (Edwards, McCarthy and Donnelly JJ): the appeal was dismissed.

Any delay in a detention should be examined to see whether it's excessive. Only an excessive delay obliges the prosecution to justify it. Waiting under an hour for the doctor wasn't excessive, so the detention remained lawful.
later: Fits with Finn (2003), where an unexplained delay was fatal, and with Brehon (2019) and Stack (2016), where explained delays were fine. The three-hour window is a backstop, not a licence.
job: Check the evidential breath-testing apparatus and its key at the start of the shift, so you don't have to fall back on a doctor.
If you must call a doctor, record the call time, what you were told, and any follow-up calls, and keep the detainee's time in custody as short as possible.
Every gap in the custody timeline needs a reason you can give in evidence.
Brassil v DPP.law: Yes. Brassil (Court of Appeal, 2021) is current: only excessive delay has to be justified.

src.t: vLex Ireland — Brassil v DPP [2020] IEHC 328

bg: A driver failed a roadside breath test on a device that shows only 'Pass' or 'Fail'. The garda formed the opinion that he was drink driving based solely on that result, and arrested him. A later evidential breath test was over the limit.
The District Court dismissed the charge, holding that a 'Fail' alone couldn't ground the opinion needed for arrest.
DPP v McGovern.q: Is a 'Fail' on a roadside breath test, by itself, enough for a garda to form the opinion needed to arrest a driver for drink driving?
dec: High Court ([2018] IEHC 577), then Court of Appeal ([2019] IECA 293): the dismissal rested on an error of law.
A 'Fail' on the preliminary breath test is by itself a sufficient basis for the garda's opinion that the driver is committing an offence, and so for arrest under s.4(8) of the Road Traffic Act 2010.
Other signs of intoxication, such as smell, speech or driving, strengthen the opinion but aren't essential.
later: DPP v Flanagan [2023] IEHC 647 applied McGovern. The threshold for the opinion is low, and a 'Fail' plus other indicators is ample, even if the garda misunderstood what the device measures.
Contrast McGuinness (2024): where a power depends on an opinion about a specific offence (such as s.4(1A) for drugs), that particular opinion must actually be formed.
job: After a 'Fail', you can form the opinion and arrest. Still record any other indicators, because they make the opinion stronger.
In evidence, say clearly that you formed the opinion that the driver had committed the offence, and why.
DPP v McGovern.law: Yes. McGovern (Court of Appeal, 2019) is current: a roadside 'Fail' alone can ground the opinion for arrest.

src.t: Irish Legal News — Garda opinion reasonably formed despite misunderstanding breathalyser result (Flanagan, applying McGovern)

bg: Gardaí saw a man driving erratically and switched on their lights. He refused to stop, drove into his brother's yard and went into the house by the back door.
Without a warrant or permission, a garda forced entry, chased him through the kitchen, along the hall and up the stairs, and arrested him on the stairs under s.49(8) of the Road Traffic Act 1961.
The District Court stated a case: was the arrest lawful, and if not, must the prosecution fail?
DPP v Delaney (2003).q: Does 'hot pursuit' of a suspected drink driver let gardaí force entry into a house to arrest him?
dec: High Court, 27 January 2003 (Ó Caoimh J): the arrest was unlawful and the prosecution failed.
The prosecution relied on a common-law power of hot pursuit. The Court followed McCreesh: entering private property against the owner's will needs express statutory provision.

Following Forbes, and the curtilage entry power then in s.39(2) of the Road Traffic Act 1994, the gardaí could have arrested him on the curtilage of the house. But they had no power to enter the dwelling itself.
As the evidence flowed from the unlawful entry and arrest, it couldn't be admitted.

keys.q: express provision should have been made for such power
keys.w: Hederman J in McCreesh, relied on here

later: The curtilage power is now in s.7 of the Road Traffic Act 2010: entry without warrant, with reasonable force if needed, to any place including the curtilage of a dwelling, but not the dwelling itself.
Under JC (2015) the question of exclusion would now turn on whether the breach was knowing or inadvertent, but entering a home without any power remains a serious breach.
For arrestable offences (e.g. dangerous driving causing serious harm), s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997 may allow entry to a dwelling on conditions.
job: In a pursuit that ends at a house, arrest in the yard or driveway if you can. Section 7 RTA 2010 covers the curtilage.
Don't follow a drink-driving suspect into the house unless you have a separate lawful basis: consent, a warrant, s.6 CLA 1997 for an arrestable offence, or a genuine threat to life.
Record where exactly the arrest happened and how you got there.
DPP v Delaney (2003).law: Yes, in substance. Delaney (2003) is still a good illustration: the curtilage but not the dwelling, now under s.7 RTA 2010.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Delaney [2003] 1 IR 363 (High Court)
Revised Acts — Road Traffic Act 2010, s.7

bg: A driver was charged with drunken driving under s.49(2) of the Road Traffic Act 1961. The arresting garda meant to arrest him under s.49(8) but cited the wrong statute.

He had given a positive breath test. At the end of the prosecution evidence, the defence argued that the wrong citation made the arrest invalid and everything that followed inadmissible. A case was stated.
DPP v Connell.q: Does citing the wrong statute when making an arrest make the arrest invalid?
dec: High Court (Geoghegan J), reported [1998] 3 IR 62: the arrest was valid.
The only reasonable inference from what the garda said was that he meant to arrest under s.49(8), so the wrong citation didn't invalidate the arrest.
An arrested person must know the reason for the arrest. He did: telling him in plain language that he was being arrested for drunk driving was enough (applying Mooney and Christie v Leachinsky).
The court added that, as a positive breath test had been taken, it wasn't even necessary to state the reason.
later: Consistent with Mooney (1992) and McCormack (1999). The reason can be given in everyday words, and the section number is optional, but the fact of arrest must always be clear.
job: Getting the section wrong isn't fatal if the reason is clear, but aim to get it right: 'I'm arresting you under section 4(8) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 for drink driving.'
The essentials are telling them they're under arrest and why, in plain words. Record what you said.
DPP v Connell.law: Yes. Connell is still good law: plain words are enough, and a mis-cited section isn't fatal where the reason is clear.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Connell (High Court, Geoghegan J)

bg: In September 2015 a driver failed a roadside breath test and was arrested for drink driving. At Westport Garda Station his details were logged and he was given his notice of rights.

The doctor service couldn't send a doctor straight away because of an emergency call, and said the doctor would come as soon as possible. He waited in the public office and gave a urine sample about two hours after arriving at the station.

The sample showed 155 mg per 100 ml, and he was charged. The defence argued the delay made the detention unlawful, and gardaí were cross-examined about having had no contact with the doctor service for about 80 minutes. A case was stated.
Brehon v DPP.q: Was he still lawfully detained when he gave a sample two hours after arriving at the station, because the doctor was delayed?
dec: High Court, February 2019 (Murphy J): he was in lawful detention.
The detention complied with the principle in Dunne v Clinton, as restated in People v Walsh and DPP v Finn. The sampling process was started promptly and wasn't delayed for an unjustified period.

The delay was judged against reasonableness. The court rejected a 'time and motion' review of every minute, and said it would be ludicrous to require the State to prove the nature of the doctor's emergency. Gardaí could rely on the doctor service's information.
The three-hour period is a backstop, not an entitlement. A detention could become unlawful within it, for example if the person were left waiting for half an hour before the process even started.

keys.q: ludicrous
keys.w: Murphy J, on requiring proof of the doctor's emergency

later: Read with Finn (2003), where an unexplained delay was fatal, Stack (2016), where an observation period was justified, and Brassil (2021), where only excessive delay needs justifying.
job: Start the procedure as soon as you arrive: log, rights, call the doctor.
Record every contact with the doctor service: times, what you were told, follow-ups. Long silent gaps invite cross-examination.
Keep the detainee informed, and make sure the delay isn't for any other purpose.
Brehon v DPP.law: Yes. Brehon (2019) is current on justified delay while waiting for a doctor.

src.t: Irish Legal News — Accused was lawfully detained when giving urine sample two hours after arrest (Feb 2019)

bg: Two drivers in separate District Court cases were arrested under s.4(8) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 and held at the station for a 20-minute observation period before giving breath specimens on the Evidenzer.

Gardaí said Medical Bureau of Road Safety (MBRS) training required the observation, to make sure the reading came from breath and not from alcohol residue in the mouth. The manufacturer's manual didn't require it.
The District Court asked whether the 20 minutes unreasonably prolonged the detention, so that the breath evidence was tainted.
DPP v Stack.q: Does a 20-minute observation period before an evidential breath test make the detention unlawful?
dec: High Court, April 2016 (Barrett J): no.
The prosecution must prove lawful detention. A delay is judged on the circumstances, and a deliberate delay needs an objective justification (the 'reasonable necessity' test from Finn).
Uncontradicted garda evidence that the MBRS trains them to observe for 20 minutes before testing supplied that justification. The wait was reasonably necessary and didn't make the detention unlawful.
The judge noted that a 20-minute delay generally won't make custody unlawful without special circumstances.
later: Distinguishes Finn (2003), where no reason for a 20-minute wait was proved. Follows DPP (Curran) v Foley (2006), which treated a needed observation period as part of the detention after arrest.
See also DPP v Fox (2008), DPP v Dardis (2015) and DPP v Lynch (2016) — waiting for a trained operator — all in this app.
job: If you observe for 20 minutes before an Evidenzer test, say in evidence that you did it because of MBRS training, to exclude mouth alcohol, and that you watched continuously.
Record the start and end of the observation period and anything that happened during it.
DPP v Stack.law: Yes. Stack (2016) is current: a 20-minute pre-test observation based on MBRS training is justified.

src.t: Irish Legal News — 20-minute observation before breath-alcohol tests does not make detention unlawful (2016)
vLex Ireland — DPP v Stack

bg: On Talbot Street, Dublin, a sergeant asked a man what money he had in his hand. The man showed a £10 note and a £5 note and said he had no other money.

The sergeant then put his hand in the man's pocket and found a £20 note he believed was forged. The man was charged with possessing forged notes. The search was justified under s.29 of the Dublin Police Act 1842, which allows a constable to stop, search and detain a person reasonably suspected of having anything stolen or unlawfully obtained.
The District Judge stated a case: before using that search power, did the garda have to tell the man the authority and grounds for the search?
DPP v Rooney.q: Must a garda tell a person the nature of the statutory search power being used before searching them?
dec: High Court, 25 May 1992 (O'Hanlon J).

Drawing on Christie v Leachinsky, where a person must be told the reason for an arrest, the Court held that before a statutory search power can lawfully be exercised, the person is entitled to be told the nature and description of the power being invoked.

Searching without giving that information wasn't a lawful exercise of the power. Precise technical language isn't required. What matters is that the person is told, in substance, what power is being used and why.

keys.q: the nature and description of the statutory powers
keys.w: The information a person searched is entitled to (as later quoted from Rooney)

later: Followed in Farrelly v Devally (1996) on Misuse of Drugs Act searches, and in DPP (O'Higgins) v Farrell (2009): the person is entitled to be told the reason for a s.23 search, though the section number needn't be cited.
The Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would put stop-and-search on a fuller statutory footing, with a formal record of every search.
job: Before searching, tell the person in plain words what power you're using and why: 'I'm searching you under the Misuse of Drugs Act because I suspect you have drugs. I saw you take something from that man.'
You don't need the section number, but you do need the substance: the power and your reason.
Record what you said, the grounds, the time and the result.
DPP v Rooney.law: Yes. Rooney is still good law: tell the person the power you're using before you search.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Rooney (High Court, O'Hanlon J, 1992)
Irish Statute Book — Dublin Police Act 1842, s.29

bg: Gardaí watching for drug activity near a Dublin shopping centre from an unmarked car approached a man after he parked nearby. One garda told him he was being detained for a search under the Misuse of Drugs Acts and that he and his car would be taken to the Garda station.
He resisted. He was convicted in the District Court of obstructing a search by refusing to be searched and of assaulting two gardaí, and the Circuit Court upheld the convictions on appeal.
He sought judicial review, arguing that the court had misinterpreted the Misuse of Drugs Acts.
Farrelly v Devally.q: Was the garda's announced intention to detain and bring him to the station for a search lawful, so that resisting it was obstruction?
dec: High Court, 19 July 1996 (Morris J): relief was refused, and the convictions stood.

The Court considered s.23 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 (as amended in 1984), which allows a garda with reasonable cause to suspect possession of a controlled drug to search a person, and to detain them for as long as reasonably necessary for the search, including at a station.
Read with DPP v Rooney, the person must be told the nature of the power being used. On the facts, the challenge to the convictions failed.
later: DPP v O'Brien (2018) [2018] IECA 166: detention for a s.23 search, including at a station, is distinct from arrest.
DPP (O'Higgins) v Farrell [2009] IEHC 368: the suspicion must relate to the individual, not just the area.
job: Tell the person the power (the Misuse of Drugs Act) and the reason before you detain them for a search.
Only move the search to a station if that's reasonably necessary, and record why.
If they resist a lawful search, obstruction may follow, but only if every step of the search was lawful.
Farrelly v Devally.law: Yes. Farrelly is an older High Court authority consistent with Rooney and O'Brien.

src.t: vLex Ireland — Farrelly v Devally [1996] IEHC 5
Irish Statute Book — Misuse of Drugs Act 1977

bg: On 7 August 1983 gardaí found a group carrying loaded firearms, including submachine guns and revolvers, at a private home in Co. Wicklow, and there was a shoot-out.
The applicant was handcuffed at the scene at about 8.10 a.m. and formally arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act at 8.50 a.m. His detention was later extended under s.30(3).

He was convicted on three firearms charges in the Special Criminal Court. He argued that the handcuffing was itself an arrest, which made the later formal arrest invalid, and that the extension was invalid because it wasn't in writing.
People (DPP) v Kehoe.q: Was handcuffing at the scene a separate arrest that invalidated the later formal arrest? And must a s.30 extension be in writing?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 17 December 1984 (McCarthy J): leave to appeal refused. The application was devoid of merit.
Handcuffing at the scene was part of a continuous sequence of events, not a separate arrest, so it didn't invalidate the later formal arrest.

A direction extending s.30 detention doesn't have to be in writing, though written directions are desirable. Nor does it have to state exact start and end times, though stating that the person is held for a further 24 hours from the expiry of the first 24 is preferable.

keys.q: devoid of merit
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on the application

later: Extensions are now routinely recorded in writing on the custody record. Braney (2021) upheld the s.30 extension regime, subject to a floor of rights.
job: Securing a dangerous suspect at a scene (handcuffs, holding) can be part of one continuous sequence. Make the formal arrest, with words and reason, as soon as it's safe.
Record extensions in writing on the custody record: who authorised, when, the grounds, and the new expiry time.
Note the times of first restraint and formal arrest, and why there was a gap.
People (DPP) v Kehoe.law: Yes, broadly. Kehoe is still cited on restraint at the scene versus formal arrest, though written recording of extensions is now standard practice.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Kehoe [1985] IR 444

bg: The accused was convicted in Cork Circuit Court in March 2009 on ten money-laundering counts and jailed for ten years.

One count concerned sterling cash found at his home in February 2005 during a search under s.29(1) of the Offences Against the State Act 1939. The warrant was issued by the superintendent who was leading the investigation.

In February 2012, while his appeal was pending, the Supreme Court in Damache declared s.29(1) unconstitutional because it allowed a warrant to be issued by someone who wasn't independent. He sought to add Damache to his grounds of appeal, and the parties agreed the validity of the warrant would decide that count.
People (DPP) v Cunningham.q: Can an appellant whose appeal was pending when Damache was decided rely on it? And what follows for evidence found under a s.29 warrant issued by the investigating superintendent?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 11 May 2012 (Hardiman J, with Moriarty and Hogan JJ): the appeal was allowed, the convictions quashed and a retrial ordered.
The evidence had been found on foot of a warrant that wasn't issued by an independent person.

The Court considered whether the declaration of unconstitutionality had retrospective effect, the finality of convictions, and whether he could rely on a ground not raised when seeking leave to appeal. On these facts, with his appeal still live, he could take the benefit of Damache.
later: JC [2015] changed how such evidence is treated: where gardaí relied in good faith on s.29 before Damache, the breach is usually inadvertent (a later legal development) and the evidence can be admitted.
Behan [2022] considered independence under the new s.29 (as substituted in 2012).
job: Warrants must be issued by someone independent of your investigation, which today normally means a District Court judge.
Cases still in the system when the law changes can be affected. Keep your paperwork, such as who issued the warrant and on what information, so the issues can be dealt with.
People (DPP) v Cunningham.law: Decided under Kenny. Since JC (2015), evidence obtained in good faith under a later-invalidated warrant power is usually admissible. The independence requirement itself is firmly established.

bg: Gardaí searched a house under a search warrant and recovered a television, a video recorder and a CD player that had been stolen in a burglary.

There were several defects. The information gave a different house number from the amended warrant, gave the wrong year for the theft, and named a different person from the accused, and the warrant was addressed to someone other than her. A new ground raised on appeal said the warrant didn't refer to the goods sought.
She was convicted of handling stolen property and appealed, arguing that the defects made the warrant, and the search, unlawful.
People (DPP) v Balfe.q: Do clerical defects on a warrant and its supporting information make the search unlawful and the evidence inadmissible?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal (Murphy J, with Lavan and Budd JJ), reported [1998] 4 IR 50.
The Court compared the case with People (AG) v O'Brien (1965), where a warrant that wrongly described the premises through pure oversight didn't lead to exclusion.

Murphy J treated O'Brien and Kenny as separate rules. Where the issuer's order is wrongly recorded and the mistake shows on the face of the warrant, the O'Brien approach applies: such slips can be treated as oversights, and admission is a matter for the trial judge's discretion. The trial judge had properly admitted the evidence.
The Court stressed that a warrant must still come from a competent, detached authority exercising an independent judgment.
later: DPP v Mallon [2011] IECCA 29 held that Balfe had not been overruled by Edgeworth and remained binding: a mere error that doesn't mislead won't invalidate a warrant.
Damache (2012) later made the detached-authority point central: the issuer must be independent of the investigation.
job: Check the information and the warrant against each other before you go: address, names, dates, offence, items sought.
Correct errors before you execute the warrant, not afterwards. A string of slips invites a challenge, and in Balfe the defence argued they should also count against the officer's credibility.
Record how you identified the premises and the person on the day.
People (DPP) v Balfe.law: Yes. Balfe is still binding (as confirmed in Mallon, 2011): clerical defects that don't mislead are judged on the O'Brien discretion.

bg: Two gardaí in plain clothes went into licensed premises in Monaghan to check whether gaming offences were being committed. They didn't identify themselves, didn't state their purpose and didn't have a search warrant under s.39 of the Gaming and Lotteries Act 1956.
Three publicans were convicted in the District Court. The defence argued the evidence was illegally obtained and should have been excluded, and a case was stated.
People (DPP) v McMahon.q: Were gardaí lawfully on licensed premises when they went in, as members of the public, to gather evidence of an offence? And if not, is the evidence admissible?
dec: Supreme Court, 20 June 1986 (Finlay CJ; Walsh, Henchy and Hederman JJ agreeing).
The Act's power of entry didn't cover licensed premises. Gardaí could enter to investigate offences only with the owner's agreement or a s.39 warrant.
A publican's implied invitation to the public doesn't extend to gardaí coming in to gather evidence of an offence, so the gardaí were trespassers.

But this was illegality, not a deliberate breach of constitutional rights. The public part of a pub isn't a dwelling protected by Article 40.5. So, applying the O'Brien majority, the evidence was admissible subject to the trial judge's discretion to exclude it.
later: An illustration of O'Brien's two tracks. Mere illegality goes to the judge's discretion, while breaches of constitutional rights (such as entering a dwelling) are now judged under JC (2015).
Many regulatory statutes now give specific inspection or entry powers. Check the power for the premises type (licensed premises, shops, gaming) before you rely on implied invitation.
job: Walking into a pub or shop as a member of the public is fine, but if your real purpose is to gather evidence of an offence, check that you have a power of entry (a statute or a warrant) or the owner's consent.
Business premises aren't 'dwellings', but a lack of power still makes you a trespasser, and the evidence then depends on the judge's discretion.
Record how you entered and under what authority.
People (DPP) v McMahon.law: Yes. McMahon is still good law on implied invitation and on the O'Brien discretion for illegally (not unconstitutionally) obtained evidence.

bg: A 16-year-old was charged with being intoxicated in a public place under s.4 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994.

Adults can be given a fixed charge notice for s.4 (under ss.23A and 23B), but the statute limits that to people aged 18 or over. He was referred to the Children Act 2001 diversion programme, found unsuitable, and sent for trial in the District Court.
He sought judicial review, arguing that excluding children from the fixed charge scheme breached the constitutional guarantee of equality (Article 40.1).
L.T. v DPP.q: Is it unconstitutional to offer adults a fixed charge for public intoxication but deny it to children?
dec: High Court, April 2024: all relief was refused.
Age is a legitimate basis for treating people differently, provided the difference isn't arbitrary or irrational.
Children facing these charges come under the Children Act 2001, which lets them avoid a conviction while still being supervised. The Oireachtas could reasonably prefer that route for children.
The exclusion wasn't an arbitrary, capricious or irrational discrimination, so there was no breach of Article 40.1.

keys.q: an arbitrary, capricious or irrational discrimination
keys.w: High Court — what the exclusion was not

later: Confirms the separate track for children: diversion under the Children Act 2001 first, and prosecution only if they're unsuitable.
job: Under-18s can't be given a fixed charge notice for ss.4 or 5. Refer them under the Children Act 2001 diversion scheme.
Follow the Children Act safeguards in custody and interview (parent or guardian, notice of rights in an age-appropriate form).
Record the referral and its outcome before any prosecution.
L.T. v DPP.law: Yes. L.T. (2024) is current High Court law on fixed charges and children.

bg: Shortly after midnight one night in October 1995, the accused kicked a woman severely, especially to the genital area. She died of heart failure caused by severe shock from the injuries and the pain.

He was convicted of murder in the Central Criminal Court in March 1997. He appealed on three grounds: that there wasn't enough evidence he caused the death, that provocation wasn't properly put to the jury, and that newspaper photos showing him heavily chained were prejudicial.
People (DPP) v Davis.q: When must provocation be left to the jury, and who has to prove what? And how closely must the accused's injuries be linked to the death?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 23 October 2000 (Hardiman J, with O'Higgins and Kearns JJ): appeal dismissed.
Causation: the injuries need only be related to the death in more than a minimal way. The jury could find they were the sole or principal cause.

Provocation: if it properly arises, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. Whether it arises is first for the trial judge. The accused's evidential burden is light, but there must be evidence, direct or by inference, pointing to each element.

Publicity: the photographs were a real concern, but with strong, uncontradicted evidence the trial was still satisfactory. Hardiman J added that shackling harms a prisoner's dignity, and that judges can restrict publication of such images.
He also remarked that provocation is a policy concession that might be narrowed or removed in future.

keys.q: in more than a minimal way
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on causation

later: DPP v McNamara (Supreme Court, 2020) later reshaped provocation into a mixed test, with a gatekeeping role for the judge. Read with MacEoin (1978).
job: In a fatal assault, gather the medical evidence on cause of death early (pathologist, treating doctors). Causation only needs a more-than-minimal link, but it must be proved.
Record everything said about what led up to the assault. It decides whether provocation goes to the jury.
Handle prisoners with dignity in public view. Restraints should be justified, and photos can be an issue at trial.
People (DPP) v Davis.law: Yes. Davis is still cited on the evidential burden for provocation and on causation, now read with McNamara (2020).

bg: In the early 1970s a girl attended a national school. Like most Irish primary schools it was funded and regulated by the State but owned by the Church and run by a priest as manager. In 1973 a teacher sexually abused her about 20 times during music lessons.

A parent had complained about the same teacher to the school manager in 1971, but nothing was passed to any State authority. More parents complained in 1973, and the teacher went on sick leave, resigned and moved to another school. A Department inspector had visited the school six times between 1969 and 1973 and received no complaint.

The abuse came to light in the mid-1990s, when a Garda investigation began after another former pupil complained. The teacher was charged with 386 offences against about 21 former pupils. He pleaded guilty to 21 sample charges in 1998 and was jailed.

She received criminal injuries compensation and obtained a default judgment against the teacher. But her claim against the State failed in the High Court and, by a majority, in the Supreme Court (2008), which held that the State wasn't vicariously liable for a teacher in a school managed by a church patron. She then applied to Strasbourg.
O'Keeffe v Ireland.q: Was the State responsible under Article 3 for failing to protect a child from sexual abuse by a teacher in a church-managed national school? And did she have an effective remedy?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber, 28 January 2014. The Court found violations of Article 3 (failure to protect) and Article 13 (no effective remedy), but no violation of the procedural limb of Article 3. The decision was by a majority, with six judges, including Charleton J, dissenting in part.

Children are particularly vulnerable, and Article 3 rights are fundamental, so the State has an inherent positive obligation to protect children from ill-treatment through special measures and safeguards. That obligation is especially strong in primary education. The State can't escape it by handing schooling to private or church bodies.

By the 1970s the State knew of the general risk of sexual abuse of children, if only from its own criminal prosecutions. Yet it entrusted most primary schools to non-State managers without any mechanism of effective State control against that risk.

The system pointed complaints about teachers to the school manager (a 1970 guidance note did this), and the inspectors looked at the quality of teaching, not at how children were treated. The Court said a detection and reporting system that allowed over 400 incidents of abuse by one teacher over so many years couldn't be called effective.
On the procedural limb, once a complaint was made in 1995, the Garda investigation and prosecution were effective, so there was no violation.

On Article 13, the Irish courts had ruled out vicarious liability, a direct negligence claim would fail for lack of a duty of care, and Ireland hadn't shown that a constitutional claim would work. So she had no effective remedy against the State. The Court awarded €30,000 in damages and €85,000 in costs.

keys.q: school authorities being obliged to protect the health and well-being of pupils
keys.w: Grand Chamber (para 145), on the duty in primary education

keys.q: the mechanisms in place did not provide sufficient protection to school children
keys.w: Grand Chamber, on the system in the 1970s

later: The State set up an ex gratia scheme for other survivors but required proof that the abuse happened after an earlier complaint that went unanswered. In July 2019 the Independent Assessor ruled that condition incompatible with the judgment, and the Department of Education began revising the scheme.

Child protection now has a statutory footing. Under the Children First Act 2015, teachers registered with the Teaching Council and members of An Garda Síochána are both 'mandated persons' who must report harm to children to Tusla.
O'Keeffe is still cited as the leading Strasbourg case on the State's duty to protect children in services it funds but doesn't run directly.
job: Treat every report of child abuse, recent or historical, as a matter for full investigation, whoever the alleged abuser is and whatever institution is involved.
You're a mandated person under the Children First Act 2015. Notify Tusla as well as investigating, and record that you did.
In historical cases, look for other victims. Here the investigation in the 1990s traced about 21 former pupils, and its thoroughness is why the procedural complaint failed.

Where you know, or ought to know, that a child is at immediate and serious risk, act. For example, use s.12 of the Child Care Act 1991 to remove the child to safety where waiting for a court order wouldn't be enough.
O'Keeffe v Ireland.law: Yes. O'Keeffe (Grand Chamber, 2014) is still the leading case on State responsibility for abuse in schools. Child protection in Ireland now rests on the Children First Act 2015.

bg: Three men dragged a woman from a car and held her companion, then raped her several times with great violence and acts of sexual perversion.

The appellant had previous convictions for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, aggravated burglary with wounding, gross indecency and burglary. He admitted his guilt at his first Garda interview, made a full statement and pleaded guilty.

He was sentenced to 21 years' penal servitude, and the Court of Criminal Appeal refused leave to appeal in January 1986. The Attorney General then certified that the case raised a point of law of exceptional public importance, about guidelines for sentencing in rape cases, so it went to the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Tiernan.q: What principles govern sentencing for rape, and how much do an immediate admission and a guilty plea count? Should the Supreme Court lay down general guidelines?
dec: Supreme Court, 13 May 1988 (Finlay CJ; Walsh, Henchy, Griffin and McCarthy JJ agreeing): the sentence was reduced from 21 to 17 years' penal servitude.

Rape must always be seen as one of the most serious offences in criminal law. It is a gross attack on human dignity and must attract very severe sanctions. Even without aggravating features, it calls for a substantial immediate period of detention or imprisonment.

The only real mitigation was the immediate admission, the full statement and the plea, which could show remorse and support a prospect of rehabilitation. The lack of premeditation didn't count as mitigation: it only meant that one aggravating factor was absent.
It was no ground of appeal that the sentence was longer than earlier rape sentences, or longer than life prisoners usually serve under the executive's release policy.
The Court declined to lay down general guidelines. It had heard argument only on this case, not on rape cases with different facts, but hoped its reasoning would help trial judges.

keys.q: a gross attack upon the human dignity
keys.w: Finlay CJ, on rape

keys.q: only established an absence of an aggravating element
keys.w: Finlay CJ, on the lack of premeditation

keys.q: a substantial immediate period of detention or imprisonment
keys.w: Finlay CJ, on what rape calls for

later: For about thirty years Tiernan was the starting point for rape sentencing. Then in DPP v F.E. [2019] IESC 85 the Supreme Court (Charleton J) set out sentencing bands ranging from about 7 years to life, before mitigation. It named violence in the home, breach of trust, domination and a background of abuse as aggravating factors.
In February 2020 the Supreme Court applied that guidance in the same case ([2020] IESC 5) and restored the trial sentence.
Tiernan's points are still applied: an early admission and a plea earn real credit, and the absence of premeditation isn't mitigation.
job: Record exactly when and how admissions were made: at the first interview, unprompted, a full statement. The court will want that detail when it gives credit.
Make sure the full previous record, the victim impact statement and the aggravating features (violence, several attackers, detaining others) are all before the court.
In rape cases, the evidence you gather on violence, breach of trust or domination helps decide which band under F.E. (2019) the sentence falls into.
People (DPP) v Tiernan.law: Partly. Tiernan's principles on the gravity of rape and on credit for admissions still apply, but the Supreme Court's guidance in F.E. (2019) now sets the sentencing bands.

bg: The prosecution case was that the accused fired a gun at a woman in a Limerick nightclub, intending to kill or seriously injure her. The gun was pushed away, and another woman in her company was shot dead.

He was tried for murder in 2004. His only defence was that he had no gun at any point and fired no shots, and accident was never raised. He was convicted of murder and of possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life.

On appeal he argued for the first time that the trial judge should have left accidental killing, and so manslaughter, to the jury. The Court of Criminal Appeal refused to let him raise the new point, and he appealed to the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Cronin (No 2).q: When can an appellant raise on appeal a point that wasn't run at trial?
dec: Supreme Court, 3 March 2006 (Kearns J, with Geoghegan, Fennelly, McCracken and Macken JJ): appeal dismissed.

A new point can be raised on appeal only where there was an error or oversight of substance at trial that gave rise to a real risk of injustice, and there must be a clear explanation for why it wasn't raised at trial.

Counsel had deliberately not relied on accident, because it contradicted the defence that he never had a gun. An accused can't run one defence, lose, and then complain that a contradictory one wasn't put to the jury.

The trial judge must keep the trial fair and direct the jury on the law, but doesn't control how the defence runs its case. A direction on accident would have undercut the defence actually run, by suggesting he may have fired the gun.
There was no miscarriage of justice. The defence team had been skilled throughout, and the point was raised about three years after the trial.

keys.q: error or oversight of substance
keys.w: Kearns J, the test for a new point on appeal

keys.q: real risk of injustice
keys.w: Kearns J, the threshold that error must meet

later: The Court of Appeal applies the Cronin test routinely. In DPP v Masznicz [2022] IECA 237 it refused a list of points not raised at trial, for which no explanation was given and no fundamental injustice shown, and called the appeal a classic instance of trawling the transcript.
It is often described as the 'Cronin exception': a new point can still succeed where a fundamental injustice is shown and the omission is explained.
job: Investigate the alternatives, not just the main case: accident, self-defence, provocation, someone else. The judge decides what goes to the jury on the evidence, whatever line the defence takes.
Brief the prosecutor on every issue in the file, including the weak points, so they're dealt with at trial. New points rarely get a hearing on appeal, so your evidence has to answer them at trial.
Note anything the suspect says that points to another account, even when the main line is a flat denial.
People (DPP) v Cronin (No 2).law: Yes. Cronin (No 2) is still the leading authority on raising new points on appeal.

bg: In November 1992 an RUC officer shot a man dead in Belfast. The man's father said the force used was unnecessary and disproportionate, and he alleged a 'shoot-to-kill' policy in Northern Ireland.

The shooting was investigated by RUC officers, from the same force as the officer who fired. The DPP decided not to prosecute and gave no reasons. The inquest was delayed for years. The officer who fired couldn't be compelled to give evidence, the family got no legal aid, and witness statements weren't disclosed to them in advance.
The father complained to Strasbourg that there had been no effective official investigation into the death.
Jordan v United Kingdom.q: What does Article 2 require when someone is killed by the police? And did the procedures in Northern Ireland meet it?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 4 May 2001, decided with three similar Northern Ireland cases. The Court found a violation of the procedural obligation under Article 2 and awarded £10,000 for non-pecuniary damage.

Where the State uses lethal force, the authorities must investigate on their own initiative. The investigation must be independent of those involved and capable of establishing the facts and identifying those responsible. It must be prompt and proceed with reasonable expedition, be open to public scrutiny, and involve the next of kin enough to protect their legitimate interests.

Here the investigating officers weren't independent of the officer involved, and the DPP gave the family no reasons. The inquest couldn't compel the officer to give evidence, couldn't reach a verdict that could lead to a prosecution, and was badly delayed. The family had no legal aid and no advance disclosure of statements.
The violation found was of the procedural duty to investigate. The Court made no finding that the shooting itself was unlawful.

keys.q: any appearance of collusion
keys.w: ECtHR, on why a prompt response to lethal force matters

keys.q: shortcomings in transparency and effectiveness
keys.w: ECtHR, on the procedures in Northern Ireland

later: The 'Jordan requirements' (independence, effectiveness, promptness, public scrutiny and family involvement) are now the standard checklist for any Article 2 investigation, including in Ireland.

The case itself dragged on, through decades of delay and repeated litigation over the inquest. In 2019 the UK Supreme Court held that the family's claim for damages for the delay didn't have to be put on hold automatically until the inquest finished.
Read with McCann v UK (1995) on the use of force itself, and on planning and control.
job: After any death or serious injury involving gardaí: preserve the scene, secure CCTV, bodycam footage and radio logs, identify witnesses, and expect an independent investigation by Fiosrú, the Office of the Police Ombudsman.
Gardaí involved in the incident shouldn't investigate it. Give a full, prompt account when required, and keep your notes separate and made at the time.
Families must be kept informed. Expect the investigation and any inquest to examine planning and control, not just the moment force was used.
Jordan v United Kingdom.law: Yes. Jordan's requirements are still the core of the Article 2 duty to investigate.

bg: In March 1988 the British authorities had intelligence that an IRA unit planned a car-bomb attack in Gibraltar, at the assembly area for the changing-of-the-guard ceremony. SAS soldiers were sent to help the Gibraltar police arrest the suspects.

Three suspects crossed from Spain into Gibraltar. They weren't stopped at the border, so as not to alert them. The soldiers had been briefed that the suspects would probably carry a remote-control device for a car bomb and might set it off if confronted.

On 6 March 1988 the soldiers shot all three dead, believing they were reaching for a detonator. None was armed or carrying a detonator, and there was no bomb in the car in Gibraltar. Explosives were later found in a car in Spain.

A Gibraltar inquest jury returned verdicts of lawful killing by nine to two. The families' civil actions were struck out after the Government issued certificates, and the European Commission of Human Rights found no violation by eleven votes to six.
McCann and Others v United Kingdom.q: When is lethal force by State agents 'absolutely necessary' under Article 2? And is it judged only at the moment of firing, or across the whole operation?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber, 27 September 1995: Article 2 was violated, by ten votes to nine.

Article 2(2) allows force only where it is 'absolutely necessary' for one of the listed aims. That is a stricter test than the necessity required elsewhere in the Convention, and the force must be strictly proportionate to the aim. Deprivations of life get the most careful scrutiny, which covers the planning and control of the operation as well as the actions of those who used force.

The soldiers genuinely believed they had to shoot to stop a bomb being detonated. Force based on an honest belief can be justified even if the belief later turns out to be wrong, so the soldiers' own actions didn't breach Article 2. The Court also rejected the claim that there had been a premeditated plan to kill.

But the operation as a whole did breach Article 2. The authorities didn't stop the suspects at the border, and they made no allowance for the possibility that their intelligence was wrong. They then relied on soldiers trained to shoot to kill, whose reflex use of lethal force reflected a lack of proper care in how the operation was controlled. So the killings weren't shown to be absolutely necessary.
The inquest, which ran for 19 days with 79 witnesses and with the families legally represented, was an adequate investigation, so the procedural duty wasn't breached.
Because the three had been preparing a bombing, the Court awarded no damages, but it ordered the UK to pay the applicants' costs.

keys.q: a stricter and more compelling test of necessity
keys.w: Grand Chamber (para 149), on 'absolutely necessary'

keys.q: the most careful scrutiny
keys.w: Grand Chamber (para 150), on deprivations of life

later: McCann is the foundation of Article 2 law on the use of force. Strasbourg examines the planning, briefing, training and control of an operation, not just the final decision to fire.
Read with Jordan v UK (2001) on the duty to investigate a death caused by State agents.
Gardaí are bound by the same standard: under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003, every organ of the State must perform its functions compatibly with the Convention.
job: Any force, and above all lethal force, must be absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate. Use the least force that will work, and keep reassessing.

In planned operations, the command decisions matter as much as the moment of firing: where and when to make the arrest, the contingency plans, and briefings that allow for the intelligence being wrong.

When you brief others, give the intelligence with its limits ('may', 'unconfirmed'). A briefing that turns a possibility into a certainty can make the operation unlawful, even if the officer who fires acts in good faith.
Record decisions and the reasons for them at every stage. Any investigation will examine the whole operation.
McCann and Others v United Kingdom.law: Yes. McCann (Grand Chamber, 1995) is still the leading Strasbourg case on the use of lethal force by State agents.

bg: The applicant, a businessman and regional politician, was suspected of ordering the killing of a former associate. The man he allegedly asked to carry it out didn't do it, and went to the security services instead.

The authorities staged the 'discovery' of two bodies at the intended victim's home and publicised the 'murder' in the media. The man then visited the applicant wearing a hidden radio transmitter, and police recorded their 16-minute conversation.

He was arrested in October 2000 and held on remand for over a year and eight months. In June 2002 he was convicted and sentenced to six and a half years, suspended with probation; the Supreme Court later reclassified one offence but left the sentence unchanged. The trial court didn't cite the recording itself as proof of guilt. It relied on experts' analysis of the conversation, the man's statements and other evidence.
Bykov v Russia.q: Did secretly recording a suspect through a participant with a hidden transmitter breach his right to privacy? And did using the results make his trial unfair?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber, 10 March 2009.

Article 8 (unanimous): the recording interfered with his private life and wasn't 'in accordance with the law'. Russian law treated it as an 'operative experiment' with no specific rules or safeguards against abuse, even though a radio transmitter is virtually as intrusive as a telephone tap.
Article 6 (11 votes to 6): the trial as a whole was fair. Article 6 doesn't set rules on the admissibility of evidence, so the question is whether the proceedings as a whole were fair.

He could challenge the recording and how it was interpreted, he did so, and the courts gave reasoned answers. The recording wasn't the only basis for the conviction: the man's accusation came before the operation and didn't depend on it. And it wasn't treated as a confession, because the courts relied on expert analysis.

There was no coercion. He was at home and free, not in custody. That distinguishes Allan v UK, where a detained, vulnerable suspect was targeted by a cellmate primed by police. He also hadn't been charged when the conversation took place.

Article 5(3) (unanimous): his long pre-trial detention was a violation, because the courts kept extending it without real reasons. The Court awarded €1,000 for non-pecuniary damage (12 votes to 5) and €25,000 in costs.

keys.q: was open to arbitrariness
keys.w: Grand Chamber, on the legal basis for the recording (Article 8)

keys.q: played a limited role in a complex body of evidence
keys.w: Grand Chamber, on the recording (Article 6)

later: Bykov confirms the line in Khan v UK (2000) and Allan v UK (2002): an Article 8 breach doesn't automatically make the trial unfair. The questions are whether the defence could challenge the evidence, how reliable it was, how far the case depended on it, and whether there was coercion.
In Ireland, covert recording with a device is governed by the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009. Get advice on authorisation before using an informant or participant with a hidden device.
Domestically, JC (2015) takes a similar approach to admissibility: a breach of rights isn't automatically fatal, but a deliberate and conscious breach leads to exclusion.
job: Before using an informant or participant to record a suspect, get the legal basis and authorisation right. Bykov's trial survived, but the Article 8 breach was unanimous.
Don't rely on a covert recording alone. Build independent evidence. Here the man's account came first and stood on its own.
Never use a cellmate or anyone else in custody to draw out admissions from a detained suspect. That is the Allan line, and it does make the trial unfair.
Keep the original recording, its continuity and any expert analysis ready for disclosure, so the defence can challenge them.
Bykov v Russia.law: Yes. Bykov (Grand Chamber, 2009) is still the leading Strasbourg case on covert recording through a participant: an Article 8 breach doesn't automatically make the trial unfair.

bg: The appellant was convicted of a sexual offence in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court in March 1994 and sentenced to five years. Child witnesses gave evidence by live television link under Part III of the Criminal Evidence Act 1992, and the trial judge overruled the defence objections.

Section 13 then let a witness under 17 give evidence by live link in sexual and violent offence cases unless the court saw good reason to the contrary, and other witnesses with the court's leave. The evidence had to be video-recorded, and the judge and barristers dealing with the witness didn't wear wigs or gowns.

He challenged the provisions. He argued he had a constitutional right to confront his accuser face to face in front of the jury, and that the procedure was unfair and discriminatory. The High Court (Costello P) dismissed the challenge in December 1996.
Donnelly v Ireland.q: Does the Constitution give an accused a right to confront a child accuser physically in the courtroom? Is evidence by live television link compatible with a fair trial?
dec: Supreme Court, 22 January 1998 (Hamilton CJ for the Court; O'Flaherty, Denham, Barrington and Murphy JJ): the provisions aren't repugnant to the Constitution, and the appeal failed.
There is no constitutional right to physical confrontation. Fair procedures require that the witness gives evidence on oath and can be cross-examined, and the live link preserved both.

Assessing credibility doesn't require the witness to give evidence in the accused's physical presence. The judge and jury could watch the witness on monitors and had ample opportunity to observe the witness's demeanour.

The accused was protected, because the court could refuse the link if good reason was shown. The Act didn't require a separate finding, child by child, that a witness would be traumatised by giving evidence in the accused's presence.
The Court accepted that children can be manipulated into making false allegations, but held that the oath and cross-examination were adequate safeguards.

keys.q: ample opportunity to observe the demeanour of the witness
keys.w: Hamilton CJ (as reported), on the live link

keys.q: physical presence of the accused person
keys.w: Hamilton CJ, on what assessing credibility does not require

later: The live-link scheme has been widened. The age limit is now 18 (Children Act 2001), and since 2018 the Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017 has let victims in other cases give evidence by live link with the court's leave.
The 1992 Act, as amended, also allows other special measures for young and vulnerable witnesses, such as video-recorded statements and screens.
job: Flag young or vulnerable witnesses on the file early. In cases covered by the Act, a witness under 18 gives evidence by live link unless the court sees good reason otherwise, and others need the court's leave.
For a child complainant, plan a video-recorded interview by specialist interviewers from the start. It can be used as evidence.
Tell the witness and family what to expect: the live link, no wigs or gowns, and that cross-examination still happens.
Donnelly v Ireland.law: Yes. Donnelly (1998) is still the authority that live-link evidence is constitutional, and the scheme has since been extended.

bg: A 16-year-old was detained in the early hours of a Saturday morning on suspicion of murder and questioned at a Garda station.

Gardaí tried several times to contact solicitors, without success, and a solicitor didn't arrive until midday. Questioning didn't start until an appropriate adult arrived, and the boy and the adult were allowed to speak alone, as they asked.

Three gardaí questioned him, although Regulation 12(3) of the Custody Regulations 1987 allows no more than two. No written statement was taken, and he wasn't asked to sign the record of his answers, until the solicitor arrived. The defence said he had a low IQ.
The trial judge admitted his answers. He offered to plead guilty to manslaughter, but the jury convicted him of murder in December 1995, and he sought leave to appeal.
People (DPP) v Darcy.q: Does a breach of the Custody Regulations, or a delay in getting a solicitor for a juvenile, make his admissions inadmissible?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 29 July 1997 (Keane J, with Budd and Moriarty JJ): leave to appeal refused.

The right of reasonable access to a solicitor is constitutional (Healy). But there was nothing like a conscious and deliberate act by gardaí to deny him access. Given the early hour and the failed attempts to reach solicitors, the delay didn't breach his constitutional rights.

Using three interviewers breached the Regulations, and detailed compliance wasn't shown. But the substance of his rights was preserved: an appropriate adult was present, he could consult the adult alone, and no written statement was taken until his solicitor arrived.

No one suggested the questioning was unfair or oppressive, so the trial judge was entitled to use his discretion and admit the statements. This fits s.7(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, under which a breach of the Regulations doesn't, of itself, make custody unlawful or a statement inadmissible.
The trial judge's charge on intent was described as impeccable, and his answer to the jury's question on 'serious injury' couldn't be faulted.

keys.q: nothing in the nature of a conscious and deliberate act
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on the delay in getting a solicitor

keys.q: substance of the applicant's rights was preserved
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on the breach of the Regulations

later: Contrast Diver (2005), where grave breaches led to exclusion. Darcy shows that a technical breach usually won't, where the purpose of the protections was met.

Safeguards for children in custody are now in Part 6 of the Children Act 2001: a parent, guardian or other adult must normally be present, and the child must be told their rights in an age-appropriate way.

Since Gormley and White (2014), once a suspect asks for a solicitor, questioning should wait until they've had a reasonable chance to consult one. Questioning before the solicitor arrived, as happened here, would now be much harder to defend.
job: With a juvenile, don't start until the parent, guardian or appropriate adult is there, and let them speak privately with the child if asked.
Keep to two interviewers. A third person asking questions is an easy breach to avoid.
Record every attempt to reach a solicitor: the time, the number and the result. If legal advice has been requested, wait for it before questioning (Gormley).
Don't take a written statement or a signature from a juvenile unless the safeguards are in place.
People (DPP) v Darcy.law: Partly. Darcy is still cited for the 'substance of the rights' approach to breaches of the Regulations, but questioning before a requested solicitor arrives is now governed by Gormley and White (2014).

bg: Two men were convicted by a jury in British Columbia of conspiracy to traffic in heroin. An accomplice gave evidence for the prosecution.

At the time, a judge had to warn the jury that it was dangerous to convict on an accomplice's uncorroborated evidence, using a technical definition of corroboration taken from the English case R v Baskerville (1916).
The defence challenged the trial judge's charge to the jury on corroboration of the accomplice. The British Columbia Court of Appeal dismissed their appeals.
Vetrovec v The Queen.q: Must a judge always give a fixed accomplice warning, with a technical definition of corroboration? Or should the judge decide whether and how to warn the jury about any untrustworthy witness?
dec: Supreme Court of Canada, 31 May 1982 (Dickson J for a unanimous court): appeal dismissed.

The law of corroboration had become unduly and unnecessarily complex and technical. The Court abolished the rule that the jury must be warned it is dangerous to convict on an accomplice's uncorroborated evidence, and disapproved the Baskerville approach.

An accomplice should be treated like any other witness. Whether to warn the jury about a particular witness, accomplice or not, is for the trial judge's discretion, depending on that witness's role and credibility.
The trial judge's instructions hadn't prejudiced the accused.

keys.q: unduly and unnecessarily complex and technical
keys.w: Dickson J, on the law of corroboration

keys.q: like any other witness
keys.w: Dickson J, on how an accomplice should be treated

later: In Canada the 'Vetrovec warning' is now standard for particularly untrustworthy Crown witnesses, such as accomplices and witnesses with an interest. R v Khela (2009) said it must point to what makes the witness untrustworthy and stress the specific danger of convicting on that evidence.

In R v Stevenson (2024 SCC 41) the Supreme Court of Canada upheld a conviction resting on a former accomplice in witness protection, because the trial judge had properly warned himself about the dangers.

Ireland hasn't followed Vetrovec for accomplices. The jury must still be warned that it is dangerous to convict on an accomplice's uncorroborated evidence (Gilligan, 2005). The Criminal Law (Rape) (Amendment) Act 1990 made the old corroboration warning discretionary in sexual offence cases.
job: Expect the defence to attack any witness with a motive: an accomplice, an informant, someone hoping for a deal. Record every benefit, promise and contact.
Look for independent evidence that confirms the key parts of such a witness's account: phones, CCTV, forensics, money, movements.
In Ireland the accomplice warning is still given, so independent corroboration is what makes the case safe.
Vetrovec v The Queen.law: Canadian law, persuasive only in Ireland. Vetrovec is still the leading Canadian case, while Irish courts keep the accomplice corroboration warning.

bg: During the G8 summit in Genoa in July 2001, the city let demonstrators use the Diaz-Pertini school as a night shelter. Around midnight on 21–22 July, riot police went in to search the building.

The applicant, then 62, was sitting against a wall with his arms raised. Officers kicked him and beat him with batons, causing multiple fractures. He never fully recovered and was left with permanent weakness in his right arm and leg.

After a three-year investigation, 28 members of the security forces were tried. Twelve were convicted at first instance in 2008, and the appeal courts upheld the main part of that judgment in 2010 and 2012. But the offences of wounding and abuse of authority became time-barred, the officers who beat him were never identified, and no one was convicted for what was done to him.
Cestaro v Italy.q: Did the beating amount to torture? And did Italy's criminal law and investigation meet the State's duty to punish ill-treatment by police?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 7 April 2015: Article 3 was violated, in both its substantive and procedural limbs.

Substantive: the beating was torture. He had done nothing to provoke it, so the force was gratuitous and disproportionate. The Court relied on the Italian Court of Cassation's finding that the violence was punitive, a reprisal.

Procedural: the officers were never identified, partly because the police didn't cooperate. The Court didn't blame the prosecutors or the courts, but held that Italian criminal law was inadequate to punish torture and had no real deterrent effect.

The Court called the problem structural. Italy's Article 3 obligations could require a proper legal framework, including effective criminal provisions, so that those responsible are punished and can't benefit from measures incompatible with the Court's case law.
The Court awarded €45,000 for non-pecuniary damage, taking account of the compensation he had already received in Italy.

keys.q: amounted to 'torture' within the meaning of Article 3
keys.w: ECtHR, on the beating

keys.q: devoid of the necessary deterrent effect
keys.w: ECtHR, on the Italian criminal law

later: In July 2017 Italy created a crime of torture (Article 613-bis of the Criminal Code), with up to 12 years where a public official abuses their powers. The debate had gathered pace after this judgment, though critics said the definition was too narrow.
Cestaro is cited as the leading case on police violence during public-order operations, on the need for identifiable officers, and on the need for an effective criminal law.
Read with McCann v UK (1995) and Jordan v UK (2001): force must be justified by the person's own conduct, and it must be investigated effectively.
job: Force must be necessary and proportionate to what the person in front of you is doing. Force on someone who is compliant or not resisting is unlawful, and it can amount to torture.
Stay identifiable during public-order operations (shoulder numbers), and cooperate fully with any investigation into the use of force.
Record any force you use, why you used it and any injuries, and get medical attention for anyone hurt.
When premises are searched during a protest or summit, the command and briefing will be scrutinised as closely as individual actions.
Cestaro v Italy.law: Yes. Cestaro (2015) is still the leading Strasbourg case on police ill-treatment in public-order operations and on the State's duty to punish it effectively.

bg: In 2012 the applicant was found with a sawn-off shotgun. He was charged under s.27A(1) of the Firearms Act 1964 (possession in circumstances giving rise to a reasonable inference that it wasn't for a lawful purpose), and under s.15 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 (articles for use in a theft). He pleaded guilty to both in 2013.

He had 26 previous convictions, including a 2009 conviction for carrying a firearm with criminal intent. While sentencing was adjourned he engaged in drug rehabilitation, and in 2014 the Circuit Court imposed fully suspended sentences.

Section 27A(8) required a minimum of five years, with no exception, for a second firearms offence or for a first s.27A offence by someone with a listed previous conviction. On the DPP's review for undue leniency, the Court of Appeal held that the judge had been bound to impose five years. His constitutional challenge to s.27A(8) failed in the High Court (Twomey J) and the Court of Appeal.
Ellis v Minister for Justice and Equalit.q: Can the Oireachtas impose a mandatory minimum sentence on a limited group of offenders, identified by a previous conviction, leaving the judge no discretion?
dec: Supreme Court, 15 May 2019 (Finlay Geoghegan J; Charleton J concurring separately): s.27A(8) is repugnant to the Constitution.
The Oireachtas has a legitimate role in setting penalty policy that applies to everyone convicted of an offence. Sentencing the individual offender is for the courts.

Section 27A(8) fixed a minimum not for everyone convicted under s.27A(1), but only for a limited group identified by one characteristic, a previous listed conviction. For that group it removed the court's power to fit the sentence to the offender, which crossed into the judicial function.
The Court expressly left open laws that let a court depart from a set sentence for stated or exceptional reasons, or that set a starting point.

keys.q: impermissibly crossed the divide in the constitutional separation of powers
keys.w: Finlay Geoghegan J

keys.q: a limited group of such offenders identified by one particular characteristic
keys.w: Finlay Geoghegan J, on who s.27A(8) targeted

later: In McManus v Minister for Justice [2021] IEHC 385 the High Court (Twomey J), applying Ellis, struck down s.27(3F) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977, the 10-year mandatory minimum for a second s.15A or s.15B drug-trafficking offence.
Only people whose sentences weren't yet final could benefit. Final sentences can't be reopened on this basis (A v Governor of Arbour Hill Prison).

The presumptive minimums survive. Section 27A(4)–(6) still requires at least 5 years for a first s.27A offence by an adult unless there are exceptional and specific circumstances. The revised Act notes that s.27A(8) was declared unconstitutional.
job: Previous convictions still matter at sentencing. Put the full record before the court, including firearms convictions.
Gather the evidence that bears on the presumptive minimum: the plea and when it was first indicated, any material assistance, and previous relevant convictions.
Don't tell anyone that a second offence carries an automatic five years (or ten, for drug trafficking). Those mandatory second-offence minimums have been struck down.
Ellis v Minister for Justice and Equalit.law: Yes. Ellis (2019) is current: mandatory minimums aimed at a limited group of repeat offenders are unconstitutional, though presumptive minimums with an exception remain.
