bg: Two men forced their way into a man's home and stabbed him. Neighbours called the police, who arrived within minutes, and the badly wounded man told them who had attacked him. He later died.

At the trial of one of the attackers, the judge admitted the victim's statement naming them as part of the res gestae, an exception to the rule against hearsay. The defence pointed out that the victim believed the accused had earlier attacked his house, which gave him a possible motive to lie, and that he had drunk well over the drink-driving limit.
The accused was convicted of manslaughter. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, and he appealed to the House of Lords.
R v Andrews.q: When can a statement by someone who isn't called as a witness (here, a victim who died) be admitted as part of the res gestae?
dec: House of Lords, 5 February 1987 (Lord Ackner, with Lords Bridge, Brandon, Griffiths and Mackay): appeal dismissed.

The key question is whether the possibility of concoction or distortion can be disregarded. The event must have been so unusual, startling or dramatic that it dominated the speaker's thoughts, so that the statement was an instinctive reaction, with no real opportunity for reasoned reflection.
Exact contemporaneity isn't required. The statement must be so closely linked to the event that the speaker's mind was still dominated by it. That it was an answer to a question is only one factor.

The judge must consider any special features that might point to fabrication, such as malice towards the accused. Ordinary error is a matter of weight for the jury, but special features such as drink or poor eyesight may require the judge to consider whether error can be ruled out.

The doctrine mustn't be used to avoid calling the maker of a statement who is available to give evidence. Lord Ackner strongly deprecated that, because it denies the defence the chance to cross-examine.

keys.q: the possibility of concoction or distortion
keys.w: Lord Ackner, the key question

keys.q: so unusual or startling or dramatic as to dominate the thoughts of the victim
keys.w: Lord Ackner, on the event

keys.q: the mind of the declarant was still dominated by the event
keys.w: Lord Ackner, on timing

later: In England, res gestae is now preserved by s.118 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, and the Andrews test still governs it.

In England, prosecutors and police increasingly try to admit body-worn footage as res gestae, especially in domestic violence cases where the complainant won't support the prosecution. Practitioners stress that it is a narrow doctrine, not a substitute for an absent witness. In one recent first-instance case, statements recorded about two hours after a stabbing, after treatment and sedation, were excluded.
In Ireland, Andrews is persuasive, and res gestae remains a common-law exception to the hearsay rule.
job: Record a victim's first words at the scene verbatim, with the exact time, what had just happened, and how they appeared (distress, injuries, crying). Spontaneity is everything.
Secure 999 calls and body-worn footage early. They are the best evidence of what was said and in what state, but footage doesn't by itself prove spontaneity.
Note anything that might suggest error or a motive to lie (drink, injuries affecting vision, a feud), because the judge will ask.
Don't treat res gestae as a way round a reluctant witness. Build the case so that it doesn't depend on it.
R v Andrews.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Andrews is still the leading test for res gestae statements.

bg: The applicant, the same man whose challenge struck down the s.29 search warrant power in Damache v DPP (2012), had become an Irish citizen by naturalisation. In July 2018 he pleaded guilty in a US court to assisting a terrorist conspiracy while living in Ireland, and he is serving a 15-year sentence there.
The Minister for Justice gave him notice of an intention to revoke his citizenship under s.19 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956.

Under s.19, the Minister started the process, appointed the members of the committee of inquiry the person could ask for, and presented the reasons for revocation. The Minister then made the final decision, without being bound by the committee's report, and there was no appeal. He challenged the procedure.
Damache v Minister for Justice and Equal.q: Does the procedure for revoking naturalised citizenship meet the standards of natural justice the Constitution requires?
dec: Supreme Court, 14 October 2020 (Dunne J): s.19 is unconstitutional.
Revoking citizenship is an executive function, not the administration of justice, so it needn't be decided by a court.

But losing citizenship, and with it EU citizenship, is a matter of grave significance. The process must be robust and meet high standards of natural justice, which requires an impartial and independent decision-maker.

The Court found no evidence that the committee members lacked independence. The flaw was in the structure: the Minister started the process, presented the case and made the final decision, wasn't bound by the committee, and there was no appeal.

keys.q: grave significance
keys.w: Dunne J, on losing citizenship

keys.q: does not meet the high standards of natural justice required
keys.w: Dunne J, on s.19

later: The Oireachtas replaced the procedure in the Courts, Civil Law, Criminal Law and Superannuation (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024. The Minister must notify the person and consider their representations, and if the Minister decides to revoke, an independent committee of inquiry can affirm or reject that decision.
Read with Damache v DPP (2012): the same insistence on an independent decision-maker runs through both cases.
job: Background for immigration and security work: revoking naturalisation is a ministerial process with its own safeguards, not a Garda power.
Don't tell a naturalised citizen that a conviction will automatically cost them their citizenship. Revocation is a separate process, now with independent review.
Any information gardaí supply for a revocation case must be accurate and sourced, because an independent committee will examine it.
Damache v Minister for Justice and Equal.law: Yes. Damache (2020) requires an impartial, independent decision-maker for revocation, and the procedure was replaced in 2024.

bg: A Myanmar national arrived in Ireland in July 2008 and applied for refugee status. Two decisions on his claim were quashed on judicial review, and his claim was still undecided years later. He spent over eight years in Direct Provision.

When he was offered a job at the accommodation centre where he lived, the Minister relied on s.9(4) of the Refugee Act 1996, which barred asylum seekers from seeking or taking up employment until their claim was finally decided. The same bar was carried into s.16(3)(b) of the International Protection Act 2015.

The High Court and the Court of Appeal rejected his challenge, with Hogan J dissenting in the Court of Appeal. He was granted refugee status after the Court of Appeal ruled, but the Supreme Court still heard the appeal as a test case.
N.V.H. v Minister for Justice and Equali.q: Can the State impose an absolute, open-ended ban on asylum seekers working?
dec: Supreme Court, 30 May 2017 (O'Donnell J, unanimous).

Non-citizens can rely on constitutional rights that go to the essence of human personality, though not on rights tied to membership of the political community, such as voting. The freedom to seek work is one of them, because work is bound up with dignity and self-worth.

It isn't a right to a job. It is a freedom to seek work, which the State mustn't block without substantial justification. The State can legitimately treat asylum seekers differently from citizens, for example because work might act as a 'pull factor'.

But s.9(4) didn't limit the right; it removed it altogether, for an indefinite period. A restriction might be permissible if processing times were limited, but there was no limit here. He had been in the system for over eight years, with damage to his self-worth.
Because several statutory provisions interacted, the Court adjourned its order for six months to let the State respond.

keys.q: contrary to the constitutional right to seek employment
keys.w: O'Donnell J, on the absolute ban

keys.q: damage to his self worth
keys.w: O'Donnell J, on eight years without work

later: The State opted into the recast EU Reception Conditions Directive (2013/33/EU). Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, applicants can seek labour market access permission if there's no first-instance decision on their claim within a set time.
In February 2021 (S.I. 52/2021) the wait was cut from 9 to 6 months, and the permission was extended from 6 to 12 months.
job: International protection applicants aren't barred outright from working. Many hold labour market access permission, so check before assuming that work is unlawful.
In employment or immigration checks, ask for the permission document and record its details and expiry date.
Applicants who have spent long periods in accommodation centres can be targets for exploitation. Consider labour exploitation or trafficking as well as possible offences.
N.V.H. v Minister for Justice and Equali.law: Yes. N.V.H. (2017) is still the leading case on non-citizens' freedom to seek work. Access is now governed by the Reception Conditions Regulations.

bg: Two Mauritian nationals came to Ireland in 2006 with student permission (Stamp 2), which allowed study and part-time work. Both families had children in Irish schools.

In 2011 the Minister introduced a policy limiting non-EEA students to seven years' residence, with transitional arrangements for those already here. When their permissions ran out, in 2012 and 2013, they applied to change their status under s.4(7) of the Immigration Act 2004. They were refused and told to leave.
The Minister argued that their right to private and family life (Article 8 ECHR) only had to be considered later, if deportation was proposed under s.3 of the Immigration Act 1999.
Luximon v Minister for Justice and Equal.q: When deciding whether to renew or vary a long-term resident's permission under s.4(7), must the Minister consider their right to private and family life?
dec: Supreme Court, April 2018 (MacMenamin J, unanimous): the refusals were quashed.

By the time of the policy change the applicants had many of the characteristics of long-term migrants, unlike short-term visitors, temporary workers or asylum seekers. They were lawful, long-duration residents.
The need to leave came from a change in Government policy, not from anything unlawful they had done. The refusal letters weren't deportation orders, but they had the effect of expulsion orders.

So their Article 8 rights were engaged and had to be assessed at the s.4(7) stage. Leaving it to the deportation stage was illogical. The ruling was confined to its facts: the Minister can still limit how long people stay, but must consider Article 8 when a decision has that effect.

keys.q: lawful, long-duration residents whose Article 8 rights were engaged
keys.w: MacMenamin J

keys.q: had the effect of expulsion orders
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the refusal letters

later: The Court of Appeal had reached the same conclusion in 2017. IHREC appeared as amicus curiae.
The ruling was expected to help many non-EEA residents whose permissions were refused after the 2011 student policy.
job: Background for immigration work: decisions on permission for long-term residents must weigh private and family life.
Before acting on someone's immigration status, check their current permission with the immigration authorities. A refusal letter isn't a deportation order.
Long-term residents with families here are often challenging decisions about their status. Record what you're told about pending applications or proceedings.
Luximon v Minister for Justice and Equal.law: Yes. Luximon (2018) is current: Article 8 must be considered in change-of-status decisions that have the effect of expulsion.

bg: In each of two cases, an Irish citizen was married to a Nigerian national who was subject to a deportation order. The marriages took place after the deportation orders had been made and evaded, and the Minister accepted that they were lawful.

The couples asked the Minister to revoke the deportation orders, and the Minister refused. In doing so, the Minister treated the couples' constitutional rights as a married family (Article 41) as going no further than Article 8 ECHR.

The High Court quashed the refusals. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, finding a prima facie constitutional right to reside in Ireland with a spouse, subject to lawful regulation. The Minister appealed.
Gorry v Minister for Justice and Equalit.q: Does an Irish citizen have a constitutional right to live in Ireland with a non-national spouse? And how must the Minister weigh the marriage when deciding whether to revoke a deportation order?
dec: Supreme Court, September 2020 (O'Donnell J; McKechnie J concurring): the Minister's appeals were dismissed, and the orders quashing the refusals stood.

The Minister erred by treating the constitutional analysis as the same as, or subordinate to, the ECHR analysis. Article 41 rights aren't absolute, but they are significant and must be given proper weight.

It is a balancing exercise. The family's choice of where to live isn't decisive, but nor is it meaningless. Recognising the constitutional rights doesn't give them automatic priority, and the balance may still favour removal.

Immigration history matters. Refusing to revoke a deportation order won't normally fail to respect the marriage where the order was evaded before the marriage. But the length of the relationship, especially if it has lasted abroad, and how long ago the order was made may become relevant.
Because the cases had become moot, the Court didn't send them back to the Minister.

keys.q: erred in law when refusing to revoke deportation orders
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the Minister's decisions

later: Gorry is the starting point whenever a deportation order affects a citizen's spouse. The Minister can still refuse revocation, but only after a proper balancing of the marriage against the State's interests.
Read with Luximon (2018) on considering Article 8 in permission decisions.
job: Background for immigration work: marriage to an Irish citizen doesn't automatically prevent deportation, but the Minister must weigh it properly.
Before acting on a deportation order against someone married to an Irish citizen, check that the order is still in force and whether an application to revoke it is pending.
Record what the person tells you about their marriage and family accurately and neutrally. It may matter to a later decision.
Gorry v Minister for Justice and Equalit.law: Yes. Gorry (2020) is the leading case on balancing a citizen's marriage against immigration control.

bg: In 2000 the President referred ss.5 and 10 of the Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Bill 1999 to the Supreme Court under Article 26, to test whether they were constitutional before signing the Bill.

Section 5 allowed listed immigration and asylum decisions, including deportation orders, to be challenged only by judicial review. Leave had to be sought within 14 days, which the High Court could extend for 'good and sufficient reason', and would be granted only on 'substantial grounds'. Irish citizens had six months to seek ordinary judicial review.

Section 10 extended detention powers. A person subject to a deportation order could be detained for up to eight weeks if suspected of having forged or destroyed identity documents, or of intending to leave the State or avoid deportation. Before, gardaí could detain only where they suspected non-compliance with the order.
In re Article 26 and the Illegal Immigra.q: Did the 14-day limit for challenging immigration decisions deny access to the courts? And were the new detention powers constitutional?
dec: Supreme Court, 28 August 2000 (Keane CJ announcing the Court's single decision, as Article 26 requires): neither section is repugnant to the Constitution, so both were upheld.

The High Court's power to extend the 14 days was wide enough. It could take account of language and communication difficulties, problems getting legal advice, and whether the applicant had acted with reasonable diligence. So the limit wasn't unreasonable in itself, and access to the courts was protected.

The detention safeguards were adequate for this kind of detention. Detention would be an abuse of power if deportation clearly couldn't happen within eight weeks, and the eight-week limit was relatively narrow. No breach of Article 5 ECHR was shown.

keys.q: good and sufficient reason
keys.w: s.5, the test for extending the time limit

keys.q: perfectly adequate
keys.w: Supreme Court (as reported), on the detention safeguards

later: The Employment Permits (Amendment) Act 2014 replaced s.5 of the 2000 Act. The time limit is now 28 days, and the 'substantial grounds' threshold and the 'good and sufficient reason' extension remain.

Because the Bill was upheld on an Article 26 reference, ss.5 and 10 can't later be challenged on constitutional grounds (Article 34.3.3°). The detention powers became part of s.5 of the Immigration Act 1999.
job: Arrest and detention for deportation must be under the specific statutory power, on the grounds it sets out (for example, a suspicion that the person intends to avoid removal). Record those grounds.
Detention is only lawful while removal is realistically possible within the time limit. Flag any obstacle at once, such as missing travel documents or pending court proceedings.
A person can still challenge a deportation decision in the courts within the time limit, so check for pending judicial review before removal.
In re Article 26 and the Illegal Immigra.law: Yes. The 2000 reference upheld the short time limit and the detention powers, and the limit is now 28 days.

bg: Two families, one of them Nigerian, applied for asylum in Ireland. Each had a child born in Ireland, who was an Irish citizen by birth under the law then in force.

Their asylum claims were refused. The Refugee Applications Commissioner and the Refugee Appeals Tribunal found the claims should be dealt with in other EU states under the Dublin Convention, and deportation orders followed. One parent hadn't disclosed an earlier asylum refusal in the UK.
The parents argued that their Irish children had a constitutional right to the company, care and parentage of their parents in Ireland, so the parents couldn't be deported.
Lobe and Osayande v Minister for Justice.q: Does an Irish citizen child's right to live in Ireland prevent the deportation of the child's non-national parents?
dec: Supreme Court, 23 January 2003 (Keane CJ, for a majority; Fennelly J dissenting): the challenges failed.

A citizen child has, in general, a right not to be expelled from the State. But the child has no right to the society of its parents in the State that would prevent the parents' deportation, even if in practice the child leaves with them.
Grave and substantial reasons associated with the common good, including the integrity of the asylum system and the Dublin Convention, justified ending the parents' residence.

Fajujonu (1990) was still good law but was distinguished, because the citizen children there had lived in Ireland for an appreciable period. In each case the Minister must consider factors such as the family's length of residence and the effectiveness of immigration control.
Fennelly J would have allowed the appeals, giving priority to the child's interests.

keys.q: the society of its parents in the state
keys.w: Supreme Court majority, on what the child has no right to

keys.q: appreciable period
keys.w: on why Fajujonu was different

later: The citizenship referendum of 11 June 2004 (the Twenty-seventh Amendment, carried with 79% Yes) ended the constitutional entitlement to citizenship by birth unless a parent is an Irish citizen or entitled to be one. The Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 2004 now governs it.
In Chen v Home Secretary (October 2004) the EU Court of Justice held that a non-EU parent of an EU citizen child could have a right to reside with that child in the EU.
Children born before the change keep their citizenship, and Lobe's balancing approach still informs decisions about families.
job: Background for immigration work: having an Irish citizen child doesn't automatically stop a parent's deportation, but the decision must weigh the family's circumstances.
When dealing with a family facing removal, record the children's details and any welfare concerns, and involve Tusla where needed.
Check a child's citizenship carefully: since the 2004 changes, birth in Ireland alone doesn't confer it.
Lobe and Osayande v Minister for Justice.law: Partly. Lobe's balancing approach is still cited, but citizenship by birth changed in 2004, and EU law (Chen) now also protects some parents of EU citizen children.

bg: A Nigerian woman claimed refugee status, saying she faced threats to her life, forced marriage and female genital mutilation (FGM) if returned. The Refugee Appeals Tribunal accepted that FGM is torture, but found she hadn't credibly linked her own circumstances to the harm she feared.

When the Minister proposed to deport her, her lawyers argued that removal would breach Article 3 ECHR and asked to submit expert evidence on FGM in Nigeria. The Minister made the deportation order, stating only that he was satisfied s.5 of the Refugee Act 1996 (the ban on refoulement) had been complied with.
She sought leave for judicial review. The High Court refused leave but certified a question: does the O'Keeffe reasonableness test apply to decisions affecting fundamental rights?
Meadows v Minister for Justice, Equality.q: How should courts review an administrative decision that affects fundamental rights? Does proportionality play a part, and must the decision give reasons?
dec: Supreme Court, 21 January 2010, by 3 to 2 (Murray CJ, Denham and Fennelly JJ; Kearns P and Hardiman J dissenting): leave for judicial review was granted.

The Court rejected the English 'anxious scrutiny' standard, but held that proportionality is part of judging whether a decision affecting fundamental rights is reasonable. The more severely a decision limits fundamental rights, the more substantial the considerations needed to justify it.
A decision affecting a person's rights should at least disclose its essential rationale. Otherwise the right of access to the courts would be unacceptably ineffective.
Fennelly J said the defect went beyond missing reasons. The decision didn't refer to the relevant material on FGM in Nigeria, so the court simply didn't know why the Minister had decided as he did.
The dissenting judges would have kept the O'Keeffe test unchanged, and Hardiman J warned against creating a two-tier standard of review.

keys.q: should at least disclose the essential rationale
keys.w: Murray CJ, on reasons

keys.q: the more substantial must be the countervailing considerations
keys.w: Murray CJ, on proportionality

keys.q: simply does not know
keys.w: Fennelly J, on why the decision failed

later: Meadows reset the standard of review in Irish administrative law. Proportionality now forms part of reasonableness where fundamental rights are affected, and decisions must disclose their rationale.
Commentators treat it as having implications for the whole of Irish administrative law, well beyond immigration.
job: Background for immigration enforcement: decisions affecting fundamental rights must be reasoned and proportionate, and deportation orders can be quashed if they aren't.
If a person facing removal raises a new risk, such as FGM or trafficking, record it and pass it on at once. It may require the decision to be reconsidered.
The same lesson applies to your own decisions: record your reasons, especially when a decision affects someone's rights.
Meadows v Minister for Justice, Equality.law: Yes. Meadows (2010) is the leading authority on proportionality and reasons in Irish judicial review.

bg: A driver gave an evidential breath test under the Road Traffic Act 1994 regime. The apparatus printed the two statements, and the garda asked the driver to sign them before the garda had signed them.
The District Court dismissed the drink-driving charge, holding that the statement wasn't 'duly completed'. At the DPP's request it stated a case to the High Court.

Section 17 of the 1994 Act required the garda to supply two identical statements, 'duly completed' in the prescribed manner, and the driver then had to sign them when asked; refusing was an offence. Under s.21, a duly completed statement was evidence of the alcohol level, and the 1999 Regulations required the garda to sign.
DPP v Freeman (2014).q: Is a breath statement 'duly completed', so that its presumption of accuracy applies, if the driver signs it before the garda does?
dec: High Court, 21 April 2009 (MacMenamin J): the District Court was right, and the dismissal stood.

Where a mandatory requirement in a penal statute is clearly not met, the certificate can't be used as evidence. Penal statutes are read strictly, and a court shouldn't create or extend criminal liability through a purposive reading.

The statutory sequence matters. The garda's signature completes the statement, and only then does the driver sign. A statement the driver signed first wasn't duly completed, so the s.21 presumption couldn't apply.
The Court followed DPP v Keogh and distinguished DPP v Moorehouse.
Supreme Court, 25 March 2014: in an ex tempore ruling, the Court took the same view.

keys.q: the far end of the spectrum of insistence on the letter
keys.w: O'Malley J in Hodgins (2024), describing Freeman

later: In DPP v Hodgins [2024] IESC 36 the DPP asked the Supreme Court to overrule Freeman under s.13 of the Road Traffic Act 2010. The Court declined, because Freeman wasn't 'clearly wrong', but said the decision shouldn't be extended by analogy to different facts or legislation.
Contrast Avadenei (2017), where a defect in the printed form was saved by the Interpretation Act 2005.
job: The statements print, you sign both, and only then do you offer them to the driver to sign. Give the driver their copy.
If the driver refuses to sign after you've signed, record it. That's a separate offence.
Check the signatures before you hand anything over. A reversed order can't be fixed afterwards.
DPP v Freeman (2014).law: Yes. Freeman stands, confirmed in Hodgins (2024): the garda must sign first, or the statement is inadmissible.

bg: On 27 May 2007 a man was shot dead at a house party in Blanchardstown, Dublin. The prosecution said the accused drove the gunman there and away on a stolen motorbike, and then burned the motorbike.

He was interviewed six times in Garda custody, with no solicitor present at any interview. The trial judge found that his constitutional right of access to a solicitor had been 'roundly and flagrantly breached and abused' and excluded most of the interviews.

One part of an interview was admitted, because it came after a brief phone call between him and his solicitor. A protected witness in the Witness Security Programme also gave evidence. In 2008 a jury convicted him of murder by 10 to 2, and he was sentenced to life imprisonment.
People (DPP) v Ryan (2011).q: Once the right of access to a solicitor has been breached, are admissions made after the suspect finally gets advice still tainted? And what follows if the jury isn't properly warned about a protected witness?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 11 March 2011 (Murray CJ, with Budd and Edwards JJ): the conviction was quashed and a retrial ordered.

The decisive ground was the corroboration warning. The trial judge had warned the jury about the benefits the protected witness received, but hadn't given the specific warning about convicting on that evidence without corroboration that the Supreme Court required in Gilligan. That fundamentally affected how the jury deliberated, so the verdict wasn't safe.

On solicitor access, the Court of Appeal later described the 2011 Court's views as consistent with admitting what followed the solicitor's call. That follows O'Brien (2005): the unlawfulness caused by denying access lasts only while access is denied.

Murray CJ observed that findings that the right of access had been breached were by no means unusual in criminal trials. He called for a uniform practice or protocol so that arrested people can routinely reach a solicitor.

keys.q: roundly and flagrantly breached and abused
keys.w: trial judge, on the right of access (quoted on appeal)

keys.q: fundamentally affected the manner in which the jury deliberated
keys.w: Murray CJ, on the missing corroboration warning

keys.q: by no means an unusual ruling
keys.w: Murray CJ, on findings of breaches of access

later: At the retrial in March 2013 he was convicted again, by 10 to 2. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in 2016 ([2016] IECA 147). It held that the trial judge was entitled to admit the later admissions, and that disputed facts about solicitor access were for the trial judge.

The law on access has moved on. Gormley and White (2014) require that a suspect who asks for a solicitor gets advice before questioning, and solicitors may now attend interviews. Commentators (Conway and Daly) criticise the idea that a breach can be 'cured' by brief later access, and contrast the European Court of Human Rights, which has rejected it.
job: When a suspect asks for a solicitor, record every attempt to reach one, and don't question until they've had a real chance to consult.
If access has been delayed or denied, anything said in that period is at serious risk. Don't rely on a later brief call to 'cure' it.
With a protected witness, gather independent corroboration from the start. The jury must be warned about convicting without it.
People (DPP) v Ryan (2011).law: Partly. Ryan is still cited with O'Brien on whether later admissions are tainted, but Gormley and White (2014) now require legal advice before questioning.

bg: In 1926 a gardener told the gardaí that the house where he worked was on fire. Six people were found dead inside, and medical evidence showed they had died before the fire started.
He was indicted for each of the six deaths but tried for one murder. He was convicted and sentenced to death.

Between 1 and 12 April 1926, while not under arrest, he had made statements to gardaí in answer to their questions. On appeal he argued that those statements should have been excluded because they weren't in his exact words, and that the jury should have been told to keep the evidence of the other five deaths separate.
Attorney General v McCabe.q: Is a statement inadmissible just because it was made in answer to Garda questions, or without a caution, or isn't recorded in the suspect's exact words?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 3 December 1927 (Kennedy CJ delivering judgment): the grounds failed.
A statement isn't inadmissible merely because it was made in answer to police questions, or because no caution was given. Admissibility is for the trial judge's discretion in all the circumstances.
The statement must be voluntary, though it needn't have been volunteered.
Recording the suspect's exact words is desirable but not a legal requirement. A statement that isn't in his exact words isn't automatically excluded, though the judge can take that into account.
The evidence about the fire and all six bodies was relevant to the prosecution case and was properly left to the jury.

keys.q: voluntary, though not necessarily volunteered
keys.w: headnote, on the test for a statement

later: McCabe is an early foundation of the Irish voluntariness rule. Later cases built the modern test on it, notably Shaw (1982) and Doyle (2017).
Questioning in custody is now governed by the Custody Regulations 1987, the caution, electronic recording and access to a solicitor, so the exact words are now captured on video.
job: Questioning isn't unlawful in itself, but every answer must be voluntary: no threats, promises or pressure.
Caution as soon as you suspect the person of an offence. An answer to an uncautioned question invites a challenge, even if it isn't automatically excluded.
Record what's said in the person's own words, as close to verbatim as you can and as soon as possible. Here the defence attacked statements that weren't in his exact words.
Attorney General v McCabe.law: Yes, as a foundation. McCabe's core points (questioning isn't unlawful in itself, and statements must be voluntary) still underpin the law, but the detailed rules now come from the Custody Regulations, recording and the right to a solicitor.

bg: The owner and the manager of a Dublin clothing company bought textiles from a man who became the prosecution's chief witness. The goods turned out to be stolen.

They were tried in the Dublin Circuit Court in 1944 on 21 counts. Both were convicted of receiving stolen goods and of offences under the wartime Emergency Powers legislation, and were sentenced to imprisonment and fines.

They said they had bought the goods believing he had come by them honestly. The trial judge told the jury to acquit on the receiving charges if that explanation might reasonably be true, and to convict if it might not.
People (AG) v Berber and Levey.q: When is a buyer of stolen goods guilty of receiving them? Is 'ordinary prudence' the test of guilty knowledge? And what follows if the accomplice warning is inadequate?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 6 July 1944 (Black J giving the Court's judgment): the convictions were confirmed.
Ordinary prudence isn't the test of guilty knowledge. The question is what the accused actually knew, not what a careful buyer ought to have realised.
The warning to the jury about acting on the evidence of the chief witness, an accomplice, was insufficient. But the Court was satisfied that no miscarriage of justice resulted.
The Court didn't decide a separate objection to the form of the indictment.
later: Later cited (in DPP v Noonan) for the principle that where a judge gives inconsistent directions on a vital matter, it's impossible to be sure the jury wasn't misled.

Handling is now governed by s.17 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001. The mental element is knowing the property was stolen or being reckless as to whether it was. Knowledge or recklessness can be inferred from the circumstances unless there is a reasonable doubt (s.17(2)).
So the modern offence reaches some buyers that a pure knowledge test wouldn't: recklessness is enough.
job: When a suspect explains how they came by goods, record the explanation exactly and check it: who sold them, where, the price, any receipt. If it might reasonably be true, the prosecution can fail.
Gather the circumstances that show knowledge or recklessness under s.17(2): a price far below value, a sale in a car park, no receipt, removed labels or serial numbers.
If the seller is your witness, treat him as an accomplice and look for corroboration, because the jury must be warned.
People (AG) v Berber and Levey.law: Partly. Still cited on jury directions and accomplice warnings, but the mental element for handling is now set by s.17 of the 2001 Act, which includes recklessness.

bg: In July 1981 three armed men tried to rob a building society branch in north London. One carried a pistol and another a sawn-off shotgun, which was fired at the security screen.

The alarm set off two security cameras, which took photographs every half-second and clearly showed the men, often facing a camera. The two accused were arrested months later: one admitted being there, and the other made admissions in interview.

At their 1982 trial the defence argued that the jury shouldn't see the photographs, which it said were prejudicial and of little value. The judge admitted them, and the jury compared them with the men in the dock. Both were convicted of attempted robbery and possessing a firearm with intent.
R v Dodson.q: Can a jury compare security-camera photographs taken at the scene with the accused in the dock, without a witness identifying them?
dec: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), 12 April 1984 (Watkins LJ, with Park and Jupp JJ). Leave to appeal was granted because there was no authority on the point.

As later courts, including the Irish Court of Criminal Appeal, have read it, Dodson holds that photographs taken by security cameras during a crime are admissible, and that the jury may compare them with the accused to decide whether it's the same person.
The Court declined to lay down a fixed formula for directing the jury. A suitable warning about the risks of identifying someone from photographs may still be needed, depending on the circumstances.
later: Followed in Ireland in People (DPP) v Maguire (1995). The jury may identify the accused from CCTV footage and stills, but the usual identification warnings apply, and relying on footage alone is unsatisfactory.
When a witness who knows the accused recognises them on footage, that is recognition evidence, and the Casey warning applies to it as well.
job: Seize the original footage and stills early, with full continuity: who recovered them, from which system, and the time offset.
Don't rely on the footage alone. Look for supporting evidence: clothing, phones, admissions, forensics.
If a garda or witness recognises someone on footage, record how well they know the person and the viewing conditions, because the identification warning will apply.
R v Dodson.law: English authority, followed in Ireland in Maguire (1995): a jury may compare CCTV stills with the accused, with appropriate warnings.

vLex Ireland — DPP v Maguire

bg: A 21-year-old farm labourer's wife had left him. He took a shotgun from his employer, sawed off the barrel and went to her mother's house, where he shot her dead.
He said he had meant only to frighten her by threatening to kill himself if she didn't come back, and that the gun went off by accident while he was showing it to her. He was charged with murder.

At the first trial the jury couldn't agree. At the retrial the judge told the jury that, once the prosecution had proved the killing, it was for the accused to show it was an accident. He was convicted and sentenced to death, and the Court of Criminal Appeal refused leave to appeal, relying on an 18th-century statement of the law.
Woolmington v DPP.q: When an accused says a killing was an accident, does he have to prove it, or must the prosecution disprove it?
dec: House of Lords, 23 May 1935 (Viscount Sankey LC, with Lords Hewart, Atkin, Tomlin and Wright; unanimous): conviction quashed.
Throughout the criminal law, it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the accused's guilt. The only exceptions are the defence of insanity and statutory exceptions.

If, at the end of the case, the evidence as a whole, whether it comes from the prosecution or the defence, leaves a reasonable doubt about whether the killing was intentional, the accused is entitled to be acquitted.
The old authorities came from a time when an accused couldn't even give evidence in his own defence, which was allowed only from 1898. The principle couldn't be whittled down.
He was released three days before his scheduled execution.

keys.q: it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt
keys.w: Viscount Sankey LC

keys.q: no attempt to whittle it down can be entertained
keys.w: Viscount Sankey LC, on the principle

later: The principle is part of Irish law. In O'Leary v AG (1995) the Supreme Court held that the presumption of innocence is implicit in the guarantee of a trial in due course of law (Article 38.1). A statute can shift an evidential burden onto the accused, but not the legal burden of proof.
The same principle is in Article 6(2) ECHR: everyone charged with a criminal offence is presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.
job: Investigate the suspect's account, don't just record it. If they say it was an accident or self-defence, the prosecution will have to disprove it beyond reasonable doubt once there's evidence of it.
Gather the evidence that tests the defence: forensics (range, trajectory, how the weapon works), witnesses to what was said, and the history between the people involved.
Never tell a suspect they have to prove their innocence.
Woolmington v DPP.law: Yes. Woolmington is still the foundation of the burden of proof, and in Ireland the presumption of innocence is also constitutional (O'Leary v AG, 1995).

bg: After a 1986 takeover, Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) inspectors investigated share dealings linked to it.

Under s.434 of the Companies Act 1985, a person questioned by inspectors had to answer, refusing was punishable, and the answers could be used in evidence. Between February and June 1987 the company's former chief executive answered questions in nine interviews.

The prosecution used those answers at his criminal trial, and in 1989–90 he was convicted on twelve counts of conspiracy, false accounting and theft. His challenges under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 and his appeals failed.
Saunders v UK.q: Can answers a person was compelled to give to inspectors, under threat of penalty, be used against him at his criminal trial?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 17 December 1996: Article 6(1) was violated, by 16 votes to 4.

The right to silence and the privilege against self-incrimination lie at the heart of a fair procedure. The prosecution must prove its case without evidence obtained through coercion or oppression in defiance of the accused's will.
The public interest in tackling complex corporate fraud can't justify using compelled answers to incriminate the accused at trial.

The privilege doesn't extend to material that exists independently of the suspect's will, such as documents obtained under a warrant, breath, blood and urine samples, and bodily tissue for DNA testing.
The Court didn't decide whether the right to silence is absolute.

keys.q: the public interest cannot be invoked
keys.w: ECtHR, on using compelled answers at trial

keys.q: existence independent of the will of the suspect
keys.w: ECtHR, on what the privilege doesn't cover

later: In the UK, s.434 was amended by the Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999 to limit the use of compelled answers at trial.
The privilege isn't absolute. In Brown v Stott the UK courts allowed a compelled answer about who was driving to be used, under s.172 of the Road Traffic Act 1988.
Read with Heaney v Ireland on the duty to account for movements under s.52 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939.
job: Statutory powers to compel information (from inspectors, regulators, or some Garda powers) aren't a short cut to admissions. Using compelled answers to prove guilt can make the trial unfair.
Caution and interview a suspect under the normal rules. Get documents and samples, which fall outside the privilege, under a warrant or statutory power.
Where a statute requires a person to give information (such as who was driving), follow its exact procedure, and get advice on how the answer can be used.
Saunders v UK.law: Yes. Saunders (1996) is still the leading Strasbourg case on using compelled answers at trial, though the privilege isn't absolute.

bg: An antiques dealer was prosecuted for handling stolen goods. At his trial the prosecution admitted that some of its evidence came from tapping his phone under a warrant issued by the Home Secretary.

He sued the Metropolitan Police Commissioner. In 1979 the English High Court held that the tapping was lawful, because nothing in English law made it unlawful, and that the Convention couldn't be enforced in English courts. The judge said the matter called for legislation.
He also complained that the Post Office had 'metered' his calls, recording the numbers he dialled, and passed the records to the police.
Malone v UK.q: Were police phone tapping and the release of call records 'in accordance with the law' under Article 8?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (plenary), 2 August 1984: Article 8 was violated, unanimously.

Tapping interfered with private life and correspondence. 'In accordance with the law' doesn't just refer back to domestic law: it concerns the quality of the law, which must be compatible with the rule of law.

Because secret surveillance carries an obvious risk of arbitrariness, the law must be clear enough to show people when and how the authorities may intercept. That doesn't mean a person must be able to foresee when they'll be tapped.

English law on interception was obscure and open to differing interpretations. It didn't indicate with reasonable clarity the scope and manner of the authorities' discretion, so the minimum legal protection was missing.

Metering: the numbers dialled are part of a telephone communication. Releasing them to the police without consent interfered with Article 8, and because no legal rules governed the practice, it wasn't in accordance with the law either. The Court found it unnecessary to rule on Article 13.

keys.q: relates to the quality of the law
keys.w: ECtHR (para 67), on 'in accordance with the law'

keys.q: somewhat obscure and open to differing interpretations
keys.w: ECtHR, on the English rules

later: The UK passed the Interception of Communications Act 1985, later replaced by the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.
With Klass v Germany (1978), Malone set the standard for surveillance law across Europe: clear, accessible rules and effective safeguards against abuse.

In Ireland, interception is governed by the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) Act 1993. In DPP v Dillon (2002) the Court of Criminal Appeal excluded evidence from an unlawful interception: an interception that is unlawful can't become lawful because of what is heard.
job: Intercepting calls or messages needs a ministerial authorisation under the 1993 Act. Never listen to or record someone's calls without it.
Get call records and other retained data through the statutory scheme (now with court orders under the 2022 Act), not informally from a provider.
Taking calls on a seized phone, or reading new messages as they arrive, may amount to interception. Get advice first.
Malone v UK.law: Yes. Malone (1984) is still a leading authority on the quality of law that surveillance requires.

bg: In late November 1988 an 81-year-old widow was alone at home. One man asked her for water while a second man, with a bedspread over his head, came into the house. About £850 kept in a tea canister was later found missing, and she had a bad fright.

Her description was limited: a stout, fair-haired man, but she couldn't give his height or age. Gardaí linked the accused to a red car she had seen outside, and detained him under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984.

About two months later gardaí drove her to Edgeworthstown. Of a man on the street she first said she thought that was him, but that she hadn't got a good look at him. Later, outside the courthouse, she identified the accused. No parade was held: the investigating garda, with 23 years' service, had never held one and thought an informal identification was more beneficial to a defendant. No details of the other people on the street were recorded.
He was convicted of larceny in Mullingar Circuit Court in November 1989 and sentenced to four years' penal servitude. Identification was the only issue at the trial.
People (DPP) v O'Reilly.q: Should a formal identification parade have been held instead of an informal street identification? And how must the judge warn the jury?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 26 April 1990 (O'Flaherty J, with Barr and Lavan JJ): the conviction was quashed.

No rule of law or practice requires a parade in every case, but the circumstances of a case may require one. Here fair procedures required a formal parade, and the reason given for not holding one was unsatisfactory.
An accused may be seriously inhibited in challenging the fairness of an informal identification at trial, not least because he is unlikely even to know it took place.

The identification warning required by Casey (No 2) must be related to the particular circumstances in which the witness saw the accused. The trial judge should have stressed the weaknesses of this identification in more detail.

keys.q: the circumstances of a case may require the holding of an identification parade
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal

keys.q: fair procedures required that a formal identification parade should have been held
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on this case

keys.q: relate the general warning to the particular facts
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on the Casey warning

later: Still followed, and cited in People (DPP) v Lee (2004).
Read with Casey (No 2) on the warning, and with Maguire (1995) on identification from CCTV.
job: If you have a suspect and a witness who might identify them, arrange a formal identification parade. Don't bring the witness to a street or courthouse to 'see if they spot him'.

If a parade genuinely isn't possible (for example, the suspect refuses or there are no suitable volunteers), record why. Record everything about any other identification: who was present, how many people, and what was said.
Take the witness's first description in detail before any identification. Its weaknesses will shape the judge's warning.
People (DPP) v O'Reilly.law: Yes. O'Reilly is still followed on when a formal parade is required and on tailoring the identification warning.

bg: The accused was charged with murder. He said he had been defending himself against a violent and felonious attack.

The Supreme Court had to decide how a jury should be directed when self-defence is raised against a murder charge, and in particular what follows if the accused used more force than was reasonably necessary.
The free reports don't give the detailed facts or the final order. The principle below is as the Supreme Court described it in DPP v Crawford (2024).
People (AG) v Dwyer.q: If an accused honestly believes force is necessary to defend himself but uses more force than is reasonable, is he guilty of murder?
dec: Supreme Court, 1972, reported at [1972] IR 416.
Self-defence against a murder charge has two sides. Whether the accused honestly believed force was necessary is judged subjectively. Whether the force used was reasonable is judged objectively.

If the force was reasonably necessary, the accused is entitled to be acquitted. If he honestly believed it was necessary but it was more than was reasonable, he lacks the intention required for murder, and the proper verdict is manslaughter. This is the 'partial defence' of excessive self-defence.
Dwyer left unclear whether reasonableness is measured against the circumstances as they actually were or as the accused believed them to be.

keys.q: partly subjective and partly objective
keys.w: Donnelly J in Crawford (2024), on the s.18 test

keys.q: the issue remains whether the accused genuinely held that belief
keys.w: Supreme Court in Crawford (2024)

later: In DPP v Crawford [2024] IESC 44 the Supreme Court held that s.22 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997 abolished the common law defences, including Dwyer's, in fatal cases too. The statutory defence of lawful use of force in s.18 now applies to murder.

Under s.18 the accused must honestly believe that the force was necessary, even if that belief was unreasonable, and the force must be reasonable in the circumstances as he believed them to be. Whether there were reasonable grounds for the belief helps the jury decide whether it was honestly held.
Dwyer still explains why an honest belief combined with excessive force gives manslaughter, not murder.
job: In any self-defence claim, record exactly what the suspect says they believed and why, as early as possible. The honesty of that belief is often the whole case.
Gather everything that bears on the circumstances as the suspect saw them: the threat, any weapons, injuries on both sides, the sequence of events, the lighting, and what witnesses saw.
Don't decide self-defence yourself. Investigate it fully and put everything in the file for the DPP.
People (AG) v Dwyer.law: Partly superseded. Since Crawford (2024), s.18 of the 1997 Act governs self-defence in murder cases, but Dwyer still explains why honest but excessive force gives manslaughter.

bg: In October 1990 a bomb at a British Army and RUC checkpoint in Co. Derry killed six people. Gardaí arrested seven men at a house nearby under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939, on suspicion of IRA membership and involvement in the bombing, and held them at Letterkenny Garda Station.

After being cautioned, the two applicants refused to answer questions. Gardaí then required them under s.52 to give a full account of their movements, which it was an offence to refuse. They still refused.
In 1991 the Special Criminal Court acquitted them of IRA membership but convicted them under s.52, and they served six months. They challenged s.52 as unconstitutional.
Heaney v Ireland.q: Can the State make it a crime to refuse to account for your movements while detained? Is that compatible with the right to silence?
dec: High Court, 29 June 1994 (Costello J): s.52 was a proportionate restriction on the right to silence. He applied a proportionality test adapted from the Canadian case R v Oakes, which is still the standard Irish test for restrictions on constitutional rights.

Supreme Court, 23 July 1996 (O'Flaherty J): appeal dismissed. The right to silence isn't absolute. The State may restrict it to keep public peace and order, provided the restriction affects the right as little as possible, and s.52 struck a proportionate balance. A citizen's wish to stand on principle must yield to the State's right to protect itself.

European Court of Human Rights, 21 December 2000 (Heaney and McGuinness v Ireland, unanimous): Article 6(1) and 6(2) were violated. The threat of prison for staying silent was compulsion that destroyed the very essence of the privilege against self-incrimination and the right to silence, and security concerns couldn't justify a provision that extinguished it.
Uncertainty about whether s.52 answers could be used in later trials, and conflicting information from the police during the interviews, made matters worse. Each applicant was awarded IEP 4,000.

keys.q: must yield to the right of the State to protect itself
keys.w: Supreme Court (1996), on the right to silence

keys.q: destroyed the very essence of their privilege against self-incrimination
keys.w: ECtHR (para 55)

keys.q: cannot justify a provision which extinguishes the very essence
keys.w: ECtHR (para 58), on security concerns

later: Quinn v Ireland, decided by Strasbourg the same day, reached the same result.
Section 52 is still on the statute book, but after Strasbourg, using it to compel answers, or prosecuting someone for refusing, is very risky.
Read with Saunders v UK (1996) on compelled answers.
job: Before using a power to demand an account, such as s.52, get guidance. Answers compelled under threat of prison are fragile evidence, and prosecuting a refusal may breach Article 6.

Prefer the inference provisions (ss.18, 19 and 19A of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, and s.2 of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1998 for membership). They come with statutory safeguards: a proper warning, legal advice and recording.
Record exactly how any demand was put, the caution given, and what the person was told about how their answers could be used. Conflicting information made things worse here.
Heaney v Ireland.law: Partly. Heaney is still the source of the Irish proportionality test, but Strasbourg found the s.52 compulsion breached Article 6, so it should be used with great caution, if at all.

bg: In 1998 the accused was on trial in the Special Criminal Court for murder. The Garda investigation had taken about 3,500 statements from about 1,350 people. Everything not in the book of evidence was made available for inspection, except 40 statements from 20 people, over which the prosecution claimed privilege.

A senior garda said disclosure could put the informants and their families at risk of serious harm. The withheld statements fell into three groups: confidential information relevant to the case and prejudicial to the accused; information about his alleged involvement in other crime; and background on criminal gangs with no bearing on the killing.

The Special Criminal Court ordered that the first group be shown to the defence lawyers only, on condition that they didn't reveal the contents to the accused. The DPP sought judicial review, and in March 1998 the High Court (Carney J) quashed that order, holding that the trial court should review the documents itself. The accused appealed to the Supreme Court.
DPP v Special Criminal Court (Ward).q: When can the prosecution withhold informant material from the defence? And can a court let the defence lawyers see it on condition that they don't tell their client?
dec: Supreme Court, 20 July 1998 (O'Flaherty J): the appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's order stood.

Informer privilege is of ancient origin and remains intact, subject only to the 'innocence at stake' exception: where the material could help show the accused's innocence, it must be disclosed or the prosecution abandoned.
An order letting the defence lawyers see material while forbidding them to tell their client was an unprecedented and wholly undesirable breach of the duty counsel owe their client.

Neither the gardaí nor prosecuting counsel can be the final judge of what would help the defence. The trial court can examine the documents itself where necessary, and prosecuting counsel must ensure the trial is fair overall.

keys.q: of ancient origin
keys.w: Supreme Court, on informer privilege

keys.q: subject only to the innocence at stake exception
keys.w: Supreme Court

keys.q: unprecedented and wholly undesirable breach
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the lawyers-only order

later: Still the leading Irish authority on informer privilege in criminal trials.
In Donohoe v Ireland (ECtHR, 12 December 2013) Strasbourg held that a claim of privilege over the sources of a senior garda's belief evidence in a membership trial didn't make the trial unfair.
job: Keep informant identities and material separate from the main investigation file, marked as sensitive, and flag them to the prosecutor.
Don't decide yourself what would or wouldn't help the defence. Give it all to the prosecution, which raises the privilege, and expect the judge to read the material.
If informant material could help show the accused's innocence, the choice is disclosure or dropping the case. Plan for that early with the prosecutor and the informant handlers.
DPP v Special Criminal Court (Ward).law: Yes. Ward is still the leading Irish case on informer privilege and the innocence-at-stake exception.

bg: A man was stabbed to death in a Limerick pub in February 1991. Two days later the accused was arrested and detained at Ennis Garda Station under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984.

He refused to agree in writing to the overnight suspension of questioning, which would have stopped the detention clock, so his first six hours ran out at 8.35 a.m. He was kept in custody anyway, an extension was purportedly made later that day, and an identification parade was held at which witnesses picked him out.

He was charged, released by order of the District Court and re-arrested, and further identifications took place. The trial judge held that all the identification procedures had happened while he was in unlawful custody, and excluded them.

The prosecution then relied on seven witnesses who identified him in the dock. The judge admitted those identifications, left their weight to the jury and refused to withdraw the case. The dock identifications were the only evidence connecting him to the killing, and he was convicted of murder.
People (DPP) v Cooney.q: Where identification parades are excluded because they took place during unlawful detention, can the same witnesses identify the accused in the dock? And can a conviction rest on that alone?
dec: Supreme Court, 29 May 1997 (Keane J for the Court; Hamilton CJ, Denham, Barrington and Murphy JJ). The Court of Criminal Appeal had refused leave but certified the question.
The trial judge's discretion to admit the dock identifications and leave them to the jury was correctly exercised in the circumstances.

There was no bad faith in the breach of the accused's constitutional rights, and those rights had been vindicated by excluding the parade evidence. The issue was whether the dock identifications were irremediably tainted by the earlier unlawful ones, and on these facts the trial judge was entitled to find they weren't. So the case didn't have to be withdrawn from the jury.
Evidence later ruled inadmissible doesn't retrospectively invalidate the return for trial.

keys.q: irremediably tainted
keys.w: the issue the Supreme Court had to decide

keys.q: sole evidence connecting the accused with the offence of murder
keys.w: the certified question

later: Cited in People (DPP) v Lee (2004). Under JC (2015), the question would now be framed as whether the breach of rights was deliberate and conscious, or inadvertent.
A dock identification on its own is weak, because the accused is obviously the person in the dock. Read with Casey (No 2) and O'Reilly (1990) on the warning and on parades.
job: Watch the detention clock. An identification parade held after lawful detention has run out can be excluded, and your best identification evidence with it.
If you want questioning suspended overnight, get the person's written consent and record it. Without it, the clock keeps running.
Hold a proper parade while detention is lawful. A dock identification on its own is a weak substitute.
People (DPP) v Cooney.law: Yes, read with JC (2015). Cooney is still cited on dock identification after unlawful parades.

bg: On the night of a murder, 19 December 1981, the accused arrived at Claremorris Garda Station at about 10 p.m. He stayed overnight, and at about 10 a.m. the next morning he made an incriminating statement.

The defence said he had been held against his will rather than staying voluntarily, which bore on whether his constitutional rights were breached. It also raised whether he had repeatedly asked for a solicitor and been refused, and whether a meeting with a co-accused had been his own idea or forced on him.

The trial judge left none of these matters to the jury, and in January 1984 he was convicted of murder. The Court of Criminal Appeal refused leave but certified two questions: when are disputed facts that go to admissibility for the jury, and at what stage of the trial should they be decided?
People (DPP) v Conroy (1986).q: Who decides the disputed facts on which the admissibility of a confession depends, the judge or the jury? And when?
dec: Supreme Court, 31 July 1986 (Finlay CJ, with Walsh, Henchy, Griffin and Hederman JJ): the conviction was quashed and a new trial ordered.
An issue of fact on which the admissibility of a statement depends is for the trial judge alone, after hearing the evidence in the absence of the jury (a voir dire).
If the statement is admitted, the weight to give it is for the jury alone.
The Court reconsidered People v Lynch (1982), which had suggested that a conflict of evidence about custody should be decided by the jury.
Because the trial judge had refused to investigate whether the accused was in unlawful custody, the trial was unsatisfactory.

keys.q: should be determined for that purpose by the trial judge alone
keys.w: Finlay CJ, on admissibility

keys.q: a matter for the jury only
keys.w: Finlay CJ, on the weight of an admitted statement

later: The voir dire, in which the judge decides admissibility with the jury absent, is now standard wherever a statement is challenged.
Read with Lynch (1982) on 'voluntary' attendance at a station, and with Healy (1990) and Kenny (1990) on unlawful custody and access to a solicitor.
job: Expect to give evidence twice: first in the voir dire, with the jury absent, on how the statement was obtained and whether custody was lawful, and then before the jury.
If someone is 'helping' at the station, be clear about whether they're free to leave, and record it. Voluntary attendance that turns into detention without an arrest is a classic challenge.
Record every request for a solicitor and every contact with a co-accused, with the times and who asked for it.
People (DPP) v Conroy (1986).law: Yes. Conroy is still the rule: the judge decides admissibility in the jury's absence, and the jury decides weight.

bg: A farmer faced 42 District Court charges under regulations to protect cattle from brucellosis, for unlawfully moving cattle and failing to keep registers and identity cards. If the penalties ran consecutively, he faced up to two years in prison, plus fines.

He was granted legal aid, but for a solicitor only. Under s.2 of the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, counsel could be assigned in the District Court only on a murder charge. The prosecution was represented by both a solicitor and counsel.

He challenged s.2 and sought a declaration that the scheme was incompatible with the ECHR. The High Court accepted the case was more complex than usual, but found no evidence that a solicitor couldn't defend him adequately, and refused relief. The Irish Human Rights Commission appeared as amicus curiae.
Carmody v Minister for Justice.q: Does an accused have a constitutional right to legal aid for a barrister in a District Court case that needs one?
dec: Supreme Court, 23 October 2009 (Murray CJ for the Court; Denham, Hardiman, Geoghegan and Fennelly JJ agreeing).
The constitutional issue came first, because a declaration of incompatibility under the ECHR Act 2003 wouldn't give him an enforceable remedy.

Criminal legal aid is a constitutional right. District Court cases are usually short and simple, but the court's criminal jurisdiction has grown a great deal since 1962, with higher penalties and complex regulatory and EU-based offences.

Equality of arms doesn't require identical representation. But where representation by both solicitor and counsel is essential in the interests of justice, because of the gravity or complexity of the case or other exceptional circumstances, an accused without means must have it.

The 1962 Act itself wasn't unconstitutional. The gap was the State's failure to provide a way to apply for counsel. The Court declared that he had a constitutional right to apply before trial for legal aid including counsel, and to have that decided on its merits, and stopped the prosecution until he had that chance.

keys.q: was a denial of a constitutional right
keys.w: Murray CJ, on refusing him the chance to apply

keys.q: essential in the interests of justice
keys.w: Murray CJ, the threshold for counsel

keys.q: essential for public confidence
keys.w: Murray CJ, on an effective defence

later: Since Carmody, District Court judges can assign counsel on legal aid where a case meets the threshold, though solicitor-only legal aid is still the norm.
job: In a complex or serious District Court case, expect the defence to have counsel on legal aid, and prepare the file and your evidence to that standard.
Regulatory prosecutions (animal health, environmental, licensing) can be complex. Make sure the file explains the regulations clearly.
Carmody v Minister for Justice.law: Yes. Carmody (2009) is current: an accused can apply for legal aid counsel in the District Court where the case requires it.

bg: In November 2008 the accused was charged with assault causing harm after an assault in a pub. The victim needed extensive stitches, and the people involved knew each other. The accused's brother, charged with common assault over the same incident, was awaiting sentence.

The DPP opposed bail on the ground that witnesses were at risk of interference. Gardaí gave evidence that witnesses had been intimidated before the brother's trial: one witness's tyres were slashed, and a statement was withdrawn. The witnesses weren't in court, and much of the evidence was hearsay.
Over the defence's objection, the High Court heard the evidence provisionally (de bene esse) and refused bail. The accused appealed.
DPP v McLoughlin.q: On a bail objection based on witness interference, what must the court be satisfied of? And can it rely on hearsay from gardaí?
dec: Supreme Court, 31 July 2009 (Denham J, with Hardiman and Geoghegan JJ): the appeal was allowed and the bail application sent back to the High Court.
The test isn't whether gardaí fear for the witnesses. The court must itself be satisfied that there is a real probability of interference with witnesses, and must say so expressly.

Following McGinley (1998), where there is evidence of a probable risk of interference, the right to liberty can yield to the public interest, and hearsay may be admitted if there are sufficient grounds for not calling the witnesses. But hearsay is admissible in a bail application only quite exceptionally.

Hardiman J stressed that hearsay from an unknown source can't be tested by cross-examination, and the court can't see the absent witness's demeanour. The weight of such evidence is for the judge, who should be careful how much weight it is given.

keys.q: The test is not whether the members of An Garda Síochána have fears
keys.w: Supreme Court, on witness interference

keys.q: may be admissible in a bail application, but quite exceptionally
keys.w: Denham J, on hearsay

later: Still followed on hearsay and witness-interference objections at bail.
Since the Bail Act 1997, bail can also be refused to prevent serious offences (s.2), but the O'Callaghan grounds, including interference with witnesses, still apply and must be proved by evidence.
job: When objecting to bail on witness interference, bring specific evidence: dates, what was said or done, by whom, and how you know.
Where possible, bring the witness or a statement from them. If you have to give hearsay, explain why the witness can't come to court (for example, fear).
Don't just say gardaí are 'concerned'. The court has to find a real probability of interference for itself.
DPP v McLoughlin.law: Yes. McLoughlin (2009) is still followed: hearsay at bail only exceptionally, and the court must itself find a real probability of interference.

bg: In the early hours of 4 April 1953, business premises on James's Street, Dublin, were broken into and property was stolen. A garda on duty saw two men on a shed roof. One jumped into the yard; the other, caught in barbed wire, freed himself and jumped down. A struggle followed for at least five or six minutes, the garda was seriously injured, and the men escaped.
A second garda arrived, shone a torch on the face of a man on the roof and called on him to come down. Neither garda had known the men before.

About a year later both suspects refused to take part in an identification parade at the Bridewell. Each was then brought in separately and stood near or in the middle of a group of men, and the first garda picked each of them out. When the accused was arrested in a cinema, he was brought to the porch, where the second garda identified him.

At his trial for store-breaking, larceny and wounding with intent to resist arrest, the defence asked for a directed acquittal, arguing that a proper identification parade was essential and hadn't been held. The judge refused.
People (AG) v Martin.q: Is a formal identification parade legally required before identification evidence can go to the jury?
dec: Supreme Court, 28 May 1956 (Lavery, Kingsmill Moore, O'Daly, Maguire and Dixon JJ).
There is no positive rule of law or practice of general application requiring an identification parade. Each case must be considered on its own evidence and circumstances.
So the absence of a parade, especially where the suspect has refused one, doesn't automatically make identification evidence inadmissible. Its weight is a matter for the jury.
The free report doesn't set out the Court's full reasoning on the informal identifications or the final order.

keys.q: There is no positive rule of law or practice of general application
keys.w: Supreme Court, on identification parades

keys.q: Each case must be considered on the evidence adduced
keys.w: Supreme Court

later: People v Marley (1985) relied on Martin for the point that identification evidence carries less weight where the suspect refused to take part in a parade.
O'Reilly (1990) built on Martin: there is no universal rule, but the circumstances of a case may require a formal parade, and fair procedures did in that case. Lee (2004) is to the same effect.
The identification warning required by Casey (No 2) (1963) applies to informal identifications too.
job: Offer a formal parade wherever a suspect is known and available. If they refuse, record exactly what was offered, the refusal and the reasons given.
If you have to fall back on another method, make it as fair as possible, with the suspect among people of similar appearance, and record who was there and what was said.
Don't confront a witness with a lone suspect (for example, in a doorway or cell) if a parade is possible. That kind of identification is the weakest of all.
People (AG) v Martin.law: Partly. Martin is still cited for 'no fixed rule', but O'Reilly (1990) and Lee (2004) show the courts will expect a formal parade where one is possible.

bg: In February 1984 a car was stolen from outside the owner's home in Templeogue. He jumped onto the bonnet to stop it, and the thieves drove him some distance before he got down. He was threatened and assaulted, and said he could identify the driver and the front-seat passenger.

Gardaí took him to a courthouse, where he picked out two youths who were already in court on other charges. His son later identified one of them as the driver. The case rested entirely on these identifications.

A fingerprint on the front passenger window belonged to another man, who gave evidence that he had been the front passenger. Both youths, aged 17, were nonetheless convicted in 1985 (after a retrial) and jailed for five years. Their appeal was dismissed in 1986.

Evidence about where the fingerprint was found emerged in 1987, and an internal Garda memorandum surfaced in 1991 suggesting the owner had identified one of the youths from police photographs before the courthouse identification. The convictions were quashed in 1995, but the Court of Criminal Appeal at first refused to certify a miscarriage of justice. The Supreme Court directed it to reconsider.
People (DPP) v Meleady (No 3).q: Did the newly discovered facts show a miscarriage of justice, entitling the men to a certificate under s.9 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 20 March 2001 (Geoghegan J, with Kearns and Murphy JJ): a miscarriage of justice was certified under s.9.
Had a jury known where the other man's fingerprint was (on the front passenger window, near the top), they might at least have had a reasonable doubt.

Had the trial judge known about the memorandum, which suggested the owner had already seen a police photograph of one accused before identifying him, the identification evidence wouldn't have been admitted.
The certificate opened the way to a claim for compensation against the State.
later: Known as the 'Tallaght Two' case, it is a leading example of a s.9 miscarriage-of-justice certificate. Read it with the later cases under the 1993 Act.
It shows why identification procedures have to be clean from the start: an identification after a witness has seen a photograph of the suspect is fatally compromised.
job: Never show a witness a photograph of the suspect before an identification procedure. If photographs are used to find a suspect, record exactly what was shown, and tell the prosecutor.
Hold a proper parade. Don't bring a witness to a courthouse to pick someone out.
Record and pass on every finding, including evidence that points away from your suspect, such as a fingerprint belonging to someone else. Non-disclosure can unravel a case decades later.
People (DPP) v Meleady (No 3).law: Yes. Meleady (No 3) is still a leading example of a miscarriage-of-justice certificate under s.9 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993.
