Irish Times — Miscarriage of justice ruled in case of 'Tallaght Two' (March 2001)

bg: The accused struck a man one blow with his fist. The man fell, fractured his skull and died.
The accused said he had acted in self-defence. He was tried in January 1963 and convicted of manslaughter, and the case went to the Supreme Court on how the jury had been directed about self-defence.
The free report gives only the headnote and later cases' descriptions of the judgment, so the bench and the final order aren't confirmed here.
People (AG) v Quinn.q: Who has to prove what when self-defence is raised?
dec: Supreme Court, 18 December 1965 (Walsh J delivered a judgment).
The accused bears only an evidential burden: there must be some evidence of self-defence for the issue to go to the jury (as later cases read Walsh J).

Once the issue is raised, it is a misdirection to tell the jury the defence must 'establish' self-defence. If the evidence leaves the jury in reasonable doubt about whether the accused acted in self-defence, they must acquit.
This is the same principle as Woolmington (1935): the legal burden of proof stays on the prosecution throughout.
later: Cited in DPP v Fitzgerald on the evidential burden, and in DPP v Forsey (2018) on the misdirection and the duty to acquit if there is a doubt.

Self-defence is now governed by s.18 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, which the Supreme Court in Crawford (2024) held applies to murder and other fatal cases too. The burden remains on the prosecution.
Read with Dwyer (1972) on honest but excessive self-defence.
job: Once self-defence is raised, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. Gather the evidence to test it: who struck first, threats, weapons, injuries on both sides, and witness accounts of the build-up.
A single punch can kill. Treat any death after a one-punch assault as a full investigation, with early CCTV and witness canvassing.
Record the suspect's account of why they used force as early as possible, in their own words.
People (AG) v Quinn.law: Yes, on the burden of proof. Quinn is still cited: the prosecution must disprove self-defence once it is raised. The defence itself is now in s.18 of the 1997 Act.

src.t: vLex Ireland — People (AG) v Quinn (SC 1965)
Irish Legal News — Supreme Court: common law defence of lawful use of force abolished by 1997 legislation (Crawford, 2024)

bg: In 1968 West Germany passed the 'G 10' Act, which allowed the authorities to open mail and tap telecommunications secretly to protect against threats to the constitutional order and national security.

There was no routine notification of the person under surveillance and no court review. Instead, surveillance had to be ordered under strict conditions, approved by an independent commission (the G 10 Commission), and overseen by a parliamentary board.
Five lawyers, a prosecutor and a judge challenged the law. They couldn't show they had been watched, because the surveillance was secret.
Klass v Germany.q: Can people complain about secret surveillance without proving it was used on them? And can secret surveillance ever be compatible with Article 8?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (plenary), 6 September 1978: no violation of Articles 6, 8 or 13, unanimously.

Victim status: the applicants could complain without proving they had been watched. Otherwise the right to complain could be reduced to a nullity, because the law itself is a menace to everyone who uses the post and phone.

Article 8: secret surveillance interferes with private life, but it can be necessary in a democratic society facing espionage and terrorism, so long as it is strictly necessary to protect democratic institutions. There must be adequate and effective guarantees against abuse.

Germany's system met that test: strict conditions for surveillance, approval by an independent commission and parliamentary oversight. Judicial control is in principle desirable but not essential. Not telling the person while surveillance continues was acceptable, because notification would defeat its purpose.
Articles 13 and 6: taken together, the available remedies were as effective as possible given the secrecy, and once the person was notified, the courts were open.

keys.q: adequate and effective guarantees against abuse
keys.w: ECtHR (para 50)

keys.q: strictly necessary for safeguarding the democratic institutions
keys.w: ECtHR (para 42)

keys.q: it is in principle desirable to entrust supervisory control to a judge
keys.w: ECtHR (para 56)

later: Klass is the starting point of Strasbourg surveillance law. Malone v UK (1984) added that the law must be clear and accessible, Kennedy v UK (2010) approved a regime with strong oversight, and Big Brother Watch v UK (2021) set 'end-to-end safeguards' for bulk powers.

In Ireland, interception is governed by the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) Act 1993, and other covert surveillance by the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009, both with judicial oversight.
job: Covert surveillance must be authorised under the statute that covers it, by the right person, with written records. Under the 2009 Act that normally means a District Court authorisation, or an approval by a superior officer in urgency.
Keep the paperwork the oversight judge will see: the grounds, the necessity, the proportionality, and when the surveillance started and stopped.
Never improvise surveillance outside the statutory schemes. A lack of safeguards is exactly what makes it unlawful.
Klass v Germany.law: Yes. Klass is still the foundation of Strasbourg law on secret surveillance.

bg: In 1990 the applicant was arrested for drunkenness and held overnight in a police cell with another man, who was found dead the next day with severe injuries. He was charged with murder and said the police had framed him to cover up their own wrongdoing.

His murder conviction was quashed in 1993, and after retrials he was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to nine years. After his release in 1996 he campaigned against miscarriages of justice and ran a removal business.

His business calls were disrupted and he received hoax calls. Suspecting that his post, phone and email were being intercepted, he complained to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), which rejected his complaint.
Kennedy v UK.q: Was the UK's interception regime under RIPA clear enough, and well enough supervised, to comply with Article 8? And were the Investigatory Powers Tribunal's secret procedures fair?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 18 May 2010: no violation of Article 8 or Article 6.
Article 8: domestic law, with the published codes, set out clearly enough how interception warrants were authorised and processed, and how intercepted material was used, shared and destroyed.

The oversight was real. The Interception of Communications Commissioner's reports showed the authorities applied RIPA with diligence and corrected errors, and anyone could complain to the IPT. So any interception of his communications would have been justified under Article 8(2).

Article 6: the IPT's restricted procedures, such as not disclosing whether interception took place, were necessary and proportionate to keep secret surveillance effective against terrorism and serious crime. Broad access to the Tribunal, with no evidential burden on the complainant, meant they didn't impair the very essence of the right.

keys.q: the absence of any evidential burden to be overcome
keys.w: ECtHR (para 190), on access to the IPT

keys.q: did not impair the very essence of the applicant's Article 6 rights
keys.w: ECtHR (para 190)

later: Kennedy is cited as a model of an Article 8-compliant interception regime: clear rules, an independent commissioner and a specialist tribunal.
Big Brother Watch v UK (2021) later found that the UK's bulk interception regime, as opposed to targeted interception, lacked adequate safeguards.
job: Interception is lawful only within the statutory scheme. In Ireland that means a ministerial authorisation under the 1993 Act, overseen by a designated High Court judge, with complaints to the Complaints Referee.
Keep records that would satisfy an oversight review: the reason, the necessity, the authorisation, and the handling and destruction of material.
Intercepted material isn't routinely used as evidence. Talk to your supervisor and the prosecutor before relying on it.
Kennedy v UK.law: Yes. Kennedy (2010) is still cited as the model of a compliant targeted-interception regime.

src.t: UK Human Rights Blog — Rules on intercept evidence not breach of human rights (May 2010)

bg: In 2013 Edward Snowden's disclosures revealed the scale of US and UK intelligence surveillance. Campaign groups, NGOs and journalists then challenged three UK regimes in Strasbourg.

The three were: bulk interception of communications travelling over fibre-optic cables, under s.8(4) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000; receiving intercepted material from foreign intelligence services; and obtaining communications data (who contacted whom, when and where) from service providers.
In September 2018 a Chamber found violations for bulk interception and the communications-data regime. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber.
Big Brother Watch v UK.q: Is bulk interception of communications compatible with the Convention? And what safeguards do bulk interception and access to communications data need?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 25 May 2021, by majorities on each issue.

Bulk interception isn't prohibited. It can be used to protect national security against serious external threats, and States have a wide margin of appreciation, but it must be subject to 'end-to-end safeguards' covering the whole process, from authorisation to the use and destruction of material.

The UK's bulk regime breached Article 8. There was no independent authorisation at the outset, and the selectors used to search intercepted material weren't properly specified or authorised. It also breached Article 10, because confidential journalistic material could be examined without authorisation by a judge or independent body.
Receiving material from foreign intelligence services didn't breach Article 8: the rules on requests, use and oversight were adequate.

The communications-data regime breached Articles 8 and 10. Access wasn't limited to fighting serious crime, there was no prior independent review, and journalists' sources weren't adequately protected.
later: Big Brother Watch is the leading Strasbourg case on mass surveillance. It confirms that bulk powers can be lawful with robust end-to-end safeguards, and updates the minimum safeguards set out in Klass and Kennedy.

The EU Court of Justice has gone further on data retention, holding (for example, in the Irish Dwyer case, 2022) that general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data to fight crime is precluded. Ireland changed its law in 2022, so access to retained traffic and location data now generally needs a court order.
job: Getting communications data now requires prior independent authorisation. Use the statutory route (court orders under the Communications (Retention of Data) Acts as amended in 2022), never an informal request.
Limit data requests to serious crime and to what you can justify as necessary and proportionate, and record why.
Flag at once any request that might involve a journalist's sources or legally privileged material. Extra protection applies.
Big Brother Watch v UK.law: Yes. Big Brother Watch (2021) sets the current Strasbourg standards for bulk interception and access to communications data.

src.t: Human Rights Law Centre — Mass surveillance not fundamentally incompatible with human rights law (2021)
Global Freedom of Expression (Columbia) — Big Brother Watch v UK

bg: On 22 July 2005, the day after attempted bombings in London and two weeks after the 7 July attacks, police wrongly believed a man was one of the would-be bombers. He hadn't been positively identified.
Specialist firearms officers followed him onto a train at Stockwell Tube station and shot him dead. He was an innocent man with no connection to the bombings.

The Independent Police Complaints Commission identified serious institutional and operational failings. The police were penalised as an organisation for failings in planning and carrying out the operation, but the prosecutor found insufficient evidence to prosecute any individual officer. His cousin complained to Strasbourg that the failure to prosecute anyone breached Article 2.
Da Silva v UK.q: Does Article 2 require the prosecution of individual officers after a mistaken police shooting? And is the English 'honest belief' test of self-defence compatible with Article 2?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 30 March 2016: no violation of Article 2, by 13 votes to 4.

The duty to investigate is one of means, not results. The investigation here was thorough and independent. The decision not to prosecute came from the prosecutor's assessment of the evidence, not from investigative failings or any tolerance of unlawful acts.

There is no common evidential threshold for prosecution across Europe, so the 'more likely than not' test was within the State's margin of appreciation. Article 2 doesn't require a prosecution where there's no realistic prospect of success, and there's no basis for a lower threshold for State agents.

On self-defence, the test under Article 2 (from McCann) is whether the person honestly and genuinely believed force was necessary. Whether there were good reasons for the belief is relevant to whether it was genuinely held, not a separate requirement, so the English test was compatible.
Four judges dissented. They thought the majority gave too little weight to the objective element and warned of de facto immunity from prosecution.

keys.q: de facto immunity from prosecution
keys.w: joint dissent, on the risk of the majority's approach

later: Da Silva is the leading Strasbourg case on investigating a police shooting where no individual is prosecuted. Read with McCann (1995) on planning and control and Jordan (2001) on the investigation.
Commentators have criticised it for softening the objective element of McCann ('for good reasons').
job: In firearms operations, positive identification and clear command decisions matter as much as the officer's belief at the moment of firing. Failures in planning can make the State liable even where no individual is.
Any death after police force will be independently investigated (by Fiosrú in Ireland). Preserve everything, and record every decision and the reason for it as it is made.
If you are involved, give a full and honest account. The honesty of your belief is the heart of any self-defence assessment.
Da Silva v UK.law: Yes. Da Silva (2016) is the current Strasbourg authority on prosecution decisions and the honest-belief test after police shootings.

src.t: Wikipedia — Armani Da Silva v United Kingdom
Human Rights Law Centre — Investigation into innocent man's death was procedurally sound (2016)

bg: In the early hours of 28 April 1992 police in Adana detained a man on suspicion of aiding the PKK. He was held at the Security Directorate until about 1 a.m. the next day, then taken to hospital, where he was declared dead on arrival.

The autopsy found marks and bruises, including a bruise on the chest and a broken sternum, but didn't determine the cause of death. The State's forensic institute attributed it to cardiac arrest brought on by the incident and pre-existing heart disease.

His widow said he had been tortured, relying on family photographs showing marks of beating on the soles of the feet ('falaka'). In 1994 ten police officers were acquitted of homicide for lack of evidence of force or torture.
Salman v Turkey.q: When someone dies in police custody, who must explain the death? And what does an effective investigation require?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 27 June 2000.

Article 2 (death), by 16 votes to 1: deprivation of life gets the most careful scrutiny. People in custody are in a vulnerable position, and where someone enters custody in good health and dies, the authorities bear the burden of giving a satisfactory and convincing explanation. The Government gave no plausible explanation, and the evidence didn't support the heart-attack theory, so the State was responsible for the death.

Article 2 (investigation), unanimously: the autopsy lacked proper forensic photographs, dissection and histopathology, and it assumed without question that the sternum was broken during resuscitation. No effort was made to identify the officers who might have ill-treated him.
Article 3, unanimously: the injuries were consistent with falaka and a blow to the chest. The ill-treatment during interrogation was severe and cruel enough to be torture.

Article 13 (16 votes to 1): the defective investigation denied his widow an effective remedy. And police officers' blindfolded questioning of her, twice, about her application to Strasbourg was an undue interference with her right of petition.

keys.q: satisfactory and convincing explanation
keys.w: ECtHR, on the State's burden after a death in custody

keys.q: the most careful scrutiny
keys.w: ECtHR, on deprivations of life

later: Salman is still the leading Strasbourg case on deaths in custody: the State must account for what happened to anyone it holds.
Read with Jordan v UK (2001) on what an effective investigation into a death involving State agents requires.
job: Everyone in your custody is your responsibility. Record their condition and any injuries on arrival, every cell check, and anything they say about their health.
Get medical help at once for any injury or illness, and record when and by whom it was given.
If someone dies or is seriously injured in custody, preserve everything: the custody record, CCTV, cell logs. Expect an independent investigation by Fiosrú and a full forensic post-mortem.
Never question a complainant or witness about their complaint against the police in a way that could intimidate them.
Salman v Turkey.law: Yes. Salman (2000) is still the leading authority on the State's burden to explain a death in custody.

src.t: ECHR Case-law Information Note (June 2000), Appendix II — Salman v Turkey
Estonian Human Rights Guide — Salman v Turkey

bg: During the conflict between the Turkish security forces and the PKK, village guards and a gendarme questioned a family about recent visits by PKK members. The family, including the 17-year-old applicant, were taken to a gendarmerie headquarters, where she was separated from them.

Over more than three days she was beaten, stripped, sprayed with high-pressure water while spun in a tyre, and raped by a man in military clothing during interrogation. She was then beaten again and warned not to report it.

When the family complained, the prosecutor sent her to a doctor with no experience of examining survivors of rape, and then to other doctors mainly to establish whether she was still a virgin. No evidence was sought at the headquarters, and the family was harassed to withdraw the complaint.
Aydin v Turkey.q: Is rape of a detainee by an official torture? And what does the State's duty to investigate require?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 25 September 1997: violations of Articles 3 and 13.

Rape of a detainee by a State official is an especially grave and abhorrent form of ill-treatment. Torture is distinguished from inhuman or degrading treatment by deliberate intent and the severity of the suffering.
The physical and mental violence, and above all the rape, amounted to torture.

Article 13: the prosecutor showed a deferential attitude to the security forces and failed to carry out a thorough and effective investigation. Because the prosecutor plays a central role in the remedies available, that failure denied her an effective remedy. Turkey was ordered to pay £25,000.

keys.q: especially grave and abhorrent form of ill-treatment
keys.w: ECtHR, on rape of a detainee by an official

keys.q: deferential attitude
keys.w: ECtHR, on the prosecutor's approach to the security forces

later: Aydin was the first case in which Strasbourg held that rape by an official is torture. It is also widely cited against 'virginity testing', which has no scientific value.
International standards for medico-legal investigation of torture and sexual violence (the Istanbul Protocol and WHO guidelines) are now the benchmark.
job: Investigate every allegation of sexual violence thoroughly and sensitively, wherever and by whomever it is said to have happened, including in custody.
Use the Sexual Assault Treatment Units and specialist examiners for forensic examination, and secure clothing and other evidence early.
Record the complainant's account and condition accurately, and protect them from intimidation.
Aydin v Turkey.law: Yes. Aydin (1997) is still the leading authority that rape by an official is torture.

src.t: LSE — Index of cases: Aydin v Turkey

bg: A woman suffered years of psychological and physical abuse from her husband, and repeatedly warned the police that he was violent and mentally unstable.

After he beat her with an electric cable, she complained to the police. With his involvement she later tried to withdraw the complaint, and with a police officer's help it was reclassified as a minor offence. No criminal investigation was opened.

About two months later police were told in emergency calls that he had a shotgun and was threatening to kill himself and the children. The calls weren't properly recorded, acted on or passed to the next shift. Two days later he shot their two children, aged five and one, and then himself.
Kontrova v Slovakia.q: Did the police's failure to act on the complaint and the emergency calls breach the State's duty to protect life?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 31 May 2007: violations of Article 2 and Article 13.

The police knew of the abuse and of the threats involving a shotgun. Under Slovak law they had to register the complaint, open a criminal investigation and act on the emergency calls to protect the family, and they did none of these things.
The direct consequence of these failures was the death of the children, so Article 2 was breached.
Article 13: no compensation for non-pecuniary damage was available to the mother in Slovakia, so she had no effective remedy.

keys.q: the direct consequence of these failures was the death of the applicant's children
keys.w: ECtHR

later: Slovakia sent the judgment to every regional court, the chief of police and all district police office directors, to improve the police response.

Read with Opuz v Turkey (2009) and Talpis v Italy (2017). In Kurt v Austria (2021) the Grand Chamber found no violation where police had carried out a proactive, comprehensive risk assessment and issued a barring order, because no real and immediate risk to the child was shown.
job: Record and investigate every domestic violence complaint, even if the victim wants to withdraw it. Withdrawal under pressure is common.
Treat any report of threats involving a firearm as urgent: respond, assess the risk and consider seizing the weapon at once.
Hand over properly at the end of your shift. A call that falls between shifts can cost lives.
Use the protective measures available under the Domestic Violence Act 2018 and record your risk assessment.
Kontrova v Slovakia.law: Yes. Kontrova (2007) is still a leading Strasbourg case on police duties in domestic violence.

src.t: ECtHR factsheet — Domestic violence (2022)
Council of Europe — Impact of the Convention: justice for the mother of two murdered children

bg: A woman suffered years of violence from her husband, which she reported to the authorities.
The authorities didn't act promptly on her complaint, and the criminal proceedings were marked by delay and passivity.
Her husband later killed their son and tried to kill her.
Talpis v Italy.q: Did the authorities' slow response to a domestic violence complaint breach the State's duties to protect life, prevent ill-treatment and avoid discrimination?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 2 March 2017.

Article 2, by 6 votes to 1: by failing to take prompt action on the complaint, the authorities deprived it of any effect. That created a situation of impunity which encouraged further violence, ending in the son's death and the attempt on her life.
Article 3, unanimously: she and her children lived in a climate of violence serious enough to amount to ill-treatment, and the State failed to protect her.
Article 14 with Articles 2 and 3, by 5 votes to 2: by underestimating the violence, the authorities in effect endorsed it, and she was discriminated against as a woman.

keys.q: failing to take prompt action on the complaint
keys.w: ECtHR, on the authorities' failure

keys.q: creating a situation of impunity conducive to the recurrence
keys.w: ECtHR, on the effect of the delay

later: Read with Opuz v Turkey (2009), the first case to find discrimination in the State's response to domestic violence, and Kontrova (2007).

Kurt v Austria (Grand Chamber, 2021) later clarified that the duty to take preventive measures depends on whether the authorities knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to life, and that a proactive, comprehensive risk assessment is central to meeting that duty.
job: Act on every domestic violence complaint promptly: take the statement, assess the risk, and use protective measures (barring, safety and protection orders) without delay.

Coercive control is an offence in Ireland (s.39 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018), and a domestic relationship is an aggravating factor at sentencing. Gather the evidence of the pattern, not just the latest incident.
Record your risk assessment and review it whenever new information comes in. Delay can itself breach the victim's rights.
Talpis v Italy.law: Yes. Talpis (2017) is still a leading Strasbourg case on domestic violence, read with Kurt v Austria (2021) on the risk test.

src.t: University of Padua Human Rights Centre — Talpis v Italy (March 2017)
ECtHR factsheet — Domestic violence (2022)

bg: A man threatened to kill his former partner and their baby daughter, and was jailed for making the threats. Psychiatrists warned that there was a strong likelihood he would reoffend without treatment, and the court ordered psychiatric treatment.
In prison he saw the doctor five times, but only for unrelated illnesses. He received no psychiatric or psychotherapeutic treatment, and there was no assessment of his risk before he was released.
Weeks after his release, he shot the mother and daughter dead and then killed himself. The relatives' complaints in Croatia were ignored, and they went to Strasbourg.
Branko Tomasic v Croatia.q: Did the State do enough to protect a mother and child from a man whose threats to kill them it knew were serious?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 15 January 2009: violation of Article 2.
The authorities knew the threats were serious, and so they should have taken all reasonable steps to protect the victims.

The Government didn't show that the court-ordered psychiatric treatment was actually and properly given, and the man wasn't assessed for risk before his release. The authorities took no adequate steps to reduce the risk that he would carry out his threats.
The family was awarded €40,000.

keys.q: strong likelihood
keys.w: psychiatrists' warning that he would reoffend without treatment

later: Croatia later adopted national strategies against domestic violence, compulsory psycho-social treatment and protective supervision for perpetrators after release, risk assessment in probation, and ratified the Istanbul Convention in 2018.
Read with Kontrova (2007), Opuz (2009) and Talpis (2017). Kurt v Austria (2021) set out the 'real and immediate risk' test and the importance of a proactive risk assessment.
job: Threats to kill in a domestic setting are a recognised warning sign of homicide. Record them exactly, assess the risk and act on it.
Know when a domestic violence offender is due for release, and what conditions or supervision apply. Make sure the victim and the local unit know too.
Consider every protective measure: barring, safety or protection orders, bail conditions, and firearms checks.
Branko Tomasic v Croatia.law: Yes. Branko Tomašić (2009) is still a leading case on the State's duty to act on known threats in domestic violence.

src.t: Council of Europe — Impact of the Convention: justice for family of murdered mother and daughter
ECtHR factsheet — Domestic violence (2022)

bg: In May 1968 a man was committed to a psychiatric hospital under the Dutch emergency procedure, on the direction of a burgomaster (mayor).

Six weeks later his wife applied for provisional detention, supported by a declaration from a GP who had examined him for the first time that day. The District Court authorised detention without hearing him or seeking expert advice. The Regional Court then made a one-year order, which was renewed ten times.
While detained, he lost the legal capacity to administer his property, again without being heard. His requests for discharge were refused, and the prosecutor declined to refer them for review.
Winterwerp v Netherlands.q: When can a person be detained as being of 'unsound mind' under Article 5(1)(e)? And what review and procedural rights must they have?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 24 October 1979.

Article 5(1)(e), no violation: except in emergencies, a person can be detained as of unsound mind only if reliably shown to be so. That requires a true mental disorder established before the authority by objective medical expertise, the disorder must be of a kind or degree warranting compulsory confinement, and continued confinement depends on the disorder persisting. His detention rested on appropriate medical evidence and wasn't arbitrary.
Article 5(4), violation: because a person's mental state can change, there must be periodic review of the continued need for detention by a court. Dutch law didn't provide that.

Article 6(1), violation: he lost capacity to manage his property without any chance to be heard. Mental illness may limit how the right to a court is exercised, but it can't justify its complete absence.

keys.q: depends upon the persistence of such a disorder
keys.w: ECtHR, on continued confinement

keys.q: cannot warrant the total absence of that right
keys.w: ECtHR, on access to a court (Article 6)

later: The 'Winterwerp criteria' are still the foundation of Article 5 law on psychiatric detention across Europe.

In Ireland, involuntary admission is governed by the Mental Health Act 2001, with independent Mental Health Tribunals reviewing every admission order. Section 12 lets a garda take a person into custody in an emergency, followed at once by a medical assessment.
job: Under s.12 of the Mental Health Act 2001, take a person into custody only where there are reasonable grounds to believe that, because of a mental disorder, there is a serious likelihood of immediate and serious harm to themselves or others. Record the grounds.
Get the person a medical assessment as soon as possible. The emergency power is a short bridge to proper medical decision-making, not a detention power in itself.
Treat the person with dignity and keep them informed. Record what you saw and heard that led you to act.
Winterwerp v Netherlands.law: Yes. Winterwerp is still the leading authority on detention on mental health grounds under Article 5.

src.t: Global Health and Human Rights Database — Winterwerp v Netherlands
Mental Health Law Online — Winterwerp v Netherlands [1979] ECHR 4

bg: A solicitor drew up a document on behalf of local residents, seeking an order to keep the peace against a man. He later sued for libel those involved.
At the trial his side suggested the document was a sham. Several of the residents who had signed it gave evidence, but none of them was asked in cross-examination whether it was genuine.
The jury found for him and awarded damages of 20 shillings. The verdict was set aside on appeal, and he appealed to the House of Lords.
Browne v Dunn.q: If a party wants to say a witness is wrong or lying, must it put that case to the witness in cross-examination?
dec: House of Lords, 1893.

If you intend to contradict a witness's evidence, or suggest they aren't telling the truth, you must put that to them in cross-examination, so they have a chance to respond. Lord Herschell called this absolutely essential to the proper conduct of a cause, and essential to fair play and fair dealing with witnesses.
If the point isn't put, the party generally can't later argue that the witness's evidence should be rejected, or that they shouldn't be believed, on that point.
The rule has three purposes: fairness to the witness, giving the tribunal opposing accounts that actually meet, and preventing ambush.

keys.q: absolutely essential to the proper conduct of a cause
keys.w: Lord Herschell

keys.q: essential to fair play and fair dealing with witnesses
keys.w: Lord Herschell

later: The rule has been adopted across the common law world, and codified in some places, such as New Zealand and Australia.

In Ireland, the Supreme Court has confirmed that the rule is part of Irish law (McNamee v Revenue Commissioners, 2016, and McDonagh v Sunday Newspapers, 2018). In DPP v PS [2021] IECA 311 the Court of Appeal said the defence must make clear that a complainant's credibility is challenged, though not in minute detail. There, treating the complainant's truthfulness as unchallenged took the heart of the defence away from the jury, and the conviction was quashed.
job: Expect the defence to put its case to you in cross-examination: that you're mistaken, didn't see what you say, or are not telling the truth. Answer the specific point calmly, by reference to your notes.
The same rule binds the prosecution. If the State will say a defence witness is lying, the prosecutor must put that to them, so give the prosecutor everything that contradicts a defence account.
Good notes made at the time are your best answer when your account is challenged.
Browne v Dunn.law: Yes. The rule in Browne v Dunn is part of Irish law and still applied.

src.t: Wikipedia — Browne v Dunn
Law Library — A question of questions (on Browne v Dunn in Ireland)

bg: A trainee journalist on a trade magazine received an unsolicited phone call from an anonymous source, with information about a company's financial difficulties. It appeared to come from a confidential corporate plan, a copy of which had gone missing.

The company got an injunction stopping publication. The High Court also ordered him, under s.10 of the Contempt of Court Act 1981, to disclose his notes identifying the source, so the company could recover the document and act against the source. His appeals to the Court of Appeal and House of Lords failed.
He refused to reveal his source and was fined £5,000 for contempt.
Goodwin v UK.q: Was ordering a journalist to disclose his source compatible with freedom of expression?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 27 March 1996: violation of Article 10.

Protection of journalistic sources is one of the basic conditions for press freedom. Without it, sources may be deterred from helping the press inform the public, and the press's vital role as public watchdog could be undermined.
So an order to disclose a source can be justified only by an overriding requirement in the public interest.

Here the injunction already stopped publication of the confidential information. The company's further interest in identifying the source, to prevent more leaks or sue an employee, didn't outweigh the public interest in protecting sources.

keys.q: protection of media sources is one of the basic conditions for press freedom
keys.w: ECtHR

keys.q: overriding public interest
keys.w: the only justification for compelled disclosure

later: Goodwin is still the leading Strasbourg case on journalistic sources, and UK courts have applied it since.

In Big Brother Watch v UK (2021) the Grand Chamber found violations of Article 10 because confidential journalistic material and sources weren't adequately protected in surveillance and data-access regimes.
job: Treat any request that could identify a journalist's source (production orders, phone records, seizures) as needing special justification and independent authorisation. Get advice first.
Record why the information is necessary and why there's no other way to get it, because that is what a court will weigh.
Leaks of Garda information should be investigated through proper channels, not by pressing journalists to reveal sources.
Goodwin v UK.law: Yes. Goodwin (1996) is still the leading authority on protecting journalists' sources.

src.t: Global Freedom of Expression (Columbia) — Goodwin v United Kingdom
Council of Europe — Impact of the Convention: greater protection for the media

bg: Under the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011, phone companies had to keep the traffic and location data of all subscribers (who called whom, when and from where) for two years. Gardaí could access it on the authorisation of a chief superintendent.

A man convicted of murder in 2015, in a case that relied partly on such data, challenged the 2011 Act in civil proceedings. The High Court granted a declaration in 2018, and the Supreme Court referred questions to the Court of Justice of the EU.

The questions were whether general retention of this data to fight serious crime is compatible with EU law, whether access decided by a senior garda is compatible, and whether an Irish court could limit the effects of any finding of invalidity.
Garda Siochana v Dwyer.q: Can States require phone companies to retain everyone's traffic and location data to fight serious crime? And who must decide whether police may access it?
dec: Court of Justice of the EU (Grand Chamber), 5 April 2022.

General and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data is precluded by EU law, even to combat serious crime. Serious crime, even murder, isn't the same as a threat to national security. Only a genuine and present or foreseeable threat to national security can justify general retention, and then only for a limited period.

To fight serious crime, States may use targeted retention (by categories of person or geographic area, such as high-crime areas, airports and stations), general retention of IP addresses and of users' identity data, and 'quick freeze' orders requiring providers to preserve data once an investigation starts.
Access can't be decided centrally by a police officer, with a court reviewing it only afterwards. It needs prior review by a court or an independent body.
A national court can't limit the temporal effects of a declaration that the law was invalid. But whether evidence obtained from retained data is admissible at trial is a matter for national law.

keys.q: The admissibility of such evidence is a matter for national law
keys.w: CJEU, as summarised

later: Ireland passed the Communications (Retention of Data) (Amendment) Act 2022. General retention now needs a High Court order on national security grounds, and access to retained traffic and location data needs a court order, with District Court orders for preservation, production and disclosure.

In People (DPP) v Smyth (2024) and People (DPP) v Dwyer (2024) the Supreme Court held that data obtained in good faith under the 2011 Act is judged by the JC test, not excluded automatically, and the convictions stood.
job: Get phone data only through the 2022 Act procedures: a preservation order to stop it being deleted, then a production or disclosure order from a court. Never ask a provider informally.
Act quickly. A preservation ('quick freeze') order is how you secure data at the start of an investigation.
Build independent evidence (attribution, witnesses, CCTV, seized phones) around any phone data, so the case doesn't depend on one source.
Garda Siochana v Dwyer.law: Yes. GD v Commissioner (2022) sets the EU law limits on data retention and access, now reflected in the 2022 Act.

src.t: eucrim — CJEU clarifies exceptions to data retention in Irish case (2022)
SCL — CJEU: blanket retention of traffic and location data for investigation of crime unlawful
Irish Legal News — Supreme Court: Dwyer appeal over admissibility of evidence dismissed (Aug 2024)

bg: Over about ten years, five men took part in consensual sadomasochistic activities in private, which caused injuries. Police discovered the activities during an unrelated investigation.
The men were charged with wounding and assault occasioning actual bodily harm under ss.20 and 47 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. None of the participants had complained.
The trial judge ruled that consent was no defence, so they pleaded guilty. The Court of Appeal certified the question for the House of Lords.
R v Brown.q: Must the prosecution prove a lack of consent to secure a conviction for wounding or assault occasioning actual bodily harm in a sadomasochistic encounter?
dec: House of Lords, 11 March 1993, by 3 to 2: the appeals were dismissed.

The majority (Lords Templeman, Jauncey and Lowry) held that consent is a defence to actual bodily harm or worse only within recognised exceptions, such as properly conducted sport, lawful chastisement and reasonable surgery. Inflicting bodily harm without good reason is unlawful.
Lord Templeman said society was entitled to protect itself against a 'cult of violence'. Lord Lowry said the 1861 Act shouldn't be relaxed for this conduct.

The dissenters (Lords Mustill and Slynn) would have allowed the appeals: consensual private conduct, even causing actual bodily harm, should be outside the criminal law, and repugnance alone doesn't justify a new crime.

keys.q: cult of violence
keys.w: Lord Templeman

later: R v Wilson (1996), where a husband branded his initials on his wife at her request, was treated differently, and critics contrast the two. R v Emmett (1999) confirmed that the Brown rules apply equally to heterosexual activity.

Brown remains the leading English authority but is heavily criticised. In Ireland, assault and harm are offences under the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, and Brown is persuasive only.
job: Where a suspect says the injured person consented, record exactly what each says was agreed, the circumstances, and the injuries (with photos and medical evidence).
Don't decide the consent question yourself. Gather the evidence and send the file to the DPP for direction.
In domestic settings, be alert to a 'consent' claim being used to cover abuse or coercive control.
R v Brown.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Brown is still the leading case on consent and harm in England.

src.t: Wikipedia — R v Brown

bg: A man was arrested in France on a European Arrest Warrant and surrendered to Belgium, where he was investigated for murder.

Under a general, mandatory Belgian statutory rule, he was questioned seven times by police and twice by an investigating judge without a lawyer. After he was remanded in custody he could consult a lawyer, but the lawyer couldn't attend interviews or other investigative steps.

He made detailed statements, which weren't strictly confessions but were used at his trial and had a decisive impact on the finding of premeditation. The jury got no warning or guidance on how to treat them.
Beuze v Belgium.q: When does restricting a suspect's access to a lawyer during questioning breach the right to a fair trial?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 9 November 2018: violation of Article 6(1) and 6(3)(c), unanimously.

The Court applied the two-stage test from Ibrahim v UK (2016) to all cases. First, was there a restriction on early access to a lawyer, and were there compelling reasons for it? Restrictions must be temporary and based on an individual assessment. Second, were the proceedings as a whole fair?
Where there are no compelling reasons, the Court scrutinises overall fairness very strictly. Here the Government showed none.

The trial was unfair because of the wide scope and length of the restrictions, the substantial impact of the statements made without a lawyer, the lack of any jury guidance on their weight, and the higher court's failure to put this right.
Four judges, concurring, said the majority had weakened Salduz, which they read as making an unjustified systematic restriction an automatic breach.

keys.q: distorts and changes the Salduz principle
keys.w: joint concurring opinion

later: Beuze is the current Strasbourg statement of the right of access to a lawyer: Salduz (2008) as refined by Ibrahim (2016).

In Ireland, Gormley and White (2014) held that a suspect who asks for a solicitor is entitled to legal advice before questioning. Solicitors may now attend interviews, and the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would put consultation before and during interview on a statutory footing (check whether it has been enacted).
job: Once a suspect asks for a solicitor, don't start questioning until they've had a reasonable chance to consult one, and allow the solicitor to attend the interview.
Any restriction must be exceptional, individual and recorded with its compelling reasons, such as an immediate risk to life.
Statements taken without legal advice will be closely scrutinised. Record every attempt to arrange it.
Beuze v Belgium.law: Yes. Beuze (2018) is the current Strasbourg test on access to a lawyer. In Ireland, read with Gormley and White (2014).

src.t: Strasbourg Observers — Unravelling Salduz and the EU: Beuze v Belgium (December 2018)
PILA — ECtHR holds restriction on early access to lawyer breached only where overall fairness compromised (2018)

bg: In March 2000 a mother began divorce proceedings, and both parents sought custody of their three-year-old son, who was moved between them, sometimes by force. She said her husband was violent towards her and asked the court for interim custody.

The court didn't examine her request until June 2000 and then adjourned it repeatedly, and she withdrew it in February 2001. Police warned the husband, but nothing more was done: under the law then, minor injuries between spouses could only be prosecuted privately by the victim, and the authorities told her it was a private matter.
She was even investigated for abduction after taking refuge with her son in a shelter. She was awarded custody in May 2001, but the husband assaulted her again in June 2002.
Bevacqua v Bulgaria.q: Did the authorities' slow and passive response to domestic violence breach the right to respect for private and family life?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 12 June 2008: violation of Article 8, by 6 votes to 1. No violation of Article 6(1) on the length of the proceedings.
Article 8 can require States to protect people from acts by private individuals, including through an adequate legal framework.
Applications for interim custody in such circumstances should normally be treated with priority. The automatic practice of postponing custody issues was unjustified, given the urgency.

Leaving it to the victim to bring a private prosecution wasn't enough. The authorities' failure to impose sanctions on the husband or enforce his obligations, and their view that the dispute was a private matter, were incompatible with their positive obligations.
Together, those failures amounted to a failure to assist the mother and child. The Court awarded €4,000 jointly.

keys.q: incompatible with their positive obligations
keys.w: ECtHR (para 83), on treating it as a private matter

keys.q: amounted to a failure to assist the applicants
keys.w: ECtHR (para 84)

later: Read with Opuz v Turkey (2009), Kontrova (2007) and Talpis (2017).

In Ireland, the Domestic Violence Act 2018 provides protection, safety and barring orders (including interim and emergency orders), and assaults in a domestic setting are prosecuted by the State, not left to the victim to pursue.
job: Domestic violence is never a 'private matter'. Record, investigate and act on every report, including while family-law proceedings are under way.
Help the victim apply for protective orders, and enforce breaches of them.
Assess the risk to any children, and involve Tusla where needed.
Bevacqua v Bulgaria.law: Yes. Bevacqua (2008) is still a leading Strasbourg case on the State's duty to respond to domestic violence.

src.t: Judgment text — Bevacqua and S. v Bulgaria (12 June 2008)
Cornell LII Gender Justice — Bevacqua and S. v Bulgaria

bg: In December 2004 a woman who had been drinking and hadn't eaten that day was pushed into a recessed doorway and raped.
The accused, who was 18 and had no previous convictions, didn't give evidence. He had told gardaí the encounter was consensual. A jury convicted him of rape in March 2007.
The nature of the attack and its serious effect on the victim were found to be worse than usual, placing the case at the upper end of the normal range.
People (DPP) v WD.q: How should a rape sentence be placed within existing sentencing practice, in the absence of guidelines?
dec: Central Criminal Court, 4 May 2007 (Charleton J), reported at [2008] 1 IR 308.

Charleton J said he wasn't setting guidelines. Instead, to promote consistency and predictability, he reviewed superior-court rape sentences from January 2005 onwards and placed this sentence within existing law and practice.
Rape is a savage attack on the bodily and psychological integrity of the victim. It is always accompanied by violence or fraud, and victims are often left in fear of pregnancy or disease.

He imposed seven years, with the last eighteen months suspended on a bond to keep the peace and attend counselling, and registration as a sex offender. Later cases describe the lowest range he identified as three to eight years.

keys.q: a savage attack on the bodily and psychological integrity of a woman
keys.w: Charleton J, on rape

later: Cited in later sentencing cases (for example DPP v J.D., 2017) for its ranges.
Superseded as the main guide by the Supreme Court's guidance in DPP v F.E. [2019] IESC 85, which set bands ranging from about 7 years to life, before mitigation. Read with Tiernan (1988).
job: The evidence you gather on the violence used and the effect on the victim drives where a rape sentence falls. Record injuries, forensic findings and the victim's state carefully.
Make sure a victim impact statement is offered, and that the court has accurate information about the offender's record and circumstances.
People (DPP) v WD.law: Partly superseded. WD is still cited, but the Supreme Court's 2019 guidance in F.E. now sets the bands for rape sentencing.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v W.D. [2007] IEHC 310
Irish Times — Rape case sentencing judgment issued by Supreme Court (Dec 2019)

bg: The accused was charged under s.15A of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 (inserted in 1999), which applies to possession of controlled drugs for sale or supply where their market value is €13,000 or more. It carries a presumptive minimum sentence of ten years.

At his trial in Waterford Circuit Criminal Court, his counsel asked the judge to tell the jury that it had to be satisfied he knew or ought to have known the drugs were worth €13,000 or more. The judge refused, and in November 2004 he was convicted and sentenced to ten years.
The Court of Criminal Appeal held that no such knowledge was required, saying any other reading would make s.15A unworkable, and certified the question for the Supreme Court.
DPP v Power.q: In a s.15A prosecution, must the prosecution prove that the accused knew, or ought to have known, that the drugs were worth €13,000 or more?
dec: Supreme Court, 26 July 2007 (Finnegan J).
No. The prosecution must prove objectively that the market value was €13,000 or more, but it doesn't have to prove that the accused knew or ought to have known that.

A contrary reading would be absurd, because s.15A doesn't even require proof that the accused knew the package contained a controlled drug. (Section 29 of the 1977 Act gives the accused a defence of lack of knowledge, which the accused must raise.)

keys.q: Any other interpretation would make section 15A unworkable
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, approved on appeal

keys.q: absurd
keys.w: Finnegan J, on requiring proof of knowledge of value

later: The ruling exposed more offenders to the presumptive ten-year sentence under s.15A, which a court can depart from only for exceptional and specific circumstances.

The mandatory minimum for a second s.15A or s.15B offence (s.27(3F)) was struck down in McManus v Minister for Justice (2021), applying Ellis (2019). The presumptive minimum for a first offence remains.
job: Prove the value properly: forensic analysis of the drug, its weight and purity, and expert garda evidence of street value at the time.
The suspect's knowledge of the value isn't an element, but their knowledge of possession still matters. Record anything they say about the drugs and how they came to have them.
Gather the evidence relevant to sentence too: the plea and when it was first indicated, any material assistance, and previous convictions.
DPP v Power.law: Yes. Power (2007) is still the law: knowledge of value isn't an element of s.15A.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Power [2007] 2 IR 509
Irish Times — Ruling exposes drug offenders to mandatory 10-year terms (July 2007)

bg: In 1982 the Minister for Justice authorised the tapping of the home phones of two political journalists, one of whom had been writing about challenges to the Taoiseach's leadership.

The Irish Times revealed the tapping in December 1982. The two journalists, and the wife of one of them (also a journalist), sued Ireland and the Attorney General, claiming a breach of their constitutional rights to privacy and freedom of expression.
The State conceded that the tapping was improper but argued it wasn't illegal and didn't breach any constitutional right.
Kennedy v Ireland.q: Does the Constitution protect a right to privacy in telephone conversations, and was it breached by the tapping?
dec: High Court, 12 January 1987 (Hamilton P).
The right to privacy is one of the unenumerated personal rights protected by Article 40.3, and it extends to private telephone conversations.

The tapping, done without proper justification, violated the plaintiffs' constitutional right to privacy. Hamilton P described it as an attack on their dignity and freedom as individuals, which couldn't be tolerated in a democratic society.
Damages of £20,000 were awarded to each journalist and £10,000 to the third plaintiff.

keys.q: an attack on their dignity and freedom as individuals
keys.w: Hamilton P, on the phone tapping

later: Interception was put on a full statutory footing by the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) Act 1993: authorisation by the Minister on strict grounds, review by a designated High Court judge, and complaints to a Complaints Referee.
Kennedy is a leading authority on the constitutional right to privacy, read with Malone v UK (1984) on the quality of law needed for interception.
job: Interception of calls or messages needs a ministerial authorisation under the 1993 Act. Never listen to, record or access someone's communications outside a statutory scheme.
Journalists' communications need extra care, because of source protection (Goodwin v UK). Flag any such request at once.
Unlawful surveillance can lead to damages against the State, as well as the exclusion of evidence.
Kennedy v Ireland.law: Yes. Kennedy (1987) is still a leading case on the constitutional right to privacy.

src.t: Wikipedia — Kennedy v Ireland
Irish Times — Judge condemned phone-tapping

bg: An 11-year-old was charged with attempted robbery, and his fingerprints and DNA samples were taken. He was acquitted.
An adult was arrested and charged with harassing his partner, and his fingerprints and DNA were taken. The charge wasn't pressed, and the case was formally discontinued.
English law allowed the police to keep fingerprints, DNA samples and profiles indefinitely, whatever the outcome of the case. Both asked for theirs to be destroyed, and the police refused.
Marper v UK.q: Is keeping the fingerprints and DNA of people suspected but not convicted of offences compatible with the right to private life?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 4 December 2008: violation of Article 8.
The mere storing of data relating to private life is an interference with Article 8.
Retention pursues a legitimate aim, the detection and prevention of crime. But the law must be precise and contain minimum safeguards on duration, storage, use, third-party access and destruction.

The blanket and indiscriminate retention of fingerprints and DNA from people suspected but not convicted failed to strike a fair balance between public and private interests. It wasn't necessary in a democratic society.

keys.q: mere storing of data
keys.w: ECtHR, on what counts as an interference with private life

keys.q: blanket and indiscriminate
keys.w: ECtHR, on the UK's retention powers

later: Marper shaped DNA database laws across Europe. In Ireland, the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014 set up the DNA database, with rules on taking samples and on destroying samples and removing profiles of people who aren't convicted.
Read with Big Brother Watch v UK (2021) on safeguards for retained data.
job: Take fingerprints, DNA and photographs only under the statutory power that applies, and record the authority and the reason.
Know the destruction and removal rules under the 2014 Act, and make sure records are processed when a person isn't prosecuted or is acquitted.
Keep retained biometric data secure and use it only for its lawful purposes.
Marper v UK.law: Yes. Marper (2008) is still the leading Strasbourg case on retention of DNA and fingerprints.

src.t: Human Rights Law Centre — S and Marper v United Kingdom (2008)
Wikipedia — S and Marper v United Kingdom

bg: A man suffering from depression walked down a street one evening with a knife, intending to take his own life. He was filmed by council CCTV cameras. Police intervened and took him to a station, and no proceedings were brought.

To promote its CCTV scheme, the council later released the footage. Stills appeared in local newspapers and film was shown on national television, without his identity being properly masked. Family and friends recognised him.
He sought judicial review and complained to media regulators, but none of these routes gave him an effective remedy.
Peck v United Kingdom.q: Does releasing CCTV footage of a person in a public place to the media breach their right to private life?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 28 January 2003: violations of Article 8 and Article 13, unanimously.

Being filmed in a public street doesn't by itself interfere with private life. But disclosing the footage to the media, to an audience far wider than anyone could have foreseen, was a serious interference, given his distress and that he wasn't a public figure.

The disclosure had a legal basis and legitimate aims (public safety and crime prevention), but it wasn't proportionate. The council could have identified him through the police and sought his consent, masked the images itself, or demanded written undertakings that the media would mask them. There were no relevant or sufficient reasons for unmasked disclosure.

Article 13: the domestic routes gave him no effective remedy. Judicial review didn't allow a proportionality assessment, and the media regulators couldn't award damages. He was awarded €11,800 for non-pecuniary damage.

keys.q: it would have been reasonable for the Council to demand written undertakings
keys.w: ECtHR (para 83), on media masking

keys.q: relevant or sufficient reasons
keys.w: ECtHR (para 85), finding none for unmasked disclosure

later: The UK then tightened its rules on CCTV, requiring systematic justification for its use and restricting the disclosure of images to third parties.

In Ireland, Garda use of CCTV and other recording devices is regulated by the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 and codes of practice, and images are personal data under data protection law.
job: CCTV and bodycam footage is personal data. Release images to the media or the public only through the proper channels, and only when it is necessary and proportionate, for example in a genuine appeal for help to identify a suspect.
Mask or blur anyone who doesn't need to be identified, especially vulnerable people and victims.
Treat footage of a person in crisis (a mental health incident, a suicide attempt) with particular care. It should never be used for publicity.
Peck v United Kingdom.law: Yes. Peck (2003) is still the leading Strasbourg case on disclosing CCTV images.

src.t: Judgment text — Peck v United Kingdom (28 January 2003)
Council of Europe — Impact of the Convention: CCTV footage of suicide attempt used for publicity

bg: In January 1980 customs officers and a police officer, investigating suspected financial offences, questioned a man and searched his home for about five and a half hours. They seized financial documents.
Customs then demanded his foreign bank statements for three years and records of a property purchase. He first agreed, then refused.

A court fined him and ordered him to hand over the documents or pay a daily penalty, which was increased on appeal. His appeals failed. After his death in 1987, his widow continued his application to Strasbourg.
Funke v France.q: Can the authorities use fines and penalties to force a suspect to produce documents they believe will incriminate him? And was the house search lawful?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 25 February 1993.

Article 6(1), by 8 votes to 1: customs, unable or unwilling to get the documents by other means, tried to compel him to provide evidence of offences he had allegedly committed. That infringed his right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself, even though French customs law allowed it.

Article 8, by 8 votes to 1: the search interfered with his home, private life and correspondence. The customs law gave officers very wide powers and lacked sufficient safeguards against abuse, so the interference was disproportionate.
He was awarded 50,000 francs for non-pecuniary damage and 70,000 francs for costs.
later: Funke was an early recognition of the privilege against self-incrimination under Article 6. Saunders v UK (1996) refined it: material that exists independently of the suspect's will, such as documents obtained under a warrant, falls outside the privilege.
Heaney and McGuinness v Ireland (2000) applied the same principle to the duty to account for movements under s.52.
job: Don't use penalties or threats to make a suspect produce evidence against himself. Get documents by search warrant, or by a production order directed at a third party such as a bank.
Statutory powers to demand documents (for example under revenue or regulatory law) need care if the person is a suspect. Get advice on how any material can be used.
Searches need a clear legal basis and safeguards, normally a warrant from an independent judge (Damache).
Funke v France.law: Yes, as refined by Saunders (1996). Funke is still cited on compelled production of documents and on searches without safeguards.

src.t: Wikipedia — Funke v France

bg: In February 1989 a Belfast solicitor, who had represented clients from both sides of the conflict, was shot dead at home in front of his wife and three children. A loyalist paramilitary group claimed responsibility.

His widow alleged that police officers had made threats against him, passed on through clients, and that the security forces had colluded in his murder. The weapon had been stolen from an army barracks.

The police investigation was carried out by the same force. The 1990 inquest didn't examine collusion. A senior British police officer led three inquiries, the third of which (reporting in 2003) found evidence of collusion, but only an overview was published. In 1995 the DPP directed no prosecution, giving no reasons.
Finucane v UK.q: Did the investigations into the killing meet the State's procedural duty under Article 2?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 1 July 2003: violation of Article 2 (procedural), unanimously. The Court made no finding on collusion itself.
The police investigation was conducted by officers from the force the widow suspected of making the threats. That raised serious doubts about its thoroughness and effectiveness.
The inquest couldn't examine collusion, and she wasn't allowed to give evidence about the threats, so it wasn't an effective investigation.

The first two inquiries weren't clearly aimed at prosecution, and their reports weren't published. The third came about ten years after the killing, so it wasn't prompt. The DPP didn't have to give reasons for not prosecuting, and that decision couldn't be challenged.
The Court didn't order a fresh investigation, leaving compliance to the Committee of Ministers. Costs of €43,000 were awarded.

keys.q: raised serious doubts as to the thoroughness or effectiveness
keys.w: ECtHR, on the police investigation

keys.q: could not be regarded as having constituted an effective investigation
keys.w: ECtHR, on the inquest

later: Finucane applies the Jordan v UK (2001) requirements: independence, effectiveness, promptness, public scrutiny and family involvement.
It is a leading example of an Article 2 failure where State involvement in a death is alleged.
job: Where State agents may be involved in a death, whether gardaí, the Defence Forces or informants, the investigation must be independent of them. Refer matters to Fiosrú where garda conduct is in question.
Take threats against lawyers, journalists and other at-risk people seriously. Record them, assess the risk, and act.
Preserve everything, and keep the family informed. Delay and secrecy are what breach Article 2.
Finucane v UK.law: Yes. Finucane (2003) is still a leading application of the Article 2 duty to investigate.

src.t: Irish Times — Court finds European Convention was violated in Finucane case (July 2003)
Kent Criminal Justice Notes — Investigating State collusion in murder

bg: In 1986 an insulting letter was sent to a judge. German authorities, trying to identify its author, got a warrant to search the office a lawyer shared with a colleague, because post for a political group had been delivered there.
The warrant was drawn in broad terms and set no limit on the documents that could be examined. Officers went through client files, though nothing was seized.
The lawyer's constitutional complaint wasn't accepted for decision, and he applied to Strasbourg.
Niemietz v Germany.q: Does Article 8 protect a lawyer's office? And was this search proportionate?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 16 December 1992: violation of Article 8.

Limiting 'private life' to an inner circle would be too restrictive. Professional and business activities can be part of private life, especially for the liberal professions, where it can be hard to separate work from private life.
'Home' can extend to business premises, as German law itself recognised. The search also reached correspondence and client files.

The aims (preventing crime and protecting the judge's reputation) were legitimate, and the offence wasn't minor. But the warrant was drawn in broad terms, there were no special safeguards such as an independent observer, and the search impinged on professional secrecy to a disproportionate extent, which could affect the administration of justice.

keys.q: too restrictive
keys.w: ECtHR (para 29), on limiting private life to an inner circle

keys.q: impinged on professional secrecy
keys.w: ECtHR (para 37)

later: Niemietz is still the leading authority that Article 8 covers business premises. Later cases (for example Kruglov v Russia, 2020) say searches of lawyers' homes or offices need especially strict scrutiny.

In Ireland, legally privileged material is protected, and the Garda Síochána (Powers) Bill 2026 would add a statutory procedure for dealing with privileged material in searches (check whether it has been enacted).
job: Searching a solicitor's or other professional's office needs a tightly worded warrant that identifies the specific items sought.
Plan how to deal with privileged material: don't read it, and seal disputed material for a court to decide.
Record the scope of the search and what was examined. A fishing expedition through client files is disproportionate.
Niemietz v Germany.law: Yes. Niemietz (1992) is still the leading authority on Article 8 and business premises.

src.t: Judgment text — Niemietz v Germany (16 December 1992)
ECHR Case Law — searches of lawyers' homes and offices need especially strict scrutiny (Kruglov, 2020)

bg: A man placed an advertisement under an assumed name and hired a former Foreign Legion member, allegedly to kill his wife. The hired man went to the police instead.

On 26 June 1981 the hired man recorded a phone call from the man, using equipment attached to a telephone, and gave the tape to the police. The Swiss courts accepted that the recording wasn't authorised by the competent authority, so it was unlawful.
The man was convicted of attempted incitement to murder and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment. The recording was used in evidence along with other evidence.
Schenk v Switzerland.q: Does using an unlawfully obtained recording as evidence make a criminal trial unfair?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (plenary), 12 July 1988.

Article 6(1), no violation by 13 votes to 4: Article 6 doesn't lay down rules on the admissibility of evidence as such, which is mainly a matter for national law. The question is whether the trial as a whole was fair.

The rights of the defence were respected. He could challenge the recording's authenticity, he obtained an investigation of the man who made it, and his counsel questioned that man at trial. And the recording wasn't the only evidence on which the conviction was based.
Article 6(2), unanimously: admitting the recording didn't mean he was treated as guilty before conviction. The Court didn't examine Article 8 separately.
Four judges dissented, saying that obeying the law when gathering evidence isn't an abstract or formal requirement, and that relying on unlawfully obtained evidence undermined fairness.

keys.q: does not lay down any rules on the admissibility of evidence as such
keys.w: ECtHR (para 46)

keys.q: not the only evidence on which the conviction was based
keys.w: ECtHR (para 48)

later: Schenk set Strasbourg's approach: the fairness of the trial as a whole, not automatic exclusion. It was followed in Khan v UK (2000), Allan v UK (2002), where the trial was unfair, and Bykov v Russia (2009).
In Ireland, admissibility of evidence obtained in breach of rights is decided under JC (2015): deliberate and conscious breaches lead to exclusion, inadvertent ones generally don't.
job: A recording made by a private person can end up as evidence. Secure the original device or file, its continuity and its metadata, and record exactly how it reached you.
Don't encourage or direct a private person to record someone. That can make them your agent and engage the rules on covert surveillance.
Never rely on a single recording. Corroborate it with independent evidence.
Schenk v Switzerland.law: Yes. Schenk (1988) is still the foundation of Strasbourg's approach to unlawfully obtained evidence.

src.t: Judgment text — Schenk v Switzerland (12 July 1988)

bg: On 1 May 2001 thousands of people took part in a demonstration in central London, and the situation at Oxford Circus became volatile, with a risk of violence and serious injury.

Police formed a cordon at Oxford Circus and held up to 2,000 people inside it for up to seven hours, with no access to food, water or toilets. The police began planning a controlled release within minutes but kept suspending it because of violence inside and outside the cordon.
One protester and three passers-by who had been caught inside complained that the containment had deprived them of their liberty, in breach of Article 5.
Austin v UK.q: Is holding a crowd inside a police cordon ('kettling') a deprivation of liberty under Article 5?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 15 March 2012: no violation of Article 5, by a majority (three judges dissented).

Article 5 is concerned with deprivation of liberty, not ordinary restrictions on movement. The Court looks at the type, duration, effects and manner of implementation of a measure, and also its context.

The cordon was coercive and uncomfortable, pointing towards a deprivation of liberty. But it was used to isolate a large crowd in volatile and dangerous conditions, it was the least intrusive and most effective means of protecting people from serious injury, and the police kept trying to release people. The Court couldn't identify a point at which it became a deprivation of liberty.

It made no difference whether a person was a protester or a passer-by. The Court stressed that crowd control mustn't be used to stifle or discourage protest, and that its ruling rested on the specific and exceptional facts.

keys.q: least intrusive and most effective means
keys.w: ECtHR, on the cordon in those conditions

later: Austin is the leading Strasbourg case on containing crowds. Its emphasis on exceptional circumstances means containment must be justified every time.
The dissenting judges would have found a deprivation of liberty that couldn't be justified under Article 5's exceptions.
job: Containment is a last resort, used only to prevent serious injury or damage. Record the intelligence, the decision, who made it and why.
Keep containment as short as possible. Release people, especially those clearly not involved, as soon as it is safe, and provide for basic needs such as water, toilets and medical help.
Never use public order tactics to discourage lawful protest.
Austin v UK.law: Yes. Austin (2012) is still the leading Strasbourg authority on 'kettling', limited to its exceptional facts.

src.t: Human Rights Law Centre — Policing of protests: European Court rules on 'kettling' (2012)

bg: In May 2003 farmers held demonstrations beside major highways to press for better agricultural policy, with permits from three municipalities.
During the protests they blocked three major highways without authorisation, causing serious disruption, until talks with the government ended the protest.

Five organisers were convicted of inciting and taking part in riots and given suspended sentences. A Chamber of the European Court found a violation of Article 11, and the case was referred to the Grand Chamber.
Kudrevicius and Others v Lithuania.q: Does convicting protesters for deliberately blocking main roads breach the right of peaceful assembly?
dec: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), 15 October 2015: no violation of Article 11, unanimously.
Article 11 protects only peaceful assembly. The protest wasn't violent, so it applied, and the convictions interfered with the right even though the farmers had permits and weren't dispersed.

The interference was prescribed by law: the organisers could foresee that long-lasting roadblocks would be treated as a serious breach of public order. The aims (preventing disorder and protecting others' freedom of movement) were legitimate.

Intentionally causing serious disruption to ordinary life, to a greater extent than is normal for a demonstration, isn't at the core of the right. The blockades weren't needed to make their point, and lawful alternatives existed. Such reprehensible conduct may justify criminal penalties.
The authorities had tolerated the blockades and kept everyone safe, so the suspended sentences were proportionate.

keys.q: serious breach of public order
keys.w: ECtHR, on what the organisers could foresee

keys.q: reprehensible
keys.w: ECtHR, on deliberately blocking the highways

later: Kudrevičius is the leading Grand Chamber case on disruptive protest. Critics say it gives States too much room to penalise disruption.
In Ireland, read with DPP v Kelly (2018) on s.8 directions and obstruction under s.9 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994.
job: Peaceful protest is protected even when it is disruptive. Show tolerance, facilitate it, and engage with organisers.
Where protesters deliberately and seriously obstruct roads, give clear directions (for example under s.8), and record the disruption and your exact words.
Prosecution of the most serious obstruction can be proportionate, but record why lesser measures weren't enough.
Kudrevicius and Others v Lithuania.law: Yes. Kudrevičius (2015) is still the leading Strasbourg case on protest blockades.

src.t: Global Freedom of Expression (Columbia) — Kudrevičius and Others v Lithuania

bg: A serial killer murdered a young woman in 1980, the last of his victims.
Her mother sued the police in negligence, alleging that their investigation had been flawed and that, but for its failings, he would have been caught before her daughter was killed.
The police applied to strike out the claim. For that purpose the courts assumed the criticisms of the investigation were true.
Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire.q: Do the police owe a duty of care in negligence to a member of the public for failing to catch a criminal who later harms them?
dec: House of Lords, 28 April 1988 (Lord Keith giving the leading speech; Lords Brandon, Templeman, Oliver and Goff): the claim was struck out unanimously.

No proximity: the young woman was one of a vast number of members of the public at risk, and faced no special or distinctive risk. The killer was never in police custody, unlike the borstal boys in the earlier Dorset Yacht case.
Public policy also weighed against a duty. Liability could lead to policing in a detrimentally defensive frame of mind, and defending such claims would divert time and resources from fighting crime.

keys.q: detrimentally defensive frame of mind
keys.w: Lord Keith, on the policy against liability

later: In Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] UKSC 4 the UK Supreme Court held that Hill doesn't give the police a general immunity. Without special circumstances, police owe no duty to protect the public from harm by others (an omission), but they do owe a duty not to cause harm by their own positive acts, such as injuring a passer-by during an arrest.

Article 2 imposes a separate duty on the State: where the authorities know, or ought to know, of a real and immediate risk to an identified person's life, they must take reasonable steps (Osman v UK, 1998).
job: Persuasive only in Ireland, but the practical lesson is the same: you owe a duty of care in your own actions, for example in pursuits, arrests and use of force.
Where there is a real and immediate risk to a known person's life, Osman requires action. Record the threat, the assessment and what you did.
Keep good records of investigative decisions. They are your answer to any later claim.
Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Hill is still the starting point on police omissions, narrowed by Robinson (2018).
