bg: A Polish national was arrested in Ireland on 5 May 2017 on three European Arrest Warrants for drug trafficking offences. He refused to consent to surrender.

He argued that sweeping changes to Poland's courts, judiciary and prosecution service meant he faced a real risk of an unfair trial. The European Commission had proposed that the EU Council find a clear risk of a serious breach of the rule of law in Poland.

In March 2018 the High Court (Donnelly J) found systemic breaches of the rule of law in Poland and referred questions to the Court of Justice of the EU about how an executing court should assess the risk.
Minister for Justice v LM.q: When can an executing court refuse to surrender someone under a European Arrest Warrant because of deficiencies in the issuing State's judicial independence?
dec: Court of Justice of the EU (Grand Chamber), 25 July 2018.

First, the executing court assesses, on objective, reliable, specific and up-to-date material, whether there is a real risk of breach of the right to a fair trial because of systemic or generalised deficiencies in judicial independence.

Second, if there is, it must assess specifically and precisely whether there are substantial grounds to believe that this person will run that risk, given their personal situation, the offence and the context of the warrant. Systemic deficiencies don't automatically mean the individual will be affected.
The executing court must seek any further information it needs from the issuing authority. Refusing surrender is an exception to mutual recognition and must be interpreted strictly.

keys.q: objective, reliable, specific and up-to-date
keys.w: CJEU, on the material for the first step

later: Back in Ireland, Donnelly J sought further information from Poland and in November 2018 ordered surrender. In November 2019 the Supreme Court (O'Donnell J, unanimous) dismissed his appeal: systemic deficiencies alone weren't enough, and nothing specific to him, including a Polish deputy minister's public remarks about him, showed a real risk to his own trial.
Later CJEU cases have confirmed and refined the two-step test.
job: When you execute a European Arrest Warrant, objections about the issuing State are for the High Court, not the arresting garda.

Show the person the warrant and give them a copy at the arrest (or within 24 hours if you don't have it then), tell them their rights (to consent to surrender, to legal advice, and to an interpreter where needed), and bring them before the High Court as soon as may be (European Arrest Warrant Act 2003, s.13).
Record anything the person says about fears for their safety or a fair trial. The court may need it.
Minister for Justice v LM.law: Yes. LM (2018) is still the leading authority on rule-of-law objections to surrender under a European Arrest Warrant.

bg: A man who had been prosecuted brought a civil action for malicious prosecution.
In that action he called the Director of Public Prosecutions as a witness, and sought to learn who had given the information that led to the prosecution.
Marks v Beyfus.q: Can a witness be required to reveal the identity of informants whose information led to a public prosecution?
dec: Court of Appeal, 1890, with Lord Esher MR stating the rule.

As a rule of public policy, in a public prosecution, witnesses can't be required to disclose the identity of informants. Protecting informants encourages people to give information that helps detect crime.

The only exception is where the judge considers that disclosing the informant's identity is necessary to show the accused's innocence. Bowen LJ described protection giving way where the information is necessary for the defence in criminal proceedings.
later: Marks v Beyfus is the classic statement of informer privilege across the common law world. Canada's Supreme Court describes the 'innocence at stake' exception as the only real exception, applying where innocence is demonstrably at stake.
In Ireland, the Supreme Court in DPP v Special Criminal Court (Ward) (1998) described informer privilege as of ancient origin and intact, subject only to the innocence-at-stake exception.
job: Protect informants' identities. Keep informant material separate from the main file, marked as sensitive, and flag it to the prosecutor.
If informant material could help show an accused's innocence, the prosecution must disclose it or drop the case. Raise this early.
Don't decide yourself what can be withheld. Flag it: the prosecutor decides what to disclose, and if privilege is claimed and disputed, the trial judge reads the material and decides (Ward, 1998).
Marks v Beyfus.law: Yes. Marks v Beyfus is still the classic statement of informer privilege, adopted in Ireland in Ward (1998).

bg: At about 2 a.m. a 19-year-old man, who had earlier done work at the house, climbed a ladder to the window of an 18-year-old woman's bedroom, intending to have sex with her, whether or not she consented. He had stripped to his socks.
As he knelt on the window sill she woke and, believing he was her boyfriend, invited him in. They had sex. When she realised her mistake, she struck him and he left.
He was convicted of burglary with intent to rape, under s.9(1)(a) of the Theft Act 1968. The trial judge rejected the argument that, because she had invited him in, he hadn't entered as a trespasser.
R v Collins.q: What does it mean to enter 'as a trespasser' for burglary, and when exactly had he entered?
dec: Court of Appeal, 5 May 1972: the appeal was allowed and the conviction quashed.

A person enters as a trespasser only if he knows he is entering another's premises without consent, or is at least reckless about whether he has consent. Civil concepts such as trespass ab initio don't apply.

The key question was where he was when she invited him in. If he was still outside, on the sill, when invited, he may not have entered as a trespasser. The jury was never asked to decide that, or whether he was reckless in relying on an invitation not meant for him, so it was misdirected.

keys.q: knowing that he is a trespasser and nevertheless deliberately enters
keys.w: Edmund Davies LJ, on entering 'as a trespasser'

later: In England the specific offence was later recast as trespass with intent to commit a sexual offence (Sexual Offences Act 2003, s.63).

In Ireland, burglary is defined in s.12 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001: entering a building or part of a building as a trespasser with intent to commit an arrestable offence, or, having entered as a trespasser, committing or attempting one. Collins is persuasive on what entering 'as a trespasser' means.
job: In a burglary, establish exactly where the suspect was when any permission was given, who gave it, and what the suspect knew or believed.
Record the means and point of entry (ladder, window, door), and any marks or forensic traces.
Where the intended offence is sexual, also consider the specific sexual offences and investigate consent fully.
R v Collins.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland on entering 'as a trespasser'.

src.t: Wikipedia — R v Collins

bg: In a department store, a man went behind an unoccupied counter area on the shop floor and opened the till. It was empty, so he left.
A store detective arrested him. He admitted that he would have taken any money he found in the till.
He was convicted of burglary under s.9(1)(a) of the Theft Act 1968: entering a building or part of a building as a trespasser with intent to steal.
R v Walkington.q: Can the area behind a shop counter be a 'part of a building' that a customer enters as a trespasser? And does an empty till defeat the intent to steal?
dec: Court of Appeal, 1979: the appeal was dismissed and the burglary conviction stood.

He argued that, as a customer, he was lawfully in the store, and that a large store couldn't be divided into separate parts. But the area behind the counter was capable of being a 'part of a building', and whether he entered it as a trespasser was a question for the jury.
An intention to steal can exist even where, unknown to the accused, there is nothing there to steal. The empty till didn't negate his intent.
later: Walkington is the standard authority that a shop's staff-only areas (behind the counter, the stockroom, an office) can be separate 'parts of a building' for burglary.
In Ireland, s.12 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 also covers entering 'any building or part of a building' as a trespasser, so Walkington is persuasive.
job: Where a customer goes into a staff-only area of a shop, consider burglary. Record how the area was marked or separated (counter, signs, door), and what the suspect did and said.
Get the CCTV showing the movement into the area and the attempt on the till or goods, and a statement from staff about who is allowed there.
Record any admission about intent. The fact that there was nothing to steal doesn't defeat it.
R v Walkington.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland on 'part of a building' and conditional intent.

src.t: Law Teacher — R v Walkington

bg: In December 1985 a constable in Northern Ireland arrested a man at his home, without a warrant, under s.12(1)(b) of the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1984. That power allowed a constable to arrest a person he had 'reasonable grounds for suspecting' to be concerned in acts of terrorism. The arrest was in connection with a murder.

The constable had no personal knowledge of the man's involvement. He said a superior officer had briefed him that the man was involved, and had ordered the arrest. The man was questioned and released without charge in January 1986.

He sued for unlawful arrest and false imprisonment. His counsel chose not to cross-examine the constable on the details of the briefing. The trial judge called the evidence scanty, but inferred that the briefing gave reasonable grounds, and the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland agreed.
O’Hara v Chief Constable.q: Can a constable who arrests on the strength of a briefing from a superior have reasonable grounds for suspicion? And whose suspicion counts?
dec: House of Lords, 12 December 1996 (Lords Goff, Mustill, Steyn, Hoffmann and Hope): the appeal was dismissed.

The test is a simple, practical one, and it relates entirely to what is in the arresting officer's mind when he arrests. It is partly subjective: he must genuinely suspect the person. It is partly objective: there must be reasonable grounds for that suspicion.

The grounds needn't come from the officer's own observations. Information from others, such as a briefing, a tip-off from a member of the public or a report from an informer, may be enough, even if it later proves to be wrong.
But the discretion to arrest belongs to the arresting officer, not to his superiors. A bare order to arrest, with no information behind it, doesn't give him reasonable grounds.
Here, the trial judge was entitled to infer from the sparse evidence that the briefing had given the constable reasonable grounds, so the appeal failed on its facts.

keys.q: he must have formed a genuine suspicion in his own mind
keys.w: Lord Hope, on the subjective part of the test

keys.q: Hearsay information may therefore afford a constable a reasonable ground to arrest.
keys.w: Lord Steyn

later: In Raissi (2008) the English Court of Appeal applied O'Hara: officers who weren't told what their superiors suspected couldn't simply assume that the superiors had good grounds.
Lord Steyn relied on Lord Devlin's judgment in Hussien v Chong Fook Kam (1969): a constable doesn't need a prima facie case before arresting.

In Ireland, s.4(3) of the Criminal Law Act 1997 lets a garda arrest without warrant where he or she, 'with reasonable cause', suspects that an arrestable offence has been committed and that the person is guilty of it. O'Hara is persuasive on what that requires.
job: The decision to arrest is yours. If you are briefed or asked to arrest someone, make sure you know the grounds, and that they satisfy you.
Record the grounds in your notebook at the time: what you were told, by whom and when, and why you suspected the person. You may have to explain them in court.
Information from colleagues, informants or members of the public can be enough, even if it later proves wrong, as long as your suspicion was genuine and reasonable at the time.
O’Hara v Chief Constable.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. O'Hara (1996) is still the leading statement of the test for reasonable suspicion.

bg: In Malaysia, a piece of timber fell from a passing lorry and killed a person travelling in a car.

The next day police arrested two men, the lorry driver and his attendant, for causing death by reckless or dangerous driving. The police didn't know which of the two had been driving, and suspected that their alibis were false.
The men were later released. They sued for false imprisonment, and the case went on appeal to the Privy Council.
Hussein v Chong Fook Yam.q: What does 'reasonable suspicion' mean? Must the police have a prima facie case before they arrest?
dec: Privy Council, 7 October 1969, with Lord Devlin giving the judgment.

Suspicion is the stage where proof is lacking. It comes at or near the start of an investigation, and prima facie proof comes at the end. So reasonable suspicion for arrest doesn't require a prima facie case.
Prima facie proof is made of admissible evidence, but suspicion can also take into account matters that couldn't be put in evidence at all.

A power to arrest on reasonable suspicion doesn't mean it should always be used. It is a discretion, and factors besides the strength of the case matter, such as the possibility of escape, the prevention of further crime and the obstruction of police inquiries.

Lord Devlin also explained when an arrest happens: when the officer says he is arresting the person, or uses force to restrain them, or makes clear by words or conduct that he will use force if necessary to stop them going where they want.
On the facts, it was reasonable to suspect that one of the two men was the driver, but not yet that the lorry had been driven recklessly or dangerously. The arrest was premature.

keys.q: a state of conjecture or surmise where proof is lacking
keys.w: Lord Devlin, on what suspicion means

keys.q: I suspect but I cannot prove
keys.w: Lord Devlin

keys.q: It means that there is an executive discretion.
keys.w: Lord Devlin, on the power to arrest

later: Lord Devlin's definition is quoted across the common law world. In O'Hara (1996) the House of Lords relied on it: a constable needn't have a prima facie case, and information from an informer or a member of the public may be enough.
Courts still describe it as one of the enduring definitions of suspicion (Supreme Court of Namibia, 2020).
In Ireland, s.4(3) of the Criminal Law Act 1997 requires reasonable suspicion of both parts: that an arrestable offence has been committed, and that the person is guilty of it.
job: You don't need proof to arrest, only genuine and reasonable suspicion. But it must cover the offence itself, not just who was involved. Ask yourself: what offence, and why do I suspect this person committed it?
Information you couldn't use in court, such as an informant's tip, can still form part of your grounds. Record it.
Arrest is a discretion. Note why arrest was needed at that point (risk of flight, further offending, interference with evidence or witnesses) rather than further inquiries first.
Hussein v Chong Fook Yam.law: Privy Council authority (correct name: Shaaban bin Hussien v Chong Fook Kam), persuasive in Ireland. Lord Devlin's definition of suspicion is still the standard one.

bg: Police stopped a car for expired registration and arrested the driver for driving on a suspended licence.

An officer took a smartphone from his pocket and, because of items linking him to a street gang, looked through it at the scene, seeing gang terms in the messages or contacts. About two hours later a gang-specialist detective searched the phone at the station and found a photograph of him in front of a car that had been involved in a shooting weeks earlier.

He sought to have the evidence excluded and lost; the California courts upheld the search. In a companion case (United States v Wurie), police had searched an arrested man's flip phone, which led them to drugs and a firearm; there, the federal appeals court ruled the evidence should have been excluded.
Riley v California.q: Can police search the digital contents of a phone taken from a person they have arrested, without a warrant?
dec: US Supreme Court, 25 June 2014, unanimously (Chief Justice Roberts; Justice Alito concurred separately).

The search-incident-to-arrest exception exists to protect officers and to prevent the destruction of evidence. Neither justifies searching a phone's data. Data can't be used as a weapon, and officers can still examine the phone physically to make sure it isn't one.

The risk of remote wiping or encryption wasn't shown to be common, and it can be met by other means, such as switching the phone off and removing the battery, or putting it in a bag that blocks signals.
Modern phones hold vast amounts of personal information, 'the privacies of life', so searching one is far more intrusive than searching the physical items a person carries.
So officers must generally get a warrant. Exigent circumstances, such as a child abduction or an imminent bomb, can still justify a warrantless search, judged case by case.

keys.q: Modern cell phones are not just another technological convenience.
keys.w: Chief Justice Roberts

keys.q: get a warrant
keys.w: Chief Justice Roberts, on what police must generally do

later: Riley is the leading US authority on searching phones on arrest.

In Ireland, the Supreme Court in Quirke (2023) held that seizing a computer under a search warrant to search its contents was unlawful, because the judge who issued the warrant hadn't been told that devices would be seized and searched.
job: Persuasive only in Ireland, but the lesson is the same: don't browse a suspect's phone on arrest. Seize it, and get proper authority (for example, a warrant that expressly covers searching devices) before examining its contents.
Preserve the data: follow Garda guidance on seizing devices (usually isolating the phone from the network, for example in a signal-blocking bag), and keep continuity.
In a genuine emergency, such as a threat to life, act to protect life, and record exactly what you looked at and why.
Riley v California.law: US authority, persuasive in Ireland. Riley (2014) still governs phone searches on arrest in the US.

TDCAA — SCOTUS has cell phones, and you need a warrant to search them after Riley v California

bg: A surgeon working as a locum at a hospital made claims for fees. The claims were for work that other doctors had carried out, or for work paid for through the National Health Service.
He was convicted at St Albans Crown Court on 29 April 1981 of four offences under the Theft Act 1968, including obtaining property by deception.
He appealed, arguing that dishonesty is a matter of the accused's own state of mind, and that the jury should have been directed to that effect.
R v Ghosh.q: How should a jury decide whether a defendant acted dishonestly?
dec: Court of Appeal, 5 April 1982 (Lord Lane CJ, Lloyd and Eastham JJ): the appeal was dismissed.
First, the jury decides whether, by the ordinary standards of reasonable and honest people, what was done was dishonest. If it wasn't, the prosecution fails.
Second, if it was dishonest by those standards, the jury considers whether the defendant himself must have realised that what he was doing was dishonest by those standards.
The trial judge's direction hadn't made the conviction unsafe.

keys.q: ordinary standards of reasonable and honest people
keys.w: Lord Lane CJ, the first stage

later: For 35 years Ghosh was the test in English criminal cases. In Ivey v Genting Casinos (2017) the UK Supreme Court said its second, subjective stage 'does not correctly represent the law'.
In R v Barton and Booth (2020) the English Court of Appeal confirmed that Ivey, not Ghosh, now applies in criminal cases.

In Ireland, 'dishonestly' is defined by statute as 'without a claim of right made in good faith' (Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, s.2(1)), so the English tests are persuasive at most.
job: In Ireland the question is whether the suspect acted without a claim of right made in good faith. In interview, ask whether they believed they were entitled to the property, and why.
A genuine belief in entitlement can defeat the charge even if it was unreasonable, but an unreasonable belief is less likely to be accepted as genuine. Test the account against the evidence.
Record exactly what the suspect says about their belief. It is often the whole defence.
R v Ghosh.law: No longer the test in England (Ivey, 2017). In Ireland, the statutory definition in s.2(1) of the 2001 Act applies.

Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, s.2 (Revised Acts)
LegalBlog.ie — Theft and dishonesty

bg: On 20 and 21 August 2012 a professional gambler played Punto Banco at Crockfords casino and won about £7.7 million.

He used 'edge-sorting'. Tiny manufacturing differences on the edges of playing cards can show whether a card is valuable. With an associate, he got the croupier, who didn't understand the significance, to turn certain cards and to re-use the same shoe, so that the valuable cards could be recognised.

The casino refused to pay, believing the game had been compromised. He openly admitted edge-sorting, said it wasn't cheating, and sued for his winnings. The High Court and the Court of Appeal both held that it was cheating.
Ivey v Genting Casinos.q: Was edge-sorting cheating? And does dishonesty depend on whether the person realised that what they did was dishonest?
dec: UK Supreme Court, 25 October 2017 (Lord Hughes, with Lord Neuberger, Lady Hale, Lord Kerr and Lord Thomas agreeing): the appeal was dismissed unanimously.

Cheating normally involves a deliberate act to gain an advantage that is objectively improper. Tricking the croupier into arranging the cards had the same effect as secretly rearranging them himself: he had fixed the deck. That was cheating.
On dishonesty, the tribunal first establishes what the person actually knew or believed about the facts. It then decides whether the conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people.

There is no further requirement that the person must have appreciated that the conduct was dishonest by those standards. The second stage of Ghosh does not correctly represent the law, and directions based on it should no longer be given.

keys.q: does not correctly represent the law
keys.w: UK Supreme Court, on the second stage of Ghosh

keys.q: ordinary decent people
keys.w: UK Supreme Court, on the standard for dishonesty

later: Because Ivey was a civil claim, its comments on criminal dishonesty were strictly obiter. In R v Barton and Booth (2020) the English Court of Appeal confirmed that the Ivey test applies in criminal cases, and that Ghosh is overruled on the point.
In Ireland, 'dishonestly' is defined by statute as 'without a claim of right made in good faith', so Ivey is persuasive at most.
job: In Ireland, focus on the statutory question: did the suspect act without a claim of right made in good faith?
In fraud investigations, establish what the suspect actually knew and believed: documents, messages, previous warnings, and their own account in interview.
Don't accept 'I didn't think it was wrong' at face value. In England that is no longer a defence; in Ireland, the question is whether they genuinely believed they had a right to the property.
Ivey v Genting Casinos.law: UK authority, persuasive in Ireland. Ivey (2017) is the current English test for dishonesty.

bg: Two men went into a woman's house.
They took her jewellery box from her bedroom. After taking it, they tied her up.

They were convicted of robbery. On appeal they argued that the theft was complete as soon as they had possession of the box, so the force (tying her up) came afterwards, not 'immediately before or at the time of' stealing, as robbery requires.
R v Hale.q: When force is used after the property has been taken, can the offence still be robbery?
dec: Court of Appeal, 1978: the appeals were dismissed and the robbery convictions stood.
To treat the theft as over the moment they picked up the box was contrary to common sense.
Appropriation is a continuing act. It doesn't end abruptly, and it is for the jury to decide when it has ended, looking at the defendants' whole course of conduct.
So the jury could find that the force used in tying her up was used at the time of stealing.

keys.q: continuing act
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on appropriation

later: Hale is the standard authority that robbery can be committed where the force follows the taking, while the appropriation is still continuing.

In Ireland, s.14 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 defines robbery in the same words: stealing and, immediately before or at the time of doing so, and in order to do so, using force on any person, or putting or seeking to put any person in fear of being then and there subjected to force. It carries up to life imprisonment.
job: Where force comes after the taking (a shop worker pushed at the door, a householder restrained before the thieves leave), consider robbery, not just theft and assault.
Record the whole sequence in order, with times: entry, taking, force or threats, and departure. The jury will decide when the theft ended.
Note what the force was for. Robbery requires force used 'in order to' steal, such as to keep the property or get away with it.
R v Hale.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland on s.14 of the 2001 Act.

src.t: Law Teacher — R v Hale (1978)
Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, s.14 (Revised Acts)

bg: Two men targeted a man for his wallet.
One of them pushed him so that he lost his balance. That let the other take his wallet.
Both were convicted of robbery. On appeal they argued that pushing or nudging someone isn't 'force' on a person, so the offence wasn't robbery.
R v Dawson.q: Is a push that makes someone lose their balance 'force' for robbery?
dec: Court of Appeal, 1976: the appeals were dismissed and the robbery convictions stood.
'Force' is an ordinary word in everyday use. The jury doesn't need a direction on what it means.
Whether force was used is a question of fact for the jury, and the jury was entitled to find that the push, which made him lose his balance, was force.
later: Dawson is the standard authority that the force needed for robbery can be slight.

In Ireland, s.14 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 also requires 'force on any person', or putting or seeking to put a person in fear of force. Whether a minor push or a snatch is enough will be for the jury.
job: Describe the force precisely in statements: who pushed, how hard, and the effect (lost balance, stumbled, fell). That is what the jury will judge.
Where contact was slight or only with the property (a bag snatched without touching the person), robbery may be hard to prove. Consider theft as an alternative.
Get CCTV and independent witness accounts of the contact. Victims often can't say exactly what happened.
R v Dawson.law: English authority (full name: R v Dawson and James), persuasive in Ireland on s.14 of the 2001 Act.

src.t: Law Teacher — R v Dawson and James (1976)
Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, s.14 (Revised Acts)

bg: Gardaí stopped a man's car after his passenger alleged that he had raped her. At the roadside he said the intercourse had been consensual.
He was detained under the Criminal Justice Act 1984, cautioned and told his rights, and he consulted a solicitor. When interviewed, he made no further statement.

At his trial in the Central Criminal Court he gave an account of consent. The prosecution argued that his silence in custody bore on his credibility, and the trial judge admitted evidence of it. He was cross-examined about what happened at the station, and convicted of rape.
DPP v Finnerty.q: Can the prosecution use a suspect's refusal to answer questions in garda custody against him at trial?
dec: Supreme Court, 17 June 1999 (Keane J, for a unanimous court of Hamilton CJ, Denham, Barrington, Keane and Murphy JJ): the appeal was allowed, the conviction quashed and a retrial ordered.
A person detained in garda custody has the right to refuse to answer questions. The Criminal Justice Act 1984, which created detention for questioning, didn't abolish that right.
The right would be significantly eroded if a jury could draw adverse inferences from the refusal. Admitting evidence of his silence, and cross-examining him about it, was wrong.
In general, a trial judge should make no reference to the accused's refusal to answer questions when charging the jury.
later: In Coddington (2001) the Court of Criminal Appeal applied Finnerty where an accused didn't give evidence at trial: the jury 'must be expressly so advised' that no inference can be drawn, and the conviction was quashed because no such direction was given.

Since 1 July 2007, s.19A of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 allows inferences from a failure to mention, when questioned or charged, a fact later relied on in the defence that clearly called for an explanation. It applies only if the suspect was told in ordinary language what the effect of not mentioning it might be, had a reasonable opportunity to consult a solicitor, and the questioning was electronically recorded (or they consented in writing to it not being recorded). No one can be convicted solely or mainly on such an inference.

Sections 18 and 19 of the 1984 Act allow similar inferences from failing to account for objects, substances or marks, or for presence at a place, again only if the suspect was told in ordinary language what the effect of failing to do so might be.
job: Without a statutory inference provision, a suspect's silence in interview can't be used against them. Don't present it in evidence as if it were suspicious.

Where you intend to rely on ss.18, 19 or 19A, follow the conditions exactly: the caution in ordinary language, a reasonable opportunity to consult a solicitor, and an electronically recorded interview. Record each step.
Put the specific facts, objects or marks to the suspect clearly, so that a later failure to mention or account for them can be relied on.
DPP v Finnerty.law: Yes. Finnerty (1999) is still the leading Irish authority on silence in custody, subject to the statutory inference provisions.

Irish Times — No inference can be drawn from accused's exercise of right not to give evidence (Coddington, 2001)
Criminal Justice Act 1984, s.19A (Revised Acts)

bg: In early 1988 a man was charged in the District Court with entering a building as a trespasser and stealing there, and with malicious damage.
The District Justice refused bail. On 11 March 1988 the President of the High Court granted it.

The DPP's only objection was that the man would continue to engage in criminal activities if released. The President held that, following O'Callaghan (1966), he couldn't consider that ground, but let evidence on it be given so that the DPP could appeal.
Ryan v DPP.q: Can a court refuse bail because the accused is likely to commit further offences if released?
dec: Supreme Court, 18 November 1988 (Finlay CJ, with Griffin and Hederman JJ; Walsh J agreeing): the DPP's appeal was dismissed.

The Court reaffirmed O'Callaghan. Bail may be refused on grounds such as a real risk that the accused won't stand trial or will interfere with witnesses or evidence, but the likelihood of committing offences on bail isn't a valid ground.

Refusing bail to prevent offending had no basis at common law before 1922, and Article 40.3 of the Constitution didn't provide one. It would be a form of preventive detention, at odds with the presumption of innocence.
The answers to offending on bail lay elsewhere: police surveillance, speedy trials and deterrent sentences.

keys.q: Is the applicant likely to stand his trial?
keys.w: Ó Dálaigh CJ in O'Callaghan, quoted in Ryan

keys.q: a form of preventative justice which has no place in our legal system
keys.w: Walsh J in O'Callaghan, quoted in Ryan

later: The Sixteenth Amendment (1996) changed Article 40.4 to allow refusal of bail where it is reasonably considered necessary to prevent a serious offence, and s.2 of the Bail Act 1997 gave effect to it.
The O'Callaghan grounds that Ryan reaffirmed (flight, and interference with witnesses or evidence) still apply alongside s.2.
job: When objecting to bail, be clear which ground you rely on: O'Callaghan (risk of flight; interference with witnesses or evidence) or s.2 of the Bail Act 1997 (necessary to prevent a serious offence).

For s.2, bring evidence on the factors the court weighs, such as the seriousness of the charge, the strength of the evidence, offences committed on bail, previous convictions and other pending charges.
A general belief that the accused will reoffend isn't enough. Give specific, recent evidence.
Ryan v DPP.law: Overtaken in part: the Sixteenth Amendment (1996) and s.2 of the Bail Act 1997 now allow refusal of bail to prevent serious offences. The O'Callaghan grounds that Ryan reaffirmed still apply.

bg: A man was charged with a murder committed in a house. No one claimed to have seen the killing, and the case against him was entirely circumstantial.
His first trial ended without a verdict. At a second trial he was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment, and his appeal was dismissed.

In the House of Lords he argued that, where a case rests wholly or substantially on circumstantial evidence, the judge must tell the jury that they can convict only if the facts proved are inconsistent with any other reasonable conclusion.
McGreevy v DPP.q: Must a judge give a special direction where the prosecution case is circumstantial?
dec: House of Lords, 1973, with Lord Morris of Borth-y-Gest giving the leading speech: no special direction is required.
The fundamental requirement in every case is that the jury must be satisfied of guilt beyond reasonable doubt. A circumstantial case is no different.

The question for the jury is whether the facts, as they find them, drive them to the conclusion of guilt. No particular form of words is mandatory; how the judge explains the burden depends on the nature of the case and the evidence.

keys.q: satisfied of guilt beyond all reasonable doubt
keys.w: Lord Morris

keys.q: It depends upon the nature of the case and the evidence.
keys.w: Lord Morris, on how to direct the jury

later: McGreevy remains the leading authority that circumstantial evidence needs no special formula of words.
The underlying rule is the same in Ireland: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, however the evidence is made up.
job: Circumstantial cases are built strand by strand: CCTV, phone and location data, forensics, movements, motive. Gather and record each, with continuity.
Look just as hard for evidence pointing away from the suspect, and record it. The jury will ask whether the facts lead to guilt and nothing else.
Put the circumstantial strands to the suspect in interview, so that their explanation, or failure to give one where s.19A applies, is on record.

bg: Two men were tried for receiving stolen goods, knowing them to have been stolen.

The prosecution relied on their possession of goods that had recently been stolen. The question on appeal was how the jury should be directed about an explanation given by an accused in that position.
R v Schama.q: Where an accused is found with recently stolen goods and gives an explanation, how should the jury approach it?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 1914.

Where the prosecution proves that the accused was in possession of recently stolen goods, the jury may infer that he received them knowing they were stolen, if he gives no explanation or gives one they don't believe.
If he gives an explanation that might reasonably be true, the jury must acquit, even if they aren't convinced that it is true. A reasonable doubt is enough.
The burden of proof never shifts to the accused.

keys.q: the onus of proof lies always on the prosecution
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal

later: Schama was cited by the House of Lords in Woolmington v DPP (1935), the leading case on the prosecution's burden of proof.

In Ireland, the Court of Criminal Appeal in Oglesby (1966) rejected any separate 'doctrine' of recent possession: possession of recently stolen goods supports an ordinary inference of fact, and the onus stays on the prosecution.

Section 17(2) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 now provides that where a person receives or handles property in circumstances in which it is reasonable to conclude that they knew it was stolen, or were reckless about it, they are taken to have known or been reckless, unless the court or jury has a reasonable doubt about it. Handling under s.17 also covers recklessness.
job: Record exactly where, when and in what circumstances the property was found, and how soon after the theft. The closer in time, the stronger the inference.
Get the suspect's account of how they came by it (who from, where, when, the price), then check every detail. An explanation that might reasonably be true means an acquittal.
Note anything that points to knowledge or recklessness: a price well below value, a sale in a pub or car park, removed serial numbers, false names.
R v Schama.law: English authority (full name: R v Schama; R v Abramovitch), persuasive in Ireland. Read with Oglesby (1966) and s.17(2) of the 2001 Act.

bg: Gardaí stopped a car in Dundalk. They suspected the man in it of involvement with an unlawful organisation. He got out when asked, and a garda told him he would search him under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939.

The garda patted both jacket pockets, felt something solid in each, and took a small walkie-talkie from the right-hand pocket. When he went for the left-hand pocket, the man pushed his hand away and turned his body — passive resistance.

The garda then arrested him under s.30, cautioned him and told him the reason, and said force would be used if necessary. The man handed over the contents of the left-hand pocket: explosives (detonators).
He was convicted in the Special Criminal Court in July 1993 of possessing explosives and sentenced to seven years. His only ground of appeal was that the search was unlawful and unconstitutional.
DPP v O'Donnell.q: When must gardaí tell a person the legal basis for a search — and what happens when a person who went along with a search starts to resist?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 28 February 1995 (O'Hanlon J, with O'Flaherty and Geoghegan JJ): leave to appeal was refused and the conviction stood.

A compulsory search is unlawful unless it can be justified under powers vested by law. Drawing on Christie v Leachinsky, the person must be informed of the legal basis relied on before the search proceeds.

Gardaí need to invoke powers of compulsion, under common law or statute, only when cooperation is withdrawn. At that point they must tell the person the legal justification for interfering with their constitutional rights.

Here the man initially went along with the search, then objected; he was then arrested and told the reason. The continued search of the left-hand pocket was lawful. Even if taking the walkie-talkie had breached his rights, there was no causal link between that and finding the explosives, so the evidence was admissible.

keys.q: unlawful unless it can be justified under powers vested by law
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on a compulsory search

later: With DPP v Rooney (1992), O'Donnell is the authority that a person must be told the legal basis before a compulsory search.

In DPP v McFadden (2003) the Court of Criminal Appeal considered O'Donnell's point that a search continued after consent is withdrawn needs lawful authority, and notice of it. McFadden also shows that consent and a statutory power are separate routes.
In DPP v Kelly [2012] IECCA 71 the Court of Criminal Appeal held there is no duty to explain the power where the person doesn't object — but the safe course is always to tell them.
job: Before any compulsory search, tell the person the power you are using and why, in plain words. You needn't quote the section.
If someone who was cooperating objects, stop. State the power and the reason before you go on — otherwise everything you find after the objection is at risk.
Record the sequence exactly: what you told them, when they objected, what you said then, and what you found where.
DPP v O'Donnell.law: Yes. O'Donnell (1995) is still the leading authority on telling a person the legal basis for a compulsory search, and on acquiescence followed by objection.

bg: A man was arrested in Ireland and extradited to England under Part III of the Extradition Act 1965.

When gardaí arrested him, they seized goods he had with him. He sued the officers for the return of the goods, and applied for an injunction to stop them parting with the goods before the action was heard.
The case raised what gardaí may seize from an arrested person, and what they may do with it.
Jennings v Quinn.q: When gardaí make a lawful arrest, what property found on the person may they seize without a warrant, and may they keep it?
dec: Supreme Court, with O'Keeffe J giving the judgment of the Court.

When effecting a lawful arrest, police may seize, without a search warrant, property in the person's possession that is: evidence in support of the charge; evidence in support of another criminal charge then in contemplation; or reasonably believed to be stolen or unlawfully in their possession.
Property seized on that basis may be kept for use at trial.
The free reports available don't show how the injunction application itself was decided; the case is cited for O'Keeffe J's statement of the law.
later: In DPP v McFadden [2003] 2 IR 105 the Court of Criminal Appeal accepted O'Keeffe J's statement as a correct statement of Irish law, and held that where a search on arrest turns up evidence of another charge, gardaí may keep it to prevent its removal or destruction.
Later cases, including DPP v Wilson (2017), cite Jennings v Quinn for gardaí's right — and duty — to retain and preserve articles that may be evidence.
job: After a lawful arrest, you may seize evidence of the offence, evidence of another offence you have in contemplation, and property you reasonably believe is stolen or unlawfully held.
Record what you seized, where it was found, and why it falls into one of those categories.
Keep continuity from the moment of seizure. The right to keep evidence carries a duty to preserve it (see Braddish).
Jennings v Quinn.law: Yes. Jennings v Quinn is still the classic statement of the power to seize on arrest, adopted in McFadden (2003).

bg: Two appeals were heard together.
In the first, a man took goods from supermarket shelves, replaced their price labels with labels showing lower prices, and paid the lower prices at the checkout. He was arrested after paying.
In the second (Anderton v Burnside), a man moved a lower price label onto a more expensive joint of pork. The checkout was alerted and he was stopped before he could leave.
R v Morris.q: Is switching price labels an 'appropriation' for theft — and must the accused assume all of the owner's rights?
dec: House of Lords, 1983 (Lord Roskill, with Lords Fraser, Edmund-Davies, Brandon and Brightman): the appeals were dismissed and the theft convictions stood.
Substituting a label showing a lower price for one showing a higher price is an appropriation of the goods, because it assumes one of the owner's rights — the right to set the price.
The prosecution doesn't have to prove that the accused assumed all of the owner's rights. Assuming any one of them is enough.
later: In Gomez (1993) the House of Lords disapproved Lord Roskill's statement in Morris that appropriation requires an adverse interference with the owner's rights, holding that appropriation can take place with the owner's consent.

In Ireland, s.4(5) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 defines 'appropriates' as 'usurps or adversely interferes with the proprietary rights of the owner' — language close to Morris.
job: Label-switching, swapping packaging or tampering with prices in a shop is appropriation — consider theft.
Record exactly what was moved or changed, and when. Get the CCTV, the till receipt and a statement from staff about the true prices.
Note when and where the suspect was stopped — before or after paying — and what they said.
R v Morris.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Read with s.4(5) of the 2001 Act and Gomez (1993).

bg: An assistant manager of an electrical goods shop agreed to supply goods to an acquaintance in return for two stolen building society cheques.

He prepared a list of goods to the value of the cheques and asked the manager to authorise the sale. The manager told him to check with the bank; he falsely reported that the bank had accepted the cheques, and the manager authorised the supply.

The goods were handed over and the cheques were dishonoured. The employees were convicted of theft. The Court of Appeal quashed the convictions, holding that because the manager had consented, there was no appropriation.
R v Gomez.q: Can there be an appropriation for theft where the owner consented to the goods being taken — consent obtained by deception?
dec: House of Lords, 3 December 1992 (Lord Keith, with Lords Jauncey, Browne-Wilkinson and Slynn; Lord Lowry dissenting): the prosecution's appeal was allowed and the convictions upheld.
An act can be an appropriation even though it is done with the owner's consent. The House followed its earlier decision in Lawrence.
Lord Roskill's statement in Morris that appropriation requires an adverse interference with or usurpation of the owner's rights was disapproved.

keys.q: notwithstanding that it is done with the consent of the owner
keys.w: Lord Keith

later: In R v Hinks (2000) the House of Lords went further: a person can appropriate property even by receiving a valid gift.

Irish law takes a different route. Theft under s.4(1) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 requires appropriation 'without the consent of its owner' — but s.4(2) provides that consent obtained by deception or intimidation is not consent. So a Gomez-type case can still be theft in Ireland.
job: In Ireland, where goods or money were handed over because of a lie or a threat, theft can still be charged: consent obtained by deception or intimidation isn't consent (s.4(2)).
Record exactly what was said to get the property, who said it, and what the owner relied on. Consider deception and fraud offences as well.
Don't rely on English cases like Gomez for the rule in Ireland — use the 2001 Act's wording.
R v Gomez.law: English authority. In Ireland the 2001 Act governs: appropriation without consent, with deceived or intimidated consent not counting.

bg: The Prime Minister announced, the day before a government function, that he would attend it.
Domestic law required organisers to give three days' notice of a demonstration. That was impossible in the time available.
About 150 people gathered outside the function to demonstrate, without giving notice. Police dispersed them. The summary available doesn't describe any disorder.
Bukta and Others v Hungary.q: Can police disperse a peaceful demonstration simply because the organisers didn't give the notice the law requires?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 17 July 2007: violation of Article 11 (freedom of peaceful assembly).
A prior-notice requirement can pursue legitimate aims — preventing disorder and protecting the rights of others — and isn't in itself a breach of Article 11.

But where a demonstration responds to an event announced too late for notice to be given, the organisers would face a choice between giving up the right to assemble and assembling without notice. Requiring them to give it up serves no legitimate aim.

Dispersing a peaceful assembly solely because notice wasn't given, without any illegal conduct by the participants, was disproportionate. Authorities must show a certain degree of tolerance towards peaceful gatherings.

keys.q: show a certain degree of tolerance towards peaceful gatherings
keys.w: ECtHR

later: Bukta is a leading authority that spontaneous, peaceful demonstrations are protected even without notice.
Kudrevičius and Others v Lithuania (2015) shows the other side: deliberate, serious disruption beyond what's normal for a protest can justify sanctions, after the authorities have shown tolerance.
job: A peaceful protest isn't unlawful just because it's spontaneous or unannounced. Facilitate it and engage with whoever is organising it.
Act on specific conduct — an offence, a danger, serious obstruction — using the right power (for example, a s.8 direction for a listed offence, DPP v Kelly (2018)), not on the absence of paperwork.
Record what you saw, what you said, and why any step you took was necessary.
Bukta and Others v Hungary.law: Yes. Bukta (2007) is still cited for tolerance of peaceful, spontaneous assemblies.

bg: An authorised political rally was held in Bolotnaya Square, Moscow, on 6 May 2012. About 5,000 people were expected; far more came.
Riot police blocked the route the organisers expected into the park and redirected the crowd. The organisers said the police wouldn't negotiate, and staged a sit-in.
Police ordered the meeting closed, but the crowd couldn't hear the announcement. Police then dispersed the crowd by force, and violent clashes followed.
The applicant, who had been peaceful throughout, was arrested, held for 36 hours, and sentenced to 15 days' administrative detention for obstructing traffic and disobeying police orders.
Frumkin v Russia.q: Did the authorities' handling of the rally, and the arrest and punishment of a peaceful protester, breach the Convention?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 5 January 2016: violations of Article 11 (assembly), Article 5 (liberty) and Article 6 (fair trial).

The authorities must keep open, prompt channels of communication with organisers. Here there was no reliable channel before the rally, too little effort to resolve the confusion over the venue, and a failure to take simple steps at the first signs of conflict, which let the situation escalate.
Ending the whole meeting wasn't shown to be necessary: the trouble was concentrated in one area while the rest stayed calm, and no attempt was made to isolate the disturbed sector.

The applicant was peaceful and not accused of violence or even passive resistance. Article 11 still protected him after the official termination, and there was no pressing social need to arrest him, let alone jail him. The 36-hour detention was arbitrary, and the courts' refusal to hear the defence evidence or examine the lawfulness of the police order breached Article 6.

keys.q: pressing social need
keys.w: ECtHR, finding none for arresting the peaceful applicant

later: Frumkin is widely cited for the State's duty to communicate with protest organisers and to target only those actually committing offences.
The Court stressed the chilling effect of arrests and punishment on others who might wish to protest.
job: At any protest, set up a reliable line of communication with the organisers early, and use it when tension rises.
Isolate trouble where it is rather than ending the whole event. If you must order people to disperse, make sure the order can actually be heard and understood.
Arrest people for what they did, not for being there — and record each person's specific conduct.
Frumkin v Russia.law: Yes. Frumkin (2016) is still a leading Strasbourg case on policing protests.

bg: Late on a December night in 1962, police stopped a driver on his way home, suspecting he was driving while unfit through drink.

He refused to get out of his car. The officers said they arrested him for being under the influence of drink and unfit to drive; he said he was never told he was under arrest. He was forced out of the car and injured in the struggle.
At the station a police doctor found he wasn't unfit to drive. He was released without charge, and no prosecution followed.
He sued the constable for assault. The trial judge treated the arrest as unlawful, and the jury awarded damages. The constable appealed.
Wiltshire v Barrett.q: Does a power to arrest a person 'committing' an offence cover someone who only appears to be committing it — and what happens if inquiries then clear them?
dec: Court of Appeal, 1965 (Lord Denning MR, Davies and Salmon LJJ). The statute allowed a constable to arrest without warrant a person 'committing' the offence of driving while unfit.

Lord Denning held that a constable is justified in arresting a driver who is apparently committing the offence. The question is whether the facts, as they appeared to the constable at the time, warranted it — a question of fact for the jury, and of reasonableness for the judge.

A later acquittal, or a decision not to prosecute, doesn't make the arrest unlawful. Lord Denning distinguished this power, used on what the officer perceives with his own senses, from powers to arrest on reasonable suspicion.

If, after arrest, the person is found on inquiry to be innocent, he should at once be set free. There is no obligation to take him before a magistrate. The free report available doesn't show the formal order on the damages appeal.

keys.q: the facts, as they appeared to him at the time
keys.w: Lord Denning MR, on judging the arrest

keys.q: he should at once be set free
keys.w: Lord Denning MR, on a person cleared after arrest

later: Wiltshire v Barrett is cited for judging an arrest on the facts as they appeared to the officer, and for the duty to release at once a person who is cleared.

In Ireland, arrest powers use similar language — s.4 of the Criminal Law Act 1997 covers anyone who is, or whom the arrester with reasonable cause suspects to be, in the act of committing an arrestable offence.
job: Your arrest is judged on what you perceived at the time. Record exactly what you saw, heard and smelt, and what was said.
If inquiries show the person isn't guilty, release them straight away. Record when, why, and who decided.
A later decision not to prosecute doesn't make a properly grounded arrest unlawful — but only good notes will prove it was properly grounded.

bg: The free reports available set out the Court of Appeal's statement of the law, not the facts of the incident, so this note covers the law only.
R v Howell.q: What is a breach of the peace, and when can a person be arrested without warrant for one?
dec: Court of Appeal (Watkins LJ). There is a breach of the peace whenever harm is actually done, or is likely to be done, to a person or, in his presence, to his property — or a person is in fear of being so harmed through an assault, affray, riot, unlawful assembly or other disturbance.
So the core is violence or threatened violence. Noise, bad language or annoyance on their own don't amount to a breach of the peace.

There is a power of arrest without warrant where: (1) a breach of the peace is committed in the presence of the person making the arrest; (2) the arrester reasonably believes the person will commit a breach in the immediate future, although none has yet been committed; or (3) a breach has been committed and the arrester reasonably believes a renewal of it is threatened.
The belief must be reasonable, not just honestly held.

keys.q: whenever harm is actually done or is likely to be done to a person
keys.w: Watkins LJ, defining a breach of the peace

later: Howell's definition is the one most often cited in later cases on breach of the peace.
In Ireland, the common-law power to arrest for breach of the peace is recognised, but it doesn't carry a power to enter a dwelling to make the arrest — DPP v O'Brien (2021).

Section 6 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 makes it an offence, in a public place, to use threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to provoke a breach of the peace, or being reckless as to whether one may be occasioned.
job: Breach of the peace means violence or threatened violence. Note the harm, or the fear of harm, you actually saw — not just that the person was loud or abusive.
For a preventive arrest, record why you believed a breach was about to happen in the immediate future, not just that it might.

Where a statutory offence fits (for example s.6 of the 1994 Act), use it and evidence it properly rather than leaning on the common-law power. The common-law power doesn't get you into a home — DPP v O'Brien (2021).
R v Howell.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Still the classic definition.

bg: In a cinema, the defendant picked up a handbag that had been left there.
He went through its contents looking for anything worth stealing, found nothing he wanted, and put the bag back with everything still in it.
He was convicted of theft of the handbag and its contents, and appealed.
R v Easom.q: Is someone who intends to steal only if they find something worth taking guilty of stealing the bag and the items actually in it?
dec: Court of Appeal, 1971: conviction quashed.
Theft under the English Theft Act 1968 needs an intention to permanently deprive the owner of the property charged. Here that was the handbag and the specific items in it.

The defendant never intended to keep any of those things. His intention was conditional — to take something only if it turned out to be worth taking — and that isn't an intention to permanently deprive the owner of the property he actually handled.
So the full offence of theft of those items wasn't made out.
later: Attorney General's Reference (Nos 1 and 2 of 1979) held that a conditional intention can be enough for an attempt to steal, if the charge is worded to fit it — for example, an attempt to steal 'all or any of the contents'.

In Ireland, theft under s.4(1) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 needs an intention of depriving the owner of the property, and 'depriving' means temporarily or permanently depriving (s.4(5)). You still need an intention to deprive the owner of the property charged.
job: If someone is caught going through a bag, car or pocket for anything worth taking, don't charge the full theft of specific items they never took.
Consider an attempt, worded to cover 'all or any of the contents' rather than named items, or another offence that fits the facts.
Record exactly what they did and said — what they opened, what they handled, what they put back — and get CCTV and witness statements.
R v Easom.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Read with Attorney General's Reference (Nos 1 and 2 of 1979) and s.4 of the 2001 Act.

bg: In April 1977 the defendant was issued a credit card with a £200 limit, which she knew about. The card's conditions required her to return it on request.
She ran up debts well beyond the limit. In early December the bank sought the card back; she agreed to return it the next day but didn't.

On 15 December 1977 she used the card to buy goods worth £10.35 in a Mothercare shop in Luton. The assistant checked the card and signature and completed the sale. The card went back to the bank four days later.

She was convicted at Bedford Crown Court of obtaining a pecuniary advantage by deception (s.16, Theft Act 1968). The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction, holding it hadn't been proved that the shop was induced by any representation. The prosecution appealed.
R v Lambie.q: When someone presents a credit card they're no longer authorised to use, what do they represent — and must the shop assistant say they relied on it?
dec: House of Lords, 25 June 1981 (Lord Roskill; Lords Diplock, Fraser, Russell and Keith agreeing): appeal allowed, conviction restored.

Following the cheque-card case Commissioner of Police v Charles (1977), presenting a credit card represents that the holder has actual authority from the bank to make the contract with the shop on the bank's behalf. That has nothing to do with the holder's credit standing, and the shop's own agreement with the bank doesn't change it.

The Court of Appeal asked the wrong question. What mattered was whether the assistant would have completed the sale had she known the truth — that the holder was using the card without authority. She plainly wouldn't.

An assistant can't be expected to remember one routine sale. The jury may infer reliance from the other evidence, and here the inference was irresistible, particularly as the defendant gave no evidence to rebut it.

keys.q: has nothing to do with the appellant's credit standing
keys.w: Lord Roskill, on what presenting the card represents

later: Lambie and Charles are the leading English authorities on cheque-card and credit-card deception.
In Ireland, deception is now charged under the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 — for example s.6, making a gain or causing a loss by deception (up to five years on indictment).
job: Prove the authority was gone: get the bank's records, letters and the date the card was cancelled or the holder was told to stop using it.

Get a statement from the shop or business that it wouldn't have completed the sale had it known the card was being used without authority. If staff can't remember the sale, reliance can still be inferred — but get the till record, receipt and CCTV.
Charge under the 2001 Act's deception offences, and record what the suspect said or did at the counter.
R v Lambie.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. In Ireland, use the 2001 Act's deception offences.

bg: A foreign student, newly arrived at Victoria Station in London with little English, got into a taxi and showed the driver a note of the address he wanted.
The driver said it was a long and expensive journey. He took £6 from the student's open wallet.
The proper fare was 10s 6d (52.5p). The driver was convicted of theft under s.1 of the Theft Act 1968, and his appeal to the Court of Appeal failed.
R v Lawrence.q: Can there be an appropriation, and so theft, where the owner consented to the property being taken?
dec: House of Lords, 30 June 1971: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld. Viscount Dilhorne gave the main reasoning.
The old law of larceny required a taking 'without the consent of the owner'. The 1968 Act deliberately left those words out, so the prosecution doesn't have to prove that the owner didn't consent.
Any assumption of the rights of an owner is an appropriation (s.3(1) of the 1968 Act). The driver plainly appropriated the money.
Whether the owner consented, or the taker believed he did, is relevant to dishonesty — not to whether there was an appropriation. There was ample evidence of dishonesty here.

keys.q: is relevant to the issue of dishonesty
keys.w: Viscount Dilhorne, on belief in the owner's consent

later: Lawrence was followed by the House of Lords in Gomez (1993) and extended in Hinks (2000) to receiving a valid gift.

Irish law is different. Theft under s.4(1) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 requires appropriation 'without the consent of its owner' — but s.4(2) provides that consent obtained by deception or intimidation is not consent. So a Lawrence-type scam can still be theft in Ireland.
job: For overcharging or 'help yourself' scams on tourists or vulnerable people, record exactly what was said to get the money, what the true price was, and what the person understood.
In Ireland, money handed over because of a lie or a threat is taken without consent (s.4(2)). Consider deception offences under the 2001 Act as well.
Don't rely on Lawrence for the Irish rule on consent — use the 2001 Act's wording.
R v Lawrence.law: English authority. In Ireland the 2001 Act governs: appropriation without consent, with deceived or intimidated consent not counting.

bg: The defendant, aged 38, befriended a 53-year-old man of limited intelligence and described herself as his main carer.

Between April and November 1996 he withdrew about £300 from his building society account almost every day. About £60,000 went into her account, and he lost most of his savings. Building society staff said she did most of the talking and interrupted him when he tried to speak.
Her defence was that the money was a gift, so it had become hers and couldn't be stolen. She was convicted of five counts of theft, and the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal.
R v Hinks.q: Can a person 'appropriate' property they receive as a gift that is valid in civil law?
dec: House of Lords, 26 October 2000, by 3 to 2: appeal dismissed. Lord Steyn gave the main speech, with Lord Slynn and Lord Jauncey agreeing; Lord Hutton and Lord Hobhouse dissented.

Following Lawrence (1971) and Gomez (1993), 'appropriation' is a neutral word covering any assumption of the rights of an owner. The owner's consent isn't decisive, so acquiring an indefeasible title to property is capable of being an appropriation.
The mental elements of theft — dishonesty and intention to permanently deprive — give enough protection against convicting the innocent. Some conflict between civil and criminal law is unavoidable.
The dissent said a valid gift can't be dishonest, and that the jury should first decide whether the gift was valid — for example, whether the donor had capacity or was under undue influence.
later: Hinks has been widely criticised by academics but remains the law in England and Wales.

Irish law is different. Theft under s.4(1) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 requires appropriation 'without the consent of its owner' — but consent obtained by deception or intimidation is not consent (s.4(2)).
job: Financial abuse of a vulnerable person: look for, and record, the pressure, lies or control used to get the money — in Ireland, consent obtained by deception or intimidation isn't consent (s.4(2)).
Get the bank or building society records and statements from staff about who did the talking, and evidence of the person's vulnerability.
Consider deception offences under the 2001 Act as well as theft, and refer to the appropriate supports for the vulnerable person.
R v Hinks.law: English authority, still the law there. In Ireland, the 2001 Act's 'without consent' wording governs.

bg: A man offered to sell furniture belonging to a friend who was in prison. The furniture was in the friend's house, and the man had no authority to sell it.
The two defendants agreed to buy it and helped take it away.
They were convicted of handling stolen goods. On appeal they argued that the handling offence didn't apply, because anything they did was 'in the course of the stealing'.
R v Pitham.q: When was the furniture stolen — when it was offered for sale, or only when it was taken away?
dec: Court of Appeal: appeals dismissed.

Offering to sell the furniture was an assumption of the rights of the owner, so the appropriation took place at that point. It didn't matter that nothing had been moved or that the owner hadn't yet lost anything.

The theft was therefore complete before the defendants did anything with the goods. Their later dealings were 'otherwise than in the course of the stealing', and they were rightly convicted of handling.
later: Pitham and Hehl is cited for the point that appropriation can happen without any physical taking — offering to sell is enough.

In Ireland, handling stolen property is an offence under s.17 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001. It also applies only 'otherwise than in the course of the stealing', and covers someone who knows the property was stolen or is reckless as to whether it was (up to 10 years on indictment).
job: Where someone offers property that isn't theirs — online, in a pub, from a van — the theft can be complete at the offer. Record what was offered, by whom, for how much and when.
Buyers who then receive, move or help dispose of the goods, knowing or reckless that they're stolen, can be charged with handling under s.17.
Get the messages, adverts or witness accounts of the offer, and record what the buyers said about where they thought the goods came from.
R v Pitham.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Read with s.17 of the 2001 Act.

bg: A publisher bought the British rights to a book, already published in several countries, aimed at school pupils aged about 12 to 18. It included a 26-page chapter on sex.
After complaints, police seized more than a thousand copies under the Obscene Publications Acts.
He was convicted of having obscene books for publication for gain, fined and ordered to pay costs. His appeal failed, and he complained to Strasbourg under Article 10.
Handyside v United Kingdom.q: Did convicting the publisher, and seizing the books, breach his freedom of expression?
dec: European Court of Human Rights, 7 December 1976: no violation of Article 10.
The conviction was an interference with free expression, but it was prescribed by law and pursued a legitimate aim — the protection of morals.

There is no uniform European view of morals, so national authorities have a margin of appreciation in judging what's necessary. 'Necessary' isn't the same as 'indispensable', but nor is it as flexible as 'reasonable' or 'desirable'.

Given the book's young readership, its direct style, wide circulation and cheap price, the measures were necessary in a democratic society. That no action was taken against a revised edition suggested the authorities had done only what was strictly necessary.

Freedom of expression is one of the essential foundations of a democratic society. It applies not only to inoffensive ideas but also to those that offend, shock or disturb the State or any sector of the population.

keys.q: offend, shock or disturb the State or any sector of the population
keys.w: ECtHR

later: Handyside is the foundation of the Strasbourg case law on Article 10, and its 'offend, shock or disturb' line is quoted in almost every expression case since.
The same approach — legal basis, legitimate aim, necessity — applies to restrictions on assembly under Article 11 (see Bukta v Hungary (2007)).
job: That a placard, chant or post offends, shocks or disturbs isn't enough, on its own, to stop it. Look for a specific offence or power that fits — threats, harassment, incitement to hatred, a s.8 direction — and record why it applies.
Any restriction must have a legal basis, a legitimate aim and be necessary and proportionate. Note the alternatives you considered.
Protecting children can justify firmer action — but still record the specific risk.
Handyside v United Kingdom.law: Yes. Handyside (1976) is still the foundation of Article 10 case law.

bg: Cattle seized under an Irish Land Commission warrant were to be sold by the sheriff at a yard in Copley Street, Cork, and a demonstration against the sale was expected.
About 200 Guards, including about 12 armed detectives, were posted outside the yard, with 40 Guards, including 10 detectives, inside.

A crowd gathered and a lorry carrying men with sticks broke through the barriers and the yard gates. After the crowd had been held back, Special Branch detectives opened fire. The plaintiff's son, who had followed the lorry, was killed.
His father sued three of the detectives and the Chief Superintendent in charge in Cork for damages under the Fatal Accidents Act 1846.
Lynch v Fitzgerald.q: When may Guards use firearms against an unlawful or riotous crowd?
dec: At trial in the High Court, Hanna J held the shooting unjustified.
Armed forces of the State may use firearms against an unlawful or riotous assembly only where it is necessary as a last resort to preserve life.
The firing here wasn't done to protect the lives of buyers or anyone else, so it couldn't be justified. Damages were awarded against Guards involved.
The case is reported at [1938] IR 382 with the Supreme Court's decision of 30 July 1938. The free sources available don't show the full judgments or the result of the appeal.
later: Courts elsewhere in the common-law world have cited Hanna J's judgment on police use of firearms — for example, a 1981 Jamaican decision.

Today the same question is also governed by Article 2 ECHR: force must be no more than absolutely necessary, and operations must be planned and controlled to minimise the risk to life — McCann and Others v United Kingdom (1995). Gardaí must act compatibly with the Convention under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003.
job: A firearm is a last resort to preserve life. It's never a way to disperse a crowd, protect property or punish.
Public order operations need planning and control: clear instructions, command, and less dangerous options ready, so the need to fire doesn't arise.
If force is used, record exactly what threat to life you perceived, what alternatives existed, and what warnings were given.
Lynch v Fitzgerald.law: Still the leading Irish authority on firearms against a crowd. Read with Article 2 ECHR and McCann (1995).

bg: The free reports available set out the court's ruling on whether a copy of a recording could be used in evidence, not the full facts of the case.
Kajala v Noble.q: Does the 'best evidence' rule stop a court admitting a copy of a film or video rather than the original?
dec: Divisional Court, 1982. Ackner LJ gave the judgment of the court.
The old rule that a party must produce the best evidence available has gone by the board long ago.
The one surviving instance is that if a party has an original document in his possession, he must produce it — he can't give secondary evidence of it by producing a copy.
If any such rule still exists, it applies only to documents. It doesn't prevent a copy of a film or video recording being admitted; questions about the copy go to its weight.

keys.q: has gone by the board long ago
keys.w: Ackner LJ, on the old best evidence rule

later: Kajala is regularly cited across the common-law world for admitting copies of tapes and films.

In Ireland, the Court of Criminal Appeal considered it in People (DPP) v Maguire (1995): security camera footage is admissible, and a jury may identify an accused from it — but with the usual identification warnings, and great care where there's no other identification evidence.
job: A copy of CCTV can be used in evidence. Make the best copy you can, in the original format where possible, and note the system's time and date difference against real time.
In your statement, record who made the copy, when, from which system and by what method — and why the original can't be produced (for example, the system overwrites, or the owner keeps it).
Keep continuity from the system to court, and exhibit the copy properly. See People (DPP) v Maguire (1995) and R v Dodson (1984) on identifying people from footage.
Kajala v Noble.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. Read with People (DPP) v Maguire (1995).

bg: In a car park, the defendant lunged at her boyfriend with a knife.

She was convicted of affray under s.3 of the Public Order Act 1986, which requires violence such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his personal safety. She appealed.
R v Sanchez.q: Where violence is aimed at one person, who is the 'person of reasonable firmness' — the victim, or a bystander?
dec: Court of Appeal, 6 March 1996 (Simon Brown LJ sitting): appeal allowed.
The person of reasonable firmness is a hypothetical third party, not the victim. Affray is a public order offence: it protects bystanders, not the person attacked.
The trial judge hadn't directed the jury to consider whether a hypothetical bystander would have feared for their own safety. Without that direction the conviction couldn't stand.
later: Sanchez is cited on the need to focus on the hypothetical bystander in one-on-one violence.

Ireland's affray offence, s.16 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994, is worded differently. It requires two or more people to use or threaten violence towards each other, at least some of it unlawful, and their conduct taken together must be such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present to fear for his or another person's safety. No such person need actually be present, and threats by words alone don't count (up to 5 years on indictment).
job: In Ireland, check the elements of s.16: two or more people using or threatening violence towards each other; at least one of them acting unlawfully; and conduct that, taken together, would make a person of reasonable firmness there fear for their own or another's safety.
Record the scene: how much space there was, who was nearby, how close, any weapons, and how people reacted.
For a one-sided attack, consider assault or another offence instead of affray.
R v Sanchez.law: English authority on s.3 of the 1986 Act. In Ireland, use the wording of s.16 of the 1994 Act.

bg: The case is reported as R v Bernhard [1938] 2 KB 264.
The defendant demanded money with menaces, honestly believing there was a legal right to it. The belief was wrong in law.
The conviction was for demanding money with menaces with intent to steal, under the Larceny Act 1916. The free reports available don't give fuller facts.
R v Bernard.q: Does an honest belief in a right to the money — one the law doesn't recognise — prevent an intent to steal?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal: conviction quashed.
A claim of right made in good faith is a defence even where the claim is unfounded in law. What matters is whether the defendant honestly believed in the right, not whether the right exists.
Because the honest claim negatived the intent to steal, the offence wasn't made out.
later: The Irish Court of Criminal Appeal applied Bernhard in People (AG) v Grey (1944).

The idea is now written into Irish law: under s.2(1) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, 'dishonestly' means without a claim of right made in good faith. Theft (s.4) requires dishonesty, and robbery (s.14) requires a theft.
job: When a suspect says 'it was mine', 'they owed me' or 'I was taking it back', record exactly what they claim and why.

Test the claim in interview: when the right arose, how much, any paperwork or messages, any earlier demands. The belief must be genuine — it needn't be reasonable or legally right, but the less reasonable it is, the less likely a court will accept it was held.
If there's an honest claim of right, there may be no theft (and so no robbery) — but force or threats used may still be an assault or another offence.
R v Bernard.law: English authority, applied in Ireland. Now reflected in s.2(1) of the 2001 Act.
