bg: During the 1984–85 miners' strike, the defendants dropped a concrete block from a bridge to frighten a working miner who was being driven to work below.
The block struck the taxi carrying him, and the driver was killed.

They admitted meaning to frighten the miner but denied intending to kill or cause serious injury. Their offer to plead guilty to manslaughter was refused, and they were convicted of murder after the judge directed the jury using the guidelines in R v Moloney (1985).
The Court of Appeal substituted manslaughter convictions, and the prosecution appealed.
R v Hancock.q: How should a jury be directed on whether a defendant who foresaw a risk of death or serious injury intended it?
dec: House of Lords, 27 February 1986: appeal dismissed; the manslaughter convictions stood.
Murder requires an intent to kill or cause serious harm — nothing less will do.

Foresight of consequences is no more than evidence of the existence of that intent. It must be weighed with all the other evidence; foresight doesn't necessarily mean intention, though a jury may infer intention from it.

The Moloney guidelines were defective because they didn't tell the jury that probability matters: the greater the probability of a consequence, the more likely it was foreseen, and if it was foreseen, the more likely it was intended.

keys.q: no more than evidence of the existence of the intent
keys.w: House of Lords, on foresight of consequences

later: Later English cases refined the direction for cases where death or serious injury was a virtually certain result.

In Ireland, s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1964 governs murder: the killing isn't murder unless the accused intended to kill, or cause serious injury to, some person; and the accused is presumed to have intended the natural and probable consequences of his conduct, but that presumption may be rebutted.
job: In murder, serious assault and arson cases, intent has to be proved, not assumed from the result.
In interview, cover what the suspect knew and expected: the height, the weight of the object, the speed and traffic, who they knew was there, and what they thought would happen.
Gather evidence of how likely the harm was — scene measurements, expert evidence, CCTV — because probability is central to proving intent.
R v Hancock.law: English authority, persuasive in Ireland. In Ireland, s.4 of the 1964 Act governs.

bg: In April 1987 a stolen car was crashed and badly damaged. The applicant was charged with offences arising from it, including unlawful taking of a motor vehicle and dangerous driving. He denied the offences.
The car was held at a Garda station. His solicitors told the Gardaí they wanted to inspect it for forensic evidence, including fingerprints.
Before that inspection could take place, the car was let go. The applicant sought an order stopping the prosecution.
Murphy v DPP.q: Can a prosecution go ahead where the Gardaí parted with evidence the defence had asked to examine?
dec: High Court (Lynch J): order granted restraining the DPP from proceeding with the prosecution.

The Gardaí knew the defence wanted to test the car. They ought not to have parted with it without a forensic examination, or at least without notifying the applicant's lawyers so they could examine it first.
That breached fair procedures. Evidence relevant to guilt or innocence must, so far as necessary and practicable, be kept until the trial.
later: The Supreme Court approved Lynch J's reasoning in Braddish v DPP (2001), where a video was returned before the defence could see it, and the duty was developed in Dunne v DPP (2002).

Later Supreme Court cases limit the remedy. In CD v DPP (2009) the accused had to show a real risk of an unfair trial that rulings at the trial couldn't avoid, and the duty to preserve was read 'in a fair and reasonable manner'. In Byrne v DPP (2010), where Gardaí had tried to copy CCTV but were told it wasn't possible, prohibition was refused.

A modern example: in DPP v O'Donoghue (Court of Appeal, February 2024) convictions for assault causing serious harm and violent disorder were quashed because Gardaí never retrieved CCTV from cameras covering the scene and kept no notes of their CCTV enquiries. The court spoke of an established duty to seek out and preserve CCTV.
job: Once you know the defence want to examine something — a car, a phone, clothing, CCTV — don't release, return or destroy it without telling them in writing and giving them a reasonable chance first.

Seek out CCTV early and record every CCTV enquiry — who you spoke to, which cameras, whether they were working, and what was viewed or downloaded. In DPP v O'Donoghue (2024) the absence of any such record helped sink the convictions.
Keep anything that may be relevant to guilt or innocence, so far as necessary and practicable, until the case is over — including material that may help the accused.

Record every request, your reply, and exactly what happened to the item and when. If something can't be kept, record why and what you did instead (photographs, a forensic examination, notice to the defence).
Murphy v DPP.law: Yes. Murphy (1989) was approved in Braddish (2001); read with Dunne (2002) and CD v DPP (2009).

bg: An elected local councillor received payments from a person who had an interest in planning applications for land in a neighbouring council's area. His own council had no role in those applications.
The prosecution alleged he tried to persuade members of the neighbouring council to grant permission and, when that failed, to change the land's zoning or bring it under his own council's control.

He was charged under s.1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1906. The prosecution relied on s.4 of the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act 2001: where an office holder receives a benefit from someone with an interest in their functions, it is deemed an inducement or reward unless the contrary is proved.
He was convicted, and appealed, arguing the jury had been told he carried the legal burden of disproving corruption.
People (DPP) v Forsey.q: Does a presumption that applies 'unless the contrary is proved' put a legal burden on the accused, or only an evidential one?
dec: Supreme Court, November 2018 (O'Malley J): conviction quashed.
Section 4 shifts only an evidential burden to the accused.

If the accused had to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the money wasn't received corruptly, he would effectively have to disprove an essential element of the offence. That would be a clear inroad on the presumption of innocence.

The jury should be told the prosecution must prove every element beyond reasonable doubt except corrupt intention. If those elements are proved, the jury may treat corrupt intention as proved — unless the evidence leaves them in doubt that the accused had a corrupt motive.

keys.q: a clear inroad on the presumption of innocence
keys.w: Supreme Court (O'Malley J)

later: Forsey is the leading Irish authority on how reverse burdens in criminal statutes are to be read.

The 1906 and 2001 Acts have been repealed by the Criminal Justice (Corruption Offences) Act 2018, which reproduces the s.4 presumption and adds others. The Supreme Court's reasoning would apply to those too.
job: A statutory presumption 'unless the contrary is proved' isn't proof of guilt. Gather evidence on every element of the offence, including the one the presumption covers.
Put the evidence to the suspect and record their explanation in full — an explanation backed by evidence can raise a doubt and displace the presumption.
In corruption cases, trace the payments, the person's interest in the office holder's functions, and what the office holder did.
People (DPP) v Forsey.law: Yes. Forsey (2018) is the leading authority on reverse burdens; read with the Criminal Justice (Corruption Offences) Act 2018.

bg: A married woman was prescribed contraceptives on medical advice.
Customs seized them because s.17 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1935 banned their importation.
She challenged the law in the High Court and then appealed to the Supreme Court.
McGee v AG.q: Did the ban on importing contraceptives breach the constitutional rights of a married couple?
dec: Supreme Court, 19 December 1973, by 4 to 1 (Walsh, Budd, Henchy and Griffin JJ; FitzGerald CJ dissenting): s.17 was unconstitutional.

Henchy J relied on the personal rights the State guarantees to protect under Article 40.3. The law violated her personal right to privacy in regard to her marital relations, and a prosecution would reach into the privacy of her marital life.

Walsh J relied mainly on Article 41 (the family). The State may not intrude on marital privacy merely to enforce private morality; it can only intrude where the exigencies of the common good justify it.

keys.q: justified by the exigencies of the common good
keys.w: Walsh J, on when the State may intrude on marital privacy

later: McGee is a landmark case on constitutional rights that aren't expressly listed in the text, and the starting point for the right to privacy in Irish law.
The right to privacy under Article 40.3 has since been recognised much more broadly — it is regularly raised in challenges to searches, phone examinations and surveillance.
job: Privacy is a constitutional right. Intrusions — entering or searching a home, examining a phone, surveillance — need a clear legal basis.
Use the power that fits the situation, and record why the intrusion was needed and why it was proportionate.
Where a warrant or authorisation is available, get it, and keep within its terms.
McGee v AG.law: Yes. McGee (1973) remains a foundation of the constitutional right to privacy.

Encyclopedia.com — extract from the Supreme Court decision in McGee v Attorney General

bg: The free reports available set out the Divisional Court's ruling on the mental element of handling stolen goods under the English Theft Act 1968, not the facts of the case.
Atwal v Massey.q: Is a handler guilty if they ought to have known the goods were stolen — or must they actually have known or believed it?
dec: Divisional Court (Lord Widgery CJ).
The question whether the defendant knew or believed the goods were stolen is a subjective one: what matters is what this defendant actually knew or believed.
It isn't enough that a reasonable person would have realised the goods were stolen, or that the defendant ought to have known.

keys.q: The question is a subjective one
keys.w: Lord Widgery CJ (as quoted in later cases)

later: Later English cases follow the subjective test. In R v Moys (1984) a direction that strong suspicion plus deliberately shutting one's eyes amounted to belief was a material misdirection, and the conviction was quashed.

Irish law is different. Under s.17(1) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, handling covers someone who knows the property was stolen or is reckless as to whether it was. Under s.17(2), where a person has stolen property in such circumstances that it's reasonable to conclude they knew or were reckless, they are taken to have known or been reckless — unless the court or jury has a reasonable doubt.
job: In Ireland, build the s.17(2) circumstances: the price paid against the true value, where, when and from whom it was got, missing paperwork or packaging, altered serial numbers, and what the person was told.
Put each circumstance to the suspect in interview and record their explanation in full — the presumption gives way to a reasonable doubt.
Recklessness is enough in Ireland: record the risks the suspect must have been aware of, and why.
Atwal v Massey.law: English authority on the English Theft Act. In Ireland, use s.17 of the 2001 Act.

bg: A campaigner challenged ss.61–62 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and s.11 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885, which criminalised sexual acts between men.
He argued they were inconsistent with the 1937 Constitution and so hadn't been carried over into Irish law (Article 50). He lost in the High Court and appealed.
Norris v AG.q: Were laws criminalising private sexual acts between men inconsistent with the Constitution, including the right to privacy?
dec: Supreme Court, 22 March 1983, by 3 to 2: appeal dismissed. O'Higgins CJ gave the majority judgment, with Finlay P and Griffin J; Henchy and McCarthy JJ dissented.
The majority relied on the Christian nature of the State and its view that the conduct was morally wrong and harmful to health and to marriage, and found no inconsistency with the Constitution.
It held that the claimed right of privacy couldn't prevail against the criminal sanctions.
later: In Norris v Ireland (1988) the European Court of Human Rights held that the laws breached Article 8 (respect for private life), following Dudgeon v United Kingdom (1981).
The laws were repealed by the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 1993.
job: Historic, but it shows that constitutional rights like privacy (McGee v AG) are interpreted in a changing society, and that the European Convention can require change where domestic courts don't.

Gardaí must act compatibly with the Convention, including Article 8, under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003. Any intrusion on private life needs a legal basis and must be necessary and proportionate.
Norris v AG.law: No — superseded by Norris v Ireland (1988) and the 1993 Act.

bg: The accused was tried at Galway Circuit Court on several counts. The jury acquitted him on all but one: attempting to procure a drug, knowing it was intended to be used to procure a miscarriage.

The prosecution's evidence was that he went to a doctor who was treating a young woman, asked for a prescription to end her pregnancy, and was refused. He then asked whether there wasn't some drug named ergot.
He gave no evidence. He was sentenced to a year's imprisonment and appealed.
People (AG) v Thornton.q: Was asking the doctor about the drug enough to prove an attempt to procure it?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal (Haugh J giving the judgment): conviction quashed.
The question about the drug could be explained in ways that didn't necessarily involve an attempt to obtain it for the purpose alleged.
In an attempt case, the trial judge must tell the jury that a mere desire to commit the crime isn't enough — and that a desire followed by an intention to act isn't enough either.

keys.q: a mere desire to commit the crime
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on what isn't enough for an attempt

later: Thornton is still cited for the rule that intention alone doesn't make an attempt — there has to be conduct towards committing the offence.
Attempt is still a common-law offence in Ireland, and the question is whether the accused's acts went beyond mere preparation towards committing the crime.
job: An attempt needs more than wanting or intending to commit the offence. Gather evidence of what the suspect actually did towards it.
Record where they went, what they had with them (tools, weapons, items), what they asked for or said, and how close they came to completing the offence.
Where the conduct is only preparation, consider other offences that fit — for example, possession of articles for use in an offence.
People (AG) v Thornton.law: Yes. Still cited on the line between intention and an attempt.

src.t: vLex Ireland — People (Attorney General) v Thornton [1952] IR 91

bg: The case is Dowman v Ireland [1986] ILRM 111 (High Court, 1985).
A young man was stopped at a supermarket for shoplifting potatoes. The assistant manager held him until a Garda arrived to make the arrest.
At the patrol car he resisted being put in without his two younger companions. A scuffle followed, and his wrist was injured. He sued for damages.
Dowman v Turner.q: Was the force used on him lawful?
dec: High Court, 1985 (Barron J): the plaintiff succeeded and was awarded £3,500 damages.
An arresting officer is entitled to use such force as is reasonably necessary to effect an arrest, and may use force to ensure the arrest is maintained.

But the Garda was holding him to stop him looking after his companions — not to arrest him or keep him in custody. So the Garda wasn't acting in the execution of his duty, and the force was an unlawful act. Whether it was reasonable didn't arise.
The judge added that force causing such an injury to a young person already effectively in Garda custody would be hard to justify as reasonable.

keys.q: such force as is reasonably necessary to effect an arrest
keys.w: Barron J

later: Dowman is cited for the rule that force must serve a lawful purpose — making or maintaining an arrest — and be no more than reasonably necessary.

Under s.19 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, force used in effecting or assisting a lawful arrest is not an offence if it is only such as is reasonable in the circumstances as the person believes them to be.
job: Every use of force needs a lawful purpose (making or keeping the arrest) and must be no more than reasonably necessary.
Deal with the person's real concern — children or companions left behind, belongings, a pet — before it turns into a struggle. Ask for help or another unit if needed.
Record what force you used, why it was needed, what it was for, and any injury. Consider whether a young or vulnerable person needs less, not more.
Dowman v Turner.law: Yes. Read with s.19 of the 1997 Act.

bg: The young accused pleaded guilty to assault causing serious harm, contrary to s.4 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997.

In July 2010, at a service station in Co. Clare, he carried out a frenzied attack lasting over four minutes: 26 punches to the head, 65 stamps to the head and two to the chest. The victim suffered a brain injury with lasting cognitive and physical effects.

The accused had been drinking and taking drugs, and had a severely dysfunctional upbringing. In November 2011 he was sentenced to 15 years, with the final 3 suspended on condition he stayed away from the victim and his family. He appealed.
DPP v Fitzgibbon.q: Was the sentence wrong in principle, and what is the proper range for assault causing serious harm?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 18 March 2014 (Clarke J giving the judgment, with Birmingham and Sheehan JJ): error in principle; appeal allowed, with the final sentence deferred to a later hearing.

The sentencing judge had misread earlier authority (DPP v Keane (2008) and DPP v Stafford (2008)) by treating the drink, drugs and dysfunctional background as carrying little or no weight. He didn't consider whether substance abuse rooted in a severely dysfunctional background took the case outside the usual rule that voluntary intoxication isn't significant mitigation.
The 15-year starting point was also out of line with comparable sentences, before any mitigation.

Before mitigation, the Court indicated: lower end 2 to 4 years; middle range 4 to 7½ years; most serious 7½ to 12½ years; above 12½ years only in exceptional cases, up to life imprisonment in wholly exceptional ones.
later: Fitzgibbon is the leading guideline for sentencing s.4 offences and is applied regularly by the Court of Appeal.

It also illustrates the rule from Keane and Stafford: voluntary drink or drugs aren't, of themselves, significant mitigation, though addiction and a dysfunctional background may be considered in appropriate cases.
job: Where the assault sits in the range drives the sentence, so evidence the gravity fully: injuries and lasting effects (medical reports, victim impact statement), the number and type of blows, kicking or stamping, any weapon, duration, and the victim's vulnerability.
Get the CCTV — it shows the court exactly what happened — and record whether the victim was on the ground or defenceless.
Record the offender's state (drink or drugs), what they said, and their background where relevant to the file.
DPP v Fitzgibbon.law: Yes. Still the leading guideline on s.4 sentencing.

bg: A Mauritian national came to Ireland in 2006 under a State education scheme that allowed students to work part-time while studying. He lived here with his family, self-supporting, and the children went to school in Ireland.

In 2011 a new scheme set time limits for full-time non-EEA students who had registered before 1 January 2011. The family's further permission was refused, and they were directed to leave by December 2013.

The High Court refused judicial review. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding the Minister had erred by not considering Article 8 ECHR. The Minister appealed; the case was heard with Luximon v Minister for Justice, which raised the same point.
Balchand v Minister for Justice.q: When deciding under s.4(7) of the Immigration Act 2004 whether to renew or vary a long-term resident's permission, must the Minister consider Article 8 (private and family life) — or can that wait until a deportation decision?
dec: Supreme Court, April 2018 (MacMenamin J): the Minister's appeal was dismissed.
The Minister argued Article 8 only had to be assessed at the final, deportation stage. The Court disagreed: on a simple reading of the Act, the s.4(7) decisions were unlawful, and they were quashed.
The Minister's approach was contrary to public policy: it could force applicants either to act unlawfully (staying without permission) or to give up their Article 8 rights.
The applicants were lawful, long-duration residents — not asylum seekers or short-term visitors — and their position changed because of a policy shift, not anything they did wrong.
The Minister is still entitled to set limits on how long people may stay. The ruling only requires Article 8 to be considered in the decision, and shouldn't be extended beyond its facts.

keys.q: lawful, long-duration residents
keys.w: MacMenamin J, on the applicants' status

later: This case and Luximon together are the leading authorities that Article 8 must be weighed when the Minister decides whether long-term residents may stay.
The European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 requires State bodies to act compatibly with the Convention, including Article 8.
job: Background for immigration work: a decision not to renew someone's permission isn't a deportation order. Check the person's current permission with the immigration authorities before acting.
Long-term residents with families here are often challenging decisions about their status. Record what you're told about pending applications or court proceedings.
Where children are involved, note their schooling and circumstances accurately — they're relevant to Article 8.
Balchand v Minister for Justice.law: Yes. Read with Luximon v Minister for Justice (2018).

src.t: Irish Legal News — 'Supreme Court: Minister erred in failing to consider Article 8 rights of applicants'

bg: A Georgian man arrived in Ireland in 2001. A deportation order was made against him under s.3(1) of the Immigration Act 1999 in December 2001, but he avoided deportation by deceptive means until November 2011.

He had married in Ireland in 2009 and the couple had two children, who weren't Irish citizens. His wife had temporary leave to remain on humanitarian grounds; in the proceedings she admitted it had been obtained with an invented story.

The family challenged the law. They argued that a deportation order of indefinite duration was an unconstitutional, disproportionate interference with family rights; that s.3(11), letting the Minister amend or revoke an order, was an unlawful delegation of legislative power; and, in the alternative, that the provisions breached Article 8 ECHR.
Sivsivadze v Minister for Justice.q: Is a deportation order that has no end date constitutional?
dec: Supreme Court, 23 June 2015 (Murray J, with Hardiman, O'Donnell, Clarke and MacMenamin JJ concurring): appeal dismissed.

A deportation order isn't necessarily unlimited in time, because the Minister can amend or revoke it under s.3(11). The Minister must exercise that power proportionately, with fair procedures, and in line with the Constitution and the ECHR.
A non-national who has no right to be in the State doesn't acquire one merely through the passage of time, so building a fixed end date into every order would be incongruous.
The delegation argument failed: the power to exclude non-nationals is inherent in a sovereign State, not created by the Act — the Act simply designates the Minister to exercise it.
Section 3(11) gives a broad discretion, and the Minister may take full account of a family's Article 8 rights when deciding whether to make or revoke an order.

keys.q: a power inherent in a sovereign state
keys.w: Murray J, on excluding non-nationals

later: Sivsivadze is the leading authority on the constitutionality of deportation orders of indefinite duration.
People subject to old deportation orders can apply to the Minister to revoke them under s.3(11), and those decisions must be proportionate.
job: A deportation order stays in force until it's revoked or amended. Before acting on one, confirm its current status with the immigration authorities.
Record anything the person says about an application to revoke the order, new family circumstances, or court proceedings, and pass it on.
Where children are involved, note their circumstances and any welfare concerns, and involve Tusla where needed.
Sivsivadze v Minister for Justice.law: Yes. Still the law on indefinite deportation orders.

bg: A child was born in Ireland in June 2013. The father had arrived in 2005 and been granted refugee status in 2006.

After a trip abroad in 2012, officials found that his fingerprints matched those of a man refused asylum in the UK in 2005. His refugee status was revoked with effect from August 2013 — after the child's birth.
In 2014 a passport application for the child was refused because the father's refugee application had been fraudulent.

The High Court refused to quash the refusal. The Court of Appeal held that permission obtained by false representations wasn't 'in force' and couldn't count towards the child's citizenship under s.6A of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, relying on the principle that 'fraud unravels everything'.
U.M. (a minor) v Minister for Foreign Af.q: Does revoking a parent's refugee status operate backwards, so that a child born before the revocation isn't an Irish citizen?
dec: Supreme Court, June 2022, unanimous: the Court of Appeal's decision was overturned.

Dunne J (main judgment): the Minister has a discretion whether to revoke refugee status, and that discretion lets the Minister consider people — like the child — who acquired rights before revocation. A declaration of refugee status remains valid until it is revoked; she couldn't accept that revocation made the declaration void from the start.

O'Donnell CJ (concurring): without clear statutory language, legislation can't retrospectively change the legal character of past events. Revocation took effect from its own date and didn't relate back.
So the father's refugee status was in force when the child was born, and the child's citizenship wasn't undone by the later revocation.

keys.q: fraud unravels everything
keys.w: the principle the Court of Appeal relied on, rejected here

later: U.M. is the leading authority that revocation of a parent's status doesn't strip a child of citizenship acquired before the revocation.
The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission intervened in the case on children's citizenship rights.
job: Don't assume a child isn't an Irish citizen because a parent's status was later revoked — citizenship depends on the position when the child was born.
Refer questions of citizenship to the immigration authorities or the Passport Office; don't decide them on the street.
When dealing with a family facing removal, record the children's dates and places of birth accurately — they can decide citizenship.
U.M. (a minor) v Minister for Foreign Af.law: Yes. Still the law on revocation and a child's citizenship.

src.t: Irish Times — 'Supreme Court overturns ruling revoking citizenship of child born in Ireland to refugee father' (2 June 2022)

bg: Each of the three applicants applied for asylum, was refused, and appealed unsuccessfully.
They then asked the Minister to let them stay on humanitarian grounds under s.3(3)(b) of the Immigration Act 1999. Deportation orders were made.
They sought leave for judicial review, arguing that the Minister hadn't given an intelligible account of his reasons for deciding to deport them. The High Court refused leave, and they appealed.
P, L & B v Minister for Justice.q: Can a refusal of asylum be a sufficient basis for a deportation order, and were the Minister's reasons adequate?
dec: Supreme Court, 30 July 2001 (Hardiman J giving the judgment, with Keane CJ, Denham, Murphy and Murray JJ): the High Court's refusal of leave was upheld.
Refusal of an application for asylum may be a sufficient basis for a deportation order.
The humanitarian applications were appeals to mercy, and the applicants didn't meet any requirement for special humanitarian consideration.

Following Laurentiu v Minister for Justice (1999), the Minister was entitled to identify maintaining the integrity of the asylum and immigration systems as an aspect of the common good. The State has a legitimate interest in controlling non-nationals' entry and residence (In re Article 26 and the Illegal Immigrants (Trafficking) Bill 1999).
later: P, L & B is still cited on the Minister's reasons for deportation after a final refusal of asylum.
The leading case on deporting parents of Irish-citizen children is Lobe and Osayande v Minister for Justice (2003), not this one.
job: Background for immigration work: after a final refusal of asylum, a deportation order can follow; humanitarian representations are for the Minister.
Before acting, check the person's current status with the immigration authorities — there may be a later application or court challenge.
Record what you're told about pending applications, family circumstances or health, and pass it on.
P, L & B v Minister for Justice.law: Yes, on reasons for deportation after refusal of asylum.

src.t: Wikipedia — P., L., & B. v Minister for Justice, Equality and Law Reform

bg: A senior Garda officer, suing under the Proceeds of Crime Act 1996, obtained High Court orders prohibiting dealings with about £300,000 held in a solicitor's client account, and appointing a receiver over it.
The respondents appealed, raising jurisdiction points — including that some of the money was in a bank in London — and challenging how the orders were made.
The appeal was heard together with a separate action challenging the constitutionality of the 1996 Act.
Murphy v GM.q: Are proceedings under the Proceeds of Crime Act 1996 criminal in nature — and is the Act constitutional?
dec: Supreme Court, 18 October 2001 (Keane CJ giving the judgment, with Denham, Murphy, Murray and Geoghegan JJ): appeal dismissed and the High Court's orders affirmed.
Forfeiture proceedings under the Act are civil in nature, even when they run alongside criminal prosecutions — so the protections that apply only to criminal trials don't apply.
The Oireachtas is presumed to have intended the Act's procedures to be operated in line with constitutional justice, with the courts correcting any departures.

The hearsay provision wasn't unconstitutional in itself, and the challengers hadn't shown the sections were repugnant to the Constitution. The Act clearly applies to property obtained before it was passed.

The courts could appoint a receiver over property outside the State under their equitable jurisdiction. And the respondents had chosen not to cross-examine the deponents or give oral evidence, so they couldn't complain about the outcome.
later: Murphy v GM underpins the Criminal Assets Bureau's civil approach: property shown to be the proceeds of crime can be frozen and disposed of without anyone being convicted.
The 1996 Act has been amended several times since to strengthen it.
job: Where someone's assets look out of line with any lawful income, consider a referral to the Criminal Assets Bureau through your supervisor.
Record evidence of lifestyle and wealth: cash found, property, vehicles, jewellery, holidays, and any known lawful income or social welfare.
Civil proceedings can run alongside a criminal investigation, so keep your notes and exhibits complete — they may be used in both.
Murphy v GM.law: Yes. Still the leading authority that proceeds of crime proceedings are civil.

src.t: vLex Ireland — Murphy v GM, PB, PC Ltd [2001] 4 IR 113

bg: The case is People (DPP) v Douglas and Hayes [1985] ILRM 25.

The two accused were convicted in the Special Criminal Court of shooting with intent to commit murder under s.14 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. They were also convicted of robbery, possession of firearms with intent to endanger life, and using firearms to resist arrest. Their appeal concerned only the shooting conviction.
Shots were fired at a Garda car before it stopped. Three hit the front of the car, and at least two might, with a slight change of aim, have killed the driver.

The trial court held that intent to murder could be found where death or serious injury was the apparent natural consequence of the shooting, or where the shooter acted with reckless disregard of the risk of killing — and that death needn't be the desired outcome, only a likely one.
DPP v Douglas.q: Does shooting with intent to commit murder require a real intent to murder — or is foresight or recklessness enough?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 21 May 1984 (McWilliam J, with the Chief Justice and Barron J).
Section 14 specifically requires proof of an intent to commit murder, and no other intent is sufficient.
So it isn't enough that death or serious injury was the natural or likely consequence of the shooting, or that the shooter acted in reckless disregard of the risk of killing.

The court noted the anomaly that murder itself can be committed with an intent to cause serious injury (s.4, Criminal Justice Act 1964), referring to English authority on attempted murder. The free report available doesn't show the court's final order.

keys.q: no other intent is sufficient
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on shooting with intent to murder

later: Douglas and Hayes is still cited on the intent needed for attempted murder and similar offences, and on the difference between intention and motive (for example in DPP v Fee).

In Ireland, murder requires an intent to kill or cause serious injury, with a rebuttable presumption that a person intends the natural and probable consequences of their conduct (s.4, Criminal Justice Act 1964). Offences requiring an intent to murder are narrower.
job: For attempted murder or shooting with intent, you must prove the intent itself — recklessness won't do.
Gather evidence of intent: what or who was aimed at, the range, the number and direction of shots, the weapon, and anything said before, during or after.
Consider alternative charges that fit the evidence of intent, such as firearms offences with intent to endanger life, or assault causing serious harm.
DPP v Douglas.law: Yes. Still cited on the intent needed for attempted murder.

Criminal Justice Act 1964, s.4 (Irish Statute Book)

bg: The case is Murphy v Independent Radio and Television Commission [1999] 1 IR 12.
A pastor's church submitted an advertisement to a Dublin radio station for a video on the evidence for the Resurrection. The station was willing to broadcast it.

In March 1995 the Independent Radio and Television Commission refused permission under s.10(3) of the Radio and Television Act 1988, which bars advertisements directed towards any religious or political end, or relating to an industrial dispute.
The pastor challenged the ban as a breach of his constitutional rights to free expression and to profess his religion, and as disproportionate. The High Court (Geoghegan J) rejected the challenge.
Murphy v Independent Radio.q: Is a total ban on broadcasting religious advertisements a constitutional limit on free expression and the profession of religion?
dec: Supreme Court, 28 May 1998: appeal dismissed; the ban was upheld.

The ban targets a type of material, not people of a particular faith, so it isn't an attack on the right to practise religion. It does limit how a person may profess or express religion, so it had to be justified.
Expression and communication are personal rights that can be limited for the common good. The question was whether the limit was proportionate to the legislature's aim.

The three banned categories concern matters that have been extremely divisive in Irish society; the legislature could fear that such advertising might cause unrest; and the wealthy shouldn't be able to buy airtime to the detriment of poorer rivals.
The restriction was minimalist: it only stopped the applicant promoting his views through paid broadcast advertising.

keys.q: extremely divisive in Irish society
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the banned categories

later: In Murphy v Ireland (10 July 2003) the European Court of Human Rights unanimously found no violation of Article 10. States have a wide margin of appreciation on religious expression; the ban covered only broadcast media, with its more immediate impact; and paid advertising would favour religions with more resources.
Compare Handyside v United Kingdom (1976) on the margin of appreciation in matters of morals.
job: Rights to expression and religion can be limited by law for the common good, if the limit is proportionate.
When restricting what people say, display or broadcast — at a protest, for example — identify the legal basis, the aim, and why the restriction goes no further than necessary.
Act on what the law actually prohibits, not on the content being religious, political or unpopular.
Murphy v Independent Radio.law: Yes. Upheld in Strasbourg in Murphy v Ireland (2003).

src.t: Irish Times — 'Pastor loses Supreme Court appeal over ban on radio ad' (29 May 1998)
IRIS Merlin (European Audiovisual Observatory) — note on the Supreme Court decision
IRIS Merlin — Murphy v Ireland (ECtHR, 10 July 2003)

bg: In August 2003 the Special Criminal Court convicted the accused of directing the activities of an unlawful organisation — the first prosecution for that offence — and sentenced him to 20 years.

The prosecution depended overwhelmingly on one witness, who had been paid by the FBI and the British Security Service and whose background gave him a questionable reputation. Much of the material about him was held outside Ireland.
The Court of Criminal Appeal upheld the conviction, and the Supreme Court heard a further appeal on a certified point about disclosure.
DPP v McKevitt.q: Are disclosure obligations met where relevant documents are held outside the jurisdiction, but all reasonable good-faith efforts were made to obtain them? And was the conviction safe?
dec: Supreme Court, 30 July 2008 (Geoghegan J, with Murray CJ, Denham, Hardiman and Fennelly JJ): appeal dismissed; the conviction was safe.

Disclosure obligations were met: all reasonable efforts had been made in good faith to obtain the documents, with a high level of co-operation. The rules of civil discovery don't apply to criminal cases.
On appeal the question isn't whether there was a risk of an unfair trial, but whether the conviction is unsafe because of unfairness.

The late disclosure of Garda surveillance notes was reasonable and not seriously prejudicial; the trial court had offered to recall the witness for further cross-examination, and the defence declined.
The Special Criminal Court believed the witness, and that finding couldn't be interfered with on appeal.

keys.q: the rules of civil discovery do not apply to criminal cases
keys.w: Geoghegan J

later: McKevitt is cited on the extent of the prosecution's disclosure duty where material is held by third parties or abroad.
Read with Braddish v DPP (2001) and Dunne v DPP (2002) on the duty to seek out and preserve evidence.
job: Disclosure covers material held by others, including outside Ireland. Make every reasonable good-faith effort to obtain it, and record each request, reply and follow-up.
Disclose surveillance notes, logs and reports promptly. Late disclosure can derail a trial even when it's eventually made.
Where a key witness is an informant or has a questionable background, everything bearing on their credibility — payments, history, other dealings — must be gathered and disclosed.
DPP v McKevitt.law: Yes. Still cited on disclosure of material held abroad.

src.t: RTÉ News — McKevitt loses Supreme Court appeal (30 July 2008)

bg: A driver was stopped and arrested on suspicion of drink-driving at about 9.05pm and brought to a Garda station, arriving at 9.21pm.

A Garda observed him for about 20 minutes, until 9.37pm, to make sure he took nothing by mouth that could affect the breath test. At 9.40pm he was required to give two breath specimens on the intoxilyser under s.13(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1994.

He didn't exhale effectively and was charged with failing to provide the specimens. Evidence from the Medical Bureau of Road Safety was that a 15 to 20 minute observation period was standard scientific practice for eliminating mouth alcohol.
The Circuit Court asked the Supreme Court whether the evidence showed that holding him for about 20 minutes of observation before the test was lawful.
DPP v McNiece.q: Is it lawful to hold an arrested driver for a period of observation before requiring breath specimens?
dec: Supreme Court, 14 July 2003 (Murray J giving the judgment, with Keane CJ, Denham, McGuinness and Hardiman JJ): the questions were answered in the affirmative — the detention was lawful.
In criminal proceedings the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was held in custody in accordance with law, for the whole period.
It was rational and logical for the State to have procedures for administering the test, and the observation period had an objective justification.
Without some controlled observation there would always be a risk that an accused could claim to have secretly taken something while the Garda was distracted.

keys.q: Unless there was some kind of controlled observation
keys.w: Supreme Court (Murray J), on the observation period

later: McNiece is cited for the lawfulness of the observation period before breath testing, and for the rule that the prosecution must prove the lawfulness of custody throughout.
Breath testing at the station is now governed by the Road Traffic Act 2010 — check its current wording.
job: Record the exact times: arrest, arrival at the station, start and end of the observation, and when the requirement was made.
Note what you watched for during the observation (nothing taken by mouth, no vomiting or belching) and who did the observing.
Be ready to explain why each part of the custody was needed — the prosecution must prove it was all lawful.
DPP v McNiece.law: Yes. Read with the Road Traffic Act 2010.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v McNiece [2003] 2 IR 614

bg: Gardaí obtained a search warrant from a Peace Commissioner and searched the accused's home. They found nothing incriminating, but arrested him on the premises and detained him under s.4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984.
He made a statement in detention, which was the main prosecution evidence on charges of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, having an article with intent to cause injury, and robbery.

The defence argued the warrant was invalid, making the entry, arrest, detention and statement unlawful. Following an earlier decision, the trial judge held there was no evidence the warrant was valid without the Peace Commissioner's own evidence, held the arrest and detention invalid, and directed an acquittal.
The DPP referred the point of law to the Supreme Court.
DPP v Owens.q: Must the person who issued a search warrant give evidence of their state of mind when issuing it?
dec: Supreme Court, 16 February 1999 (Barrington J, with Hamilton CJ, O'Flaherty, Denham and Keane JJ): yes — the Peace Commissioner had to give evidence in person to establish his state of mind when he issued the warrant.
A search warrant is a document that may affect constitutional rights, so it can't simply be accepted at face value. It doesn't speak for itself in a criminal trial.
Because that was the only question referred, the Court didn't rule on whether the arrest and detention were valid.
O'Flaherty J added that the arrest didn't depend on the warrant: Gardaí may arrest on reasonable suspicion of an arrestable offence, so the arrest wouldn't automatically be invalid.

keys.q: does not speak for itself in a criminal trial
keys.w: Supreme Court, on a search warrant

later: Owens is still cited for the principle that the issuer's satisfaction matters and a warrant doesn't prove itself.

The law on who may issue warrants has since been tightened: in Damache v DPP (2012) a warrant issued by a superintendent involved in the investigation was unconstitutional, and the issuer must be independent.
job: Your sworn information must give the issuer real grounds to be satisfied — not a form of words.
Expect to prove the warrant properly: whoever issued it may need to give evidence of what they considered.
Don't rely on a warrant to justify an arrest. If you arrest during a search, record your own reasonable grounds for suspecting the arrestable offence.
DPP v Owens.law: Yes, as to the principle. Check the current position on proving warrants.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Owens [1999] 2 IR 16

bg: The accused pleaded guilty in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court to sexual offences against children.
Before sentencing, the trial judge met counsel in chambers, and the accused then changed his plea to guilty. The judge imposed concurrent sentences of six and three years.

The DPP applied for a review under s.2 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993, on the ground that the sentences were unduly lenient. The Court of Criminal Appeal agreed and substituted ten years, declining to take account of the chambers meeting.
The accused appealed to the Supreme Court.
DPP v Heeney.q: On a DPP review of sentence, must the Court of Criminal Appeal take account of how the plea and sentence came about — including discussions in the judge's chambers?
dec: Supreme Court, 5 April 2001 (Keane CJ, with Denham, Murphy, Murray and Hardiman JJ): appeal allowed; the Court of Criminal Appeal's order was discharged and the Circuit Court sentences affirmed.
The Court of Criminal Appeal was wrong to decline to have regard to the discussions in chambers.
It was obliged to consider the whole chain of circumstances leading to the plea and the sentence — circumstances in which the DPP had participated.
There was no double jeopardy issue as such, because the accused wasn't being retried for a charge on which he'd been acquitted.
later: Heeney is cited in later cases for the principle that plea bargaining has no place in Irish law, although a judge may indicate the likely sentence.
It also shows the courts' concern with fairness where the DPP takes part in steps that lead to a plea and then seeks a heavier sentence.
job: Decisions on charges, pleas and sentence are for the DPP and the court, not the investigating Garda.
Make sure your file gives the full facts, the impact on the victims and their views, before any plea is accepted.
Record and report any approach by the defence about a plea — don't make or imply promises about charges or sentence.
DPP v Heeney.law: Yes. Still cited on chambers discussions and pleas.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Heeney [2001] 1 IR 736

bg: A driver was arrested for drink-driving in December 2001 and taken to a Garda station, where she was required to give two breath specimens under s.13 of the Road Traffic Act 1994.
On three attempts she couldn't seal her lips around the mouthpiece, and each time the machine printed that the specimen was incomplete.

She was charged with failing to comply with the requirement 'in the manner indicated by the Garda' and convicted in the District Court. On appeal, the Circuit Court asked the Supreme Court whether that was an offence, and whether simply exhaling into the device was enough to comply.
DPP v Moorehouse.q: Is it an offence to fail to give breath specimens in the manner the Garda indicates — and is just blowing into the machine enough?
dec: Supreme Court, 28 July 2005, by 2 to 1 (Kearns J giving the decision).

Section 13 is a penal provision and must be strictly construed. On that reading, it was not an offence to refuse or fail to comply with the requirement to give the specimens in the manner the Garda indicated.
But a driver must give specimens sufficient to enable the concentration of alcohol in the breath to be determined. Merely exhaling into the device isn't compliance.
McCracken J questioned how a person could be guilty for using a different method if they gave sufficient breath. The conviction on the 'manner indicated' charge couldn't stand.

keys.q: sufficient to enable the concentration of alcohol in the breath to be determined
keys.w: Supreme Court, on what the driver must provide

later: Moorehouse is cited on the strict construction of penal statutes, and on what counts as failing to provide breath specimens.
Breath testing at the station is now governed by the Road Traffic Act 2010, so check the current wording of the requirement and the offence before relying on this.
job: Charge the right failure: that the person failed to provide specimens sufficient to determine the alcohol concentration — not just that they didn't follow your method.
Record each attempt: the time, what you told them, what they did, and the machine's printout. Keep the printouts.
Note whether they appeared to be genuinely trying, and anything they said about a medical reason — it matters if a defence is raised.
DPP v Moorehouse.law: Decided under the 1994 Act — check the Road Traffic Act 2010.

src.t: Irish Times — 'Court rules on manner of giving breath specimens' (29 July 2005)
Irish Examiner — 'Supreme Court decision on drivers' breath samples'

bg: A driver was charged with drink-driving under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961.

The prosecution proved his arrest and detention, the taking of a urine sample under s.13(1)(b) of the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act 1978, and the Medical Bureau of Road Safety certificate. But there was no evidence that he had been told of his rights under the 1987 Custody Regulations.

The District Court stated a case to the High Court with six questions: whether the Regulations applied to people arrested for drink-driving; whether the prosecution had to prove compliance; whether a breach made the custody unlawful despite s.7(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984; and whether evidence obtained was inadmissible.
DPP v Spratt.q: Does a breach of the Custody Regulations make the detention unlawful, or the evidence inadmissible, in a drink-driving case?
dec: High Court, 8 February 1995 (O'Hanlon J), on a consultative case stated.

Section 7(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 provides that a failure to observe the Regulations does not of itself affect the lawfulness of the custody or the admissibility of evidence. The words 'of itself' matter.
So a breach isn't an automatic ground for excluding the evidence. Whether it affects the case is for the trial court to decide on the facts, case by case.
The free report available doesn't set out the answer to each of the six questions.

keys.q: of itself
keys.w: s.7(3), Criminal Justice Act 1984 — the words emphasised in Spratt

later: In DPP v Cullen (High Court, 2001) a District Judge was wrong to dismiss a charge for a breach of the Regulations without assessing its actual impact on the prosecution case — applying Spratt.
People (DPP) v Diver (2005) refers to Spratt as emphasising the words 'of itself' in s.7(3).
job: Follow the Custody Regulations in road traffic cases too: give the notice of rights, explain it, and record it in the custody record.
If something goes wrong (a delay, a missed notice), record exactly what happened and what you did to put it right — the court will weigh its actual effect.
Don't assume a breach is harmless: it gives the defence an argument the court must consider.
DPP v Spratt.law: Yes. Read with Cullen (2001) and Diver (2005).

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Spratt [1995] 1 IR 585
