bg: The accused was convicted by the Special Criminal Court of conspiracy to cause an explosion, contrary to s.3 of the Explosive Substances Act 1883, in connection with the Omagh bombing. He was sentenced to 14 years.

The prosecution relied on admissions he allegedly made in Garda interviews, mobile phone records, and a witness who had lent him a phone (who later tried to retract his evidence, claiming police pressure; the trial court accepted his original account).

A forensic document examiner found that a page of one interview's notes had been rewritten. Two detectives were found to have altered the notes and to have given untruthful evidence about it. The trial court excised their evidence, found no wider Garda complicity, and convicted.
DPP v Murphy.q: Once a court knows some Garda evidence is tainted, how must it treat the rest — and was the conviction safe?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 21 January 2005 (Kearns J giving the judgment): conviction set aside as unsafe and unsatisfactory; retrial ordered.

Where tainted and perjured Garda evidence comes to light, the court must evaluate the remaining Garda evidence in an extra critical fashion, and must state on the face of its judgment that it is doing so.

The alteration raised an open question whether other officers had colluded. The trial court didn't show the necessary heightened scrutiny, didn't assess earlier criticism of one detective as the defence asked, and made findings based on speculation rather than evidence.
The trial court also had regard to the accused's previous convictions, which weren't admissible because he hadn't put his character in issue. That eroded the presumption of innocence.
Challenges to the arrest and detention, the phone records and the witness's evidence failed.

keys.q: evaluate in an extra critical fashion
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on the remaining Garda evidence

later: Murphy is still cited on how courts must treat Garda evidence once some of it is shown to be tainted.
Interviews are now electronically recorded, but Garda notes, memos and statements remain evidence and are tested in the same way.
job: Your notes are evidence. Never alter, rewrite or 'tidy up' interview notes, statements or your notebook — and never give untruthful evidence about them.
Correct mistakes openly: a single line through, initialled and dated, not overwritten or replaced.
Remember the wider cost: one tainted record can cast doubt on every other Garda's evidence in the case.
DPP v Murphy.law: Yes. Still cited on tainted Garda evidence.

src.t: Irish Times law report — 'When court becomes aware of tainted Garda evidence other Garda evidence should be critically assessed' (7 Feb 2005)

bg: The case is People (Attorney General) v Murphy [1947] IR 236.
During a murder investigation, the accused made a statement in answer to questions by a police officer.
Before that, a remark had been made to him — 'you are all right' — which the defence argued meant 'you will be all right', an improper inducement to make a statement.
The free headnote available sets out the principles the court applied; it doesn't show the final order.
People v Murphy.q: Who must prove a statement was voluntary — and what if an inducement was held out before it was made?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 23 January 1947.
The onus is on the prosecution to establish that a statement was voluntary.

Where an inducement has been held out, the trial judge must be judicially satisfied that the inducement had ceased to operate on the accused's mind before the statement was made. Only then can it be admitted.
A statement made in answer to questions by the police isn't inadmissible on that account alone.

keys.q: judicially satisfied that inducement had ceased to operate
keys.w: headnote, on admitting a statement after an inducement

later: Murphy was approved by the Court of Criminal Appeal in People (AG) v Galvin (1964), on how long an inducement's effect lasts.
job: Never hold out hopes or promises to get a statement: 'you'll be all right', 'it'll go easier on you', 'tell us and you can go home', 'we'll leave your family out of it'.

If someone else has (a family member, an employer, another Garda), record exactly what was said, and make sure any statement afterwards is made free of it — a break, a fresh caution, access to a solicitor — and record those steps.
Expect to prove voluntariness: record the circumstances of every statement — who was present, what was said before it, and how it was taken down.
People v Murphy.law: Yes. The voluntariness rule still applies; read with Galvin (1964).

src.t: vLex Ireland — People (Attorney-General) v Murphy [1947] IR 236 (headnote)

bg: In July 2002 a courier arrived at Dublin Airport on a flight from Paris carrying four large slabs of cannabis — just over 20kg, worth just over €52,000. He had agreed to bring the bag to Dublin for a fee.

He pleaded guilty to an offence under s.15A of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 (possession of drugs worth €13,000 or more for sale or supply), and had made a full statement to Gardaí. He was sentenced to five years.
He appealed, arguing the sentence was too heavy compared with sentences given to other couriers, and pointing to his age, poor finances, good conduct in prison, his plea and his co-operation.
DPP v Botha.q: How does the 'exceptional and specific circumstances' exception to the s.15A minimum work — and was five years too heavy?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 19 January 2004 (Hardiman J giving the judgment, with O'Sullivan and Herbert JJ): appeal dismissed.
The trial judge was entitled to ask both sides about sentences in similar cases. Because the provisions are statutory and specific, past decisions on them are useful guidance.
The guilty plea and the assistance given to Gardaí could properly be considered in setting the sentence.

But s.27 significantly limits the court's discretion. The minimum must be imposed unless there are specific and exceptional circumstances making it unjust — both words must be satisfied. Even then, the statutory minimum and maximum still guide the court.
Cannabis isn't a separate category from other drugs: the section sets the threshold by the value of the drugs, not their type.

keys.q: exceptional and specific
keys.w: the conjunctive test under s.27, Misuse of Drugs Act 1977

later: Botha is still cited on the s.15A minimum sentence and on how 'exceptional and specific circumstances' are assessed.
Compare People (DPP) v Long (2008), where the Court of Criminal Appeal stressed that quantity and value are critical to seriousness.
job: In s.15A cases the value is the threshold: weigh the drugs, get a professional valuation, and record the weight and how it was established.
Record the suspect's co-operation and admissions accurately and fully — they count in mitigation, and the court will look for them.
For couriers, record what they knew and were paid, who sent them and who was to collect — it goes to culpability and to wider investigation.
DPP v Botha.law: Yes. Read with s.27 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977, as amended.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Botha [2004] 2 IR 375

bg: The accused was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of a firearms offence linked to a robbery, and interviewed at a Garda station in three sessions.
In the first session, after Gardaí read him a statement by a co-accused and asked him to tell the truth, he said: 'Haven't ye got the story there?'
The Special Criminal Court ruled the first two sets of admissions inadmissible, but admitted the third, and convicted him of robbery. He appealed.
DPP v Buckley.q: Does the exclusion of earlier admissions make a later admission inadmissible too?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 31 July 1989 (Finlay CJ): conviction upheld.
The trial court acted correctly in admitting the third statement.
The earlier admissions had been ruled inadmissible on grounds other than oppression, threat or inducement. So there was nothing whose effect could carry over and taint the later statement.
The free report available doesn't set out why the first two sets of admissions were excluded.

keys.q: grounds other than oppression, threat or inducement
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on why the third statement stood

later: Buckley is cited on whether excluded admissions taint later ones: where the earlier problem was oppression, a threat or an inducement, its effect may continue — read with People v Murphy (1947) and People (AG) v Galvin (1964).
Garda interviews are now electronically recorded, which makes the circumstances of each statement easier to prove.
job: If an interview goes wrong, a later interview can still be admissible — but only if it's clean and the earlier problem wasn't oppression, a threat or an inducement whose effect could continue.
Start any later interview fresh: a break, a new caution, renewed access to a solicitor, and nothing that refers back to the earlier problem. Record all of it.
Don't use material from an excluded interview to put pressure on the suspect in a later one.
DPP v Buckley.law: Yes. Read with People v Murphy (1947) and Galvin (1964).

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v Buckley [1990] 1 IR 14

bg: In 1996 the accused was charged with historic sexual offences alleged to date from the 1970s, including indecent assault under s.62 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. An earlier challenge on grounds of delay had failed.
In the Circuit Criminal Court he applied to quash the counts, arguing that s.62 was inconsistent with the Constitution and with the European Convention on Human Rights.
The judge stated a case to the Supreme Court asking whether the Circuit Court could decide those questions, and whether s.62 was valid.
DPP v MS.q: Can a Circuit Criminal Court decide that a pre-1937 statute is unconstitutional, or inconsistent with the Convention?
dec: Supreme Court, 2 April 2003 (Keane CJ, Denham, Murray, McGuinness and Hardiman JJ).

The Circuit Criminal Court had no jurisdiction to hear and determine a challenge to a pre-Constitution statute on constitutional grounds. A court of local and limited jurisdiction must apply legislation unless the superior courts have found it invalid.

Because the Convention hadn't been incorporated into Irish law by legislation, no court had jurisdiction to decide whether a statutory provision was inconsistent with it (following In re Ó Laighléis).
The free report available doesn't show the Court's view on whether s.62 itself was valid.

keys.q: could not be determined by a court of local and limited jurisdiction
keys.w: Supreme Court, on constitutional challenges

later: The European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 came into force later in 2003. Courts must now interpret laws compatibly with the Convention where possible, and the superior courts can make a declaration of incompatibility.
The constitutional point — that the District and Circuit Courts can't strike down statutes — still stands.
job: Constitutional challenges to a criminal statute belong in the High Court. In the District or Circuit Court the statute is applied unless a superior court has struck it down — so keep the prosecution moving.
If the defence signals a constitutional challenge, tell the prosecuting solicitor or state solicitor early — it can delay the trial.
DPP v MS.law: Constitutional point: yes. Convention point: overtaken by the ECHR Act 2003.

src.t: vLex Ireland — DPP v M.S. [2003] 1 IR 606

bg: The accused, in his early twenties, pleaded guilty to possessing about 1.6kg of cocaine with an uncontested street value of €111,370. Gardaí found it at his family home in 2006 while he was out.

He said he was holding the drugs for someone to whom he owed €500. A psychological report described him as immature and vulnerable; he had weaned himself off drugs and had no drug-related convictions.

The sentencing judge said the value of the drugs was not a material factor and, citing the plea, the assistance to Gardaí, his youth and the psychological evidence, imposed two years. The DPP applied for a review on the ground that the sentence was unduly lenient.
People (DPP) v Long.q: How much weight must a sentencing court give to the quantity and value of drugs?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 10 October 2008 (Kearns J, with Budd and Clarke JJ): the DPP's application was allowed, with a new sentence to be substituted after further submissions.
Quantity and value are critical factors in evaluating the overall seriousness of a drugs offence; that is implicit in the Act. The judge was wrong to treat value as immaterial.
Value isn't determinative — each case turns on its own facts, and the type of drug may also be considered — but it is the critical factor.
An earlier case involving drugs worth about €35,000 was distinguishable, largely because of the difference in value. The court also stressed the importance of giving reasons for sentence.

keys.q: critical factors to be taken into account
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (Kearns J), on quantity and value

later: Long is cited for the importance of quantity and value in drugs sentencing. Read with DPP v Botha (2004) on the 'exceptional and specific circumstances' test for going below the minimum.
The Irish Times report confirms the decision; check the neutral citation before citing it.
job: Prove quantity and value properly: weigh the drugs, get a professional valuation, and record where and how they were found.
Record exactly what the suspect says about holding the drugs for someone else, and any debt or pressure — it goes to culpability, not to whether the offence is made out.
Note the suspect's age, background and co-operation accurately in your file — courts will weigh them against the value.
People (DPP) v Long.law: Yes. Still cited on quantity and value.

src.t: Irish Times — 'Quantity and value of drugs critical for sentencing' (24 Nov 2008)

bg: An early case under s.15A of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977, which brought in a presumptive ten-year minimum for possessing drugs worth €13,000 or more for sale or supply. The drug was cannabis.
The accused was an addict and a first offender. He pleaded guilty, gave material assistance to the Gardaí, and expressed remorse.
The trial judge imposed seven years, and he sought leave to appeal.
People (DPP) v Renald.q: How should the s.15A minimum influence the sentence where the court decides it needn't be imposed?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 23 November 2001 (Murphy J giving the judgment): the court treated the application as the appeal.
It imposed seven years, with the last two suspended on terms aimed at helping him overcome his drug use.
The very existence of a lengthy mandatory minimum sentence is an important guide to the gravity of the offence — even where the court finds that the minimum needn't be imposed in the particular case.

keys.q: the very existence of a lengthy mandatory minimum sentence is an important guide
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (Murphy J)

later: The Court of Criminal Appeal endorsed Renald's approach in DPP v Ducque (2005).
Later cases set out the method: fix a notional sentence first, then consider mitigation — see Ducque (2005) and Lernihan (2007).
job: Record the factors courts weigh in s.15A cases: addiction, first-offender status, the plea, remorse and especially material assistance to Gardaí.
Note any steps the accused has taken towards treatment — part-suspended sentences are often structured around it.
Even when the minimum is set aside, expect a substantial sentence: the minimum still signals how serious the offence is.
People (DPP) v Renald.law: Yes. Read with Ducque (2005) and Lernihan (2007).

src.t: LegalBlog.ie — Drugs Sentences (People (DPP) v Renald, CCA 2001)

bg: The accused was paid €1,000 to collect and drive a car containing ecstasy tablets worth roughly €2.1 to €2.7 million. Gardaí stopped the car within minutes.
He pleaded guilty to a s.15A offence but gave no information about his contacts, citing fear. He had around forty previous convictions, mostly for road traffic offences, and a troubled childhood.
The Dublin Circuit Court imposed twelve years — two above the ten-year minimum. He sought leave to appeal.
People (DPP) v Ducque.q: How should a court approach sentence under s.15A — and can a late guilty plea take the case below the minimum?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 15 July 2005 (Geoghegan J, with Budd and O'Neill JJ): leave to appeal refused; the court was satisfied the trial judge reached the correct result.

The court should first set the sentence as if the minimum didn't exist, bearing in mind the maximum of life imprisonment. If that notional sentence is more than ten years, that is the sentence. If it's less, the ten-year minimum applies unless the exceptional and specific circumstances test is met.
A late plea would rarely if ever amount to exceptional and specific circumstances, so it won't normally displace the minimum.
The plea can be taken into account in setting the notional sentence, but it mustn't be counted twice. The minimum remains a guide to gravity even where it doesn't apply (endorsing Renald).

keys.q: would rarely if ever constitute
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on late pleas as exceptional circumstances

later: Ducque is still cited for the notional-sentence method and the weight of late pleas under s.15A.
Read with DPP v Botha (2004) on 'exceptional and specific' circumstances and DPP v Lernihan (2007) on double-counting.
job: In large seizures, the minimum is often the floor, not the sentence: record the scale and value, the person's role and what they were paid.
Record any co-operation fully — and if the suspect declines to give information (for example through fear), record that accurately too.
Note when the guilty plea was indicated: early pleas count for more than late ones.
People (DPP) v Ducque.law: Yes. Still cited on s.15A sentencing method.

src.t: LegalBlog.ie — Drugs Sentences (DPP v Ducque [2005] IECCA 92)

bg: The accused was stopped in Cork carrying a kilo of cocaine with a street value of about €72,000, which he was holding for €500. A small amount of cannabis resin for personal use was found at his home.
He wasn't an addict, was working as a painter and decorator, and had no previous convictions. He pleaded guilty early, gave limited assistance, and expressed remorse.

Cork Circuit Criminal Court imposed four years on each of two concurrent counts, with the final two and a half years suspended. The DPP applied for a review on the ground that the sentence was unduly lenient.
DPP v Lernihan.q: Was the sentence unduly lenient — and how should mitigation be applied under s.15A?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 18 April 2007 (Denham J giving the judgment): sentence quashed; seven years imposed.
The court should first determine the appropriate notional sentence, then consider the aggravating and mitigating factors, and then apply mitigation.
The life maximum and the ten-year presumptive sentence show the gravity of the offence. The trial judge didn't address this, which was an error.
The sentencing court applied the mitigating factors twice, and so erred. The plea carried less weight because the accused was caught red-handed.

On a DPP review under s.2 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993, the DPP bears the onus, and only a substantial departure from the appropriate sentence justifies intervention. Once the sentence is quashed, the court sentences afresh.

keys.q: applied the mitigating factors twice, and so erred
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (Denham J)

later: Lernihan is cited on double-counting mitigation and on the gravity signalled by the s.15A regime.
Read with DPP v Ducque (2005) and DPP v Botha (2004).
job: A plea from someone caught red-handed earns less credit — so record exactly how they were caught and what was found on them.
Record any assistance precisely, including its limits: 'limited' assistance counts for less.
Record what the suspect was paid or owed for holding the drugs — it goes to culpability.
DPP v Lernihan.law: Yes. Still cited on s.15A sentencing and undue leniency.

src.t: LegalBlog.ie — Drugs Sentences (DPP v Lernihan [2007] IECCA 21)

bg: The accused and another man broke into a house in Co. Waterford to burgle it, believing it was empty.
The elderly householder returned home and was fatally stabbed by the accused. The pathologist found fatal stab wounds to the trunk and minor defensive wounds to the arm and hand.

The accused didn't give evidence. In several inconsistent statements to Gardaí he claimed he acted in self-defence after the householder attacked him. He pleaded guilty to burglary and was convicted of the killing.
He sought leave to appeal, arguing among other things that the trial judge had misdirected the jury on self-defence and the burden of proof.
DPP v Barnes.q: Can a burglar rely on self-defence against the householder — and what force may a householder use against a burglar?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 21 December 2006 (Hardiman J, with Hanna and Feeney JJ): leave to appeal refused.

Burglary of a dwelling is more than a crime against property: it is an invasion of the victim's constitutional right to the inviolability of the dwelling. The common law no longer lets a householder kill a burglar simply for being a burglar.

A householder need not retreat from his home, and may use force to drive off, immobilise or detain an intruder. That force is judged subjectively as well as objectively: a victim isn't in the position of a calm, ordinary reasonable person weighing up the options.

There is only narrow scope for self-defence by a burglar — essentially against an attempt to kill him simply for being a burglar. Because of the burglar's initial aggression, the killing of a householder during a burglary can never be less than manslaughter.

The jury was entitled to reject the accused's account. The trial judge twice wrongly put a burden on the accused on self-defence, but corrected it on recharge, and the jury would have followed the correction.

keys.q: There is only narrow scope for the defence of self-defence by the burglar.
keys.w: Hardiman J

keys.q: not in the position of an ordinary reasonable man or woman
keys.w: Hardiman J, on the householder

later: The Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011 now provides that a person in their dwelling may use force against someone they believe has entered as a trespasser to commit a criminal act — to protect themselves or others, protect property, prevent crime or effect an arrest — if the force is only such as is reasonable in the circumstances as they believe them to be. There's no duty to retreat, and the force may include force causing death.
The 2011 defence doesn't cover force used against a Garda acting in the course of duty, or anyone assisting a Garda (s.2(2)).
job: At a burglary scene, record exactly what the householder saw, heard, feared and did, in their own words — their shock and fear are central to judging any force they used.
Treat burglary of a home as a crime against the person and the home, not just property — and record the impact on the occupants.
When entering a dwelling on duty, identify yourself clearly as a Garda: the 2011 defence doesn't protect force used against a Garda acting in the course of duty.
DPP v Barnes.law: Yes. Read with the Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011.

src.t: Irish Times law report — 'Burglary victim not in position of ordinary reasonable person weighing up what course of action is best' (Jan 2007)
Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011, s.2 (Irish Statute Book)

bg: A farmer living alone in Co. Mayo had been living in fear of burglary after a spate of local thefts.
In October 2004 a man came onto his property with his son. The farmer got a shotgun. After a struggle the man retreated, and was shot again on the public road; that second shot was fatal.

At the close of the evidence the trial judge ruled that a full acquittal on self-defence would be perverse. He left the jury only 'partial' self-defence, which could reduce murder to manslaughter — so they couldn't acquit outright.
The jury found him not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter, and he was sentenced to six years.
DPP v Nally.q: Can a trial judge take full self-defence away from the jury, so that they must convict of murder or manslaughter?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 12 October 2006 (Kearns J giving the judgment): leave to appeal granted, conviction quashed, retrial ordered.

Following People (DPP) v Davis (Supreme Court, 1993), a judge may direct an acquittal but may not direct a conviction. The jury must retain the ultimate power to decide guilt or innocence, even where it disagrees with the judge.
Whether the force used was objectively reasonable is quintessentially a matter of fact for the jury.
The court criticised both prosecution and defence counsel for not putting Davis before the trial judge — counsel must bring relevant authorities to the court's attention.

keys.q: quintessentially a matter of fact for a jury
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (Kearns J), on reasonableness of force

later: Nally is cited on the jury's role: a judge can't direct a conviction or remove a defence the evidence leaves open.

The case was part of the background to the Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011, which now sets out when a person in their dwelling may use force against a trespasser (see DPP v Barnes (2006)). It doesn't cover force against a Garda acting in the course of duty.
job: Self-defence and the reasonableness of force are for the jury, so your evidence must capture everything bearing on them.

Record the sequence of events precisely: distances, positions, who was where at each moment, what was said, what weapons were present, and where each shot or blow happened (on the property or off it).
Record what the person knew and feared beforehand — earlier incidents, reports to Gardaí, threats — and get scene measurements, forensics and witness accounts early.
DPP v Nally.law: Yes. Read with Davis (1993) and the 2011 Act.

src.t: Irish Times — 'Nally judgment' (October 2006)
Criminal Law (Defence and the Dwelling) Act 2011, s.2 (Irish Statute Book)

bg: A single mother came to Ireland in 2007, pregnant and with three young children, and sought asylum. She described violence and threats that had destroyed her family at home.

In 2010 her account was found not credible. In June 2011 the Minister refused her applications for subsidiary protection and humanitarian leave to remain, and the family was removed from the State in December 2011.

From abroad, they sought judicial review in 2012, arguing they were entitled to an oral hearing on subsidiary protection, and that judicial review wasn't an effective remedy for challenging the refusal.
A.A.A. v Minister for Justice.q: Is judicial review an effective remedy against a refusal of subsidiary protection — and is there a right to an oral hearing?
dec: Supreme Court, 21 December 2017 (Charleton J giving the judgment, with Dunne and Hogan JJ): the High Court's refusal of leave on the broader grounds was affirmed.

Since Meadows v Minister for Justice (2010), judicial review applies a proportionality test where the decision engages fundamental rights. Relying on NM v Minister for Justice and ISOF v Minister for Justice, the Court held that judicial review provides a thorough review of the refusal, and so is an effective remedy.
The EU Procedures Directive doesn't expressly require a separate appeal on the merits, and requiring one would cut across the principle of national procedural autonomy.
Following the Court of Justice in MM (C-277/11), as a rule there is no right to an oral hearing for subsidiary protection where an oral hearing has already taken place on the asylum claim.

keys.q: a thorough review of the Minister's decision
keys.w: Supreme Court, on judicial review as an effective remedy

later: A.A.A. confirms that judicial review can satisfy EU requirements for an effective remedy in protection cases.
The protection process has since been unified under the International Protection Act 2015, with a single procedure and appeals to the International Protection Appeals Tribunal.
job: Background for immigration work: once protection has been refused and the refusal has been reviewed, removal can follow.
Before acting on someone's status, check it with the immigration authorities — there may be a fresh application or court proceedings.
Where children are involved, record their circumstances and any welfare concerns, and involve Tusla where needed.
A.A.A. v Minister for Justice.law: Yes. Read with the International Protection Act 2015.

src.t: Wikipedia — AAA & Anor v Minister for Justice & Ors

bg: In August 2007, during a routine search at a courier company's compound at Dublin Airport, Gardaí found five large parcels of herbal cannabis.
Using the consignee details, Gardaí contacted the person expecting them, arranged a meeting, and handed the parcels over to a father and son, who were then arrested.

The son said a friend had asked him to collect parcels supposedly containing computer parts, and told him to use a new mobile phone and an assumed name. He couldn't drive, so he asked his father to drive a van and help; they expected to be paid about €300.

The prosecution relied on their movements and behaviour before arrest to show they knew what was in the parcels. Both were convicted in the Circuit Criminal Court of possession for sale or supply (including under s.15A) and simple possession.
DPP v Smyth.q: Under the s.29(2) defence, does the burden of proof shift to the accused — and how should the jury be directed?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 18 May 2010 (Charleton J giving the judgment): treating the application as the appeal, the court allowed it and ordered a retrial of both men.

The trial judge rightly treated the defence as subjective — based on what each accused knew and perceived. But he told the jury the burden never shifted to the defence. That was wrong, and the jury may have received inconsistent directions on a fundamental point (contrary to DPP v Noonan).

Following DPP v Byrne, Healy and Kelleher (1998), s.29(2)(a) exists so that a person isn't convicted solely because he is in possession of drugs when he neither knew nor had reason to suspect what they were. The proper construction derives from Article 38.1 of the Constitution.

The prosecution must prove possession and that the substance is a controlled drug beyond reasonable doubt. The burden then shifts to the accused to show a reasonable doubt that he didn't know, and had no reasonable grounds for suspecting, that it was a controlled drug. That is a legal burden, discharged on the lowest standard of proof — not merely a burden of adducing evidence.

He can discharge it by pointing to weaknesses in the prosecution case, relying on his statement to Gardaí, or giving evidence. He can't seek a direction of no case to answer on knowledge once possession is proved, and the prosecution may argue in closing that the defence hasn't been made out.

keys.q: discharged on the lowest standard of proof
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (Charleton J), on the s.29(2) burden

later: Smyth sets out the direction juries should now be given: the ordinary presumption of innocence; the prosecution proves possession and that the substance is a controlled drug beyond reasonable doubt; the burden then shifts to the defence to show a reasonable doubt on knowledge — 'a reasonable doubt, and no more than that'.
Compare People (DPP) v Power (2007): under s.15A the prosecution needn't prove the accused knew the drugs' value.
job: In controlled deliveries and courier cases, knowledge is the battleground. Record the suspects' movements and behaviour before arrest — counter-surveillance, false names, new or burner phones, how they handled the package, what they were paid.
In interview, put the s.29 issues squarely: what they thought was in the package, who asked them, why the false name and new phone, what they were told and paid. Record the answers in full.
Keep the chain of custody of the package from the find to the controlled delivery to the lab, and document how the delivery was set up.
DPP v Smyth.law: Yes. Still the leading authority on the s.29(2) burden.

src.t: LegalBlog.ie — Drug Powers & Penalties (DPP v Smyth and Smyth [2010] IECCA 34)

bg: An inspector from the Department of Posts and Telegraphs visited a cottage on the outskirts of Clane, Co. Kildare. He spoke to a woman there and found a television set standing on a table.

A valuation certificate named the defendant as the occupier of the cottage. He was charged under s.3 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 1926 with unlawfully keeping or having in his possession a television set without a licence. He didn't appear and wasn't represented.
The District Justice stated a consultative case to the High Court on questions of evidence and the onus of proof.
Minister for Posts and Telegraphs v Camp.q: What does it mean to 'keep or have in possession' an article — and is being the occupier of the premises enough?
dec: High Court, 13 May 1966 (Davitt P), on a consultative case stated.
A person must have control of an article to be said to keep it or have it in his possession. That statement was later cited with approval by the Supreme Court.
The occupier of premises where an article is found may be shown to have control of it — but it is control, not mere presence, that makes possession.
The free sources available don't show how the stated questions were answered on these facts.
later: Campbell is cited across possession cases for the principle that possession requires control.
Specific offences may define possession by statute (for example, the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977), so check the statutory wording too.
job: In any possession case — drugs, weapons, stolen goods — evidence of control is the key. Record who occupies or controls the premises, vehicle or bag; who has keys; whose documents and belongings are with the item; and what each person said.
Presence alone isn't possession. Where several people are present, gather evidence linking each to the item.
Photograph the item where found, before it's moved, and record exactly where it was in relation to each person's belongings.
Minister for Posts and Telegraphs v Camp.law: Yes, for the principle that possession requires control.

bg: The case is People (Attorney General) v Mills (Court of Criminal Appeal).
In December 1955 a woman felt a man jostle her in a bus queue in North Earl Street, Dublin, and her wallet containing £104 10s was stolen. She reported it to the Gardaí that day.
The next day two detectives called to her home and she described the man. They returned the same day with six or eight photographs, including one of the accused, and she picked out his photograph.

The following day she identified him at an identification parade at the Bridewell. The use of photographs came out only when the defence cross-examined; the photos weren't produced. She was the only witness to identify him, and he gave an alibi supported by his wife.
People v Mills.q: May Gardaí show photographs to a witness before an identification parade — and what does that do to the identification?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal (Maguire CJ). The grounds included the weight of the evidence, the judge's direction to the jury, and when the use of Garda photographs may be mentioned to the jury.

Later cases describe Mills as treating the evidence of a witness who has previously seen a photograph of the accused as less reliable than other identification evidence: the witness's memory of the culprit and of the photograph can merge.
It is also described as accepting that a Garda who has a description of a suspect may show photographs to the person who gave it, to confirm the description.
The free sources available don't show the court's final order.
later: Mills is cited in People (DPP) v Rapple (1999) and later identification cases on the weakness of identification after photographs have been shown.
Read with People (AG) v Casey (No 2) (1963) on the warning juries must be given about visual identification, and with People (DPP) v Maguire (1995) on identification from CCTV.
job: Get a full, detailed description from the witness first, and record it before anything else is shown.
If photographs are used, show a fair and numerous selection of similar people — never one or two — and record exactly which photos were shown, in what order, and what the witness said.

Remember the cost: once a witness has seen a suspect's photograph, any later parade identification is weaker. Where a suspect is known and available, a properly run identification parade is usually better.
People v Mills.law: Yes, as to the principle. Check current Garda identification procedures.

bg: The case is People (Attorney General) v Gilbert [1973] IR 383.

Before the trial, a Garda sergeant invoked s.107 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 — which obliges a person to give information about a vehicle and its driver — and warned the accused that refusing to answer was an offence carrying serious penalties. The accused admitted using the car.

He was tried in the Circuit Court for receiving a stolen motor car, knowing it to have been stolen, contrary to s.33(1) of the Larceny Act 1916. The admission was put in evidence, and he was convicted.
People v Gilbert.q: Is an answer given under a statutory demand — where refusing to answer is itself an offence — a voluntary statement that can be used at trial?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 13 April 1973 (Pringle J giving the judgment).
The statement wasn't voluntary: the sergeant had warned that refusing to answer was an offence carrying serious penalties.

So the trial judge shouldn't have admitted it on the Larceny Act charge of receiving. Following People (AG) v Cummins (1972), a trial judge has no discretion to admit a confession he is satisfied wasn't voluntary — the only course is to exclude it.
The court expressly gave no opinion on the position where the charges are for offences under the Road Traffic Acts.

keys.q: We express no opinion on the position
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on Road Traffic Act charges

later: That open question was answered in DPP v Burke. The High Court (2018) and the Court of Appeal (2019) held that an answer given in response to a s.107 demand isn't voluntary, but is admissible in a prosecution under the Road Traffic Acts: the limit on the right to silence is proportionate to the aim of road safety (applying Heaney v Ireland).
Gilbert remains the authority for excluding compelled s.107 answers on charges outside the Road Traffic Acts.
job: A s.107 answer ('who was driving?') given under warning of prosecution is compelled, not voluntary.

You can use it to prosecute the Road Traffic Act offence (Burke). But don't rely on it for theft, unauthorised taking, handling or other non-road-traffic offences — get that evidence another way, after a proper caution.
Record exactly how and when a s.107 demand was made, the warning given, and the answer — and keep it separate from any cautioned interview.
People v Gilbert.law: Yes, for non-road-traffic offences. Read with DPP v Burke (2019).

bg: The accused was awaiting trial in the Special Criminal Court on charges of directing terrorism and membership of an unlawful organisation.

He asked that court to order further disclosure of documents bearing on the credibility of the main prosecution witness — a paid agent — material said to be held by the British security services and the FBI. The DPP said its disclosure obligations had been met in full. The Special Criminal Court refused to order more.
In January 2003 the High Court refused him leave to seek judicial review of that refusal, finding no arguable case. He appealed to the Supreme Court.
McKevitt v DPP.q: Should the High Court review a trial court's disclosure ruling before the trial, where doing so would hold the trial up?
dec: Supreme Court, March 2003 (Keane CJ giving the judgment of a unanimous five-judge court): appeal dismissed; the High Court's refusal of leave was entirely correct.
It wasn't appropriate to grant leave for judicial review where the effect would be to restrain the trial.
The Special Criminal Court's decision on disclosure was within its jurisdiction and fair, so it shouldn't be interfered with.

The issue could arise again at the trial, and the accused could appeal any further rulings. The court took no view on whether a cataloguing or indexing system for disclosure documents should be introduced.
later: The trial went ahead. In DPP v McKevitt (2008) the Supreme Court upheld the conviction, holding that disclosure obligations were met because all reasonable efforts had been made in good faith to obtain material held abroad.

The case reflects the courts' general reluctance to interrupt criminal trials with judicial review: rulings on evidence and disclosure are normally for the trial court, subject to appeal (see also McNulty v DPP (2009)).
job: Disclosure disputes are usually decided by the trial judge, during the trial — so keep your disclosure schedule complete and up to date, because it will be revisited as the case goes on.
Record every request for material held by others (including outside Ireland), the responses, and follow-ups.
Flag anything bearing on a key witness's credibility to the prosecutor early.
McKevitt v DPP.law: Yes. Read with DPP v McKevitt (2008).

bg: The case is People (Attorney General) v Wickham [1949] IR 180.
After being arrested and properly cautioned, the accused made a statement to a police officer that amounted to a confession of the offence charged.
The statement was taken down in writing and read over to him. He acknowledged orally that it was correct, but refused to sign it.
People v Wickham.q: Is a written statement admissible if the accused acknowledged it orally as correct but refused to sign it?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal.
The document was admissible in evidence notwithstanding that the accused never acknowledged it in writing.
What mattered was that it was taken down, read over to him, and acknowledged by him as correct.
The free headnote available doesn't show the final order on the appeal.

keys.q: Document admissible in evidence notwithstanding no acknowledgment in writing
keys.w: headnote

later: Wickham is still cited for the admissibility of unsigned statements that were read over and acknowledged.
Garda interviews are now electronically recorded, which makes it much easier to prove what was said, read over and acknowledged.
job: If a suspect won't sign a statement, it isn't worthless. Read it over in full, and record their oral acknowledgment — and any corrections — word for word.
Note the refusal to sign and any reason given, and have a second member present to witness it.
Record the caution and the time of each step, and keep the original notes.

bg: The case is People (DPP) v Farrell [1978] IR 13.

The accused was convicted in the Special Criminal Court in November 1976 of causing an explosion contrary to s.2 of the Explosive Substances Act 1883 — a bomb in Mill Street, Pettigo, Co. Donegal, in September 1973 — and sentenced to 15 years' penal servitude.

The only evidence linking him to the bomb was verbal statements and one written statement, which the trial court admitted over strong objection. He had been detained under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 for over 24 hours.

On appeal he argued that the statements were obtained in breach of his constitutional rights — in particular, that he should have been told of his right to consult a solicitor, and medically examined for fitness before being questioned.
People v Farrell.q: What is the legal status of the Judges' Rules — and can statements obtained in breach of them, or of a detainee's rights, be admitted?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 29 July 1977 (O'Higgins CJ, Gannon and D'Arcy JJ).
The Judges' Rules are not rules of law. Relying on R v Voisin, the court described them as administrative directions for the guidance of those taking statements.

But a statement obtained contrary to their spirit may be rejected as evidence by the trial judge (as held in People v Cummins (1972)). So breaches matter: they give the trial judge a discretion to exclude.

On detention, the court noted that s.30 can't override constitutional rights such as access to legal advice — 'if he does not know of his right he cannot exercise it' (O'Higgins CJ in State (Healy and Foran), relied on by the accused).
The free sources available don't show the court's final order.

keys.q: The Judges' Rules are not rules of law.
keys.w: O'Higgins CJ (as quoted in later cases)

later: Farrell is cited for the status of the Judges' Rules and the trial judge's discretion to exclude statements taken in breach of them.
The Judges' Rules have largely been overtaken by the Custody Regulations 1987, the electronic recording of interviews, and the Garda Code of Practice on access to a solicitor.
job: Today's rules are the Custody Regulations, the Code of Practice on access to a solicitor, and electronic recording — but the principle is the same: breaches give the court grounds to exclude what was said.
Tell every detainee of their rights, including access to a solicitor, and record that you did and when.
Follow the rules on recording statements exactly; where you can't, record why.
People v Farrell.law: Historic on the Judges' Rules; the principle on discretion to exclude still applies.

bg: Over about 20 months, the accused subjected his partner to a campaign of violence, threats, intimidation and humiliation, and interfered with her relationships with her family and her access to friends. Some threats were made while he was in custody.

In November 2020, after a 21-day trial in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court, a jury convicted him of coercive control under s.39 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018 — the first jury conviction for that offence — together with twelve counts of assault causing harm, intimidation (committed while on bail) and perverting the course of justice (committed while on remand).

He was sentenced in January 2021 to an effective 10½ years. He appealed only the length of the cumulative sentence, arguing that the headline sentences were too high, that two assault sentences shouldn't have run consecutively, and that his age, previous good character and circumstances weren't properly weighed.
People (DPP) v Kane.q: How should coercive control be understood and sentenced alongside the individual offences — and was 10½ years disproportionate?
dec: Court of Appeal, 23 March 2023 (Kennedy J giving the judgment): appeal dismissed; the court found no error in principle.

Relying on English authority, the court held that in coercive control the individual acts must be understood within the wider pattern of behaviour. The offence is a distinct wrong, and the assaults reinforced the coercive conduct. Aggravating factors included the breach of trust, the prolonged offending and the severe impact on the victim.

The s.40 aggravating factor (an intimate relationship) was properly applied to the assaults but not to the coercive control, where the relationship is already an element of the offence (s.40(5)(b)(ii)).
Consecutive sentences were imposed with care: the assaults weren't isolated incidents, and intimidation attracts a mandatory consecutive sentence.
The overall offending was egregious. The court found it difficult to see how the overall sentence was disproportionate, and mitigation had been taken into account.

keys.q: egregious indeed
keys.w: Court of Appeal (Kennedy J), on the overall offending

later: Kane is the leading appellate decision so far on coercive control under s.39 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018, and on how it interacts with the s.40 aggravating factor.
It shows how coercive control is usually prosecuted alongside the incident offences — assaults, threats, criminal damage, intimidation.
job: Coercive control is proved by the pattern. Build a timeline of every incident, and record the controlling conduct — isolating the victim from family and friends, monitoring, threats, humiliation — and its effect on the victim's daily life.
Gather corroboration: messages and call records, social media, medical records, photographs of injuries, and witnesses (family, friends, neighbours, colleagues).

Charge the individual incidents as well, and watch for intimidation or interference with the victim while the suspect is on bail or remand — it's a separate offence and attracts consecutive sentences.
People (DPP) v Kane.law: Yes. The leading appellate decision on s.39.

bg: The accused was a serving member of An Garda Síochána.

Over more than four years he harassed, threatened, assaulted, stole from and controlled his partner. He sent her over 30,000 threatening, vile and abusive messages — 652 of them in a single 14-hour period.
He pleaded guilty to coercive control, and was sentenced in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court in July 2022.
People (DPP) v Moody.q: Where does prolonged, high-volume coercive control sit in the sentencing range?
dec: Dublin Circuit Criminal Court, 26 July 2022 (Judge Martin Nolan).
The judge found the behaviour was at the highest end of the offence.
The maximum sentence for coercive control is five years. The judge set a headline sentence of five years and reduced it to three years and three months to reflect the guilty plea.

keys.q: highest end of the offence
keys.w: Judge Martin Nolan

later: Moody is a first-instance sentence, not a precedent, but it was an early, high-profile example of a coercive control sentence near the maximum.
For the appellate approach to proving and sentencing coercive control, see People (DPP) v Kane (2023).
job: Coercive control cases are often built on volume and pattern: messages, call logs, social media and their timing can be the core evidence. Download and preserve phones and accounts early, and quantify the contact (how many messages, how often, at what hours).
Record the effect on the victim's daily life as well as the incidents, and gather corroboration from family, friends and colleagues.
No one is above the law: treat allegations against Gardaí exactly as any other. Garda systems and information must never be used for personal reasons.
People (DPP) v Moody.law: A first-instance sentence; read with People (DPP) v Kane (2023).

bg: Between May 2014 and September 2018, the accused sent anonymous handwritten letters making spurious allegations of misconduct, corruption and infidelity about three Gardaí. The letters went to the Gardaí's families, colleagues and superiors. The allegations were found to be unfounded.
He pleaded guilty to three counts of harassment under s.10 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997.
The Circuit Court, told that the maximum sentence was ten years, imposed six years with the final year suspended. He appealed.
DPP v Hutchinson.q: Was the sentence wrong in principle — and how should harassment of several victims be sentenced?
dec: Court of Appeal, 21 October 2024 (Kennedy J giving the judgment, with McCarthy and MacGrath JJ): appeal allowed and the sentence quashed.
The sentencing court had been wrongly told the maximum was ten years; the true maximum was seven. That was an error in principle.

The offending was midrange rather than high-range: the harassment wasn't persistent or daily, and he didn't follow any individual. But it was aggravated because the victims were Gardaí and their families were targeted with malicious, spurious and untrue allegations.

Because there were three separate victims, the sentences should run consecutively. The court imposed three consecutive sentences of two years and four months — seven years in all — with the final two years suspended: five years to serve, the same effective term as before.

keys.q: malicious, spurious and untrue allegations
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on the letters

later: Hutchinson illustrates the Court of Appeal's approach to harassment sentencing: where the offending sits in the range, aggravation where public servants and their families are targeted, and consecutive sentences for separate victims.
It also shows why the statutory maximum that applied when the offence was committed must be put correctly to the sentencing court.
job: Charge a separate count of harassment for each person targeted — separate victims can attract consecutive sentences.
Record the impact on each victim and their family, and how the letters or messages reached them (keep the originals, envelopes and any forensic results).
Check, and give the prosecutor, the maximum penalty that applied when the offence was committed — mistakes about it can unravel the sentence.
DPP v Hutchinson.law: Yes. A recent Court of Appeal decision on s.10 sentencing.

bg: In December 2004 an evening newspaper published articles about a man who had just appeared in the District Court charged with murder.

The DPP brought criminal contempt proceedings in the High Court against the publisher, the editor and a journalist, seeking attachment and committal (or sequestration of the company's assets) and an injunction against further publication.

In May 2005 the High Court gave the respondents a direction and refused the application. Applying the criminal standard, the judge found only a remote possibility, not a real risk, of prejudice to the trial, though she criticised parts of the articles. The DPP appealed; the respondents said no appeal lay against what was in effect an acquittal.
DPP v Independent Newspapers (Ireland) L.q: Can the DPP appeal the refusal of a contempt application — and was the High Court right to stop the case?
dec: Supreme Court, 5 March 2008 ([2008] IESC 8, Fennelly J, on a preliminary issue): when dealing with an application for attachment and committal, the High Court is not sitting as the Central Criminal Court, so the statutory bar on appeals from that court didn't apply. The DPP could appeal.

Supreme Court, 5 March 2009 ([2009] IESC 20, Geoghegan and Hardiman JJ; Murray CJ, Fennelly and Finnegan JJ agreeing): appeal allowed and the High Court order set aside. An appeal lies against the refusal of a contempt motion, whether by direction or otherwise.
The judge should have decided whether there was at least a prima facie case. Given the nature of the publication, there was clearly an arguable case of criminal contempt.

The 'fade factor' — publicity fading from memory before trial — is relevant when deciding whether to stop a trial for prejudicial publicity. It is not relevant to whether a publication was a contempt, which is judged as at the time of publication.

Contempt is essentially criminal, though not run like a trial on indictment. In a serious case a High Court judge may sit with a jury, which decides disputed facts; whether a contempt is made out is for the judge. Because so much time had passed, no new hearing was ordered.

keys.q: The nature of the remedy is determinative.
keys.w: Fennelly J (2008), on whether an appeal lay

keys.q: must take care not to pollute the fountain of justice
keys.w: Hardiman J (2009), on editors and other influential people

keys.q: a jurisdiction essentially criminal
keys.w: Hardiman J (2009), quoting Palles CB on contempt

later: Hardiman J called the common law of contempt complex and in some respects archaic, and urged the Oireachtas to consider putting it on a statutory footing.

The Court of Appeal applied the 'real risk' test in DPP v Independent News and Media plc (2017): articles attacking an accused's character after charge were contempt, even though they didn't discuss the charges.

An earlier example involving the same publisher (High Court, January 2006): an evening paper printed CCTV stills of an assault the day after two men were charged. The stills had come from a security employee. The publisher admitted the breach, apologised and was fined €25,000.
job: Once a person is charged, route every media contact through the Garda Press Office. Give no background, character, previous convictions or evidence.
Keep CCTV, photographs and suspect details secure. Release them to the media only through the Press Office, and never after charge without legal advice — especially where identification is in issue.
If prejudicial coverage appears in a case you're investigating, preserve it (date, outlet, link, screenshots) and tell the prosecutor. Contempt proceedings are for the DPP.
DPP v Independent Newspapers (Ireland) L.law: Yes. A leading Supreme Court authority on criminal contempt by publication.

bg: In 2014 a national newspaper published articles and commentary about a man who, to its knowledge, had already been charged with fraud-related offences.

The articles didn't deal with the charges themselves. They portrayed him as dishonest and lacking moral judgment, and implicated others too. Similar material had been published by others before he was charged.

In April 2015 the High Court found the publishing company and three other respondents guilty of contempt and granted an injunction against further prejudicial publication. In June 2015 it fined two of them €50,000 each and a third €100. They appealed.
DPP v Independent News and Media plc.q: Can publicity that doesn't touch the charges still be contempt — and do earlier coverage or a jury direction answer the risk?
dec: Court of Appeal, December 2017 (Edwards J; Finlay Geoghegan J agreeing; Hogan J dissenting): appeal against conviction dismissed.
The test is whether the publication created a real risk to the fairness of the trial. 'Calculated to interfere' means likely to interfere; actual interference doesn't have to be proved.
Timing was crucial. These articles were published after charge and with knowledge of it. Earlier coverage, all before charge, didn't excuse them, and they added significantly to the existing risk.

That a jury could be told to ignore the material didn't answer whether contempt had been committed. The story could have been told factually without naming him and without the prejudicial commentary, so restricting it was a proportionate limit on free expression.
Hogan J dissented: the articles added little to a long line of earlier criticism, posed no real risk to the trial, and were constitutionally protected speech.

Court of Appeal, 30 July 2018 ([2018] IECA 301, Edwards J): the offending was of moderate gravity, sitting centrally in a €20,000 to €100,000 range. The €50,000 fines were excessive and were replaced with €25,000 each.

keys.q: would seem quite permissible and not open to any legal objection
keys.w: Court of Appeal (2018), on running such a story in ordinary journalism

keys.q: lifeblood of democracy
keys.w: Edwards J on freedom of expression, as reported in commentary

later: Commentators read the case as widening contempt: material needn't discuss the charges to be prejudicial — an attack on the accused's character after charge can be enough.

In July 2019 the High Court fined the same group €111,000 after an opinion piece suggesting a defendant was guilty collapsed a six-day rape trial in the Central Criminal Court. The judge called the paper's checking system 'wholly inadequate'.
job: After charge, say nothing to the media about the accused's character, background, previous convictions or the evidence. Refer every query to the Garda Press Office.
If prejudicial coverage appears before or during a trial, record it (date, outlet, link, screenshots) and tell the prosecutor at once. It can affect the trial date or the jury.
Remind witnesses, sensitively, that comment online or to the press while a case is pending can damage the trial.
DPP v Independent News and Media plc.law: Yes. The leading modern appellate test for contempt by publication.

bg: In March 2011 the accused, aged 19, killed his mother in Co Mayo in a frenzied knife attack. Afterwards he went barefoot and injured to a neighbour's house and gave a delusional account of what had happened.
He had used alcohol and drugs heavily since the age of 13, and in the week before the killing had hallucinations and paranoid delusions.

His offer to plead guilty to manslaughter wasn't accepted. At trial he relied on diminished responsibility and on intoxication. A psychiatrist said he was grossly intoxicated and psychotic, which would have affected his capacity to form the specific intent.
The jury rejected diminished responsibility and convicted him of murder. His first appeal failed, and he appealed to the Supreme Court.
DPP v Eadon.q: How must a jury be directed on voluntary intoxication in a murder trial — and can counsel's speeches cure a defective charge?
dec: Supreme Court, 20 December 2019 (McKechnie J; Charleton J concurring; unanimous five-judge court): the murder conviction was unsafe and was quashed.

The judge was wrong to tell the jury that intoxication is not a defence in law. Voluntary intoxication can be a partial defence to murder, reducing it to manslaughter; it is no answer to manslaughter itself. The charge left out that vitally important point.
The judge also put the question as whether the accused had the capacity to form the intent. The correct question is whether he in fact formed the intent to kill or cause serious injury.
Counsel's closing speeches had told the jury intoxication could be a defence to murder, but that couldn't cure the judge's misdirection: stating the law correctly is the judge's duty.
The DPP was left to decide whether to accept the earlier manslaughter plea or to seek a retrial for murder.

keys.q: speeches from counsel cannot supplant the trial judge's obligation to correctly state the law
keys.w: Supreme Court, as reported by RTÉ

keys.q: is part of the mix
keys.w: Trial judge on intoxication; Charleton J held this was wrong

later: The case confirms the test for intent in murder: what the accused actually intended at the time. Intoxication evidence is weighed against that, not against an abstract capacity.
Defence counsel's speeches don't fix gaps in the judge's charge, so prosecutors will ask for correct directions on intoxication — make sure the evidence on intoxication and on intent is complete.
job: Record intoxication precisely: signs observed, what was taken and when (from the suspect and witnesses), and get toxicology where you can.
Gather the evidence of actual intent: threats or statements beforehand, choice and carrying of a weapon, the nature and number of injuries, and conduct afterwards.
Interview only when the suspect is fit (get a doctor's view if in doubt), and put to him what he meant to do and why.
DPP v Eadon.law: Yes. The current Supreme Court authority on directing juries about intoxication and intent in murder.

src.t: Irish Times — Supreme Court overturns man's conviction for murder of his mother (20 December 2019)
RTÉ News — Supreme Court ruling in Co Mayo murder appeal (20 December 2019)

bg: In 2013 the accused stabbed his partner's son once in the abdomen during a confrontation outside a Dublin apartment. The young man died in hospital.

The accused said it was an accident. He admitted brandishing the knife. He left without seeking medical help, drove away and disposed of the weapon. Before trial he offered to plead guilty to manslaughter.
In 2016 a Central Criminal Court jury acquitted him of murder and convicted him of manslaughter, finding he hadn't intended to kill or cause serious injury. He was sentenced to seven years.

The Court of Appeal upheld the sentence in December 2017 as consistent with other knife manslaughter cases. The Supreme Court gave leave on the proper basis for sentencing for manslaughter after a murder trial.
DPP v Mahon.q: After a manslaughter verdict on a murder charge, what facts can the judge sentence on — and how serious is bringing a knife?
dec: Supreme Court, 11 April 2019 (Charleton J, for a unanimous court): appeal dismissed.

A judge shouldn't probe how a jury reached its verdict. Only rarely, where a verdict is ambiguous, may the judge ask a limited question about which version the jury accepted. That is a discretion, and declining to ask wasn't an error.
The sentencing judge should set out a clear narrative of the facts accepted, consistent with the verdict.
Manslaughter sentences run from life or very long terms down to, very exceptionally, a non-custodial sentence. This case sat in the medium band of four to ten years.

Unless faced with a deadly attack, or reasonable grounds to fear one, producing a knife is a serious aggravating factor; bringing a lethal weapon into an emotional situation is unjustifiable. The trial judge had treated the act as spontaneous and the knife as a means of intimidation — a lenient view — so seven years stood.

keys.q: there can never be an excuse for the production of a knife
keys.w: Charleton J, outside deadly-force self-defence

keys.q: spontaneous type action
keys.w: The trial judge's finding, as quoted by the Supreme Court

later: Charleton J also said that attacks by men on women should be regarded with particular seriousness.

After a murder trial, the judge's own findings of fact drive the manslaughter sentence. They must be consistent with the verdict and clearly stated, so the evidence about the weapon and the aftermath matters at sentence too.
job: Establish who brought the weapon, and how and when it was produced — witnesses, CCTV, 999 calls, scene evidence.
Record conduct after the incident: did the suspect call for help, flee, or get rid of the weapon? Search for and recover it.
Capture the build-up — the argument, threats and words used — because it bears on intent, verdict and sentence.
DPP v Mahon.law: Yes. Supreme Court guidance on sentencing manslaughter after a murder trial, and on knives.

bg: In 2011, near Ennis, Co Clare, the accused killed a man he had met briefly in a bar earlier that evening. He then rang Gardaí and said he had killed a man.
He believed he had removed a devil from the world. The central question at trial was whether he was truly delusional or exaggerating his symptoms.

He relied on diminished responsibility under s.6 of the Criminal Law (Insanity) Act 2006, which reduces murder to manslaughter where a mental disorder substantially diminished the accused's responsibility. The judge told the jury the defence had to prove it on the balance of probabilities.
He was convicted of murder in June 2013. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in 2015, holding that the accused bears the burden of persuasion, and the Supreme Court gave leave in February 2016.
People (DPP) v Heffernan.q: Must an accused prove diminished responsibility on the balance of probabilities — and does that breach the presumption of innocence?
dec: Supreme Court, 7 February 2017 (O'Malley J; Charleton J concurring): appeal dismissed and the murder conviction affirmed.

By requiring the defence to 'establish' diminished responsibility, the Oireachtas deliberately placed a burden on the accused beyond simply raising a reasonable doubt. The balance of probabilities direction was right.

That doesn't breach the presumption of innocence under Article 38.1 of the Constitution or Article 6(2) of the ECHR. The prosecution must still prove every element of murder beyond reasonable doubt; the accused isn't asked to disprove the act or the intent.
Diminished responsibility is a separate, mitigating defence: it reduces the consequences of an offence already proved.

Charleton J agreed: legislation may put a burden on the accused where the nature of the issue requires it, as long as it doesn't fundamentally and unnecessarily undermine the prosecution's duty to prove guilt.

keys.q: It creates a new, mitigatory defence that reduces the consequences of a proven offence.
keys.w: O'Malley J, on s.6

keys.q: does not fundamentally and unnecessarily undermine the duty of the prosecution
keys.w: Charleton J, on when a burden may be placed on the accused

keys.q: clear beyond peradventure
keys.w: Court of Appeal (2015), on the burden resting on the accused

later: The same approach applies to the insanity defence, where the accused also proves the defence on the balance of probabilities.
A later Supreme Court decision cites it when describing the presumption of innocence as a bedrock principle of the criminal justice system.
job: Record everything the suspect says and does from first contact — calls to Gardaí, words at the scene, demeanour — verbatim and timed.
With proper authority, gather history from family, doctors and others about mental health, drink and drugs before the incident. The prosecution's psychiatrist will need it.
Make sure the custody record notes fitness for interview and any medical assessment. It will be examined if diminished responsibility is raised.
People (DPP) v Heffernan.law: Yes. The settled position on who proves diminished responsibility, and to what standard.

bg: In March 1997 two women were killed in sheltered accommodation at a Dublin psychiatric hospital.

Another man confessed and was charged, but the charges were later withdrawn. In August 1997 the applicant, arrested on other matters, also made admissions about the killings. Both men retracted, and no one was prosecuted at the time. A later inquiry criticised Garda handling of the confessions.
Clothing had been retained. In 2009 new DNA testing found the victims' DNA on the applicant's clothing, and he was charged in October 2009 — about 13 years after the killings.

He sought judicial review to prohibit the trial, relying on culpable delay, prejudicial publicity, the death or unavailability of witnesses and evidence, the other man's confession, and late-disclosed DNA evidence with contamination concerns. The High Court (Moriarty J) refused.
Nash v DPP.q: Should a trial be stopped because of long delay, publicity, lost witnesses and disputed DNA — or should the trial judge deal with them?
dec: Supreme Court: appeal dismissed on 10 December 2014, with reasons on 29 January 2015 (Clarke J giving the lead judgment; Hardiman and Charleton JJ also giving judgments; Denham CJ and O'Donnell J sitting).
A breach of the constitutional right to a timely trial doesn't, by itself, mean there can be no trial. The Constitution places a strong value on criminal charges being determined on the merits.
To prohibit a trial a serious factor must exist that clearly outweighs the public interest in a trial. None did here.
The trial judge's role in securing a fair trial is paramount. Publicity, missing evidence and the forensic issues, including contamination, were best explored at the trial itself.

The trial went ahead. He was convicted of both murders in April 2015. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in May 2018, holding that the scientific evidence didn't conclusively prove or disprove contamination and was properly left to the jury. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in October 2018.

keys.q: to be determined on the merits
keys.w: Supreme Court (2015), on the constitutional value of a trial

keys.q: a serious factor would have to exist
keys.w: Supreme Court (2015), on what's needed to stop a trial

keys.q: did not conclusively prove or disprove contamination
keys.w: Court of Appeal (2018), on the DNA evidence

later: His separate claim for damages for breach of his right to a timely trial was dismissed by the Supreme Court. In 2017 the Court corrected some facts in that judgment about the retention and testing of forensic items, but the outcome stood.
The case reflects the modern approach: prohibition is exceptional, and delay or gaps in the evidence are usually managed by the trial judge.
job: Package, seal, label and log exhibits so they can be retested years later. Record every movement and every examination — contamination arguments turn on the chain.
Test any confession. Is the suspect vulnerable? Does the account include details only the offender would know, and do they check out? Record the interview in full.
In cold cases, review retained exhibits for new forensic techniques, and record what was tested, when and why.
Nash v DPP.law: Yes. A leading Supreme Court authority on prohibition for delay.

bg: On 25 April 2016 two masked men entered a licensed premises in Dublin 1 and shot a man dead. The killing was linked to a gangland feud.
A car was later found partly burnt after an apparent attempt to set it alight. It contained firearms, masks and other items. The accused's DNA was found on a baseball cap and a mask from the car.

Ballistics evidence showed one of the pistols from the car fired the fatal shots. The day after the shooting the accused tried to fly to Bangkok, then got an emergency passport to travel the following day.

The prosecution case was entirely circumstantial. In January 2018, after a 21-day trial, the Special Criminal Court convicted him of murder. He received the mandatory life sentence and appealed on 28 grounds.
People (DPP) v Cumberton.q: Was a wholly circumstantial case — DNA, ballistics and flight — properly assessed, and is the verdict safe?
dec: Court of Appeal, 19 May 2020 (Edwards J, with McCarthy and Kennedy JJ): appeal dismissed.

Four grounds were dropped and none of the rest succeeded. Many concerned how the court of trial dealt with the circumstantial evidence; others included the fairness of a non-jury trial, access to certain items for examination, and the weight placed on supporting evidence.
The court used the appeal to restate the Irish approach to circumstantial evidence and to clarify how it applies in practice.
It was completely satisfied that the trial was satisfactory and the guilty verdict safe.

keys.q: completely satisfied that his trial was satisfactory
keys.w: Court of Appeal, as reported by Newstalk

keys.q: the guilty verdict is safe
keys.w: Court of Appeal, as reported by Newstalk

later: Later judgments cite Cumberton on circumstantial evidence; one notes a ground about the disputed admission of DNA evidence.
It was the first murder conviction linked to the feud.
job: Treat an abandoned or burnt-out vehicle as a major scene. Preserve it, recover everything, and send headwear, masks and gloves for DNA.
Get recovered firearms to ballistics quickly, to link them to — or exclude them from — scenes.
Check travel bookings, airport movements and passport applications soon after a serious crime. An attempt to leave can be evidence.
People (DPP) v Cumberton.law: Yes. Recent Court of Appeal authority on circumstantial cases.

bg: In March 1996 the accused's husband was killed at their pub in Co Wicklow.
She was charged with his murder and with soliciting three different men, in 1989 and 1990, to kill him. Her application for separate trials of the murder and soliciting counts was refused.

In April 2000 a Central Criminal Court jury (Carroll J presiding) convicted her on all counts. She was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, plus seven years in total for soliciting. The murder case was circumstantial.
People (DPP) v Nevin.q: Was the trial fair — given the publicity, the joint trial of the murder and soliciting counts, and a circumstantial case?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 14 March 2003 (Geoghegan, Quirke and Peart JJ): appeal dismissed on every ground, in a 60-page judgment.

The grounds were adverse publicity, the refusal of separate trials for the murder and soliciting counts, the nature of the circumstantial evidence, and the trial judge's alleged failure to analyse it properly for the jury.
The court held she had received an exceptionally fair trial in very difficult circumstances, impeccably conducted by the trial judge. It later refused to certify a point of law for the Supreme Court.
Court of Criminal Appeal, 22 November 2010 (Hardiman J, with McKechnie and Birmingham JJ): her application claiming that newly discovered facts showed a miscarriage of justice was dismissed.

The new material went only to the credibility of prosecution witnesses — a collateral issue. Garda files, which the court inspected, gave no real support to claims that witnesses were informers, and other material was too remote or vague. None of the men had been presented as of good character, and it was intrinsically unlikely that someone looking for an assassin would approach a person of known good character.

keys.q: an exceptionally fair trial in very difficult circumstances
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (2003)

keys.q: impeccably conducted
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (2003), on the trial judge

keys.q: intrinsically unlikely that someone seeking to employ an assassin
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (2010), on the witnesses' character

later: The 2010 decision restates the collateral-issue rule: questions that go only to a witness's credibility are limited and the answer is generally final, so trials aren't swamped by side issues.
To ground a miscarriage-of-justice claim, newly discovered facts must be significant; remote or vague material won't do.
job: In a circumstantial case, evidence that the suspect tried to recruit others can be central. Trace and take statements from anyone approached, however long ago.
Keep intelligence and informant records accurate and properly recorded — courts may inspect Garda files years later when disclosure is challenged.
Record the relationship history, finances and motive evidence fully, and give the prosecutor anything bearing on a witness's credibility.
People (DPP) v Nevin.law: Yes. The conviction stands; the 2010 ruling is useful on collateral issues and 'new facts'.
