bg: As part of Operation Amethyst, Gardaí obtained a warrant to search the home of a serving Circuit Court judge in Tralee.
The warrant was valid for seven days. Gardaí searched the house on 27 May 2002 — the eighth day, one day after the warrant expired — and seized a computer, discs, storage devices and other material.
He was charged with possession of child pornography and pleaded not guilty. At the trial in April 2004 the validity of the warrant was argued in the absence of the jury.
DPP v Curtin.q: Can evidence seized under a warrant executed after it expired be used at trial?
dec: Circuit Criminal Court, 23 April 2004 (Judge Carroll Moran): the warrant had expired before the search, so it gave no authority to enter and search.

Following the Supreme Court's approach, time limits on warrants must be strictly observed. Evidence obtained outside them could be admitted only in accidental or unintentional cases or in extraordinary circumstances, and the prosecution accepted that none applied.
The evidence from the search was excluded. With nothing left to go to the jury, the judge directed a not guilty verdict.

In a seven-page written judgment he called the prosecution's arguments on the warrant 'untenable and nonsensical', said the law was crystal clear, and said the prosecution knew or ought to have known that any court would exclude the evidence. He refused the accused's application for costs.

keys.q: I can't do anything about it. The gardaí were out of time
keys.w: Judge Carroll Moran, as reported by the Irish Examiner

keys.q: untenable and nonsensical
keys.w: Judge Carroll Moran, on the prosecution's arguments about the warrant

keys.q: the law was crystal clear
keys.w: Judge Carroll Moran, as reported by RTÉ

later: The collapse led to sharp public criticism of the investigation and prosecution and was discussed at Cabinet. Garda management said it would examine what the ruling meant for operations.
The Oireachtas then began a process to consider his removal from office. His High Court challenge to it failed in May 2005, and he appealed to the Supreme Court.
The exclusionary rule has since changed (People (DPP) v JC, 2015), but an expired warrant still confers no power to enter a home.
job: Before executing, read the warrant: issue date, validity period, premises and offence. Count the days.
If you can't execute it in time, apply for a fresh warrant — never stretch an old one.
Record the date and time of entry in your notebook and the search record, and show the warrant to the occupier.
DPP v Curtin.law: Yes on the rule: execute a warrant within its validity period. The test for excluding evidence has changed since (JC, 2015).

bg: On 19 May 1997 a man was seen dumping sacks of cannabis in a ditch near Drogheda. Shortly afterwards the accused drove to the spot and Gardaí arrested him.
About six kilos of cannabis were recovered. After his arrest Gardaí found £27,920 in sterling and Irish currency at his home.
He was tried at Dundalk Circuit Criminal Court for possessing the cannabis for supply to others. He didn't give evidence. He was convicted and, on 11 May 1999, sentenced to five and a half years.
DPP v Coddington.q: Can a trial judge refer to an accused's decision not to give evidence — such as not explaining cash — without warning the jury against drawing an inference?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 31 May 2001 (Murray J, with Johnson and Kelly JJ): appeal allowed.
The trial judge had referred to the accused not giving evidence, including in relation to his failure to provide an innocent explanation for the £27,920.
This was done without any direction that no inference should be drawn from his silence. The comments were therefore improper.
The conviction and sentence were quashed and a retrial was ordered.

keys.q: failure to provide an innocent explanation for the presence of £27,920
keys.w: Irish Times report of what the trial judge referred to

keys.q: This was done without any direction by the trial judge
keys.w: Irish Times report of the Court of Criminal Appeal ruling

later: The principle is long-standing: an accused can't be compelled to give evidence, and the prosecution may not comment on a failure to do so.

Inferences from silence are now available only under specific statutory provisions — mainly in Garda interview, after a warning in ordinary language and a chance to consult a solicitor — not from silence at trial.
job: If cash, property or other items found need explaining, put them to the suspect in interview and record the answer.
Where a statutory inference provision applies, give the warning in ordinary language, explain the consequences, and make sure a solicitor was available. Record it all on video and in your notes.
Build the case so it doesn't depend on the accused explaining anything: seizure records, money counts, forensic links and surveillance.
DPP v Coddington.law: Yes. Silence at trial isn't evidence of guilt; inferences need a statutory basis and proper warnings.

bg: A journalist was shot dead in June 1996. The accused was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 at about 3.30 p.m. on 16 October 1996 and taken to Lucan Garda Station, the centre of the investigation. He had been detained under s.30 before.
He saw a solicitor, who advised him of his right to silence, and he said nothing over five interviews totalling about 14½ hours.

His partner and his mother, both themselves in Garda custody at the time, were then brought to see him: his partner for about 10 minutes at 10.25 p.m. on 17 October, and his mother for 16 minutes the next afternoon. Gardaí said he made a verbal admission after each visit.
He was tried for murder in the Special Criminal Court. Apart from the admissions, the main evidence came from an accomplice who had become a State witness.
People (DPP) v Ward.q: Are admissions made after the gardaí arranged visits from a suspect's family during detention admissible? And can a conviction rest on an accomplice's evidence?
dec: Special Criminal Court, 27 November 1998 (Barr J, with Smyth and Ballagh JJ).

The Court found the visits were orchestrated meetings set up by the gardaí. During the trial Barr J had said the prosecution must show a good reason for bringing the two women to see him, and he noted that an admission came directly after each visit.
The Court was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that any admissions, if they were made at all, were the product of unfair pressure created by those meetings. It excluded them.

It still convicted him of murder, as an accessory before the fact, on the State witness's evidence. It treated that evidence with great caution because of the witness's character, but found the witness had no reason to implicate him falsely. He was sentenced to life imprisonment.

Court of Criminal Appeal, 22 March 2002 (Murphy J, with Ó Caoimh and McKechnie JJ): the conviction was quashed. The case rested almost entirely on a State witness who had lied repeatedly, and the evidence didn't show that the accused took part in planning the crime. An accomplice's evidence needs independent corroboration, or at the very least a clear warning about the danger of convicting without it.

keys.q: orchestrated meetings set up by the Gardai
keys.w: Special Criminal Court, on the family visits

keys.q: good, valid, acceptable reason
keys.w: Barr J during the trial, on what the prosecution had to show for the visits

later: Still cited on unfair pressure in custody: using a suspect's family to break their silence makes any admission unsafe, whatever the visit is called.
The 2002 appeal is a standard warning about convictions that rest on an accomplice. Read with Gilligan (2006) on State witnesses in the Witness Security Programme.
job: Never arrange or encourage a family visit to get a suspect talking. A visit should come at the wish of the detainee or the family, be allowed by the member in charge, be supervised, and be recorded accurately in the custody record.
If a suspect is using the right to silence, respect it. Pressure through family, emotion or fatigue makes any later admission vulnerable.
Record any admission at the time, in full, and offer it to the suspect to read and sign. Here the court doubted whether the verbal admissions had been made at all.
A case built on an accomplice needs independent corroboration. Look for it from the start: phone records, CCTV, forensics, money.
People (DPP) v Ward.law: Yes. Ward is still cited on unfair pressure in custody (1998) and on the dangers of accomplice evidence (2002).

bg: On 19 May 2010 gardaí in Clondalkin saw two men counting money in a car and suspected a drugs deal. One consented to a s.23 search, and nothing was found on him. €3,200 was found on the other.

Later the same car was stopped again. Nothing was found in it at the roadside, but more cash was found on the passenger. The car was taken to Clondalkin Garda Station, and the appellant was handcuffed, logged as a prisoner and held in a cell for about 40 minutes while the car was searched in detail. About 56 g of heroin was found behind the radio.

He was then released from s.23 detention, arrested under s.25 and admitted owning the drugs. He was convicted of possession, and appealed on the basis that the s.23 'detention' was really an unlawful arrest.
DPP v O'Brien (2018).q: Is detaining someone at a station while their car is searched under s.23 an unlawful arrest, so that the evidence must be excluded?
dec: Court of Appeal, 11 June 2018 (Mahon J): all grounds failed and the appeal was dismissed.

The trial judge was right to treat detention for the purpose of a s.23 search as legally distinct from an arrest. Even though the appellant was handcuffed, logged and held in a cell while the car was searched, this was not an unlawful arrest, and the evidence was admissible.
Once the search found the drugs, he was released from the s.23 detention and properly arrested under s.25 before being questioned.
later: Contrast DPP (O'Higgins) v Farrell [2009] IEHC 368: a s.23 search needs suspicion about the individual. Here the suspicion was specific (counting cash in a car, then cash found on the passenger).
job: Under s.23 you may detain a person, and a vehicle, for as long as is reasonably necessary to carry out the search, including bringing them to a station if that's needed.
Keep s.23 detention and arrest separate. When the search ends, release the person from s.23 detention, then arrest them under the proper power if there are grounds, and say so clearly.
Record your grounds of suspicion, why the search had to move to the station, the times, and every step.
DPP v O'Brien (2018).law: Yes. O'Brien (2018) is current Court of Appeal authority that s.23 detention for a search is distinct from arrest.

bg: In 1997 a special Garda unit (Operation Pineapple) was investigating money laundering and drug trafficking. It wanted files held by a Dublin firm of solicitors on property transactions linked to two clients under investigation.

Rather than seek a production order, Gardaí obtained a search warrant under s.64 of the Criminal Justice Act 1994 from a District Judge, fearing the clients would learn of the investigation and the documents would be lost.
Before the search, anonymous calls were made to the media. When Gardaí arrived, journalists were already outside the offices.
The firm sought to quash the warrant and sued the District Judge, the Garda Commissioner and the State for damages.
Hanahoe v Hussey.q: Was the warrant valid — and if it was, is the State liable for leaking the search to the media?
dec: High Court, 14 November 1997 (Kinlen J): the warrant was properly issued, so the challenge to it failed.
The leak was a deliberate, wilful act intended to embarrass and distress the firm. As a matter of probability, it came from Gardaí.
It was an outrageous interference with the firm's privacy and constitutional rights, and caused considerable and probably irreparable harm to its practice.
The firm was awarded £100,000 damages.
The judge criticised the attitude of the Commissioner and Gardaí to investigating the leak, which he said could amount to a criminal offence.

keys.w: Kinlen J, on the leak

keys.q: wilful act
keys.w: Kinlen J, describing the leak

keys.q: properly issued
keys.w: Headnote, on the s.64 warrant

later: A lawful operation can still give rise to liability if information about it is leaked: the validity of the warrant didn't protect the State from damages.

The case sits alongside the contempt cases in this app (DPP v Independent Newspapers; DPP v Independent News and Media) — all point the same way: operational and case information stays inside official channels.
job: Treat search and arrest plans as confidential. Share them only with those who need to know.
Never contact the media about an operation. Media queries go to the Garda Press Office, and only with authority.
If you suspect a leak, report it at once. Unauthorised disclosure of Garda information can be a criminal offence.
Hanahoe v Hussey.law: Yes. A leak of operational information can breach constitutional rights and lead to damages.

bg: The plaintiff ran a nightclub in Inishowen, Co Donegal.

Two Gardaí, a Superintendent and a Detective Garda, conspired to concoct false evidence that he allowed drugs to be sold on the premises. Perjured Garda evidence was given at his trial, and in 1995 a jury convicted him. He served 27 months in prison.

The conviction was later quashed with the DPP's consent, and the Court of Criminal Appeal certified a miscarriage of justice, based on newly discovered facts: the deliberate suppression of material by the two officers.
He sued the Garda Commissioner and the State. In 2005 the High Court awarded €1,923,871, refusing aggravated damages as double compensation and reducing exemplary damages. He appealed.
Shortt v Commissioner of An Garda Síochá.q: What damages should be paid when Gardaí fabricate evidence that leads to a wrongful conviction?
dec: Supreme Court, 21 March 2007 (Murray CJ, for a unanimous court with Denham, Hardiman, Geoghegan and Fennelly JJ): appeal allowed in part.

The two officers had conspired to concoct false evidence, and perjured evidence was given at trial. This was the gravest dereliction of duty and abuse of power, very damaging to the reputation of the Garda Síochána — though not to be taken as reflecting on the force as a whole.
General damages should far exceed the High Court's award. The Court made one global compensatory award, covering ordinary and aggravated damages and future loss, of €2,250,000.
Exemplary damages are not compensation: they mark the Court's disapproval and signal that such abuse of State power won't be tolerated. The Court awarded €1,000,000 under this heading.
The appeal on special damages failed. The total award became €4,623,871.

keys.q: the gravest dereliction of duty and abuse of power
keys.w: Murray CJ, on the officers' conduct

keys.q: They both engaged in a conspiracy to concoct false evidence against the plaintiff
keys.w: Murray CJ

keys.q: a stain of the darkest dye
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the misconduct

later: Murray CJ questioned whether there had been complacency within the Garda about standards of integrity.
The €1 million exemplary award was described at the time as unprecedented.
job: Record evidence truthfully and fully in your notebook at the time. Never alter or 'tidy up' notes afterwards.
Give the prosecutor everything relevant, including material that helps the defence.
If you know or suspect that a colleague has fabricated or suppressed evidence, report it. Protected disclosure routes exist.
Shortt v Commissioner of An Garda Síochá.law: Yes. The leading authority on exemplary damages for Garda misconduct.

bg: Customs officers suspected that shops in Dublin, Cork and Limerick were selling imported indecent or obscene material, which counts as prohibited goods.

District Judges issued warrants under s.205 of the Customs Consolidation Act 1876 (for the goods) and s.5(1) of the Customs and Excise (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1988 (for documents). Officers seized magazines, videos, discs and documents.

The warrants were standard forms with handwritten blanks. They recited that the officer 'hath cause to suspect and doth suspect' — not that the officer had reasonable cause to suspect, or that the judge was satisfied of that on sworn information.
The companies sought certiorari, return of the goods and damages for trespass. The High Court (Shanley J) refused in June 1998, and they appealed.
Simple Imports Ltd v Revenue Commissione.q: Is a search warrant valid if it doesn't show on its face that the statutory condition — reasonable suspicion — was met?
dec: Supreme Court, 19 January 2000 (Keane J, Barrington J agreeing; Barron J dissenting): appeal allowed.
Because search warrants authorise the forcible invasion of a person's property, the courts must ensure the conditions laid down by the legislature are strictly met.
The legislation required the District Judge to be satisfied, on sworn information, that the officer's suspicion was reasonable. It wasn't enough that the officers considered they had cause to apply.
Warrants that show on their face they were issued on a basis the statute doesn't authorise are invalid and must be quashed. The warrants were quashed and the seized goods ordered returned.
Barron J dissented: in his view no error appeared on the face of the warrants, so certiorari shouldn't issue.

keys.q: invalid and must be quashed
keys.w: Keane J, on warrants showing an unauthorised basis on their face

keys.q: hath cause to suspect and doth suspect
keys.w: The wording on the warrants

later: The case is part of a line insisting that warrants comply strictly with their statute. See also Damache v DPP (2012), on who may issue a warrant, and People (DPP) v Quirke (No 2) (2023), on searching devices — both in this app.
Whether evidence from a defective warrant is excluded at a criminal trial is now decided under People (DPP) v JC (2015).
job: Swear the information yourself, setting out the facts that ground your suspicion — not just your belief.
Before executing, check the warrant against the statute: right Act and section, right test (reasonable grounds), right premises and items, signed and dated by the right issuer.
Don't rely on old or generic forms. If the wording doesn't match the current statute, get it fixed before you go.
Simple Imports Ltd v Revenue Commissione.law: Yes. Warrants must show the statutory conditions were met; a defect on the face can be fatal.

Irish Times — Pornography search warrants ruled invalid (20 January 2000)

bg: Gardaí searched a duplex apartment in Dublin under a warrant and found the accused there with two others.

The kitchen-living area appeared to be used to make cannabis-infused jelly sweets: moulds, syringes, food colouring, a pot of green gelatinous substance, clear bags of dried cannabis and secateurs. Separate areas were set up to grow cannabis, with heating and lighting.
The accused's bank card and passport were found in the room. He faced ten charges — five linked to the kitchen-living area and five to the grow areas.

On his application under s.4E of the Criminal Procedure Act 1967 the Circuit Court dismissed the five grow-area charges. The Court of Appeal restored them ([2024] IECA 252), and the Supreme Court gave leave in February 2025.
DPP v DT.q: Can possession of drugs found in a premises be inferred from the circumstances — and can silence-based inferences be used at a s.4E dismissal application?
dec: Supreme Court, 4 June 2025 (Charleton J, with Dunne, O'Malley, Murray and Donnelly JJ): appeal dismissed. All ten charges go to trial. The Court made no findings of fact.
Possession has no single definition across the criminal law. It involves control and knowledge, and is often proved by inference from the facts and circumstances.

Kitchen-living area: his presence, the production apparatus, the dried cannabis, his personal effects, phone and passport, and the lack of any account of why he was there gave a rational prospect of conviction.

Grow areas: the same factors, plus a possible common design to possess and cultivate — the secateurs, the apparent chain from live plant to dried cannabis to infused sweets, and the heating and lighting equipment.

Inferences under ss.18 and 19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 can be taken into account if the statutory procedure was followed. But using an inference to prove possession itself risks circularity, and could undermine the prosecution's duty to prove the core of its case.
None of this means a jury will be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt. Whether possession is proved is a matter for the jury's shrewd, common-sense assessment.

keys.q: possession is not given a central definition
keys.w: Charleton J

keys.q: a matter for shrewd assessment by them
keys.w: Charleton J, on the jury's role

later: Commentators read DT as a general framework for possession cases: inferences can support the case but cannot fill an evidential vacuum, and must rest on facts proved independently.
The same reasoning may carry over to other possession offences, such as firearms.
job: Photograph every item where it lies before moving it, and record exactly where each was found. Link the suspect to the room: documents, phone, keys, clothes, bedding, fingerprints and DNA.
Put specific facts to the suspect under ss.18/19 — presence in the premises, particular objects, marks — with the warning in ordinary language and access to a solicitor.
Gather evidence of the operation as a whole (equipment, supplies, utilities, CCTV of comings and goings) to show a common design.

bg: In June 2018 a man was killed in an unprovoked stabbing in Tallaght, Dublin.
Gardaí gathered CCTV from private homes, local businesses, a Dublin bus, and public places including footpaths, roads, a public park and a shopping centre.

The accused, who was 17 at the time, was convicted of murder by a jury. At trial and on appeal he argued that using the CCTV breached his rights under the Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights, the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and data protection law.
DPP v Dunbar.q: Does using CCTV from public places and private cameras to investigate a crime breach privacy or data protection rights?
dec: Court of Appeal, 30 January 2024 (Edwards J giving judgment): all grounds dismissed.

Processing footage like this is lawful where it is necessary and proportionate for preventing, detecting, investigating or prosecuting criminal offences. Data protection rights are subject to such restrictions.

A person in a public place would not realistically have a reasonable expectation of privacy, and the presence of CCTV there is widely known. The private cameras served purposes including protecting premises, deterring crime and helping catch offenders.

Some footage gathered turned out to be irrelevant, but that was apparent only in hindsight. Gardaí, often under time pressure early in an investigation, must be given a significant margin of appreciation.

CCTV can advance an investigation, identify suspects, assist at trial — and exonerate. Failing to access potentially relevant footage could be a grave dereliction of duty. The admissibility challenge was misconceived, and such arguments shouldn't take up valuable court time.

keys.q: A significant margin of appreciation must be afforded to gardaí
keys.w: Edwards J

later: DPP v Thompson (2024), in this app, was decided the same day and also rejected a CCTV privacy argument: no one in public can expect to be immune from CCTV observation.
Read with the CCTV preservation cases in this app (Braddish v DPP, Dunne v DPP, Murphy v DPP): Gardaí must seek out and keep relevant footage, and collecting it lawfully is not a privacy breach.
job: Canvass for CCTV early — homes, businesses, transport, public cameras — and ask owners to retain footage before it's overwritten.
Record each source: location, owner, why it was sought, time window, how and when it was downloaded, and continuity (use the CCTV continuity statement).
Keep collection proportionate and store footage securely. Note at the time why footage that later proves irrelevant was taken.

bg: The accused was tried in Kerry Circuit Criminal Court on one count of sexual assault.

Before trial, his new legal team sought wide disclosure, including any counselling records. A rape crisis centre told Gardaí it held no counselling records for the complainant. She was then asked to sign consents to disclosure without first seeing any material, and she signed them.

He was convicted and sentenced to two years and nine months. After the trial it emerged that she had attended counselling sessions at the centre, and the records were disclosed to the defence in January 2022. A record of the first session suggested the abuse had happened more than once, which differed from her evidence at trial.

The Court of Appeal ordered a statement from her under s.3(3)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993; she maintained there had been one incident. It dismissed the appeal in May 2023, and the Supreme Court gave leave in February 2024.
DPP v AM.q: When must counselling records be disclosed to the defence — and what makes a complainant's consent to disclosure valid?
dec: Supreme Court, 2 May 2025 ([2025] IESC 16, Collins J giving judgment): appeal dismissed.

Counselling records attract a high level of constitutional protection. Under s.19A of the Criminal Evidence Act 1992, some compelling basis must be established before disclosure is directed: the records must be likely to be of real forensic value to the defence.

Materiality is not a bare or merely theoretical possibility; a reasonable possibility of material impact must be shown. The s.19A regime gives the defence no entitlement to surprise a complainant in cross-examination with counselling records.
A complainant's consent must be fully informed. She should see the records and have the chance to get advice before consenting — consent should be the final step.
The Court of Appeal was entitled to obtain her statement under s.3(3)(a) rather than order a retrial; the argument for a retrial was entirely fanciful.

keys.q: some compelling basis must be established for disclosure to be directed
keys.w: Collins J

keys.q: not one of bare or merely theoretical possibility
keys.w: Collins J, on materiality

keys.q: entirely fanciful
keys.w: Collins J, on the argument for a retrial

later: In DPP v WC [2024] IESC 48 (October 2024) the Supreme Court held that material seriously intruding on private life isn't generally disclosable unless directly material to an issue in the case, and that the right to silence doesn't let the defence keep its case opaque; the trial judge decides disputes. The DPP welcomed WC in March 2025 as rejecting disclosure of counselling notes merely because they're remotely or potentially relevant.

In November 2025 the DPP described WC and AM as a cultural shift: prosecutors should engage with the defence early rather than disclose everything out of caution. After AM, the ODPP and An Garda Síochána changed practice so complainants can get legal advice before agreeing to waive a disclosure hearing.

In February 2026 Cabinet approved amendments to the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026: a presumption of non-disclosure for counselling notes (a form of statutory privilege), with disclosure only where a judge orders it in the interests of justice, and mandatory pre-trial disclosure hearings in sexual offence trials. Check whether it has been enacted.
job: Never ask a complainant to sign a blanket consent to disclosure. Explain what is sought and why, let her see the records, give her time to get advice, and record each step.
When asking a service whether it holds records, be specific (name, dates, type of service) and record the answer — a wrong 'no records' reply can unsettle a conviction.
Treat counselling records as highly protected: flag them to the prosecutor and let the s.19A process decide disclosure.
Before a complainant decides whether to waive a disclosure hearing, make sure they know they can get legal advice first, and record that you told them.
DPP v AM.law: Yes. The leading Supreme Court decision (May 2025) on disclosing counselling records — watch for the 2026 statutory presumption of non-disclosure.

bg: In 2013 a man was shot dead in the car park of a pub in Co Meath.

The day after the shooting the accused met others at a fast-food restaurant in Dublin. Gardaí had placed a listening device and covertly recorded the conversation, which included remarks about the heavy Garda presence at the scene and about being followed.
A detective superintendent approved the surveillance himself under the urgency provisions of the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009, rather than applying to a District Judge.

The Special Criminal Court convicted the accused of murder in February 2019. The evidence included the recording and the evidence of a co-accused who became a State witness. He appealed on 51 grounds, several later abandoned.
DPP v Braney (2026).q: Was the urgent surveillance approval lawful — and was the rest of the trial fair?
dec: Court of Appeal, June 2026 (Kennedy J, with O'Moore and MacGrath JJ): appeal dismissed.

The defence argued that a District Court was sitting nearby, so there was no need to bypass a judge. The superintendent said he considered going to court but feared losing the chance to place the devices before the meeting. The trial court found he believed he faced an emergency — a finding of fact the appeal court called impossible to upset.
Working from transcripts, the court agreed that key passages of the recording were audible and intelligible.
The co-accused's evidence contained inconsistencies and admitted lies, but not enough to make the conviction unsafe; no error in principle or law was shown.

Privilege over the identities of eight National Surveillance Unit officers was upheld: anonymity was needed for the unit's work, and the claim that it hampered cross-examination was entirely speculative. Grounds on new evidence, perversity and a directed acquittal also failed.

keys.q: impossible to upset
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on the finding about the superintendent's belief

keys.q: no error in principle or law has been demonstrated
keys.w: Kennedy J

keys.q: entirely speculative
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on the officers' anonymity argument

later: The ruling runs to almost 200 pages — a sign of how heavily covert evidence is litigated.
The urgency route lets a senior officer approve surveillance without a judge for a short period where delay would likely lose the evidence. The reasons for using it are what the courts examine.
job: If urgent approval is needed, the approving officer should record at the time why going to a judge would risk losing the evidence — the specific meeting, timing and opportunity.
Follow the Act's steps after urgent approval: time limits, reports, and a judge's authorisation if surveillance is to continue.
Check and document the quality of covert recordings early, and prepare transcripts carefully — intelligibility will be challenged.
DPP v Braney (2026).law: Yes. Recent Court of Appeal authority (June 2026).

bg: On 7 and 8 August 2015 an IRA-organised 'inquiry' questioned suspected informants at a house in Castleknock, west Dublin.
Under a District Court authorisation granted ex parte under s.5 of the Criminal Justice (Surveillance) Act 2009, the Garda National Surveillance Unit had placed listening devices in the house.

The recordings were saved from live microphone feeds, copied to a hard drive and CDs and given to the Special Detective Unit. Investigators shared them, transcripts were made, and copies went to commercial firms to improve their presentation. They were disclosed to the defence and played in court.

In June 2018 the Special Criminal Court convicted three people of IRA membership and two of assisting the IRA's interviews. The defence argued that s.10 allowed access to surveillance material only by people the Minister authorised, that no regulations had been made, and that the evidence should be excluded under People (DPP) v JC. The Special Criminal Court and the Court of Appeal found a s.10 breach but admitted the evidence, because the exclusionary rule concerns how evidence is gathered, not how it is handled afterwards.
DPP v Hannaway.q: Does handling surveillance recordings without ministerial authorisation under s.10 make them inadmissible?
dec: Supreme Court, 4 May 2021 (O'Malley J; Charleton J concurring): appeals dismissed and the evidence held admissible.

Reading the Act as a whole, s.10 doesn't give the Minister exclusive power to authorise access to surveillance material for investigation or trial. Read with s.13, 'otherwise authorised by law' covers lawyers and investigators working for the DPP or the Garda Commissioner.

Section 10 is mainly about the secure storage of old material and has no relevance to the investigation and trial of offences. There was no relevant breach — on that point the Court of Appeal was wrong.

A JC inquiry isn't appropriate where a statutory breach after collection hasn't affected the evidence's integrity or probative value; a court should first ask whether the breach is serious enough to justify exclusion. Handling that breached an accused's rights so seriously that the State shouldn't benefit could still lead to exclusion.
Charleton J added that the authorities draw no clear line between obtaining and processing evidence; where there is illegality a balance must be struck, and the position of victims may be considered.

keys.q: section 10 has no relevance to the processes of investigation and trial of offences
keys.w: O'Malley J, as reported

keys.q: the legal authorities do not provide for any distinction
keys.w: Charleton J, on obtaining versus processing evidence

later: O'Malley J suggested the Minister could still make rules limiting access by rank or storage location.
Read with DPP v Braney (2026) in this app: authorisation is tested when evidence is gathered; later handling is tested by its effect on the evidence.
job: Keep a complete audit trail for surveillance product: every copy, transcript, enhancement, transfer and person given access.
Make enhanced or transcribed versions from a preserved master, and record who did it and how.
Store surveillance material securely and limit access to those working on the case.
DPP v Hannaway.law: Yes. The leading Supreme Court decision on handling surveillance material.

bg: In 2016 gunmen carried out a gangland shooting at a Dublin hotel and were driven away in a convoy of vehicles.

The prosecution alleged that the accused drove one of the vehicles and so facilitated a serious offence by a criminal organisation, by providing access to a motor vehicle, contrary to s.72 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006.

His defence was that he wasn't driving the vehicle at the relevant times. He served an alibi notice and called two alibi witnesses. The prosecution answered with rebuttal evidence under s.20(4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984.
The Special Criminal Court convicted him on 17 April 2023 and imposed eight and a half years. He appealed.
People (DPP) v Bonney.q: What counts as 'evidence in support of an alibi' — and can objections to rebuttal evidence be raised for the first time on appeal?
dec: Supreme Court, July 2026 ([2026] IESC 38, Hyland J giving judgment): appeal dismissed.

The objections to the rebuttal evidence, and the argument about the meaning of 'evidence in support of an alibi' in s.20(8), weren't raised at trial, and no reason was given. The interests of justice didn't require them to be raised for the first time on appeal.

Section 20(8) is concerned with geography. It covers evidence that the accused was somewhere else — not merely evidence of where someone else was. One witness's evidence, about another person's whereabouts, shouldn't have been treated as alibi evidence.
Even so, the rebuttal evidence was properly admissible in response to the evidence covered by the alibi notice, and no unfairness arose.
The trial court had independently found the accused guilty and rejected the defence evidence, so the alibi point wouldn't have changed the result.

keys.q: the section is concerned with geography
keys.w: Hyland J, on s.20(8)

keys.q: without any reason given for the failure to raise the point
keys.w: Hyland J

later: The decision reinforces that objections must be taken at trial; in long trials especially, points not raised are unlikely to succeed on appeal.
Section 20(8) is read narrowly, as relating to the accused's own location.
job: When an alibi notice arrives, interview the alibi witnesses promptly and test their account against CCTV, phone data, transaction records and other witnesses.
Record the investigation of the alibi fully, so the prosecution can decide whether to call rebuttal evidence.
Pin down the timeline of the offence precisely — an alibi only matters for the relevant times.

bg: On 25 January 2013 a detective garda was shot dead during an armed robbery at a credit union in Co Louth.
The accused later lived in the US. Two witnesses there said he had admitted the killing to them. In 2018 he was deported from the US to Ireland.

At his trial the US witnesses gave evidence by video-link under ad hoc arrangements. One resiled from her evidence and was treated as hostile; during her evidence her boyfriend interrupted. The trial ran during the Covid-19 pandemic.
In August 2020 a jury convicted him of murder. He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a 40-year minimum term and appealed on nearly 50 grounds.
People (DPP) v Brady (2024).q: Was the trial fair — given the pandemic, video-link witnesses from abroad, a hostile witness, interruptions, and the way he was returned from the US?
dec: Court of Appeal, 11 July 2024 (Edwards J giving a 363-page judgment for a three-judge court): appeal dismissed on every ground.
The trial judge had properly considered the public-health situation and was right to let the trial proceed.

The video-link arrangements for the US witnesses may not have been ideal, but they weren't an error in themselves and caused no unfairness. The claim that one witness was induced by US Homeland Security was a matter for cross-examination and the jury.

The trial judge correctly allowed the prosecution to treat the second witness as hostile after she resiled. Interruptions by her boyfriend didn't create a real and substantial risk of an unfair trial, given the judge's warnings to the jury.
The argument that his deportation was a 'de facto extradition' without legal protections was entirely without foundation.

keys.q: may not have been ideal
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on the video-link arrangements

keys.q: not a breach of the integrity of the trial
keys.w: Edwards J, on the interruptions

keys.q: entirely without foundation
keys.w: Edwards J, on the deportation argument

later: He has also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice, a matter for the Special Criminal Court.
A 40-year minimum term applies to the murder of a member of An Garda Síochána acting in the course of duty.
job: Trace and interview people the suspect may have confided in — at home and abroad — as early as possible, and record exactly what was said and when.
Take key witness statements in a form usable under s.16 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006 if the witness later resiles: with the statutory declaration, or on video.
Arrange evidence from abroad through formal channels (mutual legal assistance, video-link arrangements) and keep a full record of contact with overseas witnesses and authorities.

bg: The accused's three children, who have special needs, were abused by others; two men were later prosecuted and imprisoned.
She was arrested and interviewed under caution and denied any knowledge or involvement. The DPP initially decided not to prosecute her.

In later wardship-type proceedings about the children's care, a psychologist interviewed her five times to assess her capacity to care for them, using a polygraph. She allegedly made admissions, which were shared with the relevant agencies, and the DPP then charged her.

At trial in the Circuit Criminal Court in Clonmel the judge ruled the admissions inadmissible on grounds of fairness and directed an acquittal. The Court of Appeal reversed that ruling ([2022] IECA 248), and she appealed.
People (DPP) v BK (2023).q: Are admissions made to a psychologist during child-care proceedings — with a polygraph and no caution — admissible in a criminal trial?
dec: Supreme Court, 13 October 2023 (Charleton J, for Dunne, O'Malley, Woulfe and Murray JJ): appeal dismissed. The trial judge was wrong to exclude the statements.
The polygraph wasn't used as a tool of oppression. It was used to verify information and help find the truth, and nothing tied her answers to threatened consequences for the children's care.
The interviews weren't equivalent to arrest, detention or being placed under authority for a criminal investigation. They were a measured assessment of potential risk, not aimed at charging anyone.
In those circumstances the absence of police-style cautions didn't make the statements unfair, and there was no basis for excluding them.
The Court asked for further submissions on whether a retrial should be ordered.

keys.q: there was no basis for excluding the alleged admissions
keys.w: Charleton J

keys.q: a measured investigation into potential threat
keys.w: Charleton J, describing the assessment

later: After the Supreme Court ruling the case went back for retrial. In July 2024 she was convicted and sentenced to eight years, the last two suspended.

At the retrial the psychologist accepted that the polygrapher's remarks could have been inducements, and that she may have said what he wanted to hear — evidence the appellate courts hadn't heard before.

On 14 July 2025 the Court of Appeal (O'Moore J) allowed her appeal, unopposed by the DPP: the imbalance of power was extreme, the trial judge was wrong to feel bound by the earlier rulings, and the admissions — the only evidence — should have been excluded. She should never have been convicted.
So the principle survives — non-criminal assessments aren't automatically excluded — but voluntariness and fairness are always decided on the evidence actually given at trial.
job: Ask early whether the suspect has been through other processes (child protection, wardship, medical or psychological assessment) and whether anything relevant was said.
Obtain such records only through lawful routes (consent, court order or a statutory power), and record how you got them.
When you interview a suspect yourself, apply the full caution and custody safeguards — BK concerns non-criminal assessments, not Garda interviews.
People (DPP) v BK (2023).law: The 2023 principle stands, but the case itself ended in July 2025 with the conviction quashed and the admissions held inadmissible.

bg: In December 2012 a gang shot a man dead in north Dublin.
In 2018 Gardaí who knew the accused viewed CCTV and identified him. Some had looked him up on PULSE before viewing, and the date of the killing was displayed on the footage.

In November 2021 the Special Criminal Court convicted him of murder as a 'spotter' for the gang: he met gang members on the day, acted in concert with them and coordinated with them afterwards. He was acquitted of possessing a handgun with intent to endanger life, and in January 2022 he was sentenced to life imprisonment.

On appeal he argued the case boiled down to Garda visual identification from CCTV, that the process was contaminated, and that officers who said they knew of no link between the footage and the shooting weren't credible.
People (DPP) v Murphy (2023).q: Is Garda recognition of a suspect from CCTV reliable when some officers checked PULSE beforehand and the footage showed the date of the crime?
dec: Court of Appeal, December 2023: appeal dismissed in its entirety.
The identification process was excellent in many respects. The Gardaí viewed the footage individually, the process was recorded, and their identifications were firm and untainted.
Given the six-year gap between the killing and the 2018 identifications, the date-stamp on the footage didn't introduce an unfair or prejudicial element.
The trial court was entitled to distinguish what the officers knew at the time of the killing from what they knew in 2018, and its findings on their credibility weren't perverse.
Detailed circumstantial evidence of careful planning, advance surveillance and practice runs was enough to prove joint enterprise and murderous intent.

keys.q: firm and untainted identifications
keys.w: Court of Appeal, as reported

keys.q: excellent in many respects
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on the CCTV identification process

later: Recognition by Gardaí who know a suspect is a form of identification evidence, and the usual cautions apply — see People (AG) v Casey (No 2) and R v Turnbull in this app.
The defence focus on PULSE checks and date-stamps shows where recognition evidence is vulnerable: what the viewer knew, and what the footage told them, before they named anyone.
job: Have each Garda view the footage alone, without being told who the suspect is and without seeing PULSE material first.
Record each viewing: who, when, which clips, what they said, how sure they were, and how they know the person (how often and in what setting they've seen them).
Note anything on screen (dates, captions) that could cue the viewer, and use clean copies where you can.

bg: On 16 December 2018 armed men attacked security personnel and set vehicles alight at a property in Co Roscommon.
A journalist with a local newspaper, tipped off by a source, filmed and photographed the aftermath and published the material online.
Interviewed under caution, he offered copies of his material and gave Gardaí a USB key, but refused to reveal his sources, claiming journalistic privilege.

In April 2019 a Garda sergeant applied for warrants under s.10 of the Criminal Justice (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1997 to search his home and the newspaper's premises. The application didn't mention that he was a journalist or that he had claimed privilege. Gardaí searched his home and seized his phone; he refused the password and went to the High Court the same day. The High Court upheld the warrant; the Court of Appeal quashed it in 2022.
Corcoran v Commissioner of An Garda Síoc.q: Is a search warrant valid if the issuing judge wasn't told the target was a journalist who had claimed privilege over his sources?
dec: Supreme Court, 22 June 2023 (O'Donnell CJ, Dunne, Charleton, O'Malley, Baker, Hogan and Collins JJ): the Commissioner's appeal was dismissed unanimously, and the warrant remained quashed.

Highly relevant information wasn't before the District Judge. Without all the relevant facts — that the target was a journalist, that he had claimed privilege, and that the search aimed to identify his sources — the judge couldn't perform the independent role the law requires.

An Garda Síochána is bound by Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Protecting journalistic sources is a basic condition of press freedom, so Gardaí have a responsibility to disclose such facts when seeking a warrant.

Collins J said the warrant might still have been granted with the full facts, but that wasn't inevitable. The Court declined to decide the full constitutional scope of journalistic privilege, which hadn't been fully argued.
Hogan J identified serious, systemic shortcomings in search-warrant law — including that the s.10 power is all-or-nothing, with no power to attach conditions — and called for urgent legislation.

keys.q: highly relevant information was not before the District Court judge
keys.w: Hogan J

keys.q: without a free press, there is no democracy in the manner required
keys.w: Hogan J

keys.q: inappropriate to express any view
keys.w: Collins J, on the constitutional scope of journalistic privilege

later: The case builds on Goodwin v UK (in this app): protecting sources is a basic condition of press freedom.
Hogan J's call for legislation means the procedure may change; check for any new statutory scheme for privileged or journalistic material.
job: In any warrant application, set out every highly relevant fact — including anything that weighs against granting it, such as journalistic, legal professional or other privilege.
If the target is a journalist or may hold journalistic material, say so, say whether privilege has been claimed, and explain why the material is needed.
Record what you told the issuing judge, and get advice before examining a device over which privilege is claimed.

bg: A Garda obtained a warrant under s.26 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 to search a house in Co Offaly. She had also obtained separate warrants for two nearby properties.
At about 7.40am she and a colleague entered the house and began the search. She then left to search the other two properties, returning later.
While she was away her colleague kept searching and, near the end of the search, found suspected cocaine.

Section 26 allows Gardaí to use the warrant's powers 'accompanied by' the named Garda. In October 2023 the District Court found the colleague was not accompanied when he found and seized the substance, held the seizure unlawful and dismissed the possession charge. The DPP appealed by case stated.
DPP v Davis (2026).q: Can other Gardaí keep searching under a s.26 warrant when the named Garda leaves — and what happens to evidence found if they can't?
dec: High Court, 12 February 2026 (O'Higgins J): the colleague was not 'in any sense' accompanied by the named Garda when he found the substance, so the search and seizure were unlawful.
Read as a whole, s.26 intends the named Garda to exercise a general supervisory role. Other Gardaí may use the warrant's powers only while accompanying that Garda.

The District Judge was wrong to dismiss the charge automatically. Unlawfully obtained evidence can still be admitted in some circumstances, such as inadvertence, under People (DPP) v JC, so admissibility should have been assessed.
But the onus is on the prosecution to seek that assessment. It never asked the District Court to carry it out and gave no adequate explanation, so it couldn't raise the point on appeal.
Appeal dismissed; the acquittal was not disturbed.

keys.q: accompanied by
keys.w: The wording of s.26 that decided the case

later: The decision applies JC to an execution error: an unlawful seizure doesn't automatically exclude the evidence, but the prosecution must make the case for admitting it at trial.
A brief appearance by the named Garda is unlikely to be enough; the supervision has to be real.
job: If you're the named Garda, stay with the search. If you must leave, stop the search until you return.
Where several warrants are executed at once, name a Garda on each and plan who will be where.
Record who was present, where and when throughout the search — the timeline decides whether the search was lawful.

bg: In December 2016 the accused allegedly drove dangerously during a chase with Gardaí.
He was arrested, cautioned and charged with summary road traffic offences. Gardaí had no power to detain him for questioning on summary charges.

In February 2017 he was charged in Cavan District Court with reckless endangerment, an indictable offence. Gardaí could then have detained him for interview, but no questioning took place, and he didn't respond to the charge.

At his trial in November 2017 he applied, in the absence of the jury, to halt the endangerment charge: with no interview memo he'd have to give evidence to put his version. The judge dismissed the charge, calling the lack of a memo an insurmountable hurdle. The Court of Appeal (Birmingham P, Edwards and Kennedy JJ) held the judge was wrong to withdraw the case: he had no right to put forward a version immune from challenge or interrogation. The accused got leave to go to the Supreme Court.
DPP v JD.q: Does an accused have a right to be interviewed by Gardaí so that his account can go before the jury?
dec: Supreme Court, October 2022 ([2022] IESC 39, MacMenamin J giving the judgment of the Court): appeal dismissed.
The trial judge shouldn't have ruled on a hypothetical basis before any evidence was given. Applications to halt a trial should generally be decided in light of the evidence actually adduced.

Fair trial rights don't apply in full at the investigation stage. An investigation is a significant step in a process; the question is whether it was conducted fairly enough for a trial to take place. There is no right to be arrested and detained for questioning.

Whether an unsworn statement is admitted is for the trial judge under the rules of evidence — there's no guarantee of admission or of the weight it gets. This wasn't a lost-evidence case: those need specific material evidence actually lost, not a hypothetical lost opportunity.

The issue could have been resolved before trial if he had given Gardaí a statement, and a trial judge can direct a written response to the charge. No breach of his constitutional fair trial rights was shown.

keys.q: insurmountable hurdle
keys.w: The trial judge, on the lack of an interview memo — a view the courts rejected

keys.q: a significant step in a process
keys.w: MacMenamin J, describing an investigation

keys.q: no entitlement to be detained and questioned
keys.w: Court of Appeal (Birmingham P)

later: The reply after caution at charge is one of the recognised ways an accused can put his account, so it should always be recorded.
Investigation fairness still matters: preserving evidence and following lines of enquiry that may help the suspect remain part of a fair process.
job: At charge, caution the suspect, invite a reply, and record it word for word.
If you don't interview a suspect, note why (no power to detain, already charged, and so on) and record any offer made to take an account.
Keep the investigation fair overall — preserve evidence, follow lines of enquiry that may help the suspect, and disclose properly.

bg: At about 1am on 13 December 2013 a Garda in Dublin stopped a car that was dragging a parking cone under its bumper. He noted alcohol on the driver's breath, glassy eyes and slurred speech, and arrested him for drink driving under s.4 of the Road Traffic Act 2010.
At the station the driver was given his notice of rights and provided two breath specimens at 1.42am, showing 55 micrograms of alcohol per 100ml of breath.

The defence disputed his English, which the Garda said was good. The custody record's foreign-nationals section said nothing about whether an interpreter was needed; the Garda couldn't recall whether the member in charge had decided one wasn't required, and the driver hadn't asked for one.
The Circuit Court judge found a breach of the 2013 Regulations on interpretation and translation for persons in Garda custody, and stated a case to the Court of Appeal.
DPP v Malai.q: Does a breach of the custody regulations on interpreters make the detention unlawful — and the breath evidence inadmissible?
dec: Court of Appeal, 11 November 2020 (Ní Raifeartaigh J, with Birmingham P and Edwards J).
In the circumstances, the breaches did not render the detention unlawful.

Admissibility of the breath evidence is a matter for the trial judge's discretion. The ordinary principles for evidence obtained through illegality apply — not the stricter rules for breaches of constitutional rights.
The absence of any causal link between the breaches and the obtaining of the breath specimen is relevant, and the trial judge must weigh all the relevant factors.

keys.q: did not render the detention of the defendant unlawful
keys.w: Court of Appeal (headnote)

keys.q: no causal link between the breaches of the Regulations
keys.w: Court of Appeal (headnote)

later: The decision fits the general approach to custody-regulation breaches: they don't automatically invalidate a detention, but they can affect admissibility, especially where they're linked to the evidence obtained.
Where a person's understanding is genuinely in doubt, the consequences can be more serious — rights that weren't understood can undermine statements and consents.
job: For any foreign national, or anyone whose English may be limited, the member in charge should decide whether an interpreter is needed, tell the person, and record the decision and reasons.
If in doubt, get an interpreter and give the rights notice in a language the person understands.
Note the language used in key exchanges (arrest, caution, breath test requirement) and how you judged understanding.

bg: In October 2016 a six-year-old child said the accused had touched her while sitting beside her. She complained the next day.
In December 2016 she gave a formal video-recorded interview, later admitted as her evidence-in-chief.
The first trial collapsed in October 2019 over a non-disclosure issue. The second was abandoned because of Covid-19. The trial went ahead in May 2021, about four and a half years after the incident.

Cross-examined at 11, she said she couldn't remember the incident or its circumstances, only what she had seen on the video, though she maintained the accused was lying. The trial judge admitted the video and left the delay to the jury. He was convicted, sentenced to four years, and appealed.
DPP v MT.q: Can a trial be fair where a child, after long delay, can't remember the incident and can't be meaningfully cross-examined on her video evidence?
dec: Court of Appeal, March 2023 ([2023] IECA 65, Ní Raifeartaigh J giving judgment): conviction quashed.

The child's memory was significantly impaired, if not absent, and she was relying on the video. Cross-examination is a key right under the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights; here it lost its fundamental essence.
Decisive factors: her young age, a single brief incident, no other supporting evidence, and a dispute about whether the touching happened at all — which the delay stopped the accused exploring.
A jury warning couldn't cure the problem, because the jury could have been influenced by the video without adequate cross-examination.

The decision isn't a bright-line rule on the time between recording and cross-examination. A child not recalling every detail doesn't require a trial to stop, refreshing memory from the video isn't wrong in itself, and the concern doesn't generally arise in historic cases where all the evidence is given live.

keys.q: not to be taken as a bright-line rule
keys.w: Ní Raifeartaigh J

keys.q: loses its fundamental essence
keys.w: Ní Raifeartaigh J, on cross-examination where memory is gone

keys.q: real risk of an unfair trial
keys.w: Court of Appeal, as reported

later: The case shows the cost of delay in child cases: a trial lost to a disclosure failure in 2019 pushed cross-examination years past the interview.
Supporting evidence — a prompt-complaint witness, contemporaneous observations, forensic or digital evidence — can make the difference when a child's memory fades.
job: Hold the specialist interview promptly and cover the context and circumstances as well as the incident itself.
Look for supporting evidence from the start: first-complaint witnesses, others present, physical, forensic and digital evidence.
Get disclosure right first time and flag child cases for early trial — every adjournment costs the child's memory.

bg: A garda attached to a Dublin traffic unit was investigated over a video clip he allegedly forwarded on WhatsApp in 2019.
Gardaí searched his office, home and car under a warrant. He handed over his phone and its passcode.

In May 2020 the DPP decided not to prosecute. Disciplinary processes followed, relying on material from the phone — including images of Garda computer screens showing suspects, PULSE entries and command-and-control incidents, and CCTV stills linked to Garda investigations — along with other allegations.
He challenged the use of the material. The High Court found against him, the Court of Appeal reversed that, and the Commissioner appealed to the Supreme Court.
Hyland v Commissioner of An Garda Síochá.q: Can material found on a phone lawfully seized in a criminal investigation be used in a Garda disciplinary inquiry?
dec: Supreme Court, 6 November 2025 ([2025] IESC 54, Murray J, with O'Donnell CJ and Dunne J; Woulfe and Hogan JJ dissenting).
He couldn't insist on the return of material unlawfully held on the phone; the Commissioner could remove it before returning the device.

The Commissioner was entitled to use the knowledge obtained from the lawful search to start the disciplinary inquiry. His privacy rights weren't exhausted by the seizure, but on the evidence the use was lawful and proportionate to enforcing Garda discipline.

Copying or downloading material after the no-prosecution decision and after he demanded the phone's return wasn't permitted, and that material shouldn't be used. Material copied earlier raises further legal and factual questions.
The dissent held there was no lawful basis for using the material in an internal investigation, and that any such search needed authorisation from a judicial or other independent body.

keys.q: privacy rights were not exhausted
keys.w: Murray J, on the lawful seizure

keys.q: lawful and proportionate to the objective of enforcing garda discipline
keys.w: Murray J

keys.q: was entitled to use the knowledge obtained to initiate the disciplinary inquiry
keys.w: Murray J, on the Commissioner

later: With a 3–2 split, the dissent's view — that using seized data beyond the criminal investigation needs independent authorisation — may be argued again.
Seized data must be handled according to the purpose and stage of the process: what's lawful during an investigation may not be after a decision not to prosecute.
job: Never keep images of PULSE, Garda screens, CCTV or case material on your own phone or messaging apps.
When you seize a device, record what is extracted, when and why. Stop copying when the purpose ends (for example after a decision not to prosecute) and get advice before any further use.
Return devices promptly when no longer needed, removing anything that can't lawfully be returned.
Hyland v Commissioner of An Garda Síochá.law: Yes. Supreme Court decision (November 2025), by a majority.

bg: The accused was a chaplain at the complainant's school. The complainant said he didn't report the abuse at the time because he'd been told not to tell anyone.

In 2017 he first disclosed it to a doctor and, shortly afterwards, to his mother. A priest gave evidence that he disclosed the abuse in two counselling sessions in late 2017. In May 2018 he told a lifelong friend. He also made two statements to Gardaí.
At trial the complaint evidence was admitted — the friend's over objection, the doctor's without objection — and the prosecution relied on it in closing.

In March 2022 the accused was convicted of six counts of sexual assault under s.2 of the Criminal Law (Rape) (Amendment) Act 1990. The trial judge gave no direction on the limited use of the complaint evidence, and the defence didn't ask for one.
People (DPP) v BFJ.q: What must the jury be told about evidence that a complainant told others — and can the point be raised on appeal if it wasn't raised at trial?
dec: Court of Appeal, June 2023 ([2023] IECA 127, Kennedy J): convictions quashed.
Complaint evidence is admitted as an exception to the hearsay rule. It goes to consistency — it is not evidence that the abuse happened.
Where it's admitted, the jury must be told how it can and can't be used. Without that direction a jury may treat the complaints as confirming that the complainant's account is true.

The prosecution introduced the evidence and relied on it in closing, so it was clearly important. The missing direction was an oversight or error of substance giving rise to an apprehension of real injustice, so the Court allowed the ground although no requisition was raised at trial.

keys.q: oversight or error of substance
keys.w: Kennedy J, on the missing direction

later: Complaint evidence remains admissible and can be powerful; the problem was the missing direction, not the evidence itself.
Later disclosures (to counsellors or friends) may raise questions about whether they qualify as complaint evidence at all — prosecutors decide what to lead, so give them the full picture.
job: Take statements from each person the complainant disclosed to: when, where, the words used, who raised the subject, and the complainant's demeanour.
Record the timeline of disclosures accurately — the first complaint and how soon it was made both matter.
Note, in the complainant's own words, anything that explains a delay in reporting (fear, being told not to tell).

bg: The accused and his wife, who had a child together, separated after their relationship deteriorated.
In May 2014, during a row, he produced a knife and threatened to cut her face, then raped her overnight. He threatened her again the next day.

Over the following weeks he confronted her at work and at the child's creche, and in June 2014 told her he would next come armed with a hammer. In August 2014 he struck her several times on the head with a hammer at her parents' home, and struck her mother too.

He pleaded guilty to the hammer attack and was convicted after trial of rape and the threats. The Central Criminal Court imposed 10 years in total; the Court of Appeal cut it to eight and a half. The DPP appealed, arguing the rape had been treated in isolation from a pattern of violent and abusive behaviour.
DPP v FE.q: How should rape be sentenced — and can the background of abuse in a relationship be taken into account?
dec: Supreme Court, 6 December 2019 ([2019] IESC 85, Charleton J): the Court of Appeal was wrong to consider the rape, and the earlier threat, in isolation.

The circumstances of a crime are relevant to sentence. But events entirely separate in time and character, or offences for which the accused was acquitted or never charged, can't be used to aggravate it.

A rape ordinarily merits a headline sentence of about seven years before mitigation, and custody is all but inescapable. A category of more serious cases merits 10 to 15 years, and some may require up to life.
Aggravating factors include violence in the home, breach of trust, domination and a background of abuse.

Consecutive sentences are wrong in principle if they punish twice for what is really one crime, subject to totality; here the hammer attack and later threats could justify consecutive terms. After further submissions the Court restored the original 10-year sentence in 2020.

keys.q: all but inescapable
keys.w: Charleton J, on custody for rape

keys.q: wrong in principle
keys.w: Charleton J, on consecutive sentences that punish twice for one crime

later: Section 40 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018 now makes it an aggravating factor that an offence was committed against a current or former spouse, civil partner or intimate partner.
Sentencing guidance for sexual offences has continued to develop since; check the current position before advising a victim about likely outcomes.
job: Record the full history of the relationship: earlier threats, violence, control, breaches of orders, and their dates.
Charge each distinct offence (threats, assaults, breaches) — only matters charged and proved can aggravate the sentence.
Explain and offer the victim impact statement process.
DPP v FE.law: Yes. The Supreme Court's framework for rape sentencing (December 2019).

bg: On 21 July 2008 the applicant was stopped in Co Roscommon and later charged with drink driving under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961, as amended.
Before trial his lawyers asked for their expert to examine the evidential breath-testing machine, and for its servicing history.
The District Judge refused without giving reasons, and on 5 June 2009 convicted him.
He sought judicial review. The High Court (Charleton J) refused to quash the conviction, holding that he had to establish reasons for wanting the inspection. He appealed.
Oates v Browne.q: Can a court refuse, without reasons, a defence request to inspect the breath-testing machine — and must the defence justify the request?
dec: Supreme Court, 29 February 2016 ([2016] IESC 7, Hardiman J, with Laffoy and Dunne JJ): appeal allowed.
The applicant had a right to apply for inspection of the machine. The District Judge fell into substantial error by refusing the application without giving reasons.
The High Court was wrong to treat him as needing to establish reasons for the inspection. Requiring that would offend fair procedures and constitutional justice.

Breath specimens are transitory — none can be kept for independent analysis. So, as the Court said quoting McGonnell v Attorney General, the opportunity for independent assessment is critical to fair procedures.

keys.q: had fallen into substantial error
keys.w: Supreme Court, on refusing without reasons

keys.q: is critical to fair procedures and constitutional justice
keys.w: Supreme Court, quoting McGonnell v Attorney General

later: The decision concerns the older Road Traffic Act 1994 regime, but the principle — fair access to test the machine evidence — carries over to evidential breath testing under the Road Traffic Act 2010.
Read with DPP v Avadenei and DPP v Hodgins in this app on the breath statement itself.
job: Keep the station's evidential breath-testing machine records — service, calibration, faults, maintenance — complete and retrievable.
Pass any defence request about the machine to the prosecutor promptly; don't refuse it yourself.
Note the machine's identity and any error messages on the night.

bg: Over about an hour and forty minutes in Dublin, the accused slapped his partner in public and then forced her into the boot of her car for about ten minutes.
Later he punched her repeatedly while she was driving, punched the windscreen, and assaulted her again. A witness filmed the first incident and alerted Gardaí.
He pleaded guilty to false imprisonment and assault, and an assault causing harm was taken into consideration. The trial court took a five-year headline and imposed three years after mitigation.

The Court of Appeal raised the headline to eight years, discounted by two and a half years for mitigation. He appealed to the Supreme Court on how s.40 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018, and offences taken into consideration, should operate.
People (DPP) v Mountassir.q: How does s.40 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018 affect sentence — and can offences be taken into consideration?
dec: Supreme Court, December 2025 ([2025] IESC 53, O'Malley J giving the leading judgment): appeal dismissed; the Court of Appeal's sentence stands.

Section 40 is a victim-centred provision. It doesn't impose mandatory punishment, but it requires a more severe sentence where the offender has a specified connection with the victim, because of the additional psychological harm. The s.40(5) exception may apply where no such additional harm was caused.

Section 40 should be weighed when assessing the gravity of the offence, and the judge should refer to it expressly. It shouldn't be applied in an overly literal way, and a fixed percentage uplift would risk a rigid tariff.
Offences taken into consideration aren't invalid. The court must avoid any impression of a 'free ride', either by separate penalties or by making clear the final sentence reflects them.

The false imprisonment facilitated the assaults, so separating them would be entirely artificial. The trial court's headline was too low and didn't adequately reflect the assault or s.40; the victim's ongoing distress and fear supported the higher sentence. The Court declined to give a guideline for false imprisonment, given its range of circumstances.

keys.q: victim-centred provision
keys.w: Supreme Court, on s.40

keys.q: should not be applied in an overly literal manner
keys.w: O'Malley J, on s.40

keys.q: entirely artificial
keys.w: Supreme Court, on separating the false imprisonment from the assaults

later: In 2026 the judiciary adopted a sentencing guideline for many domestic violence offences, pointing to heavier sentences — check it alongside Mountassir.
Factors for sentencing false imprisonment include its purpose, the means used, its duration and the victim's vulnerability, avoiding double counting.
job: Record the relationship between the accused and the victim (s.40) and the evidence of its effect — fear, distress, control.
Secure independent evidence quickly: witness footage, 999 calls, CCTV, dash-cam, and photographs of injuries.
Charge each distinct offence; if some are to be taken into consideration, make sure the prosecutor has the full details.

bg: In February 2017 the accused was driving on the M7 in a vehicle that had no current tax, and he wasn't insured to drive it.

Gardaí detained the vehicle under s.41 of the Road Traffic Act 1994 and the 2011 regulations on the detention, removal, storage and disposal of vehicles. It was removed and stored at a Garda compound.
At the compound a Garda opened the boot and found a large quantity of amphetamines, worth about €137,000.
He was convicted in the Circuit Court in June 2023 of possessing drugs for sale or supply under s.15A of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977.

In October 2024 the Court of Appeal (Burns J) quashed the conviction. The trial judge had let a Garda tell the jury about a phone call from an inspector who had received confidential information about drugs in the car. The inspector didn't give evidence: it was hearsay with a significant prejudicial effect. The case was sent back to Naas Circuit Court.
The Supreme Court gave leave (January 2025) on the separate question whether opening the boot was authorised by law.
DPP v Noonan.q: Does lawfully detaining a vehicle under s.41 allow Gardaí to open the boot and seize what they find — without a warrant or a separate search power?
dec: Supreme Court, 2025 ([2025] IESC 22, O'Donnell CJ giving the lead judgment): the accused's appeal was dismissed — opening the boot was lawful.
Detention under s.41 gives Gardaí lawful possession and control of the vehicle. That includes opening its compartments and taking items found in it, including evidence of a crime.
There was no need to rely on a separate common-law power of search, or on s.23 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977.
The search was lawful in the circumstances, so the evidence of the drugs was admissible.

keys.q: the search of the vehicle in the circumstances was lawful
keys.w: Supreme Court, as summarised by Decisis

keys.q: a breach of the rule against hearsay
keys.w: Burns J (Court of Appeal, 2024), on the tip-off evidence

later: Commentators expect the principle to apply wherever a lawfully detained vehicle turns out to hold evidence of an unrelated offence.
Everything turns on the lawfulness of the detention: if the s.41 grounds weren't there, the possession — and anything found — could be challenged.
The Court of Appeal's 2024 ruling is a separate lesson: evidence that Gardaí acted on a confidential tip-off, given by a Garda who didn't receive it, is hearsay and can sink a conviction.

One case summary describes the conviction as affirmed by the Supreme Court; news reports of the 2024 ruling say it was quashed and sent back for trial. Check the current position before relying on the outcome.
job: Record the s.41 grounds precisely (tax, insurance and licence checks and their results) before detaining the vehicle.
Keep the chain: who drove or towed it, where it was stored, and who had access.
When opening compartments, photograph items in place and record the time, place and Gardaí present before seizing anything.
Explain the grounds for a stop or search by what you saw and checked yourself. Don't tell the court about a tip-off you didn't receive — it's hearsay.
DPP v Noonan.law: Yes on the search point (Supreme Court, 2025). The conviction itself was quashed by the Court of Appeal in 2024 on a hearsay ground.

bg: In August 2021 a man was prosecuted in the District Court for possessing a small quantity of cannabis. He denied the charge.
The case was presented by a Garda other than the one who had instituted it, under a District Court rule allowing this — the long-standing court presenter system.
In May 2022 the High Court (Bolger J) held that rule invalid: s.8(2) of the Garda Síochána Act 2005 limited the role to the Garda who instituted the prosecution. She paused the effect of her ruling.

Thousands of District Court prosecutions were at risk. Emergency legislation was enacted the next day so that any Garda could conduct a prosecution instituted by another. The DPP appealed to the Supreme Court.
DPP v Davitt.q: Can a Garda who didn't institute a prosecution present it in the District Court?
dec: Supreme Court, 14 July 2023 (Dunne J for a five-judge court with O'Donnell CJ, Charleton, O'Malley and Collins JJ): appeal allowed and the High Court ruling overturned.
The appeal wasn't moot despite the emergency legislation.
The ordinary meaning of s.8(2) clearly contemplates different Gardaí instituting or conducting summary proceedings.

Gardaí had acted as prosecutors since at least 1948. Abolishing that would have been a radical step that the Oireachtas would have had to take explicitly; the emergency legislation, restoring the previous position the next day, reinforced that view.

Rights of audience fall within the District Court Rules Committee's rule-making power. The rules have the force of law unless declared invalid, and the District Court can't question them through a consultative case stated.

keys.q: clearly contemplates different members of An Garda Síochána instituting or conducting
keys.w: Dunne J, on s.8 of the 2005 Act

keys.q: The rules have the force of law, unless declared invalid.
keys.w: Dunne J

later: The case shows how much of the District Court's daily work depends on court presenters — and how quickly a narrow reading of a statute can disrupt it.
Check the current statutory basis for Garda prosecutions under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024.
job: Prepare every summary file so a court presenter who has never seen it can run it: clear summary, statements, exhibits, previous convictions and witness availability.
Flag any legal issues on the file (warrant points, custody issues) for the presenter.
Be available to give evidence even when someone else presents your case.
