bg: In September 2012 the accused was arrested on suspicion of IRA membership, over his presence at a funeral, and released without charge.

In December 2012 he was arrested again, without a warrant, during the investigation into the murder of a prison officer in Northern Ireland. It was alleged that he had bought, in Dublin, the car used in the shooting. In 2014 he was acquitted of a separate charge of withholding information.

In 2017 the Special Criminal Court convicted him of IRA membership and imposed five years. A Detective Chief Superintendent gave belief evidence that he was a member and claimed privilege over its basis, which the defence said made meaningful cross-examination impossible.
The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and the Supreme Court gave leave on issues of general public importance.
People (DPP) v Banks.q: Was the second arrest lawful without a warrant — and was the evidence enough to prove membership?
dec: Supreme Court, 10 February 2022 (O'Malley J giving the decision of a unanimous five-judge court): appeal allowed and the conviction quashed.

Arrest: the Act provides a straightforward route — a District Court warrant — where the statutory limits on re-arrest apply. The Special Criminal Court was wrong to hold that no warrant was needed because the second arrest concerned a different incident and investigation.
Leaving that question to be resolved at trial would gravely weaken the protection against abuse of arrest powers.

Evidence: belief evidence of membership needs strong independent support. There were grounds for grave suspicion about his role in sourcing the car, but the evidence wasn't strong enough to prove membership beyond reasonable doubt.

keys.q: grave suspicion
keys.w: O'Malley J, on his role in sourcing the car

keys.q: not sufficiently strong to prove the offence of membership beyond reasonable doubt
keys.w: Supreme Court, as reported

keys.q: gravely weakened
keys.w: Supreme Court, on protection against abuse of arrest powers

later: Under s.30A of the Offences Against the State Act 1939, a person arrested under s.30 and released without charge generally can't be re-arrested for the same offence without a District Court warrant based on new information.
Membership is a continuing offence, so a 'new incident' doesn't by itself avoid the re-arrest safeguard.
job: Before any re-arrest, check the suspect's arrest history (PULSE, custody records) for earlier arrests for the same or a related offence.
If the re-arrest rules apply, get a District Court warrant on new information — don't rely on the new arrest being for a 'different incident'.
In membership cases, gather independent evidence (surveillance, communications, conduct, items found) to support any belief evidence.

bg: In March 2017 a garda on duty at a Garda station was taking a statement from a woman. He engaged in a sexual act with her and didn't record the statement.

Under the Garda Síochána (Discipline) Regulations 2007 a Board of Inquiry found breaches of discreditable conduct and neglect of duty. It recommended retirement or resignation for the first and a two-week pay deduction for the second. In October 2018 the Commissioner ordered resignation.

On appeal, the Appeal Board found resignation disproportionate and substituted a four-week pay deduction. The Commissioner didn't implement that within the seven days required; instead the garda was suspended pending a decision under s.14 of the Garda Síochána Act 2005.

In March 2020 the Commissioner decided dismissal under s.14(2) was necessary to maintain public confidence. The High Court quashed the dismissal as fundamentally unfair — a second process for the same conduct on unchanged facts — and the Court of Appeal dismissed the Commissioner's appeal.
Hegarty v Commissioner of An Garda Síoch.q: Can the Commissioner dismiss a garda under s.14(2) after disciplinary proceedings imposed a lesser penalty?
dec: Supreme Court, July 2025 ([2025] IESC 36, Murray J giving the lead judgment): the Commissioner's appeal was allowed and relief refused.

Section 14(2) is separate from the disciplinary regulations, as its 'notwithstanding' wording shows. Both serve public confidence, but s.14(2) is a protective power for the most unusual and extreme circumstances; using the regulations doesn't stop the Commissioner later using it.

The Commissioner must form the view that dismissal is necessary to maintain public confidence. Conduct that is wrongful or disgraceful, or briefly angers some of the public, isn't enough — and the threshold is higher for lower-ranking members.
Findings of a Board of Inquiry or Appeal Board don't bind the Commissioner under s.14(2). Where the member accepts the allegations there are no facts to resolve, so no prior recommendation is needed.
Section 14(2) decisions are reviewable on ordinary public-law grounds. The Commissioner gets no special deference, and the discretion to refuse a remedy follows general principles.

keys.q: confers an extreme power
keys.w: Murray J, on s.14(2)

keys.q: in the wholly exceptional situation
keys.w: Murray J

keys.q: necessary to maintain that confidence
keys.w: Murray J, on the test

later: A separate costs judgment later in 2025 dealt with who should pay the costs of the litigation.
Read with Hyland v Commissioner (2025) in this app, on using seized phone material in discipline.
job: Keep every interaction with victims and witnesses strictly professional — and recorded.
Record statements and contacts properly; failing to record can itself be a breach of discipline.
If you become aware of a colleague abusing their position, report it.
Hegarty v Commissioner of An Garda Síoch.law: The leading Supreme Court decision on s.14(2) (July 2025); check how the dismissal power now works under the 2024 Act.

bg: On 17 December 2017 a 74-year-old man was attacked with a machete near a yard in Rathkeale, Co Limerick, where many people and vehicles were present.

During the canvass, a woman whose house camera covered the scene told Gardaí her system was operational and that they could view it. No Garda went back to view or retrieve it, and no notes of the CCTV enquiries were kept.
The defence later had an engineer survey the area, who said there were about 30 cameras.

In November 2021 a jury at Limerick Circuit Criminal Court convicted the accused of assault causing serious harm and violent disorder, and acquitted him of producing a machete and of threats to kill. He was sentenced to 10 years, and appealed.
DPP v O'Donoghue.q: Does a failure to retrieve available CCTV make a trial unfair — and should the judge have directed an acquittal?
dec: Court of Appeal, 16 February 2024 (Burns J speaking for the court): appeal allowed and the convictions quashed.
It is an established duty of Gardaí to seek out and preserve CCTV evidence.

There were significant failings in how CCTV was handled: footage the owner offered was never retrieved, and there were no notes of the CCTV enquiries. The State offered no evidence to rebut the householder's account.
That unfairness removed a realistic prospect of a defence relating to the missing CCTV, so the trial judge should have directed an acquittal.

keys.q: established duty
keys.w: Burns J, on seeking out and preserving CCTV

keys.q: a realistic prospect of a defence existed in relation to this missing CCTV
keys.w: Burns J

later: The case applies the long line on the duty to seek out and preserve evidence — Braddish v DPP, Dunne v DPP and Murphy v DPP in this app.
Contrast DPP v Dunbar (2024): collecting CCTV widely is lawful and expected; here the problem was failing to collect it.
job: When an owner offers CCTV, retrieve it straight away or fix a time to return, and ask them to preserve it in the meantime.
Log every CCTV enquiry — location, owner, coverage, whether working, what was taken, or why not.
Before charge, check that all CCTV identified in the canvass has been retrieved, viewed and recorded.

bg: On 23 November 2023 a large crowd gathered in Dublin city centre after an incident at a school earlier that day. What followed became known as the Dublin riots.

CCTV showed the accused throwing rubbish bags at Gardaí and kicking and stamping on a patrol car, breaking its windscreen. He then placed a burning box in a second patrol car, which was set alight, and afterwards wiped the door handle he had used.
He also threw a bicycle saddle at a building housing about 90 international protection applicants — an attack he admitted was racially motivated.

Arrested in January 2024, he admitted his involvement in interview and pleaded guilty to riot, arson and criminal damage, with violent disorder and further criminal damage taken into consideration. In November 2024 he received headline sentences of 10 years (arson), 6 years (riot) and 4 years (criminal damage), reduced by 35% for mitigation, concurrent, with the last year of the arson sentence suspended.
DPP v Donaghey.q: Was a 10-year headline for arson during the Dublin riots excessive?
dec: Court of Appeal, May 2026 ([2026] IECA 105, Butler J giving the judgment of the Court): appeal dismissed.
The offending was part of what was rightly described as the gravest public disorder incident in the history of the State, which made the case unique.
The attack on Gardaí was extremely frightening — they shouldn't have to fear for their own safety. The attack on the centre was racially motivated and left its residents in a terrifying situation.

The arson was the first of its kind that evening and marked an escalation. He had been in the area earlier and returned with his face covered, intending to take part, and he removed forensic traces from the car — so his actions weren't simply opportunistic and impulsive.

Sentences in other riot cases had limited value as comparators, since each turns on its own facts and culpability. The question was whether the judge erred in principle; no error was shown, and mitigation had been properly applied.

keys.w: Butler J, adopting the description of the events

keys.q: should not have to fear for their own personal safety
keys.w: Butler J, on Gardaí

keys.q: These actions were not simply opportunistic and impulsive.
keys.w: Butler J

later: The Court referred to DPP v Shannon [2023] IECA 325 on how arson is categorised for sentencing.
The case shows how CCTV-led identification, interviews and admissions brought riot participants to court months after the event.
job: Preserve footage from every source quickly — CCTV, Garda cameras, media and public uploads — and map each person's acts across the clips.
Record attacks on Gardaí and Garda property in detail (injuries, damage, fear) as aggravating evidence.
Note evidence of planning or clean-up (face coverings, returning to the scene, wiping surfaces) — it goes to culpability.

bg: In October 2022 the plaintiff bought a van for about €2,000 but didn't register himself as owner, so the seller remained the registered owner.

On 16 October 2022 the van was parked, untaxed and uninsured, in a residential car park in Dublin. A Garda seized it under s.41 of the Road Traffic Act 1994, and a recovery contractor towed it to their compound. The plaintiff reported it stolen.
Notices were sent to the registered owner, who didn't respond. After the statutory period the van was crushed.

The plaintiff sued, alleging theft, destruction of property and discrimination, pointing to his nationality and to another uninsured vehicle nearby that wasn't seized. The case reached the High Court on appeal from the Circuit Court.
Pysz v An Garda Síochána.q: Were the seizure and disposal lawful — and is there liability for alleged discriminatory policing?
dec: High Court, 4 December 2025 ([2025] IEHC 698, Gillane J, ex tempore): claim dismissed in full.

A residential car park that the public can access with vehicles, by right or permission, is a public place for s.41, using the s.49 definition. The seizure was lawful, and the Garda didn't know the owner's identity or nationality.

Disposal followed the statutory notice and waiting-period process. The Court accepted that a Garda had phoned the plaintiff and told him the van could be crushed. There was no negligence, so the s.41(5) protection for acts done in good faith and without negligence applied.

Racism, if proven, is odious and abhorrent. But such an allegation can be an ugly one where it isn't founded in evidence; there was no evidence of discriminatory motive, and the comparator-vehicle point was unsupported.

keys.q: can be an ugly allegation where it is not founded in evidence
keys.w: Gillane J, as quoted in commentary

later: Read with DPP v Noonan (2025) in this app: a lawful s.41 detention also gives possession and control of the vehicle, including opening its compartments.
Clear records and proactive contact with the person affected were what protected the Gardaí here.
job: Record why the location is a public place (vehicle access, signage, use) and the tax and insurance checks made.
Send and log the statutory notices to the registered owner, and diarise the disposal date.
Record any contact with the person claiming the vehicle — date, time, and what you told them about the deadline.

bg: The applicant was arrested for a second time over an alleged breach of a protection order under the Domestic Violence Act 2018.

The member in charge refused station bail under s.31 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1967, for two case-specific reasons: he was already on bail for an earlier alleged breach, and conditions were needed that only a court can impose, such as no contact.

He sought judicial review, arguing that a 2017 Garda HQ directive — since rescinded — required station bail to be refused in domestic violence cases, so the member's statutory discretion had been unlawfully fettered.
He had previously been granted station bail, which undercut the claim of an inflexible policy.
GW v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána.q: Was the refusal of station bail an unlawful application of a blanket policy?
dec: High Court, 2025 ([2025] IEHC 336): relief refused.
The evidence of the arresting Garda and the member in charge showed case-specific reasons for refusing station bail. The applicant didn't show that the directive influenced the decision.

His affidavits were incomplete and contradicted by objective evidence, and he didn't seek to cross-examine the Gardaí. Factual disputes on affidavit generally need cross-examination by the party asserting the facts.
The burden of proof lies on the challenger, and the threshold is high. A mere coincidence between the existence of a policy and an unfavourable decision isn't enough.
Because the factual basis failed, the Court didn't rule on whether the directive itself was valid.

keys.q: the burden of proof lies squarely on the challenger
keys.w: Commentary on the High Court's approach

later: The principle that a statutory discretion can't be replaced by a rigid rule (as in DPP v Cullen (2014) on handcuffing) applies to station bail too.
Deferring to the court where conditions beyond Garda powers are needed — common in domestic violence cases — was treated as a legitimate, case-specific reason.
job: Decide station bail on the facts of each case and record the specific reasons in the custody record.
Where only a court can impose the conditions needed (no contact, stay away), say so expressly as your reason.
Don't cite a policy or directive as the reason for refusal; if guidance informed your thinking, record how it applied to this person.

bg: The applicant was charged with violent disorder in November 2013 and refused bail in the District Court, so he was remanded in custody.
In December 2013 the High Court granted bail on conditions: a specified residence, a curfew, daily signing at a Garda station, and no contact with his co-accused.

About three months later bail was revoked for breaches. He later got bail on relaxed conditions, but travelled to Portugal, returned early, didn't surrender his passport and didn't live at the agreed address. Gardaí sought an arrest warrant, and the High Court found breaches of the residence condition, rejecting the argument that the conditions were ambiguous.
He brought an Article 40 challenge seeking release, arguing the Bail Act 1997 was a complete code that left no power to revoke bail.
Roche (Dumbrell) v Governor of Cloverhil.q: Can the courts revoke bail outside the Bail Act 1997 — and is habeas corpus the way to challenge a revocation?
dec: Supreme Court, 31 July 2014 (Charleton J giving judgment, with O'Donnell and MacMenamin JJ): appeal dismissed and the High Court order affirmed.

The Bail Act 1997 is not an exhaustive code. It added statutory grounds for refusing bail and amended the law, but the courts keep their common-law powers to grant and revoke bail, as People (AG) v O'Callaghan shows.

The High Court is a full jurisdiction that may be asked to deal with bail by the accused or the prosecution. Bail may be revisited where there is a relevant and appropriately probative change of circumstances.
Following The State (McDonagh) v Frawley, a detention is not unlawful for habeas corpus purposes merely because some defect attaches to it. The bail issue wasn't a matter for Article 40.4.2.

keys.q: a full jurisdiction
keys.w: Charleton J, on the High Court's bail jurisdiction

keys.q: relevant and appropriately probative change of circumstances
keys.w: Charleton J, on revisiting bail

later: Later High Court decisions have applied Roche, for example Corcoran v Governor of Castlerea Prison [2016] IEHC 267.
Read with People (AG) v O'Callaghan in this app on the purpose of bail.
job: Check bail compliance actively — signing records, curfew checks, residence visits, passport surrender — and record each check.
When a breach occurs, gather the evidence (dates, times, who saw what) and bring it to the prosecutor or court promptly.
Make sure conditions are clearly worded when sought, so breaches can't be excused as ambiguous.

bg: In early 2014 the accused was tried at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court for burglary, endangerment and arson.
In a voir dire the trial judge ruled CCTV footage inadmissible.

The judge also excluded the memo of a Garda interview, holding that the Gardaí had wrongly invoked s.19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 (inferences from failure to account for presence at a place), which raised doubt about whether the admissions were voluntary.

With no other evidence of value left, the judge directed the jury to acquit. The DPP appealed under s.23 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2010, which allows an appeal against an acquittal where compelling evidence was wrongly excluded.
DPP v AMcD.q: Were the CCTV and the interview wrongly excluded — and should there be a retrial?
dec: Supreme Court, December 2016 (McKechnie J giving the unanimous judgment of a four-judge court): appeal allowed.

CCTV footage is generally real evidence, not hearsay. It carries no presumption of reliability and must be proved, including its provenance and authenticity; once admitted, its weight is a matter for the jury.
The trial judge misread s.19 and was wrong to hold that the Gardaí had no jurisdiction to invoke it, so the question of voluntariness didn't arise.
Both rulings were erroneous in a point of law, and the excluded material could properly be treated as compelling evidence under s.23.

A fair retrial was possible: the delay hadn't impaired recollection, the exhibits had been preserved, and the public interest in prosecution remained strong. A retrial was ordered, to be conducted in accordance with due process.

keys.q: erroneous in a point of law
keys.w: Supreme Court, on both rulings

keys.q: in accordance with due process
keys.w: Supreme Court, on the retrial

later: The case is a key authority on how CCTV is treated at trial: proved like other real evidence, then weighed by the jury.
Preserved exhibits made the retrial possible — another reason to keep everything until a case is finally over.
job: For each CCTV source, record the location, owner, system time against real time, who extracted it, how and when, and how it was stored — the provenance and authenticity chain.
Keep an unaltered master copy; make working copies and record any enhancement.
Before invoking s.18, s.19 or s.19A in interview, confirm the statutory conditions are met and record why.

bg: An elderly woman was robbed at the back door of her home in Co Laois. The robber was alleged to have followed her home.
The suspect refused to take part in a formal identification parade.

At Portarlington Garda Station, Gardaí ran an informal parade. Without his knowledge, seven men including him walked with a Garda along a corridor while the woman sat watching; she was to squeeze her daughter's hand if she recognised the robber. She identified him. As he passed, he spoke to a Garda.

The prosecution said CCTV and clothing fibres supported the identification. The trial judge excluded the identification and directed an acquittal. The DPP appealed under s.23 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2010.
DPP v Unnamed (informal ID parade, 2022).q: Was the informal identification fair — and should it have been excluded?
dec: Court of Appeal, 29 July 2022 (Kennedy J giving the judgment of a three-judge court): appeal allowed.
The accused speaking to a Garda as he walked past wasn't significant: the woman had already recognised him, instantly, before he spoke.
There was no obligation to tell him that Gardaí would hold an informal parade if he refused a formal one. That information might induce a suspect to agree to a formal parade.
The exclusion of the identification was wrong. The acquittal was set aside and he was returned for retrial.

keys.q: might induce him or her to agree to a formal parade
keys.w: Kennedy J

keys.q: quite a high standard
keys.w: Counsel for the DPP, on how the line-up was run

later: Corroboration mattered: CCTV and clothing fibres supported the identification, making it more robust.
The accused can't be named for legal reasons, so the case is listed here without his name.
job: If a suspect refuses a formal parade, record the refusal, then consider an informal identification planned in advance.
Choose a fair group of people of similar appearance, and keep the suspect from interacting with Gardaí or the witness during the procedure.
Record exactly when and how the witness indicated recognition, what was said and how sure they were — and look for corroboration (CCTV, forensics).

bg: The accused accepted a postal package containing about €6,000 of methamphetamine, addressed to a housemate.
In the same search, drugs were found in his bedroom. He pleaded guilty to cannabis and amphetamine supply charges arising from those finds.
At his trial on the remaining counts, the judge excluded references to the guilty pleas and related items as more prejudicial than probative. The jury acquitted.
The DPP appealed under s.23 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2010. The Court of Appeal found the exclusion erroneous, quashed the acquittal and ordered a retrial. He appealed to the Supreme Court.
DPP v JS.q: Was the related evidence wrongly excluded — and if so, should there be a retrial after a jury acquittal?
dec: Supreme Court, 11 July 2025 ([2025] IESC 32, O'Malley J, with O'Donnell CJ, Woulfe, Hogan and Murray JJ): appeal allowed; the acquittal was reinstated.
A prosecution appeal on a point of law was available, even though the ruling involved the exercise of discretion.
The exclusion was wrong. The evidence was reliable and probative of his knowledge and intent, and met the s.23(14) definition of compelling evidence.

But the DPP didn't show a retrial was in the interests of justice under s.23(12). The case was over five years old though still triable, there was no identifiable victim, the quantity made it routine and below the s.15A threshold, and he had already been punished for the related offences.

Correcting the legal error at appellate level already served the systemic purpose. After a full jury trial in a routine case, a retrial is exceptional and needs a distinct public-interest justification — strengthening the evidence isn't enough.

keys.q: exceptional remedy
keys.w: Commentary on the Supreme Court's view of a retrial after a jury acquittal

later: Read with DPP v AMcD (2016) and the 2022 informal identification case in this app — both s.23 appeals where retrials were ordered after directed acquittals.
Trial judges are expected to analyse both probative value and prejudice expressly when excluding evidence.
job: Record every related find in a drugs search — where, what, how much — and link each to the suspect (room, belongings, phone).
Gather the evidence of intent: scales, bags, cash, debt lists, messages.
Give the prosecutor a clear schedule of related charges and pleas so the admissibility argument can be made at trial.

src.t: Casemine — commentary on DPP v JS [2025] IESC 32

bg: In late 1983 a businessman was kidnapped and held in a hideout in Co Leitrim. During the rescue a Garda recruit and a soldier were shot dead, and the kidnappers escaped, leaving behind objects bearing fingerprints.
The applicant was a suspect. He had been serving a sentence in Northern Ireland, escaped from the Maze in 1983, was arrested in the Netherlands in 1986 and returned to Northern Ireland.
In 1998 he was arrested in the State under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 and charged with false imprisonment and firearms offences.
Gardaí had lost the items bearing the fingerprints. He sought judicial review to prohibit the trial for loss of evidence and delay, and the High Court prohibited it on the lost evidence.
McFarlane v DPP.q: Should a trial be stopped where Gardaí lost key exhibits and there was long delay?
dec: Supreme Court, 2006 ([2006] IESC 11), on the DPP's appeal: there was no real risk of an unfair trial from the loss. Photographs of the prints survived and the forensic examination had been completed before the items were lost.
Supreme Court, 5 March 2008 ([2008] IESC 7, Kearns J, unanimous): the delay argument also failed.
It was legitimate for Gardaí to wait for his release in Northern Ireland before arresting him in the State, so the pre-arrest delay didn't justify prohibition.

An accused must show specific prejudice, or delay well outside the norm. The Court weighed the length of delay, its reasons, whether he asserted the right, and prejudice (drawing on Barker v Wingo and DPP v Byrne), and treated systemic delay the same way. No breach of his right to a trial in due course of law was shown.

keys.q: adequate resources or facilities for the disposal of litigation
keys.w: Supreme Court, describing systemic delay

later: The trial then went ahead before the Special Criminal Court, but collapsed when the Garda evidence was ruled inadmissible, and the charges were dismissed.
In 2010 the European Court of Human Rights found that Ireland had no effective remedy for excessive delay in criminal proceedings.
job: Photograph every exhibit in detail (including marks and prints) before and after examination, and keep the images securely with the file.
Get forensic examination done promptly and record the results fully — they may outlive the item.
Log storage and movement of exhibits in long-running cases, and review retention periodically.
McFarlane v DPP.law: Yes, on lost evidence and delay (2006, 2008).

bg: The applicant, who had a mental illness, had stopped taking his medication. He asked to be admitted voluntarily to a Dublin hospital but was refused because he lived outside its catchment area; the hospital where he was a patient asked Gardaí to arrange his assessment and transfer if he came to their attention.

That evening his brother told a consultant psychiatrist that he had stopped his medication, had a samurai sword, and that he feared for everyone's safety. The brother also raised his concerns with Gardaí, who agreed to wait until morning.

Next morning two Gardaí asked the applicant to come to the station, and he went voluntarily. They called a retired GP, who spoke with him for about ten minutes behind the station and concluded he needed hospital care. The application for a recommendation was signed by the brother, not a Garda, and the GP signed the recommendation.

He was taken by ambulance to hospital. A junior doctor saw him around noon and the consultant phoned to say he should be admitted, but didn't see him in person until more than seven hours later, when the admission order was signed. The Mental Health Commission received it after the 24-hour deadline. He sought release.
MZ v Khattak.q: Do defects in the s.12 process — and later delays — make an involuntary detention unlawful?
dec: High Court, 28 July 2008 (Peart J): release refused. He was lawfully detained under the admission order, despite a somewhat unusual sequence of events.
The application for the recommendation should have been made by a Garda, but the brother's signature didn't justify release.
The GP's ten-minute conversation was too informal a way to conduct the examination, but given his experience there was no reason to doubt the basis of the recommendation.
'As soon as may be' allows some latitude, so the consultant's seven-hour delay — not ideal, and not clearly explained — didn't make the detention unlawful.
The late notice to the Mental Health Commission was a technical breach that didn't affect his rights in any fundamental way.

keys.q: a somewhat unusual sequence of events
keys.w: Peart J

keys.q: too informal manner in which to conduct such an examination
keys.w: Peart J, on the GP's examination

later: The court tolerated the defects here, but each was a breach; a different combination, or a weaker clinical basis, could lead to release.
Mental health law has been under reform; check the current Act and forms before relying on older procedure.
job: When you take a person into custody under s.12, make the application for a medical recommendation yourself, on the correct form, straight away.
Ask the doctor for a proper examination in suitable conditions, and record its time, place and duration.
Don't leave a situation of serious risk overnight without a plan; record the risk factors (weapons, stopped medication, threats) and your reasons for acting or waiting.
MZ v Khattak.law: Yes, on the approach to procedural defects (2008); check current mental health legislation.

src.t: Irish Times — Man legally detained in hospital (High Court, July 2008)

bg: On 18 April 2013 a 17-year-old was drinking with a group of young men in Dublin city centre.
Two Gardaí approached the group. He was very drunk and was warned about the offence of intoxication in public.
While a Garda was speaking to him he pulled down his trousers and underwear. Told to stop, he didn't, and he ran off. He wasn't caught that evening but was later summonsed.

The District Court convicted him of offensive conduct under s.5 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 and placed him on probation for six months. Whether he should first have been warned that failing to desist was an offence went to the High Court.
DPP v Unnamed youth (s.5 offensive condu.q: Must a Garda warn that continuing is an offence before s.5 offensive conduct is complete?
dec: High Court, June 2015 (Kearns P): no warning was required, and the conviction stood.
The defence argued that a s.5 request to desist should carry the same warning as s.8(2), where failing to follow a direction is an offence only if the person disobeys a warning.
But the Act doesn't specifically require a warning to be given first for s.5.
The conduct here was so self-evidently and notoriously criminal that no warning was needed.

keys.q: so self-evidently and so notoriously criminal in nature
keys.w: Kearns P, on the conduct

keys.q: does not specifically require a warning be first given
keys.w: Kearns P, on s.5

later: The ruling leans on how obvious the misconduct was. Where conduct is less clearly offensive, a clear warning remains good practice.
Contrast s.8: a direction to leave or desist must be accompanied by a warning before failure to comply becomes an offence.
job: Outside midnight to 7am, request the person to desist clearly — the request is part of the offence — and record the exact words, time and response.
Add a warning that continuing is an offence; s.5 doesn't require it, but it strengthens the case.
For s.8 directions, always give the warning and record it.

src.t: Irish Times — Court rules garda not required to warn youth (26 June 2015)

bg: The applicant was charged with rape.
Prosecution witnesses referred to the complainant's previous sexual history. He argued that Gardaí had failed to seek out and make available witness statements about it, so his trial would be unfair.
He sought judicial review to prohibit the trial. The High Court refused leave, and he appealed.
DC v DPP.q: When should a trial be prohibited because of an alleged gap in the Garda investigation?
dec: Supreme Court, 21 November 2005 ([2005] IESC 77, Denham J, with McGuinness and McMenamin JJ concurring): appeal dismissed.
Prohibition of a trial succeeds only in exceptional circumstances. The test is whether there is a real or serious risk of an unfair trial.
The onus is on the applicant to show that risk. The court must assess the whole situation; it should not pick out one element and infer a mere possibility of unfairness.
He hadn't established even an arguable case of a serious risk of an unfair trial.
Courts should be slow to interfere with the DPP's decision to bring a prosecution.

keys.q: real or serious risk of an unfair trial
keys.w: Denham J, on the test for prohibition

keys.q: should not merely pick out an element
keys.w: Supreme Court, on assessing the whole situation

later: The same idea — a real risk of an unfair trial that the trial judge can't avoid — runs through later prohibition cases in this app, including McFarlane v DPP (2008) and Nash v DPP (2015).
Evidence of a complainant's previous sexual history is tightly restricted at trial (s.3 of the Criminal Law (Rape) Act 1981), which also bears on what investigators should seek.
job: Pursue reasonable lines of enquiry, including those that may assist the accused, and record decisions not to pursue others, with reasons.
Give the prosecutor everything relevant; the prosecutor and the court decide what is disclosed and admitted.
In sexual offence cases, take advice before seeking material about a complainant's sexual history — it is restricted.
DC v DPP.law: Yes. The standard test for prohibition (2005).

bg: In June 1998 the applicant's car collided with another car in Co Cork, and the other driver died.
Engineers for her concluded that a tyre had deflated and the car went out of her control.
In early December 1998 her solicitor was told the DPP had decided not to prosecute.

The deceased's family wrote asking the DPP to reconsider. The decision was reviewed, and on 23 December 1998 a summons issued for dangerous driving causing death. The DPP's office said it had reviewed the decision at the highest level, but gave no reasons.
The High Court (Kearns J) held the reversal arbitrary and perverse and restrained the prosecution. The DPP appealed.
Eviston v DPP.q: Can the DPP reverse a decision not to prosecute after it has been passed on to the suspect?
dec: Supreme Court, 31 July 2002 ([2002] IESC 62; Keane CJ, Denham, McGuinness and Geoghegan JJ; Murphy J dissenting): the DPP's appeal was dismissed, 4–1. The prosecution could not go ahead.

The DPP is entitled to review an earlier decision not to prosecute and come to a different view. Keane CJ held this could be done even without new evidence, if the DPP believed the first decision was wrong.
But fair procedures apply. There was no new evidence or change of circumstances, and she had not been told the decision could be reviewed. In those circumstances reversing it was unfair.
McGuinness and Geoghegan JJ went further: once she had been told without qualification that there would be no prosecution, reversing that decision breached fair procedures.
Murphy J dissented: as a matter of law the DPP could change his mind and was not barred from prosecuting.

keys.q: was arbitrary and perverse
keys.w: High Court (Kearns J), on the reversal

keys.q: had not been informed that the decision would be reviewed
keys.w: Law report headnote, on why it was unfair

keys.q: entitled as a matter of law to change his mind
keys.w: Law report headnote, on Murphy J's dissent

later: Eviston doesn't stop the DPP reviewing decisions. It turns on fairness in the particular case: what the suspect was told, and whether anything had changed.

Victims now have a right to ask for a review of a decision not to prosecute (EU Victims' Rights Directive, 2012). Passing on a decision as final, without qualification, risks the problem in this case.
job: Never tell a suspect or solicitor there'll be no prosecution unless the decision has been made by the right authority and you're authorised to pass it on.
When passing on a decision not to prosecute, say in writing that it may be reviewed — especially in fatal or serious cases where the family may ask for a review.
Keep the victim's family informed through the proper channels, and record what was said to each side and when.
Eviston v DPP.law: Yes. The leading authority on reversing a communicated decision not to prosecute (2002).

src.t: vLex Ireland — Eviston v DPP [2002] IESC 62
Irish Times — DPP acted unfairly in road death case (1 August 2002)

bg: The applicant was charged with three counts of gross indecency against a relative, alleged to have happened between 1982 and 1985, when the complainant was a teenager.
The complaint to Gardaí came many years later. He was arrested and questioned in July 1999 and later charged.
He sought to prohibit the trial, relying on the complainant's delay in reporting and on further delay by the prosecuting side after the complaint.

The High Court refused to stop the trial for the complainant's delay, but halted it because of blameworthy prosecutorial delay. The DPP appealed, arguing that an accused must show prejudice to the defence.
PM v DPP.q: Can blameworthy delay by the prosecution side stop a trial even where the defence hasn't been prejudiced?
dec: Supreme Court, 5 April 2006 ([2006] IESC 22; Kearns and Geoghegan JJ giving judgments, with Murray CJ, Denham and Hardiman JJ agreeing): the DPP's appeal was dismissed, so the trial stayed halted. The applicant's cross-appeal also failed.
Blameworthy prosecutorial delay does not, by itself, entitle an accused to stop a trial.

The court must balance the accused's interest in being protected from stress and anxiety caused by unnecessary and inexcusable delay against the public interest in prosecuting and convicting offenders, applying the test in PM v Malone.

Prejudice to the defence isn't always needed. Serious blameworthy delay is a factor in its own right, but a short delay won't be enough just because some delay occurred. Stress and anxiety needn't be measured precisely — an innocent person suspected of a sexual offence will naturally suffer some.
Here, about 34 months of delay that the DPP had not adequately explained caused significant extra anxiety, and the balance favoured stopping the trial.

keys.q: a balancing exercise must be carried out
keys.w: Geoghegan J

keys.q: serious blameworthy prosecutorial delay
keys.w: Geoghegan J, on a factor to be weighed in its own right

later: In Devoy v DPP (2008) the Supreme Court approved PM v DPP but allowed the DPP's appeal, so that prosecution went ahead — the balance often favours a trial.
Nash v DPP (2015), in this app, stresses the constitutional value of deciding charges on the merits. Prohibition for delay remains exceptional.
job: Treat historic complaints as urgent: take statements, trace witnesses and records, and get the file to the prosecutor without avoidable gaps.
Record the reason for every period of delay (awaiting records, forensic results, directions). Unexplained gaps count against the State.
Chase outstanding directions and queries. Don't let a file sit.
PM v DPP.law: Yes, as refined in later cases. The leading authority on the balancing test for prosecutorial delay (2006).

Irish Times — DPP's delay in abuse cases not cause for halting trial (6 April 2006)

vLex Ireland — Devoy v DPP [2008] IESC 13

bg: A former teacher faced 50 charges of indecent assault (s.62 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861) involving four boys, aged about 7 to 10, in his care in the mid-1960s.
The complaints to Gardaí came more than 30 years later, and charges were brought from 2001.
He sought to stop the prosecutions, arguing that the lapse of time created a real risk of an unfair trial. The High Court (Ó Caoimh J) refused in July 2004, and he appealed.
SH v DPP.q: When should a trial for historic child sexual abuse be stopped because of delay — and does the reason for the complainant's delay matter?
dec: Supreme Court, 31 July 2006 ([2006] IESC 55; Murray CJ for a unanimous court with Denham, Hardiman, Geoghegan and Fennelly JJ): appeal dismissed. The prosecutions could proceed.

The court reviewed the cases of the previous decade, under which the prosecution had to explain a complainant's delay in reporting — often with psychiatric or psychological evidence, which itself caused long delays in the courts.
It held that the reasons for the complainant's delay are no longer the issue. The question is whether the delay has caused prejudice giving rise to a real or serious risk of an unfair trial.
The onus is on the applicant to establish that prejudice. Without it, only wholly exceptional circumstances would make it unfair to let a trial go ahead.
The court noted that these prosecutions reflected a society only recently able to speak openly about child abuse, and that many victims face real barriers to reporting.
No such prejudice, and no wholly exceptional circumstances, were shown here.

keys.q: wholly exceptional circumstances
keys.w: Supreme Court, on when a trial may still be stopped without proven prejudice

later: SH v DPP replaced the earlier approach and speeded up historic abuse prosecutions. Pre-trial challenges now need concrete prejudice — for example, specific lost evidence or witnesses that would have mattered to the defence.
Read with DC v DPP (2005), PM v DPP (2006) and Nash v DPP (2015) in this app.
job: Don't spend time trying to justify why the victim took years to report — that's no longer the legal question. Record the account, and any reasons they give, in their own words.

Trace what still exists from the time: school or institutional records, rolls, photographs, other pupils and staff. Record what has been lost or destroyed, and who has died or can't be found, with dates.
Check early whether key people are alive and contactable, and take statements promptly. Losses after the complaint can found a prejudice argument.
SH v DPP.law: Yes. The leading Supreme Court test for delay in historic child sexual abuse cases (2006).

Irish Times — Ruling to speed up prosecution of sex abusers (1 August 2006)

bg: In March 1976 the Dublin–Cork mail train was robbed at Sallins, Co Kildare, and about £200,000 was taken. The IRA later claimed the robbery.

The accused was arrested and questioned in Garda custody, and was denied access to a solicitor. He said he was assaulted and eventually signed a confession; Gardaí denied any ill-treatment. Allegations about a Garda 'Heavy Gang' were the subject of a 1977 Amnesty International report.

In 1978 the non-jury Special Criminal Court convicted him and two co-accused, Kelly and McNally, largely on their statements. He was sentenced to 12 years. Kelly had left the jurisdiction during the trial and was convicted in his absence.
People (DPP) v Breathnach.q: Can a confession be relied on where the suspect was denied a solicitor and questioned in oppressive conditions?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, May 1980 ((1981) 2 Frewen 43; Finlay P presiding): the convictions of Breathnach and McNally were quashed and both were released. Breathnach had served about 18 months.

The prosecution must prove a statement was voluntary. The court couldn't be satisfied that their statements were, and ruled that his confession had been obtained under oppression, so the statements were inadmissible.
The court described the denial of access to a solicitor while he was in custody as inexcusable.
Court of Appeal, 21 July 2026 (Kennedy J for a three-judge court): a certificate of miscarriage of justice was granted under s.9 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993, with costs.

The newly discovered fact came from another man questioned in 1976 but never charged. He said he had been forced to sign a statement Gardaí concocted, and produced alibi evidence. A later review had also concluded that a prosecution would have been unlikely on the later information.

The DPP accepted that the accused had no part in the robbery. The court said that concession implies actual innocence, and stressed that the application rested on evidence of innocence, not only on procedural defects.

later: The 2026 certificate followed a later review of the case that found significant concerns about the reliability of the evidence. The accused and the Irish Council for Civil Liberties called for an independent public inquiry.

The modern protections go further: a suspect has a constitutional right to legal advice before questioning (People (DPP) v Gormley and White, 2014, in this app), interviews are electronically recorded, and treatment in custody is governed by the Custody Regulations.
job: Arrange a solicitor promptly when one is requested, record the request and each step, and don't start questioning until legal advice has been obtained — unless a recognised exception applies and is recorded.
Record interviews electronically and in full. Never draft, prompt or 'tidy up' a statement for a suspect to sign.
Keep the custody record accurate — times, breaks, meals, rest, visits and complaints — and report any allegation of ill-treatment at once.
Test every admission against independent evidence. A confession with nothing to support it is a warning sign, not the end of the investigation.
People (DPP) v Breathnach.law: Yes. An early landmark on oppression and solicitor access (1980); certified a miscarriage of justice in 2026.

bg: In December 2014 Gardaí saw the accused driving in convoy with another man, who was found with two improvised explosive devices.

In June 2017 the Special Criminal Court convicted him of IRA membership. The prosecution relied in part on the belief evidence of a senior Garda officer. The officer assured the court that his belief wasn't affected by the book of evidence — but he hadn't seen it.

In June 2018 the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction: the intelligence behind the belief overlapped with the book of evidence, so the same material risked being counted twice. At a retrial in 2019 he was acquitted; the court couldn't rely on the belief evidence because the officer wasn't independent of the investigation. He had served 14 months.

In April 2021 the Special Criminal Court certified a miscarriage of justice under s.9 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993. The DPP sought judicial review; the High Court (Simons J) dismissed it in December 2023, and the DPP appealed.
DPP v Special Criminal Court (Connolly).q: Does a senior Garda's careless assurance about the basis of belief evidence, which contributed to a wrongful conviction, justify a certificate of miscarriage of justice?
dec: Special Criminal Court, April 2021: the officer's assurance had given the trial court false comfort that double counting didn't arise, and that court would probably have acquitted had the issue been considered. He had been careless, not knowingly misleading, but this was a grave defect in the administration of justice.

High Court, December 2023 (Simons J): the DPP's challenge failed. A certificate doesn't require the person to prove factual innocence, and can rest on a grave defect in the administration of justice. The presumption of innocence stands after an acquittal.
Court of Appeal, 31 July 2026 (O'Moore J giving judgment): the DPP's appeal was allowed and the certificate quashed — reported as the first time the Court of Appeal has overturned such a certificate.

Granting the certificate was not an option reasonably open to the Special Criminal Court. The officer's carelessness, though regrettable, was not a basis for a certificate, and there was no finding of improper, deliberate conduct by the State.
The acquittal is untouched. The 2026 ruling concerns only the certificate, which would have opened the way to compensation.

keys.q: grave defect in the administration of justice
keys.w: Special Criminal Court (2021)

keys.q: seriously incomplete and misleading
keys.w: Special Criminal Court, on the officer's assurance

later: However the certificate question ends, the conviction was lost because of how the belief evidence was given, and the case took more than a decade to resolve.

Belief evidence is still used in membership trials (see People (DPP) v Kelly (2006) and Redmond v Ireland (2015) in this app). Here the retrial court rejected it because the officer wasn't independent of the investigation and the basis of his belief overlapped with the other evidence. See also People (DPP) v Banks (2022) on membership arrests.
job: If you give belief evidence, know exactly what your belief rests on — and what is in the book of evidence — before you swear that one doesn't depend on the other.
Keep a record of the intelligence material reviewed, when, and by whom, separate from the investigation file.
If your evidence proves incomplete or inaccurate, correct it at once through the prosecutor. Never leave a court with a false assurance.
DPP v Special Criminal Court (Connolly).law: The acquittal stands. The July 2026 Court of Appeal ruling quashed only the miscarriage of justice certificate; check for any further appeal.

bg: In September 2019 a man was killed at his home in Cork. The killing followed a long-running dispute over a family home, which had been before the civil courts.

The accused was found to have used a billhook in the attack: his blood was on the handle and the victim's on the blade. A taxi driver found blood in his cab after carrying the accused and a co-accused, and a DNA sample taken from the accused by Gardaí matched it.

Gardaí obtained search warrants from a District Judge who heard the application in chambers, where there were no recording facilities. The defence said the detective was unclear about the oath administered.
In December 2021 a jury at the Central Criminal Court sitting in Cork convicted him of murder and burglary. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and appealed against the murder conviction.
DPP v O'Hara.q: Was a DNA sample admissible where the authorising Gardaí allegedly didn't state their grounds — and must a search warrant application be recorded?
dec: Court of Appeal, 26 March 2026 ([2026] IECA 65; McCarthy J giving judgment, with Collins and Owens JJ): appeal dismissed.

DNA: the defence argued the sample wasn't taken in accordance with s.13 of the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014, because a sergeant and a superintendent didn't state the grounds on which authorisation was sought or granted — breaching his constitutional right to bodily integrity.

The superintendent's authorisation rested on reasonable suspicion of the accused's involvement and a belief that the samples would confirm or disprove it. The court held the reasonable grounds were plainly present, the superintendent had sufficient grounds, and the Garda evidence had been tested in cross-examination. The trial judge was entitled to admit the evidence.
Search warrants: there is no requirement that a Garda's application for a warrant be recorded. The District Judge heard the application reasonably and rightly granted the warrants on their merits.
A co-accused's separate appeal, about the wording of a detective's oath for a search warrant, had already failed in June 2024.

keys.q: plainly and unequivocally present
keys.w: McCarthy J, on the grounds for the DNA sample

keys.q: no meaningful proposition that the order was unreasonably made
keys.w: McCarthy J

later: The court looked at substance: grounds that existed, and were proved at trial, were enough despite the complaint that they hadn't been stated.

Read with the search warrant cases in this app (Simple Imports, Damache, Quirke (No 2), and DPP v Unnamed (oath on warrant information, 2024) — the co-accused's appeal): the warrant itself must still comply with its statute.
job: When seeking or giving an authorisation for a sample, record the grounds at the time: the offence, the suspicion, and why the sample will confirm or disprove involvement.
Tell the suspect what is being taken and why, and record that you did.
When swearing information for a warrant, make sure the oath is properly administered, and note who administered it, where and when — especially if heard in chambers.

bg: In September 2019 a man was killed in Cork after a long-running family dispute over the family home.
A search warrant was issued on 10 September 2019 on a detective's sworn information, heard by a District Judge. The application wasn't recorded.
In December 2021 the man's sister was convicted of his murder at the Central Criminal Court sitting in Cork, and received the mandatory life sentence.

On appeal she argued the warrant was unlawful. The information hadn't been sworn as the law requires: the words of the detective's oath covered answers to any questions the judge might ask, not the information itself. She also complained that the application wasn't recorded.
DPP v Unnamed (oath on warrant informati.q: Is a search warrant invalid because the detective's oath was worded to cover answers to the judge's questions, rather than the information itself?
dec: Court of Appeal, 6 June 2024 (Ní Raifeartaigh J for a three-judge court): appeal dismissed. The conviction stands.
The statutory requirement that the information be given on oath was met: the detective took an oath before the information was read to the judge.

An oath's purpose is to impress on the witness the duty to tell the truth, and that purpose was achieved. Read sensibly, the oath implicitly covered the information read to the judge, not just answers to questions.
Quashing a murder conviction over a particular formula of words would be an absurd triumph of form over substance.
Recording the basis on which a warrant is granted is best practice, but there is no legal requirement to note everything said, and the lack of a recording caused no harm.

keys.q: an absurd triumph of form over substance
keys.w: Ní Raifeartaigh J

later: The co-accused's appeal — on a DNA sample and on warrant applications heard in chambers — failed in March 2026. See DPP v O'Hara in this app.
Contrast Simple Imports (2000) in this app: a warrant that shows on its face that the statutory test wasn't applied can be fatal. Here the substance of the oath was there.
job: Make sure the oath covers the information you are swearing — not just answers to questions — and is taken before you read it to the judge.
Keep your own note of the application: date, time, place (courtroom or chambers), the judge, who administered the oath, and any questions asked and answers given.
Check that the information and the warrant match the statute before you leave the court.
DPP v Unnamed (oath on warrant informati.law: Yes. Court of Appeal authority (June 2024) — substance over form on the oath.

bg: The accused was charged with two sexual assaults said to have happened in summer 1991, at locations in the West of Ireland.
He said his wife would confirm that the complainant didn't stay at their home on the night between the two incidents — which, he argued, would undermine her account of the second assault, in a car.
Gardaí didn't take a statement from the wife, saying she was unwell. She died before the trial.
In 2024 a jury at Galway Circuit Court unanimously convicted him on both counts, and he was sentenced to two years. He appealed, arguing the missing statement made his trial unfair.
DPP v Unnamed (witness not interviewed,.q: Does the Garda failure to take a statement from a potential defence witness, who has since died, make the trial unfair?
dec: Court of Appeal, 5 May 2026 (Burns J for a three-judge court): the ground failed.
The court accepted that the missing statement was the fault of the investigating force: an effort should have been made to speak to her, even though she was unwell.
But it was uncertain whether her statement would have been admissible at trial, given her death. And his own account of what she would have said was put before the jury.
The trial judge warned the jury to take account of the delay and the lost evidence.

Crucially, the complainant was never challenged on whether she stayed at the accused's home. A party who doesn't contest the main evidence on an issue can't then argue that missing material on that issue makes the trial unsafe — an insuperable difficulty for the appellant.
The trial was imperfect, but the court held it could not be said that an unfairness arose.

keys.q: insuperable difficulty for the appellant
keys.w: Burns J

keys.q: it cannot be said that an unfairness arose
keys.w: Burns J

later: The investigators were found at fault; the conviction survived because of how the defence ran the trial. A different trial could have ended differently.

Read with DPP v SQ (2023) in this app — the Supreme Court's 'lost chance of acquittal' test for evidence Gardaí failed to collect — and with Braddish v DPP and Dunne v DPP on the duty to seek out and preserve evidence.
job: When a suspect or anyone else names a witness who could support the suspect's account, make a real effort to get a statement.
If a witness is unwell, try again later, take a short statement, or ask whether they can be seen at home or in hospital — and record every attempt and the reason it failed.
In historic cases, treat elderly or ill witnesses as urgent: their evidence can be lost for good.

bg: On Christmas Eve 2007 a man was arrested in Carrick-on-Suir, Co Tipperary, while travelling in a car with three others. A rucksack beside him contained six bars of cannabis resin.
He was detained at a Garda station. During the detention the shift changed and a new member in charge took over. The incoming member didn't satisfy himself that continued detention was necessary.
The trial judge held the detention unlawful from that point and ruled the man's statement inadmissible. He was acquitted.

The DPP referred the point to the Supreme Court, without prejudice to the acquittal: did s.4(2) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 require a relieving member in charge to consider whether there were reasonable grounds for both the original detention and its continuation?
DPP v Roche (2015).q: Does a detention become unlawful when a new member in charge takes over and doesn't re-satisfy himself that it's still necessary?
dec: Supreme Court, July 2015 ([2015] IESC 67; 4–1 majority): the detention was lawful.
Nothing had happened during the detention to change the original reason for it. In those circumstances the change of member in charge didn't make the continued detention unlawful.
The trial judge was therefore wrong to exclude the statement on that ground.
Because the reference was made without prejudice to the acquittal, the acquittal stood.
later: The ruling rests on the absence of any change in circumstances. If something happens during a detention that affects the grounds — new information, an admission, a decision not to charge — the member in charge must act on it.
The Custody Regulations (1987) still require the member in charge to keep the custody record and oversee the detainee's treatment throughout.
Read with DPP v McGuire (member in charge, 1996) in this app: the member in charge is whoever is actually in charge — a question of fact.
job: At handover, the incoming member in charge should read the custody record, confirm the grounds for detention still apply, and record that review with the time.
Record anything that might affect the grounds — new information, an admission, an alibi checked — and decide promptly whether detention is still necessary.
Never let a detention run on autopilot: the reasons and the timeline must be clear from the record.

bg: The accused was tried for rape in the Central Criminal Court. His defence was that the sexual activity was consensual.
The evidence included medical and forensic evidence and text messages he sent shortly afterwards, including one apologising and asking for forgiveness.

About 20 to 22 hours after the incident, before making her statement, the complainant met a work colleague and his girlfriend. They went with her to the Garda station, and the girlfriend stayed with her while she made her statement.
Neither was asked for their details, and no statements were taken. The prosecution didn't know of them either; the defence learned of them only from her victim impact statement at sentencing.
The Court of Appeal accepted that Gardaí should have sought them out, but held any unfairness was entirely speculative, as no one knew what they would have said, and dismissed the appeal.
DPP v SQ.q: When Gardaí fail to collect evidence the defence never knew about, how does an appeal court decide whether the trial was fair?
dec: Supreme Court, 31 March 2023 ([2023] IESC 8; Baker J giving judgment, with Dunne, Charleton, O'Malley and Woulfe JJ): appeal dismissed. The conviction stands.

The duty to seek out, preserve and disclose evidence is central to fair trial rights. The State must take reasonable and proportionate steps — and here it plainly fell short: the companions' presence was obvious and their details easy to get.
Where the State's failure left the defence unaware of the evidence, it is unfair to require the accused to show what it would have said. The Court of Appeal was wrong to impose that requirement.
Instead the court assesses the fairness of the trial as a whole, the role the missing evidence could have played, and whether there was a chance of a lost acquittal.

Recent complaint evidence isn't evidence of the facts; it goes only to consistency. Its value to the defence would have been limited, and there was significant evidence beyond the complainant's account. The trial wasn't unfair.

keys.q: central to, and supports, fair trial rights
keys.w: Baker J, on the duty to seek out and preserve evidence

keys.q: a chance of a lost acquittal
keys.w: Baker J, on the test on appeal

keys.q: entirely speculative
keys.w: Court of Appeal — the approach the Supreme Court rejected

later: The court reaffirmed Braddish v DPP: the duty covers evidence that may help either side, limited by what is necessary and practicable (Murphy v DPP).
See also DPP v Unnamed (witness not interviewed, 2026) in this app, where the Court of Appeal again found Gardaí at fault but upheld the conviction.
job: Record the name and contact details of anyone who comes to the station with a complainant, or is with them soon after the incident, and note what they saw or were told.
Take statements from early-complaint witnesses — friends, colleagues or family who heard the account first — and pass them to the prosecutor.
Tell the prosecutor about anyone present while the complainant's statement was taken.

bg: On 19 March 2010 two raiders hid in the ceiling of a bookmaker's in Swords, Co Dublin, and dropped down about 35 minutes later to rob it. A passing car was hijacked at gunpoint and later abandoned in Finglas.
A phone dropped at the scene was linked to a number the accused had given in a passport application, and to phones found on him when arrested.

A detective who had worked in Finglas for 17 years — and had met the accused on patrols and arrested him before — viewed the CCTV at a Garda station. No suspect was named to him; he was told only that there had been a robbery and the getaway car was found in Finglas. He said he was 100 per cent certain it was the accused.

No contemporaneous notes or record were kept of the viewing or the procedure. The Special Criminal Court convicted him in May 2021, and he appealed on the single ground that the recognition evidence should not have been admitted.
DPP v Byrne (2024).q: Is a Garda's recognition of a suspect on CCTV admissible when no record was kept of how the footage was shown?
dec: Court of Appeal, 23 July 2024 ([2024] IECA 218; Edwards J giving judgment, with McCarthy and Kennedy JJ): appeal dismissed.
Recognition evidence — a witness who knows the person recognising them — is distinct from identification of a stranger, following DPP v Tynan (2017).
The recognition evidence was relevant and probative and was properly admitted.

The trial court acknowledged the defence criticisms, including the absence of contemporaneous notes, and weighed them in assessing the evidence. It warned itself about the dangers of recognition evidence.

It could safely rely on the evidence because high-quality CCTV footage and stills were available to test the witness's reliability. Its approach was impeccable; the trial was satisfactory and the conviction safe.

keys.q: impeccable
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on the trial court's approach

keys.q: 100 per cent certain
keys.w: The detective, on his recognition

later: The State argued — and the outcome reflects — that the missing record went to weight, not admissibility, here. With poorer footage or no supporting evidence, the lack of a record could matter far more.

See DPP v Tynan in this app — the 2017 recognition case Byrne followed, whose conviction was later quashed and certified a miscarriage of justice — and DPP v Unnamed (informal ID parade, 2022) and People (AG) v Casey (No 2).
job: Before asking a Garda to view CCTV for recognition, don't name or hint at a suspect. Record exactly what the viewer was told.
Keep a viewing log: who showed the footage, when and where, which clips and stills, for how long, and the viewer's exact words and level of certainty.
Record how the viewer knows the person — how often, in what context, and when they last saw them. That's what the court will test.

bg: On 13 December 2012 three men attacked customers in a bookmaker's in Tallaght, in the context of a feud. Two men pleaded guilty.
The prosecution case against the accused rested on one witness: a Garda who identified him from the bookmaker's CCTV. The accused always denied it.

A Garda bulletin circulating the CCTV hadn't produced an identification of him — including by the Garda who later identified him. An internal Garda email naming suspected brothers and their associates wasn't disclosed to the defence, and notes of the identification process weren't kept.

He was convicted in the Circuit Criminal Court and sentenced in January 2017 to four years, with the final year suspended. In July 2017 the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, which focused on the dangers of visual identification ([2017] IECA 202).
Months later another man came forward and made a statement claiming to be the third attacker. The case was referred to UK experts in visual identification.
DPP v Tynan.q: How far can a conviction rest on a Garda's recognition of a suspect on CCTV — and what happens when it proves wrong?
dec: Court of Appeal, July 2017 ([2017] IECA 202): appeal dismissed. The court treated the Garda's evidence as recognition evidence — distinct from identification of a stranger — an approach later followed in DPP v Byrne (2024).

Court of Appeal, April 2018: the conviction was quashed under s.2 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993. The DPP didn't oppose, without conceding the facts. No retrial was ordered. He had served about 11 months.
Court of Appeal, 28 July 2023 (McCarthy J giving judgment): a certificate of miscarriage of justice was granted. The miscarriage was not in controversy.

An expert evaluation by the UK Metropolitan Police, comparing photographs of the accused and of the man who came forward with CCTV stills, confirmed his innocence. Without it, the civil standard for a certificate would not have been met.

The core issue was the Garda identification process, together with a lack of disclosure material that could have helped the defence test its reliability. The court made no criticism of the investigation itself: the identifying Garda's opinion was honestly held and in good faith.

keys.q: one witness case

later: At the 2023 hearing the State accepted that the undisclosed material should have been disclosed, and said the real failing was that notes weren't kept.
Read with DPP v Byrne (2024) in this app: recognition from CCTV is admissible, but it is only as reliable as the record of how it was made.
job: Record every CCTV viewing for recognition: who showed it, when, what the viewer was told, what was shown, and the viewer's words — including any earlier occasion when they saw the footage or a bulletin and didn't recognise anyone.
Give the prosecutor all material bearing on identity, including internal emails or intelligence naming other suspects.
Where a case rests on a single recognition, look for supporting or undermining evidence (phones, forensics, alibis, other witnesses) before charging, and consider an expert image comparison.

bg: In April 2008 the applicant arrived at Dublin Airport with children she said she had been asked to bring with her.

She was arrested and charged under s.12 of the Immigration Act 2004 with failing to produce a passport or equivalent document, and failing to give a satisfactory explanation. She was later re-arrested, charged again and granted bail; she never produced any documents.
Section 12 let a Garda or immigration officer demand a passport from any non-national. Failing to produce one without a satisfactory explanation was an offence punishable by up to a year in prison.
She applied for asylum and brought judicial review proceedings challenging s.12. The Irish Human Rights Commission appeared as amicus curiae.
Dokie v DPP.q: Was it constitutional to make failing to produce a passport 'without satisfactory explanation' a crime?
dec: High Court, 25 March 2011 (Kearns P): s.12 was declared inconsistent with Article 38.1 (trial in due course of law) and Article 40.4.1 (personal liberty) of the Constitution.
'Satisfactory explanation' was undefined. That created uncertainty and room for arbitrary application by individual Gardaí, failing the basic requirements of a criminal offence.
The explanation appeared to form part of the offence itself rather than a defence. It would have been clearer to frame it as a defence, as British legislation does.
Silence could be treated as a failure to give a satisfactory explanation, potentially breaching the right not to incriminate oneself.

The court accepted that the State has a right and duty to control the movement of non-nationals, and that a criminal sanction for having no passport on entry is not in itself disproportionate. But on the facts, s.11 (entry requirements) would have been more appropriate.

keys.q: serious problems faced by immigration authorities
keys.w: Kearns P, accepting the State's difficulty

later: Section 34 of the Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2011 (August 2011) amended s.12. A non-national can be required to produce a valid passport or equivalent document to establish that their presence in the State isn't in breach of s.5. Failing to do so is an offence, but it's a defence to prove reasonable cause for not complying.
Under-16s are excluded, and EEA nationals and their family members exercising EU free movement rights are excluded from ss.11 and 12.
job: Use s.12 only for its purpose — establishing whether the person's presence in the State is lawful — and record why you made the demand.
Don't apply it to under-16s or to people exercising EU free movement rights. Check the current text of the section.
Note any explanation the person gives. Whether it amounts to reasonable cause is for the court.
Dokie v DPP.law: No for the original s.12 (struck down in 2011). The amended s.12 applies.

bg: The accused was convicted of IRA membership by the non-jury Special Criminal Court in November 2003 and jailed for four years.

Under s.3(2) of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1972, a Chief Superintendent's belief that a person is a member of an unlawful organisation is evidence of membership. The prosecution relied in part on such a belief.
The officer claimed privilege over the sources of his belief without further explanation, so the defence couldn't test them in cross-examination.
The Court of Criminal Appeal certified the point for the Supreme Court.
People (DPP) v Kelly (2006).q: Is a conviction fair where it rests partly on a senior Garda's belief whose sources are kept from the defence?
dec: Supreme Court, 2006 (Fennelly J for a unanimous court of five): appeal dismissed. The conviction stood.
The right to cross-examine one's accusers is essential to a fair trial, but it can be restricted in the interests of overall balance and the efficiency of the criminal justice system.

Belief evidence was justified: it applies only to dangerous organisations, such senior officers are presumed to have high integrity, and the Special Criminal Court is presumed to apply high standards of fairness.
Restricting the accused's access to the identity of the sources — to protect informants and potential witnesses — went no further than strictly necessary.

The Special Criminal Court had sufficient other evidence of membership. It should have explained the weight it gave the officer's belief, especially as privilege was claimed without explanation, but there was no overall unfairness.
later: The ruling cleared the way for pending membership trials. In 2015 the Supreme Court upheld s.3(2) against a direct constitutional challenge — see Redmond v Ireland in this app.
The Connolly certificate case (2026) in this app shows the risk when the basis of a belief overlaps with the other evidence.
job: Build membership cases on independent evidence; don't rely on belief evidence to carry the case.
If privilege is to be claimed over the sources of a belief, raise it with the prosecutor in advance so it can be properly justified to the court.
Keep the material underlying a belief organised, dated and separate from the investigation file.
People (DPP) v Kelly (2006).law: Yes. Supreme Court authority (2006), confirmed by Redmond v Ireland (2015).

bg: The applicant was convicted of IRA membership by the Special Criminal Court. The trial focused on forensic evidence linking him to weapons.

The court also relied on a Chief Superintendent's belief that he was a member, admissible under s.3(2) of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1972. The sources of the belief were privileged.
He never challenged the truth of the belief, sought access to the underlying material, or gave evidence at trial.

He argued that s.3(2) breached his right to a fair trial under Article 38.1: the informants would never testify, and a Chief Superintendent could be misled by bogus information yet still appear credible.
Redmond v Ireland.q: Is it constitutional to allow a senior Garda's belief, based on secret sources, to be evidence of membership of an unlawful organisation?
dec: Supreme Court, December 2015 (Charleton J giving judgment): the challenge failed and s.3(2) was upheld.

Belief evidence has no special status. It is merely admissible and can be rejected, contradicted or challenged like any other evidence. The officer isn't presumed truthful: credibility and expertise can be tested in cross-examination.
The statute doesn't require corroboration, but a practice has developed of not convicting on belief evidence alone.

Undisclosed material doesn't by itself make a trial unfair. The defence can ask the prosecution and the court to examine it for anything bearing on innocence, and privilege can yield where the material could raise a reasonable doubt.

The court stressed the danger to informers in the IRA context. The provision applies only in the Special Criminal Court, for membership of an unlawful organisation, with a written ruling — it isn't a precedent for belief evidence elsewhere.
The court must still be satisfied of guilt beyond reasonable doubt on all the evidence. Where belief evidence is supported by other evidence, s.3(2) complies with Article 38.

keys.q: complies with article 38 of the Constitution
keys.w: Supreme Court, on s.3(2)

later: Read with People (DPP) v Kelly (2006) in this app, on privilege over the sources of a belief, and the Connolly certificate case (2026) on double counting.
job: Treat belief evidence as support, not a substitute: gather independent evidence of membership — forensics, surveillance, association, conduct.
A senior officer giving belief evidence should expect cross-examination on credibility and expertise, and be clear about what the belief rests on.
Keep the underlying material organised so the court can examine it if asked, and flag anything that could help the defence to the prosecutor.
Redmond v Ireland.law: Yes. The leading Supreme Court authority (2015) on the constitutionality of belief evidence.
