bg: In July 2016 a man was shot dead outside a shop in Dublin 8. The shop's CCTV fixed the time of the shooting at 4.11pm.

The prosecution relied on CCTV from multiple locations showing four vehicles operating together before and after the shooting. The accused's car drove past the shop about four minutes before — described at trial as a final check.
His fingerprints and DNA were found in two cars used in the attack, and inferences were drawn from his silence in interview. He was arrested in 2017 after flying into Dublin.

Gardaí gave evidence recognising him on a disputed piece of footage. One officer's statements were undated, he kept no notes of the basis for his recognition, and he had viewed other footage from the investigation first — which he denied influenced him. A second officer's statement was dated about four months after the killing.

After a 12-day trial the Special Criminal Court convicted him of murder in 2018. On appeal he challenged the recognition evidence and the quality of the footage, and argued the CCTV breached his privacy and data protection rights.
DPP v Thompson (2024).q: Was Garda recognition evidence from CCTV reliable enough despite gaps in the record — and did gathering the CCTV breach his privacy?
dec: Court of Appeal, 30 January 2024 ([2024] IECA 22; Ní Raifeartaigh J giving judgment, with Birmingham P and Edwards J): appeal dismissed on all grounds. He continues to serve a life sentence.
The court rejected the arguments that the footage was of insufficient quality and that the lack of Garda records relating to the identification made the evidence unsafe. The CCTV was admissible.

There was no breach of privacy. People walking on a public street, driving on a public road or eating in a public restaurant cannot reasonably expect their movements to be immune from CCTV observation in the current day and age.

keys.q: immune from CCTV observation
keys.w: Ní Raifeartaigh J, on privacy in public places

later: Later judgments cite Thompson for the admissibility of CCTV from public spaces, and for the point that privacy rights and data protection breaches are distinct questions.
Decided the same day as DPP v Dunbar (CCTV and privacy). Read with DPP v Byrne (2024) and DPP v Tynan on recording how a recognition was made.
job: Date every statement, and record the basis for any recognition at the time: how you know the person, how often you've seen them, and when last.
Log each viewing: what footage you saw, in what order, and what you'd been told — especially any footage viewed before the clip you identify from.
Build the case on several strands (CCTV movements, forensics, phones), so it doesn't rest on recognition alone.

bg: In September 2018 a Garda stopped the accused in Co Clare. He held a learner permit but not a driving licence, and no qualified driver was with him.

He produced a certificate of insurance. The Garda gave evidence that an employee of the insurer had told him the insurer would compensate any third party for a loss, but would seek to recover the cost from the driver.
He pleaded guilty to unlicensed driving, but denied using the vehicle without insurance (s.56(1) of the Road Traffic Act 1961).

The District Judge took the view that a policy only operates if the driver holds a licence; a learner permit is a conditional licence, the condition wasn't met, so he wasn't insured. He stated a case to the High Court asking whether he was right to uphold the charge.
DPP v Sherlock.q: Is an unaccompanied learner driver who holds an insurance certificate automatically 'uninsured' because the permit's conditions weren't met?
dec: High Court, June 2020 ([2020] IEHC 362, Humphreys J): the answer to the case stated was no — he couldn't be convicted under s.56(1) on that evidence.
The real question is whether an approved policy of insurance was in force covering the user at the time. That depends on the wording of the policy, not on whether the driver held a valid licence.
Whether a policy condition was breached must be proved in each case, by admissible evidence.

The insurer's employee's account, relayed by the Garda, was inadmissible hearsay. Even if admitted, it showed only that the insurer would seek recovery from the insured, not that it would refuse to indemnify him.
The judge noted that s.56(1) had been replaced by s.34 of the Road Traffic Act 2004, but the replacement had never been commenced — an unhappy situation that had lasted 16 years.

keys.q: inadmissible hearsay
keys.w: Humphreys J, on the insurer's account relayed by the Garda

keys.q: an unhappy situation
keys.w: Humphreys J, on the uncommenced replacement section

later: It applied DPP v Spendlove (2014), in this app: an unaccompanied learner is liable for the licensing offence, but isn't uninsured unless the policy itself makes cover depend on the permit's conditions.
The outcome turns on each policy's wording: where a policy expressly excludes or conditions cover for learners, a breach can be proved with the right evidence.
The court welcomed the DPP's suggestion that District Court audio recordings be attached to cases stated, to avoid disputes about what evidence was given below.
job: Get a copy of the policy, or a statement from the insurer identifying the clause relied on (for example, a condition that learners must be accompanied).
Take the insurer's evidence formally, in a statement or certificate, rather than relaying a phone call in your own evidence.
Record the permit details and the absence of an accompanying driver, and prosecute the licensing offence separately.
DPP v Sherlock.law: Yes. High Court authority (2020) — check the current wording of the insurance offence.

bg: On 19 November 2012 a Garda stopped the accused driving in Kilrush, Co Clare.
He produced an insurance certificate that appeared valid, and a learner permit issued the previous month. He had never held a driving licence of any kind.
He had no L-plates and no qualified driver with him, as the learner permit conditions require.
The insurance certificate covered him 'provided that the person holds a licence to drive such a vehicle or, having held such a licence, is not disqualified'.

He was charged with driving without insurance (s.56 RTA 1961), failing to produce an insurance certificate (s.69), and driving without a licence (s.38). The District Judge stated a consultative case to the High Court.
DPP v Spendlove.q: Does an unaccompanied learner, driving in breach of the permit's conditions, drive without a licence — and without insurance?
dec: High Court, 20 November 2014 ([2014] IEHC 558, McDermott J).

A learner permit has effect under s.35(4) in accordance with its terms and conditions. The usual answer to a s.38 charge is that a permit was in force and authorised the driving — but driving without L-plates or a qualified accompanying driver isn't authorised. He was liable to conviction for driving without a licence.
The insurance certificate wasn't made conditional on complying with the learner permit's terms. He was therefore insured on the day, and there was no s.56 offence.
The court distinguished a Northern Irish authority (McGimpsey v Carlin, 1969) as entirely distinguishable, relying instead on the Irish statutory scheme.

keys.q: entirely distinguishable
keys.w: McDermott J, on the Northern Irish authority

later: DPP v Sherlock (2020), in this app, applied Spendlove: whether a learner is insured turns on the wording of the policy, and any breach of a policy condition must be proved by admissible evidence.
job: At the roadside, check and record the permit, L-plates and whether a qualified driver is present.
Read the insurance certificate's wording before deciding on a no-insurance charge, and note any clause about permits or accompanied driving.
If the policy wording is unclear, get a statement from the insurer before charging.
DPP v Spendlove.law: Yes. High Court authority (2014), followed in 2020.

bg: In August 1994 Gardaí running a radar speed check recorded a motorcycle at 80 mph. It didn't stop — it sped up.
Gardaí pursued it, and a roadblock was attempted. The motorcycle went around the roadblock and continued through Cashel. The pursuing car lost sight of it.
On a bend the motorcycle crossed onto the wrong side of the road and struck an oncoming car, whose driver was not at fault. The plaintiff, a pillion passenger, was severely injured.
Gardaí had no information that the occupants had committed a crime, though one officer had a gut instinct that something serious might have happened.

The plaintiff sued the Minister for Finance as the Gardaí's employer, claiming the pursuit made the driver panic and speed. The High Court found for her, holding that the pursuit caused the excessive speed.
Hayes v Minister for Finance.q: Do Gardaí owe a duty of care to the occupants of a vehicle they pursue after it fails to stop — and were they liable for the crash?
dec: Supreme Court, 23 February 2007 ([2007] IESC 8; Kearns J giving judgment, with Hardiman and Finnegan JJ): the State's appeal was allowed and the High Court's finding overturned.
The motorcyclist's failure to stop gave the Gardaí a reasonable and genuinely held suspicion of criminal activity.
Pursuing the vehicle in the course of their duty to detect and prevent crime did not breach any duty owed to its occupants.

The trial judge was wrong to treat the pursuit as one seamless unitary process. There was no breach of duty over the final stretch either, even treating the passenger as an involuntary participant by then.
In any event, the plaintiff's injuries were caused by the motorcyclist's driving.

keys.q: one seamless unitary process
keys.w: The trial judge's approach, which the Supreme Court rejected

later: Applied in Galazka v Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform (2024), in this app: breaching Garda policy isn't automatically negligence — but an unnecessary, risky stop can be.
job: Before and during a pursuit, weigh the suspected offence against the risk to the public, the occupants and yourself.
Follow the Garda Code and current pursuit policy, and keep control informed throughout.
Record why you started, continued and ended the pursuit, with times and locations.

bg: Gardaí received information about an aggravated burglary and followed two suspect vehicles. Neither was involved in the burglary; one was the plaintiff's car.

A Garda in an Armed Support Unit Audi Q7 began a 'compliant stop' to halt the plaintiff. The Audi approached from his right rear and, he said, cut across his path as he neared a roundabout. The front right of his car struck the Audi's left rear wheel.
He said he hadn't seen the flashing lights. The court accepted that, given how briefly the Audi had been behind him.

He sued the State. Duty of care and causation weren't disputed; the issues were breach — measured against the Garda Code's provisions on chasing and stopping vehicles — and contributory negligence. The case reached the High Court on appeal from the Circuit Court.
Galazka v Minister for Public Expenditur.q: Were Gardaí negligent in how and where they carried out a 'compliant stop'?
dec: High Court, 2024 ([2024] IEHC 266, O'Connor J): the State was fully liable, and damages of €10,070 were awarded.
Applying Hayes v Minister for Finance (2007): Gardaí must balance arresting suspects against protecting the public, and a breach of policy isn't automatically negligence.
But there was no satisfactory explanation for stopping the plaintiff before the roundabout rather than letting him proceed through it. Under the Garda Code, taking that risk wasn't imperative.
No adequate regard was paid to the Code's advice to tail suspects, or to the road conditions at the roundabout. The court assessed events without hindsight, as the Gardaí would have faced them.
The plaintiff wasn't negligent: his reaction was reasonable, and the Garda car had entered his blind spot.
later: Read with Hayes v Minister for Finance (2007) in this app: pursuing a vehicle that fails to stop isn't negligent in itself, but the manner and place of a stop are judged on the facts.
job: Before a compliant stop, ask whether it's imperative now, or whether you can tail the vehicle to a safer place.
Avoid junctions, roundabouts and bends, and give the driver time to see and react to lights and sirens.
Record the reasons for the stop, the location chosen and the manoeuvre, following the Garda Code and current policy on stopping vehicles.

bg: On 17 November 2014, at about 9.40pm, a double-decker bus turned at a T-junction in Dublin 4. The prosecution's evidence was that the bus appeared to cut the corner.
The bus knocked a cyclist off her bicycle. She died two days later from head injuries.
In October 2018 a jury in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court convicted the driver of careless driving causing death. He was disqualified from driving for four years.
After retiring, the jury asked for the legal principles in layman's terms; the judge re-charged them using terms such as 'appreciable', 'due care and attention' and 'prudent'.
On appeal he argued the re-charge confused the jury, that there was no evidence of phone use, conversation or other distraction, and that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence.
DPP v Irabor.q: What must be shown for careless driving causing death — and was the jury properly directed?
dec: Court of Appeal, 19 October 2021 ([2021] IECA 271; Edwards J giving judgment): appeal dismissed. The conviction stands.
Neither side raised requisitions about the re-charge, and the directions — including the requirement of an 'appreciable' falling below the standard — were adequate.

Careless driving requires no proof of intention or recklessness. The question is whether the driver fell below the standard of care expected of a reasonably prudent driver in the circumstances. It sits below dangerous driving, but above mere inattention.
There was evidence capable of supporting the verdict. A bus had collided with a cyclist, causing her death — far from a marginal case — and the perversity argument was rejected without hesitation.

keys.q: far from a marginal case
keys.w: Court of Appeal

keys.q: without hesitation
keys.w: Court of Appeal, rejecting the perversity ground

later: The court relied on earlier authority placing careless driving below dangerous driving but above mere inattention, and requiring an appreciable departure from the standard of a reasonably prudent driver.
job: Record the scene in detail: road layout and markings, the vehicle's path through the turn, final positions, lighting and visibility.
Recover CCTV — including on-board cameras — and vehicle data quickly, before it's overwritten.
Take statements on what each road user could see, and arrange a collision reconstruction of the turning line and speeds.

bg: In February 2014 Gardaí surveilling suspected IRA members at a pub in Phibsboro, Dublin, saw the accused exchange a package with a man at a table.
The man was stopped after leaving and found with 400 counterfeit €50 notes in two bundles — €20,000 face value.

The accused was searched. He had genuine cash and a set of keys. The keys opened a leased unit in Dunboyne, Co Meath, holding two offset printers and other printing equipment, paper, completed counterfeit €50 notes (about €189,000 face value) and part-finished notes (about €2 million).

He declined to answer questions. He pleaded guilty to having custody or control of materials or implements for counterfeiting (s.36 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001); delivering counterfeit currency (s.34(1)(b)) was taken into consideration. In November 2015 he was sentenced to six years, and he appealed against severity.
DPP v Molloy (2016).q: How should a large-scale counterfeiting operation be sentenced — and what must a sentencing judge show about mitigation?
dec: Court of Appeal, 28 July 2016 ([2016] IECA 239; Edwards J giving judgment, with Sheehan and Mahon JJ): appeal allowed.

The sentencing judge's reasons were insufficiently detailed for the court to be satisfied that adequate credit had been given for mitigation — the plea, previous good character, remorse and personal circumstances. That was a significant error of principle.
Re-sentencing, the court set a headline sentence of eight years to reflect the gravity of the offending.
It allowed a 30-month discount for mitigation, and suspended a further 18 months on a bond for two years after release, in light of his progress towards rehabilitation.

keys.q: significant error of principle
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on the sentencing judge's reasons

later: The scale of the operation — presses, finished notes and about €2 million in part-finished notes — drove the eight-year headline even on a guilty plea.
The charges show how counterfeiting is prosecuted under the 2001 Act: delivering counterfeit currency (s.34(1)(b)) and having materials or implements for counterfeiting (s.36).
job: Seize keys, fobs and access cards on arrest, and trace what they open — here a set of keys led to the print unit.
Photograph and record counterfeit notes, printers and materials where found; count, bundle and exhibit notes separately.
Match the charge to the evidence: delivery of counterfeit notes (s.34) or having counterfeiting materials or implements (s.36).
DPP v Molloy (2016).law: Yes. Court of Appeal sentencing authority (2016).

bg: On 9 January 2024, in a Garda Economic Crime Bureau investigation, two smartphones and a computer belonging to the applicant were seized at his home under a District Court search warrant issued under s.48(2) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001.
Following People (DPP) v Quirke, the District Judge was satisfied that there were reasonable grounds to search the digital space as well as the physical premises.

Gardaí required him to give the passwords under s.48(5)(b)(i). He refused, was arrested under s.49(2), and was charged with three offences under s.49(1)(c) of failing, without lawful excuse, to provide passwords for the three devices.

He sought to prohibit the prosecution and a declaration that the provisions were invalid: compelled passwords breached the privilege against self-incrimination and freedom of expression, and Article 6 ECHR.
The High Court (Bradley J) refused, holding the privilege wasn't engaged because the devices existed independently of his will. The Supreme Court allowed a leapfrog appeal.
Poptoshev v DPP.q: Can the law compel a suspect to unlock seized devices — and what can the prosecution then use?
dec: Supreme Court, November 2025 ([2025] IESC 47, Charleton J giving judgment): appeal dismissed. Section 49 is valid and compatible with the Constitution and Article 6 ECHR; there was no basis to prohibit the prosecution.
Departing from the High Court: stating a passcode or operating a device biometrically could be evidence of possession and use, so s.49 engages the right to silence and is potentially incriminating.

The key safeguard is use immunity. The compelled act — giving the password or key — cannot be used to prove that the person owned, controlled or operated the device. Ownership and control must be proved from other evidence.
Material already on the device is outside the compulsion and can be used: what already exists does not infringe the privilege.

Section 49 is a targeted response to the need to search the digital sphere. The suspect's choice is analogous to opening the door to a room, cupboard or safe in a physical search, or defying the warrant — and refusal exposes him to a much lesser offence.

Searching the digital space must be judicially mandated on reasonable grounds: where investigators propose to operate a computer to search it, reasonable justification of necessity and proportionality must be put before the issuing judge.

keys.q: targeted response to the need to search the digital sphere
keys.w: Charleton J, on s.49

keys.q: What exists already does not infringe
keys.w: Charleton J, on the device's existing contents

keys.q: analogous to opening the door to a room
keys.w: Charleton J, on the suspect's choice

later: Read with People (DPP) v Quirke and Quirke (No 2) in this app: warrants must specifically address the search of devices and the digital space.
Commentators expect similar compelled-password powers in other serious-crime statutes to be read the same way. The applicant remains presumed innocent on all charges.
job: In the warrant application, justify searching the digital space: why the devices are likely to hold evidence, and why examining them is necessary and proportionate. List electronic devices and electronically held material expressly.
When requiring a password under the warrant power, state the requirement clearly, explain that refusal without lawful excuse is an offence, and record the request, the answer and the time.
Prove ownership and use independently — where the device was found, SIM and account details, contacts, photos, cell-site data — never from the fact that the suspect unlocked it.

A&L Goodbody — Password protected: Supreme Court clarifies the privilege against self-incrimination where access to devices is compelled

bg: On New Year's Day 2005 a man was shot in Coolock, Dublin, and seriously injured. Two men were charged with assault causing harm under the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997. The Garda described an ongoing feud between two families.

At the District Court bail hearing on 6 January 2005 the prosecution objected to bail on the seriousness of the charge and a fear that witnesses would be intimidated. The Garda identified no witnesses and called none.
The defence objected that the Garda's evidence was hearsay, and that no objection under s.2 of the Bail Act 1997 had been raised.

The District Judge refused bail. He said this was an ongoing feud, and that the test was whether the man would go out and murder someone, or assault someone again with a gun. The High Court refused to order their release, and they appealed.
McDonagh v Governor of Cloverhill Prison.q: Can a judge refuse bail on his own fear of further violence, without evidence or notice of a s.2 objection?
dec: Supreme Court, 28 January 2005 (McGuinness J, with Hardiman and Fennelly JJ): appeal allowed. Both applicants had been released on 17 January; the reasons followed.

The District Judge didn't address the prosecution's objection or the hearsay objection, made no finding on either, and didn't consider the matters listed in s.2(2) of the Bail Act, which are mandatory.

His refusal rested on an apprehension he appeared to raise himself, with no supporting evidence. His remarks were improper and wrong in principle; the applicants were entitled to the presumption of innocence.
Under s.2, bail may be refused only where that is reasonably considered necessary to prevent a serious offence — and the refusal must rest on relevant evidence.

As a matter of natural and constitutional justice, an accused must be told that a s.2 objection is being made and have a proper chance to answer it by evidence or submissions. The procedural failings meant the detention was not in accordance with law.
later: Read with DPP v Mulvey (2014) in this app: refusing bail for risk to witnesses also needs evidence linking the accused to any interference.
The Bail Act 1997 has been amended several times since, including in 2007 and 2017. Check the current text of s.2 and the factors the court must consider.
job: Make clear, through the prosecutor, which grounds you rely on — the O'Callaghan grounds, s.2, or both.
Give evidence, not apprehension: identify the witnesses at risk, any threats or incidents, and the basis for your belief, and be ready to be cross-examined on it.
For a s.2 objection, address the s.2(2) factors — including the seriousness of the offence, the strength of the evidence and the accused's previous convictions, especially offences committed on bail.

src.t: Irish Times — Refusal of bail unlawful where District Judge acted on his own apprehensions (2005)

bg: In August 2013 the accused was arrested on six charges, including violent behaviour, trespass, demanding money with menaces, violent disorder, wrongful intimidation and criminal damage.
The prosecution alleged that he and three others went to a house in Finglas and demanded €8,000 over a drug debt owed by a former resident.
Bail was refused in the District Court and then in the High Court. Before a later bail hearing, all four complainants withdrew their statements.

The High Court again refused bail on the O'Callaghan grounds, finding that the complainants had been intimidated into withdrawing and that there was a risk of interference with witnesses. It described the intimidation as wholly and completely plain.
DPP v Mulvey.q: Can bail be refused for risk of interference with witnesses because the complainants withdrew their statements?
dec: Supreme Court, 25 February 2014 ([2014] IESC 18; Dunne J giving judgment, with Denham CJ and MacMenamin J): appeal allowed and the matter remitted to the High Court.
There was no evidence that, as a matter of probability, the accused would interfere with witnesses.
There was also no evidence that he was involved in any intimidation of the complainants.
The finding that the witnesses had plainly been intimidated lacked evidential support. Because the refusal rested on that unsupported conclusion, it couldn't stand.

keys.q: wholly and completely plain as a pike
keys.w: The High Court judge — a finding the Supreme Court held had no evidential basis

later: Read with McDonagh v Governor of Cloverhill Prison (2005) in this app: bail decisions must rest on evidence.
job: When a complainant withdraws a statement, take a statement about why, and whether anyone has contacted or pressured them.
Gather evidence linking the accused to any interference — threats, contacts, messages, third parties — before relying on it to oppose bail.
If interference is suspected, consider witness intimidation offences (s.41 of the Criminal Justice Act 1999) and protective bail conditions, and tell the prosecutor.

bg: On 3 June 2009 a firearm was discharged at a house in Blanchardstown, Dublin. Witnesses said they saw the accused and a co-accused at the scene.
The accused was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of involvement in the unlawful discharge of a firearm.

In interview Gardaí invoked s.19 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 (as inserted in 2007), asking him to account for his presence at named places on the basis that a Garda reasonably believed he was there to take part in the firearm discharge.

He was never charged with a firearms offence. He was charged with burglary under s.12(1)(b) of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001; the trespass involved an assault causing harm, and there was no evidence a gun was produced during it.

At trial in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court the judge allowed reliance on s.19. The Court of Appeal rejected his appeal, and the Supreme Court gave leave on whether s.19 can be used at a trial for a different offence.
DPP v Wilson (inferences, 2017).q: Can inferences under s.19 be drawn at a trial for an offence other than the one the suspect was questioned about?
dec: Supreme Court, 13 July 2017 ([2017] IESC 53; Denham CJ giving judgment, with McKechnie, O'Donnell, Clarke and O'Malley JJ): appeal allowed and conviction quashed.

The wording of s.19 is clear. The inference provisions can be relied on at trial only where the offence charged is the same as the offence the accused was questioned about when the section was invoked.
The caution had been invoked for the firearm offence, not the burglary, so no inference could be drawn at the burglary trial.

An earlier authority relied on by the prosecution didn't assist. The Chief Justice noted that, if the men had been tried separately, the firearm evidence would probably have been inadmissible against him — changing the position would need legislation.
Whether there would be a retrial was a matter for the DPP.

keys.q: could not be utilised in a trial for an offence other than
keys.w: Denham CJ, on s.19

later: Read with Rock v Ireland (1997) and DPP v DT (2025) in this app on inferences. Sections 18 and 19A are also framed around a specific offence, so name it in every inference warning.
job: Name in the inference warning the specific offence or offences you are investigating — including any you may charge.
If the investigation moves to a different offence, take advice on re-arrest or a fresh inference warning for that offence, and put the relevant facts again.
Record the exact wording of each inference warning and the offence it relates to.

bg: Between 2011 and 2013, over about 18 months, the accused — a Detective Sergeant in the Garda Crime and Security Division — sent abusive letters and emails to the home and workplace of a State solicitor who worked in the DPP's office deciding on prosecutions.

The victim didn't know the accused. One email purported to come from a dangerous criminal, others were abusive and insulting, and leaflets were placed on cars and pillars in the victim's neighbourhood.

In 2017 a jury in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court convicted her of harassment under s.10 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997. In January 2018 she was sentenced to three years; in July 2019 the Court of Appeal suspended the balance, finding an error in principle.

Section 10 covers harassing a person by persistently following, watching, pestering, besetting or communicating with them. The Supreme Court considered whether communications sent to other people, rather than directly to the victim, can count.
DPP v Doherty (harassment, 2020).q: Can harassment by 'communicating with' a person be committed without addressing the victim directly — and what does 'besetting' mean?
dec: Supreme Court, 24 July 2020 ([2020] IESC 45; O'Donnell J giving the lead judgment, with MacMenamin, O'Malley and Baker JJ; Charleton J dissenting on besetting): appeal dismissed. The conviction stands.

'Communicating with' takes its plain and ordinary meaning. It doesn't necessarily require the victim to be directly addressed; the jury could reasonably find the conduct amounted to communicating with the victim.
Persistence was clearly satisfied. A number of incidents, or a single continuing action, can amount to persistence (DPP (O'Dowd) v Lynch).

On besetting, a majority held the prosecution's argument failed: besetting requires some physical presence or physical action, even at a distance. Charleton J would have held that persistent communications besetting the victim's life fall within it.

All five judges described 'besetting' as an archaic term unsuited to a criminal statute and said s.10 should be reviewed and updated; O'Donnell J stressed that technology had only emphasised the harm such conduct causes.

keys.q: does not necessarily require the victim to be directly addressed
keys.w: O'Donnell J, on 'communicating with'

keys.q: arcane word in the modern era
keys.w: Supreme Court, on 'besetting'

keys.q: email blitz
keys.w: Charleton J, describing the conduct

later: Section 10 was amended by the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020, which also created new offences for sharing intimate images and threatening or grossly offensive communications. Check the current wording before charging.
job: Gather every communication — letters, emails, social media posts, leaflets, messages to third parties — and the dates, so the course of conduct is clear.
Prove who sent them: devices, accounts, IP and subscriber data, handwriting, CCTV of leafleting, and admissions.
Take a full statement from the victim on how the communications reached them and their effect, and consider the 2020 Act offences.
DPP v Doherty (harassment, 2020).law: Yes. Supreme Court authority (2020); check the amended s.10.

bg: In 2017 the applicant faced an allegation of sexual assault. His conviction was quashed on appeal, and at the retrial a jury unanimously acquitted him.
He applied for a small public service vehicle (SPSV) driver licence. A Garda Superintendent decided the application as the licensing authority under the Taxi Regulation Act 2013.

At an interview on 25 September the authority told him only that it had 'one side of the events'. It didn't identify the documents or statements it was relying on, so he couldn't respond to the specific material.
On 7 November 2023 the application was refused because of concerns arising from the 2017 allegation. He sought judicial review.
PK v VS (SPSV licence, 2025).q: Can the SPSV licensing authority rely on an allegation that ended in acquittal — and what must it tell the applicant first?
dec: High Court, 28 April 2025 ([2025] IEHC 244, Phelan J).

Under s.10(1) of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, a licence shall not be granted unless the authority is satisfied as to the applicant's suitability. Section 10(2) lists matters the authority may consider, such as good character and concerns raised by An Garda Síochána; the list isn't exhaustive.
Considering an allegation that ended in acquittal was within the authority's discretion, because it bore on the safety of vulnerable passengers — even though it didn't lead to a conviction.

But fair procedures require the applicant to be told the material on which adverse concerns are based, so he can respond. The authority hadn't adequately identified that material, so the refusal was unfair.
The refusal was quashed and remitted for reconsideration, with notice of all material relied on. A statutory appeal to the District Court is also available against licensing decisions.

keys.q: one side of the events
keys.w: The licensing authority, at the applicant's interview

later: Read with McKenna (SPSV licence conditions, 2023) in this app: licensing decisions and conditions must be fair, reasoned and proportionate.
job: Identify the specific material behind any concern — statements, Garda records, court outcomes — and give the applicant a summary or copies and a real chance to respond before deciding.
Weigh allegations that ended in acquittal carefully: record why they bear on passenger safety and how you've treated the acquittal.
Give written reasons for the decision, and note the applicant's right of appeal to the District Court.

src.t: Casemine — Fair procedures in SPSV licensing: considering acquitted allegations and ensuring material disclosure (PK v VS [2025] IEHC 244)

bg: Gardaí refused the applicant a small public service vehicle (SPSV) licence. He had previous convictions for drugs offences.
He appealed to the District Court, which allowed the appeal and granted the licence.
Gardaí then issued the licence with a condition restricting him to working for one named private-hire business run by a relative.
He sought judicial review of the condition. The Taxi Regulation Act 2013 lets the licensing authority attach conditions as it sees fit.
McKenna (SPSV licence conditions, 2023).q: How far can the Garda licensing authority restrict an SPSV licence that the District Court has ordered to be granted?
dec: High Court, July 2023 (Meenan J): the condition was quashed.
The power to attach conditions has limits. Conditions must be rational, reasonable and proportionate, and must be balanced against the applicant's constitutional right to earn a living.
A condition can't be so restrictive that it effectively overrides the District Court's decision — and this one did.
It was also fragile: if the business changed its name the licence would become invalid, and the driver could trade under the business name anyway, defeating the condition's purpose.

Supervision-type requirements might not have been unreasonable given his record, but this restriction was irrational and unreasonable. The application went back to An Garda Síochána to grant the licence.

keys.q: irrational and unreasonable
keys.w: Meenan J, on the condition

later: Read with PK v VS (SPSV licence, 2025) in this app on fair procedures in SPSV licensing.
job: Tie any licence condition to a specific, recorded risk, and explain why less restrictive options won't address it.
Check that the condition is workable — it shouldn't depend on things outside the licensee's control, like a business name.
Where the District Court has ordered a licence to be granted, don't use conditions to undo that decision.

src.t: Echo — Judge quashes 'unreasonable' restriction on man's public service vehicle licence (21 July 2023)

bg: The National Transport Authority prosecuted the accused for carrying a passenger for hire or reward in a vehicle without an SPSV licence, under the Taxi Regulation Act 2013.
The journey was arranged in a mobile phone call that treated him as a taxi service. He arrived at the agreed time and place in a particular vehicle.
There was no prior agreement on the fare and no payment up front, but he admitted asking for a fare after the journey. He stopped the activity after the incident.
The District Court acquitted him, apparently because there was no prior fare agreement or immediate payment. The NTA appealed.
NTA v Granaghan.q: Is a passenger carried 'for hire or reward' if no fare was agreed or paid in advance?
dec: High Court, 21 April 2020 ([2020] IEHC 224, Barr J): the acquittal was overturned and the case remitted to the District Court.
The District Court applied too narrow a test by focusing only on a prior fare agreement or immediate payment.
The court looked at all the circumstances: the booking by phone, the arrival at the agreed time and place, the request for a fare after the journey, and the fact that the activity stopped afterwards.
Together these pointed to an expectation of payment, which was enough for carriage 'for hire or reward'.
later: The test is contextual: payment doesn't have to be agreed or made in advance. Read with NTA v Beakhurst (2020) in this app on owners' liability.
job: Record how the journey was booked — call logs, messages, apps — and what was said about the service.
Take a statement from the passenger about the pick-up, the journey and any payment asked for or expected.
Note any advertising, signage or pattern of trips suggesting a business.

src.t: Casemine — Redefining 'for hire or reward' in taxi regulation: NTA v Granaghan [2020] IEHC 224

bg: A taxi was driven by a person without the required licence.
The National Transport Authority prosecuted the vehicle's owner under the Taxi Regulation Act 2013 for allowing this.
The owner argued that, as with possession offences, he couldn't be liable unless the prosecution proved he knew of or consented to the unlicensed driving.
NTA v Beakhurst.q: Must the prosecution prove that a taxi owner knew or consented before he can be liable for an unlicensed driver using the vehicle?
dec: High Court, 2020 ([2020] IEHC 301, Barr J): no — the offence (reported as s.22(4) of the 2013 Act) is one of strict liability.
The Act is regulatory, aimed at public safety and an orderly taxi service.

Possession offences (such as in DPP v Ebbs) require awareness because knowledge is part of the offence. Operating a vehicle is different: it concerns control, and the owner's duty to prevent unauthorised use.
As reported, an owner can avoid liability by showing that all reasonable steps were taken to prevent unauthorised use.
later: Read with NTA v Granaghan (2020) in this app on what counts as 'for hire or reward'. This summary comes from a published commentary; check the judgment for the exact section and defence.
job: Identify and record the vehicle owner, the driver, and the licences each holds (or doesn't).
Ask the owner how use of the vehicle is controlled — keys, rosters, checks on drivers — and record the answers.
Report the matter to the NTA where appropriate, and keep evidence of the journey and any payment.

src.t: Casemine — Strict liability for vehicle owners in taxi regulation: NTA v Beakhurst [2020] IEHC 301

bg: In February 2020 the Garda licensing authority for the Dublin region changed its policy: SPSV driver licences would not be granted to people holding temporary immigration permission while a residence application was pending.
The applicant had temporary permission to live and work in Ireland while his application to retain residence was pending.
He was granted a time-limited SPSV licence, which expired in April 2020 when his permission lapsed.
On renewal he was refused as not a 'suitable person', after an adverse immigration finding against him. He sought judicial review of both decisions.
Unnamed (SPSV licence and temporary perm.q: Can the licensing authority refuse SPSV licences under a blanket policy based on immigration status — and can it issue licences for shorter terms?
dec: High Court, April 2022 (Simons J).
The refusal to renew was valid: the authority could rely on the adverse immigration finding as a red flag bearing on good character, even though that finding was subject to review.

But the judge had grave reservations about the legality of the policy. The authority hadn't justified systematically refusing family members of EU citizens the right to drive while their immigration matters were pending.
The ad hoc introduction of the policy was unsatisfactory, to say the least; changes of that kind should be made by the National Transport Authority through regulations.
The original time-limited licence was invalid: SPSV licences must last five years. A five-year licence could be issued with conditions, such as a requirement to hold renewed immigration permission.
With much of the case narrowed, the judge listed it for submissions on the final orders.

keys.q: unsatisfactory, to say the least
keys.w: Simons J, on how the policy was introduced

later: Read with PK v VS (SPSV licence, 2025) and McKenna (SPSV licence conditions, 2023) in this app: SPSV decisions must be individual, fair and proportionate.
Several similar appeals against SPSV refusals were pending in the District Court at the time. Check the current NTA regulations and Garda licensing policy.
job: Assess each applicant individually on the evidence — don't refuse under a blanket policy the regulations don't support.
Record what each adverse finding is and why it bears on suitability, including whether it's still under review.
Issue licences for the statutory period and manage specific risks with conditions.

bg: Four children — represented by their parents and solicitors — were interviewed by Gardaí about alleged offences, with legal representation present.

They were then considered for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. Under s.23(1)(a) of the Children Act 2001, admission requires the child to accept responsibility, having had the opportunity to consult parents or guardians and get legal advice.
Before deciding whether to accept responsibility, they asked for access to the Garda investigation files. Access was refused.
They sought judicial review, relying on s.23, constitutional fair procedures and EU Directive 2012/13/EU on the right to information in criminal proceedings.
JM v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána (.q: Must a child be given the Garda file before deciding whether to accept responsibility for youth diversion?
dec: High Court, 1 February 2022 ([2022] IEHC 149, Heslin J): all four applications dismissed.
The court applied the literal meaning of s.23. There was no ambiguity or absurdity requiring a purposive reading, and nothing in it entitled the children to the files.

The programme's purpose (s.19) is supportive diversion to prevent further offending — not to give access to prosecution evidence. The Director's admission decision operates independently of any later decision by the DPP to prosecute.
Neither the EU Directive nor the constitutional arguments overrode the statutory scheme.
The children had been told the allegations and the complainants' identities in interview, and their solicitors had enough information to advise them.
later: Read with S v Director of the Garda Juvenile Diversion Programme (2019) and Unnamed v DPP (juvenile delay and diversion, 2023) in this app. This summary comes from a published commentary.
job: Put the allegation clearly to the child in interview, so they understand what they'd be accepting responsibility for.
Make sure the child has had the opportunity to consult parents or guardians and get legal advice before accepting responsibility, and record it.
Explain how the programme works and that admission isn't guaranteed.

src.t: Casemine — Legal advice rights in juvenile diversion: J.M. v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána [2022] IEHC 149

bg: In May 2017, when he was 16, the applicant allegedly committed an assault.
While he was being considered for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme, he made a partial admission under caution to a Juvenile Liaison Officer. He was refused entry to the programme.

He wasn't summonsed to the District Court until February 2021. In the meantime he had come to Garda attention as an adult, been before the courts several times, and served a custodial sentence on unrelated matters.
The prosecution explained the delay by the investigating Garda's caseload of some 40 other cases and difficulty serving him at the address he'd given. He sought to restrain the prosecution.
Unnamed v DPP (juvenile delay and divers.q: Should a youth prosecution be stopped because of culpable delay in summonsing — and what of admissions made at the diversion stage?
dec: High Court, 4 July 2023 ([2023] IEHC 384): the application to restrain the prosecution was refused.
There was culpable prosecutorial delay, but it didn't tip the balance of justice in favour of stopping the prosecution.

The loss of the anonymity he'd have had as a child wasn't prejudicial, because he had come to Garda attention after reaching adulthood. The roughly two years of delay after he turned 18 caused no additional prejudice.
later: Commentary (a barrister, writing in the Gazette): the Children Act makes evidence of acceptance of responsibility inadmissible where a child is admitted to the programme (s.48(1)), but is silent where a child is considered and refused. Accepting responsibility for entry shouldn't happen under caution, and is different from the formal caution given after admission (s.25).
Read with PM v DPP (2006) on blameworthy prosecutorial delay, and S v Director of the Garda Juvenile Diversion Programme (2019) on eligibility, in this app.
job: Process youth files promptly; record the reason for any delay, and escalate if caseload is holding a file up.
At the diversion consideration stage, take advice before cautioning a child in a way that turns acceptance of responsibility into evidence.
Confirm and update the young person's address for service, and record each attempt to serve.

src.t: Law Society Gazette — Juvenile admission subject of significant High Court ruling (11 July 2023)

bg: S was 17 when he committed the offences in 2017, and was arrested after turning 18.
He was charged with child sexual exploitation and child pornography offences under the Child Trafficking and Pornography Act 1998.
His solicitors argued he met the criteria for the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. Juvenile Liaison Officers recommended against admission.
In July 2018 the Director found him unsuitable, and kept that position in September 2018 after further submissions, giving no reasons. He sought judicial review.
S v Director of the Garda Juvenile Diver.q: Can someone who offended as a child be excluded from youth diversion simply because they're now over 18 — and must the Director give reasons?
dec: High Court, November 2019 ([2019] IEHC 796, Simons J).

The Director's admission decision is amenable to judicial review. It doesn't attract the restricted standard that applies to the DPP's decisions, though the court still shows deference and intervenes only where a decision is unreasonable or irrational.
In the circumstances there was a duty to give reasons: the material showed a prima facie case that the decision rested on a mistaken reading of the eligibility criteria.

The Director had applied a blanket policy that once a young offender turned 18 they couldn't be admitted, regardless of their age at the time of the offence. That misinterpreted s.23 of the Children Act 2001.

Refusing reasons in those circumstances — a Sphinx-like approach — risked letting a serious error of law go unchecked. The decisions were quashed and remitted for reconsideration; the order restraining the DPP from prosecuting stayed in force.

keys.q: Sphinx-like approach
keys.w: Simons J, on refusing to give reasons

later: Read with JM v Commissioner (diversion, 2022) and Unnamed v DPP (juvenile delay and diversion, 2023) in this app on the youth diversion process.
job: Assess diversion on the person's age when the offence was committed, even if they've since turned 18.
Record the reasons for any Juvenile Liaison Officer recommendation, so the Director's decision can be explained.
Deal with youth files promptly so that eligibility questions don't arise from delay.

src.t: Irish Legal News — High Court: Director of Juvenile Diversion Programme incorrectly interpreted Children Act 2001 (26 November 2019)

bg: In July 1980 two Gardaí were shot dead after a bank robbery in Ballaghaderreen, Co Roscommon.

The accused was arrested and detained under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939. The prosecution relied mainly on an admission of involvement he allegedly made after detectives questioned him in custody.

In November 1980, after a 23-day trial, the Special Criminal Court convicted him and two others of capital murder and robbery, and he was sentenced to death. In 1981 the sentence was commuted to 40 years' imprisonment.
People (DPP) v Pringle.q: Can a conviction resting mainly on an alleged admission in custody stand when doubt later emerges about how it was recorded?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 22 May 1981 (O'Higgins CJ, Finlay P, Costello J): leave to appeal refused for all three accused.

In June 1994 he applied under s.2 of the Criminal Procedure Act 1993 to have the conviction quashed. The court ordered full discovery of State documents, and allowed documents obtained in his civil proceedings to be used in the application.

Court of Criminal Appeal, 16 May 1995 (O'Flaherty J giving judgment): the conviction was quashed as unsafe and unsatisfactory — reported as turning on a disputed entry in a Garda notebook. He was released after 14 years and 10 months in prison.

keys.q: unsafe and unsatisfactory
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal (1995), as reported

later: His civil claims against the State were dismissed for delay in 2019, reinstated by the Court of Appeal in 2022 because a key legal issue hadn't been addressed, and struck out after his death in 2023 — so no court ruled on their merits.
Read with People (DPP) v Breathnach and DPP v Murphy (2005) in this app: convictions lost because of doubts about Garda accounts of interviews and notes.
job: Make notes at the time, in your official notebook, in sequence — never add entries afterwards or on loose pages.
Correct an entry by striking it through, initialled and dated, so the original can still be read.
Record interviews electronically. If something is said outside the recorded interview, note it at once and put it to the suspect on the recording.
People (DPP) v Pringle.law: Overtaken: the conviction was quashed in 1995.

Irish Times — Damages claim by man whose murder conviction was quashed fails (22 December 2019)

bg: Two applicants, armed with knives, killed a man in a stabbing attack after a long-running family dispute. They were convicted of murder.
The first applicant's interview ran to four hours. She declined an offer to adjourn it. Gardaí hadn't kept a contemporaneous note of her first interview.
For the second applicant, privilege was claimed over the source of the information behind a search warrant. Gardaí had offered her access to a solicitor and made calls on her behalf.
During the trial the jury learned that the second applicant had been in prison, implying previous convictions. Both applied for leave to appeal.
People (DPP) v Reddan and Hannon.q: Does a breach of the Custody Regulations or the Judges' Rules make a later statement inadmissible?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 4 December 1995 (Blayney J giving judgment, with Flood and Kinlen JJ): leave to appeal refused; the convictions stood.

Regulation 12(4) of the 1987 Custody Regulations requires an interview that has lasted four hours to be terminated or adjourned for a reasonable time. This interview should have been interrupted — but the breach did not of itself render the statement inadmissible.
The failure to keep a contemporaneous note of the first interview didn't make the later statement inadmissible either, because that statement was taken in compliance with the Judges' Rules.
Privilege over the source behind the search warrant was upheld, because revealing it could have endangered a civilian contact. The arrest and detention were lawful.

The jury shouldn't have learned of the prison reference, but given the strength of the evidence it caused no miscarriage of justice, and no retrial was ordered. The court also held there is no defence in law of a 'flawed intent'.

keys.q: did not of itself render the applicant's statement inadmissible
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal, on the regulation breach

keys.q: There is no defence in law of a flawed intent
keys.w: Court of Criminal Appeal

later: Read with People (DPP) v Darcy (1997) in this app — a three-Garda interview breached the regulations, but the statements were admissible because the substance of the rights was preserved.
Today interviews are electronically recorded, and the JC test (2015) governs evidence obtained in breach of rights.
job: Stop or adjourn an interview at four hours, and record the time, the offer and any decision to continue.
Keep a contemporaneous note of every interview, including informal or preliminary ones.
Record every offer of a solicitor, every call made, and the reasons for any delay; and protect informant sources through the prosecutor.

src.t: Irish Times law report — Failure to end interview within prescribed time does not render statement inadmissible (25 March 1996)

bg: In February 2016 the plaintiff was arrested at a sod-turning ceremony attended by a Government minister.

The arresting Garda observed insults, the plaintiff touching a Garda's epaulette, threats about the minister, and a refusal to obey a s.8 direction to leave. He was convicted in the District Court but acquitted on appeal to the Circuit Court.

In March 2017 a Garda complained of harassment through Facebook posts. A warrant under s.10 of the Criminal Justice (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1997 was issued for 'electronic devices capable of forwarding messages on social media' at a property. Devices were seized and forensically examined; the DPP later directed no prosecution.
He sued Gardaí, the DPP and the State for €500,000 for false imprisonment, malicious prosecution and malicious procurement of a search warrant.
Rochford (civil claims over arrest and d.q: Was the public order arrest lawful — and does an acquittal, or a no-prosecution decision after a search, make the Gardaí liable?
dec: High Court, 2025 ([2025] IEHC 251, Simons J): all three claims dismissed.

False imprisonment: the arrest under s.24 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 was lawful. The Garda had reasonable cause to suspect a s.6 offence (threatening or abusive behaviour), and a valid s.8 direction had been given and disobeyed.

Malicious prosecution: the acquittal satisfied the first element, but the plaintiff couldn't show a lack of reasonable cause or malice. The Garda's observations, and a supervising Superintendent's review, gave objective grounds.

Malicious procurement of the warrant: there were reasonable grounds to suspect harassment and to believe evidence was on the devices. The warrant expressly sought to search digital devices, as People (DPP) v Quirke requires. There was no malice.

keys.q: electronic devices capable of forwarding messages on social media
keys.w: The warrant application, as quoted by the court

later: Read with DPP v Kelly (2018) in this app on s.8 directions, and Poptoshev v DPP (2025) and People (DPP) v Quirke on device warrants. This summary comes from a published commentary.
job: Record exactly what was said and done, the s.8 direction you gave (in clear words) and how it was disobeyed, before and after arrest.
Have a supervisor review the decision to prosecute where it's contentious, and record the review.
In device warrant applications, set out why evidence is likely to be on the devices and ask expressly for authority to seize and search them.

src.t: Casemine — Reasonable grounds for public order arrests and digital evidence search warrants ([2025] IEHC 251)

bg: From June 2026 criminal defence solicitors withdrew their services in the District Court in protest at a new 'one accused, one fee' legal aid model, introduced on 1 July 2026: a fixed €520 fee replaced payment per appearance.
Many accused appeared at District Court bail hearings without a solicitor and were remanded in custody. They brought Article 40 challenges in the High Court, arguing their detention was unlawful.

In one case a man charged with stealing two cans of cola, worth €3.60, had bail refused and his existing bail revoked. He wasn't able to question the Garda, and was only able to mention a new address after bail had already been refused.
Unrepresented accused at bail hearings (.q: Is a remand in custody lawful where the accused had no solicitor at the bail hearing?
dec: High Court, 29 July 2026 (Gearty J): 11 accused succeeded and were entitled to immediate release. There had been a fundamental denial of justice in their bail hearings, though this wasn't the fault of the District judges; the cases turned on what happened at each hearing, not on legal aid rules.

High Court, 5 August 2026 (Twomey J): an Article 40 inquiry was refused for a man charged with firearms offences whose solicitor declined to act in the District Court over fees but acted for him in the High Court. Habeas corpus, a stable bulwark of liberty, shouldn't be used that way; the remedy was an appeal of the bail refusal.

High Court, 18 August 2026 (Simons J): the €3.60 theft case was a very minor offence, and refusing and revoking bail without the accused being heard did not constitute a hearing. His detention wasn't in accordance with law, and he was released.

High Court, 26 August 2026 (Simons J): Twomey J had misread the case law — no solicitor can cause another person's detention. But lack of representation doesn't of itself make a bail hearing fundamentally flawed: an unrepresented accused may still have a meaningful opportunity to answer the case for detention. Two applicants who'd had that opportunity were refused relief.

keys.q: fundamental denial of justice
keys.w: Gearty J (29 July 2026)

keys.q: did not constitute a hearing
keys.w: Simons J, on the €3.60 case

keys.q: stable bulwark of our liberties
keys.w: Twomey J, on habeas corpus

later: The rulings conflict on when Article 40 is the right route; written judgments and any appeals may settle it. Read with McDonagh v Governor of Cloverhill Prison (2005) and DPP v Mulvey (2014) in this app: bail decisions must rest on evidence and fair procedure.
job: When objecting to bail against an unrepresented accused, state the grounds plainly and give your evidence so they understand what is alleged.
Expect questions and allow the accused to answer and to put their side — address, ties, conditions they'd accept — before the court decides.
Keep objections proportionate to the charge, and be cautious about seeking revocation of existing bail without the accused being heard.

bg: On 3 November 1985 a Peace Commissioner issued a warrant under s.42(1) of the Larceny Act 1916 to search a house in Swords, Dublin, for stolen property. It was granted on a Garda's sworn information in an investigation into stolen electric cookers.
The Peace Commissioner's power to issue the warrant came from s.88(3)(b) of the Courts of Justice Act 1924.
Stolen equipment was found in an upstairs bedroom. The applicant, who lived in the house with a friend, was arrested outside and charged with burglary, larceny and receiving stolen property.

He sought judicial review: the information didn't justify the warrant, the warrant wrongly purported to authorise his arrest, and the search breached his constitutional right to be free from unwarranted search.
Berkeley v Edwards.q: Was the Peace Commissioner's warrant valid — and does an unlawful clause about arrest invalidate it?
dec: High Court, 9 October 1987 (Hamilton P): the application was dismissed.

Issuing a search warrant isn't an administration of justice in a criminal matter under Articles 34 and 37, following Ryan v O'Callaghan. Section 88(3)(b) wasn't inconsistent with Article 40.5 (inviolability of the dwelling).
The sworn information was sufficient for the Peace Commissioner to be satisfied that stolen property would be found at the house.
The passage purporting to authorise arrest was severable, so it didn't invalidate the rest of the warrant.
Even if grounds had been made out, the court would have refused relief in its discretion: the warrant was spent, and the admissibility of the evidence was a matter for the Circuit Court at trial.

keys.q: reasonable cause to believe
keys.w: The statutory threshold for the warrant

later: The statutory scheme has moved on: the Larceny Act 1916 was replaced by the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001, and Damache v DPP (2012) requires warrants to be issued by someone independent of the investigation.
Read with Byrne v Grey, Simple Imports (2000) and People (DPP) v Edgeworth (2001) in this app on what makes a warrant valid.
job: Set out in the sworn information the facts behind your belief or suspicion — not just the statutory words.
Check the warrant authorises only what the statute allows; don't rely on a warrant for powers (such as arrest) it can't give.
Raise any doubt about a warrant's validity before executing it, not after.
Berkeley v Edwards.law: Older authority (1987); the statutory framework has changed.

src.t: vLex Ireland — Berkeley v Edwards [1988] IR 217

bg: In August 1995 a suspect was linked to a burglary. A Garda sergeant sought search warrants under s.42(1) of the Larceny Act 1916 for several flats in a Dún Laoghaire complex.
The warrant for the plaintiff's flat was sought on the basis that the suspect might move there from the next-door flat over the rear balconies to escape.
Executing the warrant, Gardaí broke down the plaintiff's door to arrest the suspect.

She sued for damages, including aggravated damages, for personal injuries and breach of her constitutional rights, saying she was injured inside her home. The court found her account unreliable in material respects: she was probably injured outside, during hostile action by a crowd against the Gardaí as they left.
Osbourne v Minister for Justice.q: Can a householder recover damages from the State because Gardaí executed a technically invalid search warrant on her home?
dec: High Court, 13 April 2006 (Clarke J): the claim was dismissed.

The warrant was technically invalid. Section 42 is about property in a person's possession on the premises — not about a possible escape route. Failing to strike out the alternative 'District Judge' description on the form didn't itself invalidate it.
The sergeant genuinely and reasonably held his beliefs, and the warrant was sought and granted in good faith.

Applying People (AG) v O'Brien: no damages claim, in tort or for breach of constitutional rights, arises from acting on a warrant that appeared valid but was technically defective, unless the defect was relied on in a deliberate or conscious violation of rights.

That could happen where a false basis is given to obtain the warrant, where the applicant knows the basis doesn't justify a warrant, or where those executing it know of the defect beforehand. An innocent error nobody knew about, in a warrant obtained in good faith, doesn't support damages. Nor did the manner of execution.

keys.q: deliberate or conscious violation
keys.w: Clarke J, on when damages can arise

keys.q: bona fide sought and bona fide granted
keys.w: Clarke J, on the warrant

later: Entry to arrest is now governed by s.6 of the Criminal Law Act 1997 — see DPP v O'Brien (2021) in this app. Whether evidence from a defective warrant is admissible at a criminal trial is decided under People (DPP) v JC (2015).
job: Use a search warrant only for the purpose its statute allows — finding property or evidence on the premises named.
If you need to enter to arrest, rely on the power that actually covers it, and record the grounds.
If you learn of a defect in a warrant before executing it, don't execute it — get a valid one.

src.t: Irish Times law report — No damages claim in respect of execution of invalid warrant where no deliberate violation of rights (29 May 2006)

bg: The accused was charged in the District Court with drink driving — having more than 80mg of alcohol per 100ml of blood within three hours of driving.

At about 1am a Garda took over as member in charge, relieving a colleague who had held the role since 10pm. The new member in charge performed all the duties, including completing the custody record and informing the accused of his rights.
He did not sign the station diary, as a Superintendent's directive required. The relieved Garda remained in the day room during the process.
The District Judge dismissed the charge, holding that without the diary entry he couldn't be the member in charge, and stated a case to the High Court.
DPP v McGuire (member in charge, 1996).q: Can a Garda be the member in charge without signing the station diary as a local directive requires?
dec: High Court, 31 July 1996 (Kelly J): yes — the District Judge was wrong in law.

Regulation 4(1) of the Treatment of Persons in Custody Regulations 1987 defines the member in charge as the member actually in charge of the station when a duty under the Regulations arises. That is a question of fact.

The Superintendent's directive was, at most, an administrative mechanism for identifying the member in charge. Failing to comply with it didn't change who the member in charge actually was; making the diary entry decisive might even exceed the Superintendent's powers.

Although not necessary to decide, the judge noted that under s.7(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 a breach of the Regulations doesn't automatically exclude evidence: there must be a causal link between the breach and prejudice to the accused.
The case was remitted to the District Court to continue the hearing.

keys.q: actually in charge
keys.w: Kelly J, on the test in reg. 4(1)

later: Read with DPP v Roche (2015) in this app: a change of member in charge doesn't by itself make a detention unlawful.
job: At every handover, record in the custody record (and any station diary) who is taking over as member in charge, and the time.
Make sure the incoming member in charge actually performs and records the duties: rights, custody record entries, reviews.
If a local directive applies, follow it — even if non-compliance isn't fatal, it gives the defence an argument.

bg: The accused was charged with driving with excess alcohol under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961.
At the Garda station he was required under s.13(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act 1994 to permit a doctor to take blood or, at his option, to give urine. He chose urine.
He couldn't produce a sample within about 15 minutes, despite attempts to help him. The doctor, under pressure to attend another station, then took a blood sample.
The District Judge dismissed the charge: the accused hadn't been given a reasonable opportunity to provide urine, so blood wasn't properly an option. The DPP appealed by way of case stated.
DPP v O'Connor (urine specimen, 1998).q: How long must Gardaí allow a person who opts for urine before a blood sample is taken?
dec: High Court, 10 July 1998 (Geoghegan J): the appeal was refused.
Being allowed to provide urine, if it can be provided, is a condition precedent to any absolute obligation to give blood.

The District Judge wasn't laying down a rule that 30 minutes must always be allowed. He assessed the time against all the circumstances, including the pressure on the doctor and the accused's distress.
His view was open to him and wasn't perverse, so no question of law arose. The certificate showing the accused was well over the limit was irrelevant to whether the option had been properly offered.
later: The blood-or-urine option continues under the Road Traffic Act 2010. Read with the station-procedure cases in this app (DPP v Finn, DPP v Stack, Brassil v DPP).
job: Record the time the person opts for urine, each attempt, any help offered (water, time, privacy), and the time you move on.
Allow a genuinely reasonable time in the circumstances; don't cut it short because the doctor needs to leave.
If moving to blood, record why the urine option was exhausted, and tell the person clearly.

src.t: Irish Times law report — Accused person must be given reasonable opportunity of providing urine sample (28 September 1998)

bg: In October 1993 the accused was seen driving erratically in Dublin and was arrested under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 for drunk driving.

At the Garda station a doctor was called. The Garda told him he was required to allow a blood specimen to be taken or, at his option, to give urine — and that refusing was an offence carrying a possible prison term, a fine or both.
The Garda closely paraphrased the statutory wording but didn't name the section authorising the requirement. The accused gave urine.
He was convicted in the District Court, fined £75 and disqualified for 12 months. The High Court upheld the conviction on a case stated, and he appealed.
Brennan v DPP (specimen requirement, 199.q: Must a Garda name the statutory section when requiring a specimen?
dec: Supreme Court, 1 November 1995 (O'Flaherty J giving judgment, with Hamilton CJ and Denham J): appeal dismissed.
Where a valid requirement is made, the accused is told of the requirement and the consequences of refusal, and he complies, there's no need for the Gardaí to invoke the actual section.
That involves no encroachment on the accused's constitutional rights.

DPP v McGarrigle was distinguished: there, the section had to be invoked because non-compliance was the basis of the charge. Arrest was also distinguished: the operative section generally must be invoked, because an arrest deprives a person of liberty.

keys.q: no need for the Gardai to invoke the actual section
keys.w: O'Flaherty J

keys.q: no encroachment on the accused's constitutional rights
keys.w: O'Flaherty J

later: Specimen requirements are now made under the Road Traffic Act 2010. Read with DPP v Connell (1997) and DPP v McCormack (1999) in this app on telling a person why they're arrested and that they're under arrest.
job: State the requirement in plain words — what specimen, and that it's required by law — and the consequences of refusing.
Record exactly what you said and the response.
Where refusal or failure may become the charge, be precise about the requirement made and the power relied on.

bg: A Garda allegedly saw the accused move into the back seat of a car as a passenger moved into the driver's seat.
He was arrested on suspicion of drink driving. At the station he refused to provide two specimens of breath.
He said he hadn't been driving; his girlfriend told Gardaí and the District Court that she had been.

In January 2007 the District Court convicted him of refusing to provide the specimens under the Road Traffic Act 1994. The judge had doubts about whether he'd been driving — so driving wasn't proved — but didn't find that he hadn't been. He challenged the conviction in the High Court.
Finnegan v DPP (refusing breath specimen.q: Can a person be convicted of refusing breath specimens if it isn't proved that they were driving?
dec: High Court, November 2008 (Clark J): the challenge failed, with costs to the DPP.
The requirement for breath specimens was lawfully made, and he couldn't challenge the arrest on the ground that his driving hadn't been proved.
Driving a vehicle was not a prerequisite to a conviction for refusing, without good and substantial reason, to provide a breath specimen.
The conviction stood, although the District Judge had doubts about who was driving.

keys.q: driving a vehicle was not a prerequisite to a conviction
keys.w: Clark J

later: Refusal offences are now in the Road Traffic Act 2010. Read with DPP v Moorehouse (2005) in this app on what the failure-to-provide offence involves.
job: Record the observations that founded your opinion that the person was driving or in charge — such as a seat swap — with times and positions.
Record the grounds for arrest, the requirement made, the warning about refusal, and the exact response.
Take statements from any passenger claiming to be the driver, and check them against CCTV or witnesses.

bg: At about 3.30pm on 6 January 2013 a Garda saw the accused's car being driven erratically — failing to keep a steady course and veering onto a grass verge.

On stopping him the Garda noticed a strong smell of alcohol and slurred speech, and arrested him to carry out an evidential breath test at the Garda station. No preliminary roadside breath test was done.
He was charged with exceeding the breath alcohol limit under s.4 of the Road Traffic Act 2010. The defence argued the arrest was unlawful because no preliminary breath test had been carried out.
The District Court referred questions on the meaning of s.9(2) of the 2010 Act to the High Court.
DPP v Moran (no roadside test before arr.q: Must a Garda carry out a roadside breath test before arresting a suspected drink driver?
dec: High Court, 4 July 2014 (Kearns P): no.

Section 9(2) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 is clear and unambiguous. Where a Garda forms the opinion that a person should be arrested on suspicion of an offence, the mandatory duty to carry out a preliminary breath test doesn't arise.
The Garda's opinion was entirely reasonable, given the erratic driving, the smell of alcohol and the slurred speech.
That reading didn't breach the principle that penal statutes are strictly construed, nor undermine the legislature's intention. The questions were answered in favour of the prosecution.

keys.q: clear and unambiguous
keys.w: Kearns P, on s.9(2)

later: Read with DPP v McGovern (2019) and DPP v Flanagan (2023) in this app on forming the opinion for a drink-driving arrest.
job: Record every observation behind your opinion — the manner of driving, smell of alcohol, speech, balance, eyes, any admission.
If you decide to arrest without a roadside test, note that decision and why.
Tell the person why they're being arrested, in ordinary words, and that they're under arrest.

bg: At about 3am on 25 November 1996 Gardaí in Kilkenny saw a car leave a pub with its lights off, being driven on both sides of the road.
They followed with flashing lights. The driver didn't stop for about half a mile; he indicated and was blocked in near his home.
A Garda noticed a smell of alcohol. The roadside breath test was positive, and he was arrested.

At the close of the prosecution case the District Judge dismissed the drink-driving charge: the Garda's evidence didn't describe the place where he was spoken to, tested and arrested as a public place. The DPP appealed.
DPP v Morrissey (public place, 1998).q: Must the prosecution prove that the vehicle was still in a public place when it was stopped?
dec: High Court, 15 December 1998 (O'Higgins J): the DPP's appeal was allowed and the case remitted to the District Court.
The prosecution didn't need to offer evidence that the vehicle was still in a public place when it was stopped, unless there was evidence to the contrary.
The District Judge was wrong to dismiss the charge on that ground.
later: Read with Murphy v DPP (2004) in this app on recording the public-place element of public order charges.
job: In your statement, name the road where the driving was seen and describe it as a public road.
Record where the vehicle eventually stopped, and whether that was a public road or private property (a driveway, a yard).
Note the times and the route of any pursuit.

src.t: Irish Times — Decision to dismiss drink driving charge overturned (16 December 1998)

bg: On 9 December 1996 a Garda stopped the accused's car in Co Limerick. He reportedly admitted drinking four pints; the roadside breath test was positive, and he was arrested and charged with drink driving.
At the District Court hearing the defence produced a photocopied map to argue that the car was stopped about 15 feet before the junction the Garda had identified.
The Garda said he couldn't read the photocopied map, and the prosecution asked for time to consider it.
The District Judge had a substantial doubt about where the offence occurred, dismissed the charge, and asked the High Court whether he was right.
DPP v Sheehan (location in the summons,.q: Should a drink-driving charge be dismissed because of doubt about the exact location of the stop?
dec: High Court, 14 October 1998 (Kelly J): the District Judge wasn't justified in law in dismissing the charge.
The District Court has power under its rules to amend a summons.
A case shouldn't be dismissed on its merits unless there is a possibility of injustice not capable of being remedied by an adjournment or an amendment of the summons.
The DPP's appeal was allowed and the case remitted to the District Court.

keys.q: a possibility of injustice not capable of being remedied
keys.w: Kelly J, on when to dismiss rather than amend

later: Read with DPP v Morrissey (public place, 1998) in this app on proving where the driving happened.
job: Record the location precisely: road name, nearest junction or landmark, direction of travel, and distances.
Check the summons wording against your notes before the hearing.
If a discrepancy arises in court, ask the prosecutor to apply to amend the summons or for an adjournment.
