bg: In February 2012 a man was arrested at the plaintiff's home on a European Arrest Warrant and bailed to her address for a High Court appearance on 24 July 2012. She said he left for Poland on the morning of that hearing.
On 19 August 2012 four Gardaí came to the house looking for him. She said he wasn't there, asked to see a warrant, and refused consent to a search. They had no warrant.

One officer said she had seen movement at an upstairs window; the plaintiff said it was likely her dog. A detective pushed the door open against her foot, and she fell and injured her ankle. No one else was found in the house.

The Gardaí's account was that a hand had been seen at the window, giving reasonable grounds to believe the man was inside. The High Court preferred her evidence that only movement had been reported, but still dismissed her claim, finding reasonable suspicion and justified force.
Rozmyslowicz v Minister for Justice.q: When may Gardaí force entry to a home without a warrant to arrest someone they believe is inside?
dec: Court of Appeal, August 2018 ([2018] IECA 289, Hogan J): the appeal was allowed.
Section 6(1) of the Criminal Law Act 1997 permits forcible entry to arrest only if the person is in the house, or the Garda has reasonable cause to believe they are.
That must be read against Article 40.5 of the Constitution: the home enjoys the highest level of protection that could reasonably be afforded in a democratic society.

The belief rested on the hand-at-the-window account. Once the court accepted that the officer had reported only movement, that basis simply disappeared. There were no other grounds, so the Gardaí hadn't discharged the burden of showing reasonable cause.

Hogan J also criticised the defence for not putting key evidence to the plaintiff in cross-examination. The case was remitted to the High Court to assess damages for trespass, personal injury and breach of constitutional rights.

keys.q: enjoys the highest level of protection
keys.w: Hogan J, on the home

keys.q: simply disappears
keys.w: Hogan J, on the basis for the Gardaí's belief

later: Read with DPP v O'Brien (2021) in this app — no common-law power to enter a home to arrest for breach of the peace — and with The People (DPP) v Laide and Ryan and DPP v Gaffney on entering homes.
job: Record at the time the specific grounds for believing the person is inside: sightings, vehicles, phone or intelligence information, admissions — and who observed what.
Movement at a window, or a general suspicion, isn't enough. If grounds are thin, keep observation and seek a warrant.
Use only the force necessary, and record what was done and any injury.

src.t: Irish Legal News — Court of Appeal: Gardaí did not have reasonable grounds to forcibly enter woman's home without warrant (27 August 2018)

bg: On 1 August 2011 the plaintiff, who had applied for asylum, was arrested in Dundalk and detained because he didn't hold a valid passport or visa to enter Northern Ireland, his intended destination.
He was held for 25 days. He was released after an Article 40 application succeeded on appeal to the Supreme Court because of technical defects in the warrant.
He sued for false imprisonment. The High Court awarded €7,500 — a figure reflecting his lack of credibility about his right to remain — and made a differential costs order.

The Commissioner and the State appealed, arguing he was entitled only to nominal damages because he would have been lawfully detained had proper procedures been followed — the approach of the UK Supreme Court in Lumba.
GE v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána.q: Is someone unlawfully detained entitled to real damages if they could have been detained lawfully anyway?
dec: Court of Appeal, April 2021 ([2021] IECA 113, Murray J): the appeal was dismissed and the €7,500 award upheld.

The Lumba principles have never been recognised in Irish law, and the court declined to adopt them. The 'but for' test negates the essence of the cause of action, and the UK approaches suffer from a striking lack of clarity, including on the burden of proof.
Because liberty is a constitutional right, compensatory damages are the starting point. They reflect the loss of liberty and its impact, and include a vindicatory element.
A trial judge may reduce the award where the plaintiff's own conduct made him liable to lawful detention and the unlawfulness was purely procedural or technical.

Supreme Court, December 2022 ([2022] IESC 51; Hogan J, with O'Donnell CJ, Dunne, O'Malley and Baker JJ): both the State's appeal and the plaintiff's cross-appeal were dismissed, and the €7,500 award stood.

Accepting the 'but for' argument would devalue the remedy for false imprisonment and undermine personal liberty and the rule of law; nominal damages suit only the most technical or fleeting cases. His own conduct — leaving the State without permission, and his lack of credibility — reduced the award, which would otherwise have been appreciably higher; but that conduct didn't justify detaining him under a defective warrant.

keys.q: negates the essence of the cause of action
keys.w: Murray J, on the 'but for' test

keys.q: striking lack of clarity
keys.w: Murray J, on the UK approaches

keys.q: appreciably higher
keys.w: Hogan J, on what the award would otherwise have been

later: Read with Shortt v Commissioner (2007) in this app on damages against the State for Garda wrongdoing, and Dokie v DPP (2011) on immigration document offences.
job: Before detaining anyone on a warrant or order, check it: correct person, correct power, properly completed and signed.
If you spot a defect, don't detain on it — get it corrected or obtained afresh, and record what you did.
Record the grounds and the legal basis for every detention, and review it as circumstances change.
GE v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána.law: Yes. Court of Appeal (2021) and Supreme Court (2022) authority.

bg: Late at night in Dublin 1, a Garda cordon was extended after a fire.
The applicant went inside the cordon to retrieve his bicycle, and kept a piece of crime scene tape.

He was arrested, searched and detained at Store Street Garda Station, then released on bail. He was charged under the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 and, over the tape, under the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001.

His central complaint was that he was never given a direction to leave before being charged. He sought leave for judicial review: declarations that the arrest was unlawful, prohibition of the prosecution, compensation, and orders preserving CCTV and body-camera footage.
Harford v Commissioner of An Garda Síoch.q: Can a public order prosecution be stopped by judicial review on the ground that no direction to leave was given?
dec: High Court, 26 August 2025 ([2025] IEHC 476, Egan J): leave to seek judicial review was refused — no stateable ground or arguable case.
Prohibiting a prosecution is exceptional. It needs an unavoidable risk of an unfair trial that the trial judge cannot cure, and none was shown.
Judicial review during pending criminal proceedings is available only in wholly exceptional cases.
Whether a direction was given, and where the applicant was standing, are factual disputes for the District Court at trial.
A claim for wrongful arrest or false imprisonment belongs in a plenary action for damages — an adequate alternative remedy.
later: Read with DPP v Kelly (2018) in this app on what a valid s.8 direction requires, and Rochford (2025) on civil claims after a public order arrest.
job: At a cordon, give a clear direction to leave in plain words, and record to whom, when, where and the response.
Record when the cordon was set up and extended, and its boundaries.
Preserve CCTV and body-camera footage of the incident as soon as possible.

src.t: Casemine — Judicial review is not a shortcut to halt pending prosecutions (Harford v Commissioner [2025] IEHC 476)

bg: On 23 August 2014 Gardaí searched the plaintiff's truck business yard in Swords, Co Dublin, on foot of a search warrant. The yard had been linked to a vehicle seen there at a particular time, which had been used in an attack on a company's premises.
Gates were cut open with an acetylene torch, and documents of his trading companies were seized.

He sued the Garda Commissioner and the State, alleging that Gardaí harassed him over several years, that the information used to obtain the warrant was untrue, that the damage was unnecessary, and that the documents belonged to his companies.

He sought discovery of the sworn information supporting the warrant and a legible copy of the warrant. In October 2016 the High Court refused, after the judge viewed the document and upheld claims of public interest and informer privilege.
McGuinness v Commissioner of An Garda Sí.q: Can a person whose premises were searched see the sworn information behind the warrant — and when will a civil claim over a search succeed?
dec: Court of Appeal, January 2018 (Edwards J): the discovery appeal was dismissed.
Discovery depends on relevance to the pleaded claim, and he hadn't established that the sworn information was relevant.

Even if he had, public interest and informer privilege had been asserted, and the High Court judge was right to view the document before deciding to uphold those claims. A possible audio recording of the warrant application wasn't before the court, and no application had been made for it.

Court of Appeal, January 2025 (Allen J): his appeal against the dismissal of the action failed on all 16 grounds. He had never pleaded that the search was carried out without a warrant, there was no suggestion the copy warrant was not genuine, and the evidence of the detective sergeant who applied for it was unchallenged.
later: Read with Hanahoe v Hussey (1997) and Osbourne v Minister for Justice (2006) in this app on civil liability arising from searches.
job: Draft the sworn information as if a judge will read it later — accurate, specific, and with informant material identified so privilege can be claimed through the prosecutor.
Record the search fully: who was present, entry method and any damage (with the reason), and an itemised list of what was seized.
Return or account for seized documents promptly once no longer needed, and record it.

src.t: Irish Legal News — Court of Appeal: Businessman loses appeal for discovery of information supporting search warrant (11 January 2018)
Echo — Brother loses appeal over search on business premises (28 January 2025)

bg: Gardaí moved in on a suspected break-in at a house in Templeogue, Dublin, using a loud bang as a distraction.
The accused ran onto the lawn and was made to lie down. He was overpowered, handcuffed and kept face down on the ground, with armed Gardaí present.

A Garda searched him and found gloves, a balaclava, car keys and a mobile phone — no weapon — and then questioned him. Having no notebook, he later wrote the questions and answers on an A4 sheet at the office.

According to the Garda, the accused said he had no gun, that the gun was 'in the bag', and that the car was full of items from the house. Only then was he arrested. At the station he answered with silence or 'no comment'.
He was convicted in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court in October 2007 of possessing a firearm and sentenced to seven years. The trial judge had found no breach of the Judges' Rules.
DPP v Breen.q: Can answers given by a suspect who is restrained and handcuffed, but not yet arrested, be used against him?
dec: Court of Criminal Appeal, 16 December 2008 (Fennelly J giving judgment, with Budd and Hanna JJ): the appeal was allowed on the admissibility ground; the conviction was quashed and no retrial ordered.
The questioning took place in highly unusual circumstances.
Gardaí were entitled to subdue the accused for their safety. But they should have arrested and detained him under their statutory powers before questioning him to gather evidence.
He was physically restrained, lying face down and handcuffed, with armed Gardaí present: he was not arrested, yet he was not free. The answers should not have been admitted.
The court didn't need to decide the other grounds (the 'no comment' evidence, the firearm definition, and corroboration).

keys.q: He was not arrested. Yet he was not free.
keys.w: Fennelly J

keys.q: highly unusual circumstances
keys.w: Fennelly J, on the questioning

later: Read with DPP v McCormack (1999) — an arrest needs words making clear the person isn't free to go — and the Judges' Rules cases in this app, such as People (AG) v Cummins.
job: Once a suspect is restrained, arrest them — tell them they're under arrest and why — before questioning them about the offence.
Caution before questions, and record the questions and answers in your notebook at the time; have the suspect read and sign it where possible.
Safety questions (for example, 'Is there anything sharp on you?') are different — keep them to what safety needs, and record them.
DPP v Breen.law: Yes. Court of Criminal Appeal authority (2008).

bg: In November 2003 a driver was stopped at a checkpoint on the Templeogue Road, Dublin.
The Garda noticed a smell of alcohol and slurred speech and formed the opinion that he was intoxicated to such an extent as to be incapable of proper control of the vehicle.
The Garda then asked him to pull over to the side of the road. He drove a short distance into a nearby park, where he was arrested; he later gave a breath sample.

He was charged with drink driving under s.49 of the Road Traffic Act 1961. Because the point was novel, the District Judge stated a consultative case: was the arrest lawful, and was the Garda's opinion vitiated by requiring him to drive on?
DPP v Penny.q: Does asking a driver you believe is drunk to move the car undermine the arrest or your opinion?
dec: High Court, 27 July 2006 (Dunne J): the arrest was lawful, and the opinion was not vitiated.

All the ingredients of a valid s.49 arrest were present. The arrest didn't depend on the request to move, no evidence was obtained because of it, and the driver suffered no prejudice. Moving the car wouldn't necessarily have been an offence anyway, as the breath test might have come back under the limit.
Applying Lynch v Attorney General, the court wouldn't interfere with an otherwise proper procedure merely because it disapproved of one step in it.
The Garda's formation of the opinion was a finding of fact that later events couldn't undo.

As a matter of practice, though, the Garda shouldn't have asked the driver to move. It would be better to have motorists pull in before dealing with them, or to arrange removal of the vehicle after an arrest.
later: Read with DPP v Moran (2014) in this app on forming the opinion and arresting without a roadside test.
job: At a checkpoint, have the driver pull in to a safe spot before you assess them.
Once you've formed the opinion that the driver is impaired or over the limit, don't ask them to drive the vehicle again.
Arrest, then arrange for the vehicle to be moved or secured, and record it.

src.t: Irish Times law report — DPP v Penny (16 October 2006)

bg: The accused was arrested under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 on suspicion of unlawful possession of explosives.
After about 11.5 hours of questioning on that offence, his detention was extended.

On 2 July 2003 he was interviewed twice about IRA membership, with s.2 of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1998 — which allows inferences from failing to answer material questions — to be invoked.

Those interviews took place at a station without video recording facilities, chosen for its proximity to his family and solicitors. The Gardaí's verbal explanation of s.2 wasn't recorded, the questions were compound and loaded, and his phone call to his solicitor was made in a public office.
People (DPP) v Kelly (interview fairness.q: What does fairness require when Gardaí invoke an inference provision in interview?
dec: Special Criminal Court, 26 November 2004 (O'Donovan J, Judge Mathews and Judge Malone): the arrest was lawful, and the extension of detention couldn't be invalidated because the statute set no preconditions for it.

There was no statutory duty to use a station with video recording, but where s.2 is to be invoked, fairness requires taking the prisoner to a station with video recording facilities where that is possible.
Fairness also required telling him that the focus of questioning had changed, and reminding him of his right to legal advice.

The questioning was unfair: the questions were compound and loaded, making straightforward answers difficult; the explanation of s.2 wasn't recorded; and the call to his solicitor in a public office breached his privacy.
The two interviews were tainted with unfairness and their products were excluded.

keys.q: tainted with unfairness
keys.w: Special Criminal Court, on the interviews

later: Read with DPP v Wilson (inferences, 2017) in this app — inferences are tied to the offence named — and DPP v AMcD on strict compliance with the inference provisions.
job: Record every interview where an inference provision is invoked, including your explanation of it, word for word.
When the questioning moves to a different offence, say so clearly, give the relevant warning afresh, and remind the suspect of their right to a solicitor.
Ask one clear question at a time, and make sure calls and consultations with solicitors are private.
People (DPP) v Kelly (interview fairness.law: Yes, as a ruling on interview fairness (2004).

bg: The applicant was arrested at 10.55pm on 5 March 2006 under s.30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939, in connection with a murder by shooting in Coolock, Dublin.
He was detained for 24 hours, and then for a second 24 hours; the second period wasn't challenged.

Towards the end of the second period Gardaí applied to the District Court under s.30(4) for a third 24-hour extension. The hearing began before the period expired — 10.26pm according to the warrant, 10.35pm on the Garda evidence.
The District Court didn't make the order and warrant until 11.20pm, 25 minutes after the detention had expired at 10.55pm. He sought his release under Article 40.
Finnegan v Member in Charge (Santry Gard.q: Is an extension of detention valid if the application started in time but the order was made after the detention had expired?
dec: High Court, 8 March 2006 (O'Neill J): no — the continuing detention was unlawful and he was ordered released that night.
Statutory detention periods can't be extended by the courts or by implication. Starting the application within the period didn't prevent the period expiring.

A District Court extension under s.30(4A) requires continuing lawful detention under s.30(3). Once that ended at 10.55pm, the court had no jurisdiction to make the order, and the later order couldn't cure the illegality.
The suspension provision in s.4(8A) of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 (and the 1997 Act provisions) didn't apply to s.30 detention — a significant and express omission by the legislature.

keys.q: a significant and express omission
keys.w: O'Neill J, on the suspension provisions

later: Read with DPP v Roche (2015) and DPP v McGuire (member in charge, 1996) in this app on managing detention.
job: Diary the exact expiry time of every detention period, and the time for any review or extension.
Apply for an extension early enough that the order will be made before expiry — allow for travel, court lists and the length of the hearing.
Know whether a suspension provision applies to the power you're using; if an order won't be made in time, take advice before the period expires.
Finnegan v Member in Charge (Santry Gard.law: Yes, on the strictness of detention periods (2006).

src.t: Irish Times law report — District Court has no jurisdiction to extend detention after statutory period has expired (3 April 2006)

bg: The suspect was arrested on suspicion of murdering his wife, whose body had been found in Dublin. He was held at Santry Garda Station and released without charge the same day.

Under s.10 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984, a suspect released from custody can be re-arrested for the same offence only on a warrant from a District Court judge satisfied that new information has come to the Gardaí since the release, relating to the suspect's participation in the offence.

The application relied on: a witness who said she saw a man near where the body was later found and identified the suspect from a photo album; a landlord's account of remarks the suspect made about being accused of the murder; and evidence that a bag of clothing linked to the couple was thrown into a river, while he couldn't account for his movements in the early hours.
He was re-arrested at his home at 8.15am and challenged the lawfulness of the re-arrest in the High Court.
Murphy (re-arrest under s.10, 1996).q: Was there new information to justify a re-arrest under s.10 — and does the detention clock stop while a court decides?
dec: High Court, September 1996 (Kelly J): the re-arrest was lawful; the District Court application was properly made and granted.
The witness's identification was new information that amply justified the application. The landlord's account was less compelling, but also new. Together they justified the order.
The judge rejected arguments that the information was insufficient to incriminate the suspect, or that the application wasn't made in good faith.

But judgment was delivered at 8.30pm, 15 minutes after a six-hour extension of the detention had expired. The judge had no jurisdiction to stop the clock once the detention was challenged, so the suspect was no longer detained and was free to go.

keys.q: amply justified
keys.w: Kelly J, on the new identification evidence

later: Read with Finnegan v Member in Charge (Santry Garda Station) (2006) in this app: detention periods are strict, and courts can't extend them by implication.
job: For a s.10 re-arrest, set out specifically what new information has come in since release, when, and how it links the suspect to the offence.
Show that the information is genuinely new — not material already known at the first arrest.
Plan the interview strategy and any extension around the remaining detention time; a court challenge won't stop the clock.

src.t: Irish Times — Suspect's re-arrest legal in murder hunt, judge rules (4 September 1996)

bg: Gardaí carried out surveillance on the accused in Rathcoole, Co Dublin.

They sought a search warrant for a truck wash and parking business — a commercial premises owned by a third party. Learning that a judge wouldn't be available for some hours and that a Peace Commissioner wasn't at home, they obtained a warrant under s.26(2) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 from a Detective Superintendent.
Cannabis resin worth about €2 million was found inside a white van at the premises. The accused was convicted of possession for sale or supply and sentenced to 13 years.

On appeal he argued that the issuing officer wasn't independent, that there was no genuine urgency (or it was self-created by not having a judge or Peace Commissioner on standby), that the warrant was issued within one minute, and that his arrest was unlawful.
People (DPP) v Boggans.q: Can an accused challenge a Superintendent's urgent warrant for someone else's commercial premises?
dec: Court of Appeal, 9 March 2015 ([2015] IECA 46; Sheehan J giving judgment, with the President and Edwards J): appeal dismissed.
The court rejected the claim that the evidence was contrived: the accused's presence at the location was needed before any warrant could be sought.

Damache v DPP was distinguished. That case concerned a warrant for the applicant's home; here the premises were commercial and owned by a third party, so the accused couldn't invoke any proprietary or constitutional interest.
The warrant's authority hadn't been exceeded; a contrary finding would be entirely disproportionate.

The trial was fair: he hadn't shown that missing CCTV would have helped his cross-examination, the judge's intervention to resolve a dispute about a witness's answer was nothing unusual, and the charge dealt with any prejudice.

keys.q: invoke any proprietary or constitutional interest
keys.w: Court of Appeal, distinguishing Damache

keys.q: entirely disproportionate
keys.w: Court of Appeal, on finding the warrant exceeded

later: Read with Damache v DPP (2012) — a warrant must be issued by someone independent of the investigation — and DPP v Davis (2026) on executing s.26 warrants, both in this app.
job: Use the urgent Superintendent route only where a judge or Peace Commissioner genuinely can't be reached in time, and record the attempts made.
Where possible, have the warrant issued by an officer with no involvement in the investigation.
Set out the grounds properly even under time pressure; a warrant issued in a minute invites challenge.
People (DPP) v Boggans.law: Yes, as Court of Appeal authority (2015).

bg: In 2015 gardaí were investigating cocaine delivered in packages to two Dublin hostels. A co-accused was arrested carrying the accused's driving licence and receipts in his name.

Gardaí got a District Court warrant under s.26 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977 for the accused's registered flat. When they arrived, the owner said he had recently moved to another flat in the same building because of renovations.

Gardaí didn't enter the second flat. They went back to the District Court and got a second warrant. The sworn information for it was almost identical to the first — only the flat number changed. The garda who prepared it said he did so after a colleague contacted him.

Cocaine was found. In November 2017 a Circuit Court jury convicted the accused of conspiracy to import (s.71 Criminal Justice Act 2006), possession and possession for sale or supply. He was sentenced to five years.

His single ground of appeal was that the warrant was invalid: the information contained untruths, left out the most up-to-date reasons, and had plainly been prepared for the earlier address — so the search breached the inviolability of his dwelling.
People (DPP) v Theaddus.q: Is a warrant valid where the sworn information was largely copied from an earlier application for a different flat?
dec: Court of Appeal ([2019] IECA 93; Kennedy J): appeal dismissed.

The trial judge had found that the District Judge was fully informed, including through further questions put at the hearing, and that the gardaí acted appropriately and showed restraint by not entering before the second warrant was issued.

The Court of Appeal agreed. The same District Judge heard sworn evidence on both applications and was fully aware of the circumstances of each. There was no reason the wording should change significantly when the only difference was a move from one flat to another.

The District Judge was clearly satisfied, on information on oath, that there were reasonable grounds for suspicion under s.26(1)(a). The warrant was valid, so the search and the evidence found were lawful.

keys.q: a firm basis in granting the warrant
keys.w: Trial judge's ruling, upheld by the Court of Appeal

later: Read with People (DPP) v Boggans (2015) and DPP v Unnamed (oath on warrant information, 2024), both in this app.
job: If the target has moved, stop and get a fresh warrant for the right premises before entering.
Update the information so it explains why this premises, now — don't rely on the judge's questions to fill the gaps.
Note what the judge asked and what you said on oath; you may need to prove it later.
People (DPP) v Theaddus.law: Yes, as Court of Appeal authority (2019).

src.t: Irish Legal News — Court of Appeal: conspiracy to import cocaine, appeal against conviction lost (Theaddus, 2019)

bg: The accused was found in a car parked on a Dublin footpath with the engine running. The garda noticed a strong smell of alcohol and slurred speech.
He was arrested for being in charge of a vehicle with excess alcohol and taken to a Garda station, arriving at 2.40am.

The Intoxilyser procedure called for a 20-minute observation to make sure nothing was taken by mouth. He was observed for 27 minutes; the breath reading was 66 µg per 100ml, and he was charged by 4.45am.

The garda conceded he gave no reason for the extra seven minutes. The District Judge held the detention unlawful at the time of the test and excluded the result, and stated a case. The High Court answered in the accused's favour; the DPP appealed.
DPP v Fox.q: Does an unexplained seven-minute overrun of the 20-minute observation period make the detention unlawful?
dec: Supreme Court, 22 July 2008 ([2008] IESC 45; Murray CJ, Denham and Hardiman JJ agreeing): DPP's appeal allowed; the question was answered no.
The Act sets no fixed time within which the station procedures must be done, but the detention must be processed with reasonable expedition.
Relying on DPP v Finn, the court held that not every delay is unreasonable, and a delay that isn't unreasonable doesn't need to be objectively justified.

Looking at the whole process from arrest to charge with common sense, the extra seven minutes was not unreasonable. Absent special circumstances, it couldn't make the detention unlawful, so the breath result was admissible.

keys.q: Not every delay is unreasonable
keys.w: Supreme Court, adopting DPP v Finn

later: Relied on by the Court of Appeal in DPP v Dardis (2015) — a restarted 20-minute period. See also DPP v Finn, DPP v McNiece and DPP v Stack (2016) on the observation period, all in this app.
job: Keep the custody timeline tight and record each step with times.
If something holds things up — machine busy, another prisoner, observation interrupted — note the reason at the time.
Don't run the procedure by blanket policy; be ready to explain why each step took the time it did.

bg: The accused was arrested under s.4(8) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 in March 2014 and brought to a Dublin Garda station.

At 00.45 the garda began a 20-minute observation to make sure he took nothing by mouth. About a minute before the end, the garda briefly looked away and was then unsure whether anything had been taken. He had also noticed the Evidenzer was in use.
He began a second 20-minute observation at 01.12. Afterwards the accused gave two valid samples showing 64 µg per 100ml.

The District Judge held the second period unjustified — the garda should have checked whether the machine was free before starting, and a momentary look-away didn't reasonably suggest anything had been ingested — and dismissed the charge.
On a case stated, the High Court held that this was a finding of fact reasonably made, which a case stated couldn't correct. The DPP appealed.
DPP v Dardis.q: Can a garda restart the 20-minute observation if it may have been compromised, and is that a question of law?
dec: Court of Appeal, 11 December 2015 ([2015] IECA 284; judgment delivered by the President): DPP's appeal allowed.

The court reviewed the Supreme Court line: Finn (unexplained, policy-based delay unlawful), McNiece (justification for the 20 minutes accepted) and Fox (only unreasonable delay needs explaining; a short overrun insignificant).
Whether the second period was justified, and whether the charge should have been dismissed, were questions of law, not findings of fact (citing DPP v Fox).
The District Judge was not correct to find the extra 20 minutes unjustified, and not correct to dismiss the charge.
later: Builds on DPP v Fox (2008), DPP v Finn and DPP v McNiece; see also DPP v Stack (2016) on the observation period with the Evidenzer — all in this app.
job: If the observation may have been compromised, restarting it is defensible — say so and note why at the time.
Check the machine is free before starting the observation, so the reason for any wait is clear.
In evidence, explain the reason for any extra period, not just the times.
DPP v Dardis.law: Yes, as Court of Appeal authority (2015).

bg: The accused failed a roadside breath test at an authorised checkpoint and was arrested at 11pm. He arrived at Kilrush Garda station at 11.25pm and was processed.

At 11.40pm gardaí asked Ennis Garda station, about 43km away, for a garda trained to operate the Evidenzer. That garda arrived at 11.56pm and began the 20-minute observation at 11.59pm; the test followed. The arresting garda wasn't trained on the machine at the time.

The District Judge found the wait of about 29 minutes unjustified: 'procedure' wasn't a sufficient explanation, and the arresting garda could have started the observation. He was minded to dismiss the charge and stated a case.
DPP v Lynch (2016).q: Does waiting about half an hour for a trained Evidenzer operator make the detention unlawful?
dec: High Court, 21 November 2016 ([2016] IEHC 723; Ní Raifeartaigh J): both questions answered no.

The court grouped the earlier cases: the general policy of a 20-minute observation (Finn, McNiece, Stack); waiting to reach the station rather than observing in transit (McNiece and a 2015 High Court case); an unexplained seven minutes (Fox); and a restarted observation (Dardis).
None had directly decided whether waiting for a trained garda, who would both observe and test, made detention unlawful.

This case didn't fall within the Finn policy category, and the delay wasn't of a kind that would normally take detention into illegality. The accused wasn't held longer than was reasonable, and the District Judge wasn't correct to dismiss.
later: Read with DPP v Fox (2008), DPP v Dardis (2015) and DPP v Stack (2016), all in this app.
job: If you have to wait for a trained operator, note when you asked, when they arrived, and why the observation couldn't start sooner.
Where a trained member is on hand, start without waiting.
Keep the overall time from arrest to test as short as practicable.

bg: At about 2.25am on 2 December 2017 a garda on mobile patrol in Swords, Co Dublin, observed a vehicle being driven.
He formed his opinion to arrest partly on the result of a roadside breath test on a Dräger device. He didn't first observe a 20-minute period, which the device's operating instructions mention.
The accused was charged under s.4(2) and (5)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 2010 — blood alcohol over 50mg per 100ml within three hours of driving; the summons alleged 147mg.
The District Judge dismissed the charge because the 20-minute period wasn't observed, and stated a case asking whether he was right to do so despite the other factors behind the garda's opinion.
DPP v Feghiu.q: Must a garda wait 20 minutes before a roadside breath test, as the device's instructions suggest?
dec: High Court, 28 April 2020 ([2020] IEHC 235; Meenan J): no — the District Judge was not correct in law.

The court fully agreed with DPP v Slattery [2017] IEHC 442 (in this app as DPP v Slattery (2017)): the threshold for forming an opinion to arrest is low, and the apparatus's operating instructions form no part of the offence itself.
It followed that the garda wasn't obliged to observe a 20-minute period before using the roadside device.

keys.q: a low threshold
keys.w: DPP v Slattery (2017), adopted by the High Court

keys.q: do not form any part of the offence itself
keys.w: DPP v Slattery (2017), on the device's operating instructions

later: Followed in DPP v Foley (roadside test, 2023), in this app — a garda with no reason to suspect drinking in the previous 20 minutes needn't wait. For the station evidential test see DPP v Stack (2016), DPP v Fox (2008) and DPP v Dardis (2015), all in this app.
job: Base your opinion to arrest on all the circumstances, including the roadside result, and note them all.
A roadside device's instructions aren't a legal precondition, but follow them where you can and note why if you didn't.
At the station, follow the evidential observation procedure and record it.

bg: In Cork in August 2021 a garda stopped a driver after seeing him drive at speed. The garda noted a strong smell of alcohol, slurred speech and glassy eyes, and required a roadside breath specimen under s.9(2) of the Road Traffic Act 2010.
The result was a 'fail'. The garda formed the opinion that the driver had consumed an intoxicant to the extent of being unable to properly control the vehicle, and arrested him.

In cross-examination the garda accepted that the driver had volunteered having a few drinks before driving, with no time given and no inquiry made; that he was coming from a property five minutes from the stop; and that the garda didn't know the device's instruction to allow at least 20 minutes after a last drink.

The District Court asked whether, in those circumstances, the roadside test was invalid and the arrest unlawful. The defence accepted that no law requires the 20-minute wait — it comes from the instruction manual — but argued it applies where the garda knows or has reason to suppose recent drinking.
DPP v Foley (roadside test, 2023).q: Is a roadside breath test invalid if the garda doesn't wait 20 minutes after being told of drinking with no time given?
dec: High Court, 20 December 2023 ([2023] IEHC 734; O'Regan J): both questions answered no.
The roadside test wasn't invalid, and the arrest wasn't unlawful, even though the garda — acting in good faith — didn't know the device's instruction and didn't wait or ask when the last drink was.

The State relied on DPP v Slattery (2017) and DPP v Feghiu (2020). As summarised in commentary, the court treated the 20-minute period as coming from the device's instructions rather than statute, and as needed only where the garda knows or has reason to suspect drinking within that time.
later: Follows DPP v Feghiu (2020), in this app. For the station evidential test see DPP v Stack (2016), DPP v Fox (2008) and DPP v Dardis (2015).
job: Know your roadside device's instructions, including the wait after a last drink.
If you know or have reason to suspect the driver drank in the last 20 minutes, wait before testing and note the times.
Record everything behind your opinion — driving, smell, speech, eyes, the result — not just the 'fail'.

bg: At a mandatory alcohol testing checkpoint in Co Mayo in November 2013, a garda stopped the accused and required a roadside breath specimen under s.10(4) of the Road Traffic Act 2010. It gave a 'fail', which was shown to him.

The garda formed the opinion that he had consumed an intoxicant to the extent of being incapable of proper control of a vehicle, and arrested him. A urine specimen at the station showed 281mg per 100ml.

The defence argued that the garda hadn't asked whether he'd had nothing by mouth for 20 minutes. The device's instructions say that at least 20 minutes should pass before use, because residual mouth alcohol can distort the reading — and the defence said those instructions were approved by the Medical Bureau of Road Safety.

The prosecution relied on a 2003 High Court case and the House of Lords decision in DPP v Carey (1970): an officer acting in good faith with no reason to suspect a very recent drink doesn't invalidate the test, and a garda has no power to compel an answer about drinking.
DPP v Slattery (2017).q: Before a roadside breath test, must a garda observe the driver for 20 minutes or ask about a drink in that time?
dec: High Court, 4 July 2017 ([2017] IEHC 442; Binchy J).
The garda was under no obligation to ask whether the driver had a drink in the previous 20 minutes.
The garda's opinion rested on the breath result. Its reasonableness and good faith weren't challenged, so the District Judge had to accept it, and the argument for dismissal fell away.
As later summarised in Feghiu, the court held that the threshold for forming the opinion is low and that the device's operating instructions form no part of the offence itself.

keys.q: a low threshold
keys.w: High Court, on the garda's opinion to arrest (as quoted in Feghiu)

keys.q: do not form any part of the offence itself
keys.w: High Court, on the device's instructions (as quoted in Feghiu)

later: Followed in DPP v Feghiu (2020) and DPP v Foley (roadside test, 2023), both in this app. For the station evidential test see DPP v Stack (2016) and DPP v Fox (2008).
job: You needn't ask every driver when they last drank before a roadside test.
If you have reason to suspect a drink in the last 20 minutes, wait before testing and note the times.
Record what your opinion rested on — the result and everything else you saw.
